papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) offer complementary routes to post-training. For visual agents, however, tool use presents two related challenges. Models may overlook useful tool-returned observations, while poorly grounded actions can limit the evidence available for subsequent distillation. We introduce Reframe, a post-training framework that treats the observation state, rather than only the output distribution, as an object of alignment. First, Ground-Drop-GRPO (GD-GRPO) trains spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and stochastic removal of the original visual input, encouraging them to acquire grounded evidence and use the returned observations. Second, Observation-Gated-MOPD (OG-MOPD) replaces deficient tool actions with canonical ones mid-rollout and resumes distillation from the repaired observation. The two stages complement each other, as learning to rely on tool-returned observations can help the policy benefit from observation repair. Neither stage requires a task-specific SFT cold start. Extensive experiments over 14 image and video benchmarks demonstrate that Reframe outperforms both Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD. Ablation results show that GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain compared with outcome-based GRPO.
bullets: Addresses agents overlooking useful tool-returned observations and taking poorly grounded actions that limit later evidence.
Uses Ground-Drop-GRPO to train spatial and temporal specialists with evidence-aware rewards and randomly removed original visual input.
Uses Observation-Gated-MOPD to replace deficient tool actions with canonical actions and continue distillation from the repaired observation.
Evaluated on 14 image and video benchmarks, Reframe outperforms Mix-RL and vanilla MOPD.
Ablations show GD-GRPO increases observation dependence and tool gain over outcome-based GRPO.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of GD-GRPO. The policy samples multi-turn tool-use rollouts. After the first successful tool call, the original input o0 is dropped with probability 0.5 while tool-returned observations ot remain visible, so the answer must rely on what the tools have retrieved. Rollouts are grouped by their pre-sampled drop flag di, and advantages are normalized within each subgroup so that dropout does not confound the comparison.

Figure 4. Overview of OG-MOPD. Tool actions of the student policy are checked against annotated evidence using an IoU threshold. Missing, invalid, or poorly grounded actions are replaced with annotation-derived actions to obtain query-relevant observations. Injected action tokens receive NLL supervision, while retained student-generated tokens are trained with MOPD.

Figure 1. Overview of Reframe: visual agents should produce reliable intermediate results and truly look at them. (a) Outcome-based RL without explicit grounding rewards can permit observation neglect. (b) Vanilla MOPD may supervise trajectories conditioned on a poorly grounded observation state. (c) Our GD-GRPO rewards grounded actions and encourages reliance on tool-returned observations. (d) Our OG-MOPD repairs deficient tool actions before continuing distillation.

Figure 2. Construction pipeline of Reframe-100K. We first collect public data sources and preprocess them into a raw data pool. We then drop samples answerable from text alone, and audit the rest with 8 rollouts on the full input (F ) and on the annotated evidence alone (E), discarding samples that are (1) too easy or too hard; (2) insufficiently supported by their evidence. Remaining suspicious samples are diagnosed by Qwen and removed only when a final reviewer confirms an answer or evidence error.

Table 2. Comparison of training paradigms. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best scores. Image-RL, Video-RL, and MixRL use GD-GRPO; MOPD and Reframe distill the same specialists with vanilla MOPD and OG-MOPD. Video-MME-v2, VSI-Bench, and V-STaR report Non-Lin Score, accuracy/MRA, and 100×mAM, respectively; MLVU reports M-Avg.

Table 1. Comparison with representative visual agents. Reframe adopts a predominantly on-policy paradigm to consolidate image and video reasoning within a unified model, while achieving the highest observation dependence and tool gain among the compared models. Observation dependence is measured on V∗. Tool gain is measured across seven image benchmarks.

Table 5. Optimization and reward settings. MOPD denotes the shared configuration of vanilla MOPD and OG-MOPD. The observation gate and injected-action loss are enabled only in OG-MOPD. The tool-reward settings apply only to GD-GRPO.
Table 6. Rollout and batch settings. Counts refer to independently sampled trajectories before turn splitting. Repeated optimization of a rollout does not create additional independent samples.
Table 4. Comparison with existing visual agents. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best averages. Video metrics follow

papers.selection_reason: Presents a post-training framework for visual agentic reasoning with tool-use observation alignment, directly relevant to multimodal LLM post-training and interleaved multimodal reasoning.
papers.title: Reframe: Observation-Aligned Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Agentic Visual Reasoning
papers.tldr: Reframe improves visual agents’ tool use by aligning both their actions and the observations those actions produce during post-training.

papers.abstract: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript
bullets: Addresses the limitation that demonstrations from other scenes lack feedback about the robot’s current world.
RoboScript implements WICL by combining one demonstration with simulated rehearsal, reflection, and frozen Task Memory.
Achieves 83.4% mean success across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks using one demonstration per task and no gradient updates.
The approach generalizes across visual distributions, benefits from larger foundation models, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment adaptation.
Scope: performance is demonstrated for agentic manipulation, with deployment inputs isolated to information available on the real robot.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces World In-Context Learning (WICL) for robot manipulation, fitting Robot Learning and Manipulation. The paradigm of learning world dynamics/context rather than weights fits Latent Action Models.
papers.title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: World In-Context Learning lets a frozen robot model rehearse a demonstrated task in simulation, store feedback in context, and transfer the resulting task memory to new scenes without gradient updates.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) integrate information across modalities, but become unreliable when those modalities disagree. Under conflicting inputs, MLLMs may favor modalities that are not the most reliable for the task, thus motivating inference-time control of modality arbitration. We identify a small set of attention heads, termed arbitration heads, that causally influence whether predictions follow visual or textual evidence. Building on this, we introduce a lightweight, training-free intervention that biases these heads toward a designated trusted modality at inference time. The identified heads are stable across calibration set sizes and generalize across settings, and steering them enables effective bidirectional control of modality reliance across diverse benchmarks. Our findings identify an effective control mechanism to align MLLM predictions with task-specified modality priorities. The code is available at https://github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.
bullets: MLLMs can make unreliable predictions when modalities disagree, sometimes favoring the less reliable source.
The work identifies a small set of causally influential attention heads, called arbitration heads, that control visual-versus-textual reliance.
Biasing these heads at inference time enables bidirectional control over modality preference across diverse benchmarks.
Arbitration heads remain stable across calibration-set sizes and generalize across settings.
Code is publicly available at github.com/zhaoyingpan/modality-arbitration.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of our method. (a) Arbitration head localization: we causally identify attention heads that causally influence modality preference by patching head activations from image-only and text-only inputs into conflicting multimodal inputs and measuring their effects on the answer logit margin. (b) Inference-time intervention: we select the most influential arbitration heads and steer predictions toward a designated modality by adjusting their attention to visual and textual tokens.

Figure 4. Preserving multimodal benefits under sparse modality conflict. The left and right panels evaluate MPS and our method steered towards image and text, respectively. Dotted lines denote unimodal performance. Although unimodal inference avoids modality conflict, it cannot exploit complementary information when the modalities are aligned. Adaptive steering retains this benefit while remaining robust to conflict.
Figure 13. Robustness to visual degradation.

Figure 3. Modality conflict detection for adaptive steering. Top50 union-logit cosine similarities for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context, where lower similarity indicates stronger modality conflict. The dashed line marks the threshold, selected to maximize conflict-detection accuracy on the calibration set.

Figure 5. Effect of steering strength α. Increasing α progressively shifts predictions toward the target modality, with performance saturating at moderate steering strengths. α = 0 denotes the unmodified baseline, and α = ∞ corresponds to hard masking of the competing modality.

Figure 6. Effect of the number of arbitration heads (top-k). Steering an increasing number of top-ranked heads progressively shifts predictions toward the target modality, with the effect saturating at moderate values. The top-k of 0 denotes the unmodified baseline.

Figure 7. Robustness of modality conflict detection using centered logits. Top-50 union-logit cosine similarities after centering each logit vector, for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context. Lower similarity indicates stronger modality conflict. The dashed line marks the conflict-detection threshold calibrated to maximize accuracy on the calibration set.

Figure 8. Robustness of modality conflict detection to calibrationset selection. Top-50 union-logit cosine similarities for samples paired with conflicting or aligned context, using a calibration set generated with random seed 43. The dashed line marks the detection threshold selected to maximize conflict-detection accuracy on the calibration set.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates controlling modality arbitration in MLLMs at inference time, fitting Multimodal Large Language Models. The identification of arbitration heads is a technically meaningful contribution.
papers.title: Beyond Modality Preference: Controlling Multimodal Arbitration under Modality Conflict in MLLMs
papers.tldr: A lightweight, training-free inference intervention steers MLLMs toward a task-designated modality when visual and textual inputs conflict.

papers.abstract: Motivated by reinforcement learning subject to communication constraints, we study a policy evaluation problem with linear function approximation over a rate-limited channel. In our setup, an agent interacting with an unknown environment (modeled as a Markov Decision Process) transmits quantized estimates of a temporal-difference (TD) learning update direction to a server over a finite-capacity channel. Our goal is to investigate to what extent one can preserve the statistical convergence rates achievable when the channel has infinite capacity. To that end, we propose a new algorithm called Batched Adaptively Quantized TD (BAQ-TD), which uses batching to reduce the variance of the transmitted information, and adaptive quantization to encode innovations. We prove a high-probability finite-time error bound for BAQ-TD, and show that, above a certain finite channel capacity, BAQ-TD preserves the convergence rate of unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors. Specifically, for a $d$-dimensional value function parameter, we establish that transmitting a total of $\mathcal{O}(d \log(T))$ bits over a horizon of length $T$ suffices to achieve the order-optimal rate of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/T)$, marking an exponential improvement in communication-complexity over prior work.
bullets: Studies linear-function-approximation policy evaluation when TD updates must cross a rate-limited channel.
Batches updates to reduce transmission variance and adaptively quantizes innovations.
Provides a high-probability finite-time error bound for the proposed method.
Above a finite channel-capacity threshold, matches unquantized TD up to logarithmic factors.
Uses O(d log T) transmitted bits over horizon T to attain the order-optimal Õ(1/T) rate, improving communication complexity over prior work.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Agent-server architecture for BAQ-TD, presented in Algorithm 1. During each epoch k, the agent uses H transition samples from the unknown MDP under policy µ to estimate the TD direction and transmits the encoded innovation over a noiseless, rate-limited channel. The server reconstructs the direction, updates its parameter to θk+1, and returns this parameter exactly over an unconstrained noiseless reverse channel.

Fig. 2. (Left) Evolution of the estimation error Ek = ∥θk−θ⋆∥2 for BAQ-TD with batch sizes H ∈ {512, 2048, 8192}, precision m = 16, and K = 1000 epochs. (Middle) Results for precisions m ∈ {10, 12, 16}, compared with unquantized TD. (Right) Terminal estimation error EK = ∥θK − θ⋆∥2 versus sample budget T for BAQ-TD with m ∈ {12, 16} and unquantized TD. The dashed line shows the T−1/2 scaling suggested by our square-error bound.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses reinforcement learning (TD learning) over rate-limited channels, which is relevant to communication constraints in robotic systems. Fits Robot Learning and Manipulation.
papers.title: Adaptive Quantization Preserves Fast Rates for TD Learning over Rate-Limited Channels
papers.tldr: BAQ-TD uses batching and adaptive quantization to preserve TD learning’s fast convergence rate over sufficiently capable finite-rate channels.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.
bullets: Addresses the irreversibility of feed-forward 3D reconstruction predictions.
Injects sparse geometric constraints through a lightweight point correspondence adapter.
Targets ambiguities from repetitive textures, symmetry, viewpoint changes, and textureless regions.
Introduces a challenging benchmark focused on failure modes of existing methods.
Reduces reconstruction error with as few as one correspondence click on standard and curated benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CLICK3R architecture. A shared ViT encoder processes the two input images. Correspondence prompts are tokenized using our correspondence tokenizer (Section 3.2). A symmetric point correspondence adapter, implemented as a lightweight transformer with self-attention and cross-attention (Section 3.3), updates the decoder-input features for each view. The asymmetric decoder then interprets the updated embeddings and passes them to the original DUSt3R [44] heads to predict 3D pointmaps and confidence.

Figure 1: Overview. Given (a) an image pair and sparse correspondences (colored dot clicks), CLICK3R conditions DUSt3R [44] to produce accurate 3D reconstruction. (b) DUSt3R fails on a scene with limited overlaps. (c) With as few as two clicks, CLICK3R recovers correct geometry.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. Each example features challenging geometry, such as large baselines, limited co-visibility, or substantial viewpoint changes. The input image pair with user-provided correspondence prompts (colored dots) is shown on the left, followed by each model’s reconstruction. CLICK3R produces more accurate and consistent 3D reconstructions, with prompted correspondences aligning more closely in 3D. Additional qualitative results are provided in Appendix Figure 13.

papers.abstract: As multimodal agents accumulate increasingly long interaction histories, effectively retrieving and utilizing past information becomes critical for long-term interaction. Existing memory systems typically rely on semantic retrieval over compressed memories and expose predefined representations, which may miss relevant memories and overlook heterogeneous evidence needs across queries. We introduce \textbf{\hivemem}, a multimodal memory framework that interleaves \textbf{\textsc{H}}or\textbf{\textsc{i}}zontal Memory Expansion with \textbf{\textsc{Ve}}rtical Evidence Composition. For horizontal memory expansion, \hivemem organizes memory episodes into a relational graph using textual and visual anchors, expanding semantically retrieved seeds with related neighbors to recover complementary information. For vertical evidence composition, each retrieved memory retains multiple evidence forms, including compact summaries, captions, grounded visual views, raw images, and interaction history. A lightweight trainable selector independently composes an evidence subset for each retrieved memory, enabling query-adaptive utilization of heterogeneous multimodal information. This two-dimensional design jointly broadens memory coverage and adapts the evidence contributed by individual memories. Experiments across three multimodal memory benchmarks show that \hivemem consistently improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90\% compared with the most efficient competing multimodal baselines.
bullets: Addresses missed relevant memories and fixed representations in semantic-retrieval memory systems.
Builds a relational graph of memory episodes using textual and visual anchors, then expands retrieved seeds with neighbors.
For each memory, selects among summaries, captions, grounded views, raw images, and interaction history based on the query.
Across three multimodal memory benchmarks, improves task performance across base models while reducing token consumption by about 90% versus efficient multimodal baselines.

papers.abstract: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
bullets: Problem: Action learning can weaken pretrained language–video alignment, but guidance on data and supervision design is limited.
Method: Systematically evaluates language–video, language–video–action, and joint supervision using about 47,000 hours of general, egocentric, UMI, and robot videos.

Key findings: Egocentric video mixed with UMI demonstrations improves control generalization under a fixed training budget; architecture and joint-training choices affect how well these data are used.
Scaling the selected pretraining setup and post-training on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations yields 88.10% success in Easy and 61.56% in Hard conditions.
The model reaches 40.00% success across three real-world tasks, versus 23.33% for the strongest baseline, and the authors release data, code, and weights.

papers.abstract: Soft powered descent landings are becoming evermore important in the field of space exploration and scientific advancement, because of their ability to deliver mission critical payloads, both highly accurately and safely. The high efficiency restriction on planetary landings due to the severely limited fuel supply results in the need for optimal guidance trajectories and control. Model based reinforcement learning is proving to be an important tool in simplifying the highly complex process of generating optimal guidance trajectories and control. In this work, we present DreamLander, a state of the art model based reinforcement learning algorithm based on DreamerV3, to generate optimal guidance and control for a realistic 6 degree of freedom entry descent landing problem. The model based approach creates a sample efficient and highly generalizable model that can be applied to a variety of scenarios whilst maintaining a high degree of accuracy, landing within 2 meters of the designated landing zone, and with velocity norm less than 0.3 meters per second. DreamLander makes use of state sensor observations, making progress toward End-to-End solutions of the Entry Descent Landing problem.
bullets: Targets soft powered descent, where limited fuel demands efficient guidance trajectories and control.
Uses model-based reinforcement learning built on DreamerV3 for the entry-descent-landing problem.
Operates from state sensor observations, advancing toward end-to-end landing solutions.
Reportedly lands within 2 m of the designated zone with velocity norm below 0.3 m/s.
Designed to be sample-efficient and generalizable across landing scenarios.

papers.abstract: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.
bullets: Robot probe pressure alters vascular anatomy, motivating fast biomechanical simulation for autonomous access.
The simulator used Stable Neo-Hookean tissue and a Vertex Block Descent solver on one GPU.
In a cylindrical phantom, artery predictions stayed within 5 percentage points and vein predictions within 3 points through 11 mm of compression.
A selected setting reduced solver time from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms per frame while staying within 1.03 points of the finest reference; the full stack ran at 56.4 ms per frame.
A realistic digital leg reproduced the expected clinical signal: the vein collapsed more than the artery.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining heterogeneous tactile data despite sensor-specific physics and limitations.
Supports piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors, with extensibility to new sensor types.
Produces plug-and-play tactile tokens compatible with diffusion policies and VLA models, including π₀.₅ and LingBot-VLA.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots across multiple hardware platforms show benefits for complex manipulation while retaining computational efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of LingBot-Touch. Top: what tactile data look like at scale. Our 5,000-hour corpus is multi-source, pooling egocentric recordings from human tactile gloves with teleoperated robot hands across piezoresistive, magnetic, and optical sensing (left); heterogeneous in taxel geometry, resolution, and channels, which we reconcile in a canonical fingertip space (middle); and sparse, with most taxels silent most of the time (right). Bottom: what one encoder trained on this corpus enables. Frozen features recover contact force, location, extent, and dynamics and align with vision (left); the same tokens plug into imitation-learning and VLA policies on real dual-arm hands (middle) and into reinforcement learning in simulation (right). LingBot-Touch transfers to a sensor model unseen in pretraining without retraining, and its 5.46M-parameter Tiny variant adds under 0.2% to the parameters of the policies it augments.

Figure 3. Overview of LingBot-Touch. LingBot-Touch learns unified tactile representations through self-supervised prediction in latent space. Heterogeneous spatiotemporal signals from magnetic, piezoresistive, and visuotactile sensors are mapped to a canonical spherical space and incorporated into pretraining through weighted sampling. Modality-specific tokenizers convert these signals into tokens for a shared Transformer backbone equipped with 5D rotary positional embeddings (RoPE). The context encoder processes only visible tokens, and its outputs are concatenated with mask tokens before being passed to the corresponding modality-specific predictor. The target encoder processes the unmasked input, providing latent targets for the context loss on visible positions and the prediction loss on masked positions. Its parameters are updated through an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the context encoder, with gradients stopped through the target branch.

Figure 7. Scaling with pretraining data and model size. Frozen-encoder probing on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom) for Tiny and Small encoders pretrained on 1K to 5K hours with fixed source proportions. Small improves or holds on every task with every increment of data on both hands; Tiny saturates at about 4K hours and loses retrieval recall at 5K.

Figure 8. Single-source versus multi-source pretraining. Blue: probed on Sharpa Wave. Orange: probed on XHand1. Top: adding 441 hours of piezoresistive data and the other sensor’s data to a fixed 331 or 228 hours of a sensor’s own data improves seven of eight sensor-task pairs. Bottom: at a fixed 1,000-hour budget, a single-source model beats the three-source mixture on its own sensor on seven of eight pairs, by the widest margins on the spatial tasks. Bold marks the better of each pair. LingBot-Touch uses the HaT-Tiny backbone.

Figure 2. Composition and diversity of the LingBot-Touch pretraining dataset. Our dataset comprises 4,983 hours of tactile recordings, spanning 464K episodes and 1.33 billion frames across piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensing modalities. To support representation learning for downstream understanding of contact physics and robotic dexterous manipulation, it covers diverse real-world human and robot manipulation tasks, encompassing varied sensing principles, spatial resolutions, sampling frequencies, and physical taxel layouts.

Figure 6. Comparison with FTP-1 using frozen pretrained backbones. Results on Sharpa Wave (top) and XHand1 (bottom). Gray bars show FTP-1 with sensor-specific adapters trained for each platform. Colored bars show LingBot-Touch with the HaT-Small backbone, pretrained on 5K hours of tactile data and evaluated without sensor-specific encoder adaptation. Arrows indicate whether lower or higher values are better.

Figure 5. Contact-physics probing tasks. Five frozen-encoder probing tasks on two dexterous hands, Sharpa Wave and XHand1: fingertip force recovery, contact center and coverage estimation, future force prediction, and tactile-to-video retrieval. They test contact intensity, spatial structure, short-term dynamics, and cross-modal correspondence. Each task trains its own attentive probe on the multi-level features of the frozen EMA target encoder. For fingertip force recovery, labels are obtained by averaging the per-finger resultant force vectors over each pair of consecutive frames and then computing their magnitudes. Contact centers are computed as contact-strength-weighted centroids of valid taxels above the activation threshold, while contact coverage is the fraction of valid taxels that are active. Future force labels represent per-finger changes in force magnitude at each of the next four frames relative to the final history frame. Contact centers are supervised only when contact is present.

Figure 9. Latent prediction versus signal reconstruction. VAE, MAE, and LingBot-Touch are pretrained on identical data with matched hyperparameters. Top left: pretraining losses. Bottom: frozen-encoder probing with 1K and 4K hours of pretraining data. Top right: real-world manipulation success rates with the pretrained tactile encoders integrated into LingBot-VLA.

Figure 12. Reinforcement-learning curves on twelve dexterous tasks, Sharpa Wave (a–h) and XHand1 (i–l). Lines show the mean episode return over three seeds; bands show one standard deviation across the smoothed per-seed curves.

Figure 10. Contact separation and continuity in the latent space. Non-contact windows form one cluster, and contact windows form continuous structures that track the strengthening and weakening of the responses.
Figure 4. Spatial mask-ratio warm-up. The masking ratio increases linearly from 40% to 80% over the first 300 training steps, then remains fixed. Red and green denote masked and visible taxels.

papers.tldr: LingBot-Touch learns a unified, sensor-agnostic tactile representation that can improve dexterous manipulation across diverse tactile sensors and policy models.

papers.abstract: A challenging bottleneck in manipulation research is reproducibility and comparability of methods in real-world environments. Since manipulation is an interactive task, it cannot be evaluated on a static dataset of observations. Benchmarking in simulation is a common remedy, but cannot cover the whole complexity of real-world tests. This paper proposes a new paradigm of stochastic challenges. Like the well-known YCB objects, it is based on reproducible real-world scenes and therefore allows system-level innovation and comparability between different platforms. Due to their stochastic nature, our challenges however, mimic the rigor and surprise of hidden test sets. To this end, we show how different robots in different labs can be compared based on their success rate over different random task samples, if these samples come from the same distribution. We propose stochastic challenges as a general paradigm for robot benchmarking and implement this paradigm in a novel benchmark for mobile manipulation, on which we compare two robots tested in two different labs.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of evaluating interactive manipulation using static datasets or simulation alone.
Uses reproducible real-world scenes with randomized task samples to emulate hidden-test-set rigor and variability.
Enables comparison across platforms when task samples are drawn from the same distribution.

papers.abstract: Modern digital phenotyping pipelines require the precise measurement of a range of 3D morphological plant traits. The accurate, high throughput acquisition of these traits helps breeders and researchers accelerate the development of new varieties, techniques and products. Recent advances in 3D technologies have enabled a rapid transition from 2D to 3D pipelines, but high throughput acquisition of digital 3D twins of plants remains a significant challenge due to complex morphology, thin structures and occlusions. In this paper we present Plant Orbiter, a new approach to generating 3D plants that leverages recent advances in video diffusion to produce high quality 3D Gaussian Splats of plants from a single image. We show that our method more accurately recreates plant morphology than other state-of-the-art methods, achieving the highest 3D F-score against all baselines, while being more practical for high throughput pipelines due to easier alignment and reduced cost of camera placement. Combined with a 2D diffusion model, we show that our method also achieves state-of-the-art results in the generation of 3D plant models from a text prompt.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of high-throughput 3D plant acquisition under complex morphology, thin structures, and occlusions.
Uses video diffusion to generate orbit-camera views and reconstruct plants as 3D Gaussian Splats.
Produces more accurate plant morphology than prior methods, attaining the highest 3D F-score against reported baselines.
Offers easier camera alignment and lower camera-placement costs for high-throughput pipelines.
Combined with a 2D diffusion model, achieves state-of-the-art text-to-3D plant generation.

papers.abstract: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.
bullets: Targets the evidence and governance requirements of deploying LLMs in regulated industries.
Separates trusted performance measurement by NVIDIA AIPerf from experiment design and post-measurement decisions.
Uses a shared storage model to support both caching and auditability.
Finds that engine rankings change with concurrency, newer GPUs may lower cost per request, and speculative decoding varies by engine under load.
Shows that configuration choices can matter more than the engine choice itself.

papers.abstract: World models have increasingly been applied as a model-based control method for robotics tasks such as manipulation and locomotion. While early world model architectures relied on decoders to prevent mode collapse and learn a predictable latent space, recent works on world models, such as Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture or LeWorldModel, increasingly aim to learn embeddings without a grounding decoder, utilising only a latent forward dynamics predictor and a stabilising entropy term. In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
bullets: Targets more effective, real-time model-based control for robotics.
Extends LeWorldModel with a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor.
Uses these auxiliary latent losses to impose additional structure on learned embeddings.
Evaluated on standard world-model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

papers.tldr: Σ-LeWM improves decoder-free world models for robot control by adding backward and inverse-dynamics losses that structure latent representations and enhance performance and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Post-LayerNorm Transformers have seen limited practical adoption due to enduring difficulties in scaling them to large depths. While prior research has focused on stabilising Post-LayerNorm by improving conditioning at initialisation, stability often deteriorates when models are trained with large learning rates, forcing additional compromises. In the decoder-only settings we study, existing Post-LayerNorm methods fail to outperform strong Pre-LayerNorm baselines. We propose KiteNorm, a post-norm training method designed to break this trend by constraining hidden-state variance. This approach is motivated by a bound on the LayerNorm Jacobian suggesting that variance growth contributes to gradient vanishing, alongside empirical evidence linking it to rank collapse. KiteNorm combines residual scaling and variance regularisation to maintain stability throughout training, supported by scalarised double-normalisation that provides separately learnable scales for the skip and residual branches. Across decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves training stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates, with scaling laws favouring KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget. Ablations show that each component is necessary for the full stability and performance gains.
bullets: Post-LayerNorm Transformers can become unstable at large learning rates and depths, limiting their practical use.
KiteNorm combines residual scaling with variance regularisation to constrain hidden-state variance and reduce gradient vanishing and rank collapse.
Scalarised double-normalisation gives the skip and residual branches independently learnable scales.
In decoder-only Transformers up to 1.3B parameters, KiteNorm improves stability and outperforms leading baselines at their optimal learning rates.
Scaling laws favour KiteNorm across depth, width, batch size, and training budget; ablations indicate both components are necessary.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.
bullets: Outcome-only reinforcement learning improved aggregate reward yet encouraged premature commitment, asking only one question, and failures on rare high-risk cases.
The study evaluates medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration in controlled environments with hidden states, query costs, adaptive oracles, and verifiable outcomes.
In diagnostics, dense credit for uncertainty-reducing questions improved held-out value and moderate-case support across three seeds without the observed high-risk seed collapse.
Separating exploration from exploitation increased best-checkpoint high-risk support but caused excessive information gathering for low-acuity cases.
Reinforcement learning can trim useful questions after supervised warmup and does not reliably fix rare behavior gaps from biased supervised data.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Experimental framework and effects of reward design on clinical multi-turn decision procedures. A, The LoRA-adapted MedGemma-4B-it policy interacts with a partially observed patient simulator across medication-refill triage, acute diagnostics and dosing titration. Each environment provides an exact adaptive oracle and deterministic outcome verifier. The three GRPO methods use different training reward formulations or exploration strategies, with policy optimization and rollout generation distributed across two compute nodes. All policies are evaluated on held-out cases using the same unshaped terminal verifier. B, Selected trajectories for the same simulated high-risk abdominal-pain case illustrate different information-gathering procedures. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four targeted findings before emergency treatment. Outcomeonly GRPO commits prematurely after one finding. Credit-assignment GRPO reaches the correct terminal action after four requests and receives an oracle-grade reward despite following a different evidence sequence. Decoupled exploration reaches the correct terminal action after eight requests, including additional non-decisive findings. The learned trajectories are selected illustrative examples, not representative estimates of typical policy behavior. Oracle-grade reward does not necessarily establish sufficient gathered clinical evidence. C, Held-out diagnostics performance measured by high-risk verifier value and mean questions asked. Outcome-only and credit-assignment GRPO show mean ± standard deviation across three training seeds; the base model and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references (hatched bars). The dashed line indicates the exact adaptive oracle’s mean question count. All methods are scored using the same unshaped evaluation reward. Decoupled GRPO is shown at its step-40 checkpoint, selected on held-out data; its final checkpoint does not retain the high-risk advantage (Table 3). The held-out diagnostics set contains only two high-risk cases.

Figure 3: Diagnostics performance by risk subgroup in the held-out hidden condition. Every method is evaluated with the pure verifier reward. Plain GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO show mean±standard deviation over three training seeds; base and decoupled GRPO are single-seed references. Outcome-only GRPO raises aggregate value but reduces and destabilizes high-risk performance. Credit assignment improves the moderate subgroup and maintains high-risk support of 0.50 (one of two high-risk cases) across all three seeds. Decoupled GRPO produces the highest high-risk value and support, but requests substantially more information.

Figure 10: Attempted repair of a mildly biased diagnostics SFT policy by risk subgroup, using the held-out hidden condition and n=200 cases. Both RL methods lose most of the initialization’s high-risk oracle-grade support; support falls from 1.00 for the SFT initialization to 0.14 with credit-assignment GRPO and 0.36 with decoupled GRPO, even as high-risk value rises. The methods fail in different directions. Credit assignment reduces gathering, while decoupled GRPO increases question burden and lowers benign support from 0.92 to 0.16. This figure complements Table 5 and Figure 9.

Figure 9: Attempted reinforcement learning repair of the biased SFT policy. Credit assignment and decoupled GRPO move away from the initialization in opposite directions. Credit assignment reduces gathering and loses high-risk support; decoupled GRPO increases gathering and damages benign support. Both methods reduce the SFT policy’s strong aggregate support, and neither restores the missing high-risk procedure.

Figure 2: Agent–simulator dialogues rendered in plain language. The dialogues are simplified simulator traces, not real clinical conversations. The replying party is a rule-based simulator, not a patient or clinician. It looks up each requested finding in the case’s hidden record and reports whether it is present. Findings are binary, so the simulator returns no numeric values; each question and answer paraphrases one requested finding and its revealed value. (A) The same held-out high-risk diagnostics case as Figure 1. The exact adaptive oracle gathers four findings before emergency treatment (reward +0.83). The outcome-only GRPO rollout shown is that policy’s most common behaviour on this case (6 of 12 samples). It asks one question and admits the patient (reward +0.17). (B) Exact adaptive oracle trajectories for one held-out case in each task, matching Appendix B. Rewards are terminal utility minus 0.03 per question. Hidden risk is never shown to the agent.

Figure 6: Training diagnostics derived from the run logs. Top, diagnostics GRPO over 60 optimisation steps. The panels show the optimised reward, KL divergence from the initialization, policy entropy, and mean questions per rollout for outcome-only GRPO, credit-assignment GRPO, and decoupled GRPO. The question trajectory reveals the characteristic procedural differences among the methods; outcome-only GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO both settle well below the oracle gathering level of approximately 3.9, with credit assignment slightly higher, while decoupled GRPO rises above it. Bottom, training loss for the biased SFT warmup. Loss converges to approximately 0.002, showing that the supervised trajectories are closely fit before RL begins.

Figure 4: Information credit coefficient sweep on the titration task. Mean questions remain below the oracle level when λ≤0.03, approach the oracle at λ=0.1, and exceed it at λ=0.2. The coefficient therefore behaves as a task-specific control parameter for gathering depth, rather than as a constant that can be transferred without calibration.

Figure 8: Refill triage performance by risk subgroup in the held-out hidden condition, evaluated with the pure verifier reward. The figure compares the base model, the SFT v3 warmup, outcome-only GRPO, and creditassignment GRPO at their final checkpoints. The SFT warmup already achieves the strongest high-risk result. Both RL policies subsequently reduce high-risk value and move toward shorter, under-gathered trajectories, despite preserving high support under stochastic sampling.

Figure 5: Effect of supervised coverage bias on aggregate performance and latent support. Left, the biased SFT retains high overall support despite poor high-risk value. Right, severe bias removes the high-risk action emergent_tx from sampled trajectories and fails Gate 2. Mild bias retains a 21% sampling rate and passes Gate 2. The subsequent repair experiment shows that nonzero latent support is necessary but not sufficient for RL to restore the missing behaviour.

Figure 7: Checkpoint trajectory for decoupled GRPO on diagnostics. Evaluation uses the held-out hidden condition and the pure verifier reward. High-risk oracle-grade support and high-risk value peak at checkpoint 40, reaching 1.00 and +0.248, respectively. The same checkpoint also shows increased gathering; mean questions approach and then exceed the oracle level of approximately 3.9. The trajectory illustrates the method’s central tradeoff between high-risk coverage and information burden.

Table 2: Final held-out results across tasks and training methods. All policies are evaluated in the hidden condition using the pure verifiable reward and k=12 sampled rollouts per case. High-risk value and high-risk oracle-grade support are the primary safety-focused metrics. Overall value, overall support, and mean questions describe aggregate performance and interaction burden. Bold marks the strongest non-exploitative high-risk result within each task. The SFT initialization samples an oracle-grade trajectory for every high-risk case (support 1.00) but performs poorly on a typical high-risk rollout (value −0.285). Both RL methods raise high-risk value but sharply reduce high-risk support, and both reduce overall support. Credit-assignment GRPO under-gathers; decoupled GRPO over-gathers and damages benign support. Neither converts the sampled behaviour into a reliable procedure. “supp” denotes oracle-grade support@12.

Decoupled GRPO instead alternates exploration updates based on state recoverability with exploitation updates based on env.score. Every policy is evaluated using the same unshaped terminal verifier.

All environments use a question cost of 0.03 and an oracle-grade tolerance of 0.03. Diagnostics contains the largest finding space and is designed to reveal hedging and premature commitment on rare emergency cases.

Table 3: Diagnostics results in the held-out hidden condition using the pure verifiable reward. Plain GRPO and credit-assignment GRPO are reported as mean±sample standard deviation over three training seeds. Base and decoupled GRPO are single-seed reference policies. Credit assignment improves overall value, high-risk value, and moderate oracle-grade support relative to the outcome-only control. One plain GRPO seed loses the supported high-risk case, whereas credit assignment retains it in each tested seed. “supp” denotes oracle-grade support@12 and should be interpreted as sampled capability rather than single-trajectory reliability. The held-out high-risk subgroup contains only two cases; every policy with high-risk support of 0.50 supports the same abdominal case, so high-risk values in this table are illustrative rather than precise estimates. §The step-40 checkpoint was selected on the held-out evaluation set and is therefore an optimistic estimate; the final checkpoint is shown for comparison.

Plain GRPO and λ=0.03 produce high one-question rates and under-gathering. At λ=0.2, the policy asks more than the oracle and loses aggregate value. The analytically motivated setting λ=0.1 places mean questioning close to the oracle level and preserves high clot support. The absence of an overall value gain is consistent with the small best constant gap of +0.075, which leaves limited adaptive headroom.

papers.selection_reason: RL reward design for multi-turn LLM agents is relevant to LLM reasoning and sequential decision-making methods.
papers.title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
papers.tldr: For multi-turn clinical agents, dense process rewards that value uncertainty-reducing questions can produce safer procedures than outcome-only rewards, but reward strength and exploration must be tailored to the task.

papers.abstract: In production systems, 3D geometry is represented by primitives such as points, lines, and triangles, as rendering hardware is optimized to generate images from them very efficiently. Learning such primitives from images by volume rendering is challenging, as they are Dirac masses defined at infinitesimal locations in space. EWA splatting, Poisson reconstruction, and 3D Gaussian Splatting overcome this by convolving Dirac masses with a low-frequency kernel, a recipe that generalizes along two axes: the kernel and the primitive. As points and triangles have already received significant attention, we investigate this recipe for curvilinear primitives, and introduce Spaghetti Splatting. We approximate curves by polylines whose convolution converges to that of the continuous curve, and volume render each segment so that connected segments composite without overcounting at their joints. For fast training and inference, we linearize the camera projection per segment, which also accommodates kernels beyond Gaussians, such as Beta kernels. As a point is a curve of zero length, our representation is a strict superset of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It remains competitive with the state-of-the-art on general scenes, outperforms methods specialized to line-like geometry, natively supports anti-aliasing, and produces long connected strands that are directly amenable to physics simulation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning infinitesimal curve-like Dirac masses from images.
Approximates continuous curves with polylines whose convolved representation converges to the curve.
Composites rendered segments at joints without overcounting and linearizes camera projection for efficiency.
Supports kernels beyond Gaussians, including Beta kernels, and strictly generalizes 3D Gaussian Splatting.
Remains competitive on general scenes, surpasses line-specialized methods, supports anti-aliasing, and produces physics-ready connected strands.

figures.caption: Figure 7. Comparison on Mip-NeRF 360, Shelly, and Fuzzy – (a, b) Unlike point-based primitives [8, 14, 29], our method can reconstruct thin elongated geometry effectively. (c) We can also model wide texture-less areas, like the dark shadow on the figure, with wide kernels, unlike Line Primitives [34]. We mark the three best values in each column with gold, silver, and bronze medals.

Figure 4. Overview – (Left) Our representation is a set of learnable polyline primitives convolved with Gaussian or Beta kernels. (Middle) Without loss of generality, we render each segment individually: we first project it onto the image plane, and then evaluate the integral of the convolution along the ray in screen space using the closed-form integrals of Section 3.3, which yields a per-segment screen-space rendering. The segments are then composited along each ray to obtain the accumulated color. (Right) We compute the L1 loss between the rendered image and the ground-truth image, and backpropagate its gradient to the parameters of the primitives.

Figure 3. Inside our spaghetti – We visualize the Dirac measure of Kheradmand et al. [14] (left), and of our Spaghetti Splatting (right) for the Bonsai scene from Mip-NeRF 360 [2]. (middle) We show one RGB render, not repeated, as it is visually identical for both representations. While 3DGS models thin strokes with scattered points (e.g. the bicycle spokes), our segments form continuous strokes that follow edges.

Figure 8. Comparison with Gaussian Haircut [43] – averaged over two datasets: GeomHair [15] (selected 8 hairstyles) and the curly hair model of Yuksel [42]. Top: strands of the curly hair model in a held-out view, one random color per strand. Our strands closely match the ground-truth strands, whereas those of Gaussian Haircut are poorly structured.

Figure 2. Kernel ⊛ dirac – Since Dirac masses and convolution kernels are independent degrees of freedom, we can modify either one to obtain a different differentiable primitive. The first column shows that convolving a point mass with a Gaussian or a Beta kernel yields the primitives of 3DGS [13] and DBS [16], respectively. Replacing the point mass with a line segment, while retaining either kernel, yields the primitives in the middle. Finally, we connect these segments into a polyline, which yields our curvilinear primitive. In the bottom row, we convolve the same Dirac masses with an anisotropic Beta kernel. For visualization, we shade the primitives with the normals of their convolution surfaces [4].
Figure 5. Convergence – A curve rendered as a polyline of 4, 8, 16, and 32 Beta segments rasterized independently converges to the smooth curve without knots at the joints.

Figure 6. Densification – We take inspiration from the densification strategy of 3DGS MCMC [14], but adapt it to our primitives. When the opacity of a segment falls below a threshold, MCMC relocation moves it, potentially breaking up the polyline it was in. The relocation target is then sampled in two ways. Long segments are split into two, short segments are cloned.

Table 1. Ablations – Averaged over Fuzzy, Shelly, and MipNeRF 360; each row removes one component (✗). The size of a connected component is its number of segments; a segment without a joint has size 1.

papers.selection_reason: Novel curvilinear primitive representation for 3D scene rendering, extending 3D Gaussian Splatting.
papers.title: Spaghetti Splatting: Differentiating Curvilinear Dirac Masses via Convolution
papers.tldr: Spaghetti Splatting enables efficient differentiable rendering and learning of curvilinear 3D primitives by convolving curves with kernels and volume-rendering their polyline approximations.

papers.abstract: In ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing images, the objects that questions count in a region or relate by direction often span only a few pixels. Existing methods mainly decide where a vision-language model (VLM) should look and trust its answer in the chosen view. We show that this assumption fails for counting, and measure VLMs as one calibrates a sensor. All eight open VLMs tested fall increasingly short once a view holds more than a certain number of objects, about five for most on DOTA aerial images. This counting horizon narrows as views grow and objects appear smaller. An empirical power-law response model predicts the undercount a split recovers and the spurious counts it adds, and supports the rule of splitting only views beyond the horizon. In GeoScope, a text-only language model parses the question into a typed spatial program that fixes the region and its resolution. The VLM only grounds and counts within its operating range, and directions are computed explicitly from the grounded boxes. To our knowledge, it is the first UHR method to split views by a measured limit of the VLM. Without training, it improves Qwen3-VL-8B by 16.3 points on regional counting and 10.5 on spatial relations in XLRS-Bench, and has the highest reported accuracy, trained methods included, on regional counting and on the whole benchmark by question. On UHR-Micro it improves global and regional counting by 16.8 and 36.2 points, 15.6 of the former from splitting. On MME-RealWorld counting it gains 11.4 points, and we show that an option that is almost never correct yet often chosen distorts comparisons there. Project page: https://avalon-s.github.io/GeoScope/
bullets: VLM counting accuracy degrades sharply beyond a view-dependent horizon of roughly five objects, especially as objects become smaller.
A text-only language model converts questions into typed spatial programs that specify regions and resolution.
GeoScope splits only views exceeding the measured counting horizon, while the VLM grounds and counts within its reliable range.
It computes directional relations explicitly from grounded object boxes rather than relying solely on VLM judgments.
Without training, it reports substantial gains across XLRS-Bench, UHR-Micro, and MME-RealWorld counting tasks.

papers.selection_reason: VLM-based spatial reasoning for counting and spatial relations in ultra-high-resolution imagery, directly fitting spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GeoScope: Training-Free Program Execution beyond the Counting Horizon for Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing Question Answering
papers.tldr: GeoScope improves ultra-high-resolution remote-sensing QA by measuring when VLMs undercount and selectively splitting overly crowded views, without training.

papers.abstract: A world model predicts how a scene changes after an action, and a planner uses it to search for actions that reach a goal. If the camera moves or the controller changes, the same command moves the robot differently: when its commands are turned by 90 degrees, a frozen planner with the LeWM world model that succeeds in 77.5% of episodes succeeds in only 7.8%. Current fixes retrain the model, need training data, or forget a set-up when it returns. We propose Library of Hands (LoH), a training-free method that keeps the world model frozen and corrects only the map from commands to applied actions, which we call the hand. LoH reads the hand through the frozen model, with no extra sensor: it finds the action that best explains the change between two camera images (a reading). It stores every hand it identifies, so a returning set-up is recognised rather than re-learnt. In closed-loop tests, LoH more than doubles success on three simulated tasks, from 28.6% to 62.3%, and loses only 0.6 percentage points when nothing changes. It also works, unchanged, with two other world models and on two of three models pretrained on real robot data, and its gain grows with the quality of its readings.
bullets: Problem: Camera or controller changes can make a planner’s commands produce different motions, sharply reducing performance.
Method: Infer the current command-to-action mapping—or “hand”—from image changes using the frozen world model, without extra sensors or training data.
LoH stores identified hands so previously seen setups can be recognized instead of relearned.
In closed-loop tests, success increased from 28.6% to 62.3% across three simulated tasks, while unchanged setups lost only 0.6 percentage points.
The method also transferred unchanged to other world models and most tested models pretrained on real-robot data; performance depended on reading quality.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free adaptation of command-to-action mapping for frozen world-model planners, with a reusable library of hands for closed-loop control.
papers.title: Library of Hands: Fix the Hands, Not the World Model
papers.tldr: Library of Hands (LoH) adapts a frozen world model to changing robot command mappings without retraining by identifying and reusing the current action-to-motion mapping.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.
bullets: Studies how dataset size, training updates, checkpoint selection, and simulation affect VLA adaptation for precise chess-piece manipulation.
Fine-tunes π₀.₅ on teleoperated real demonstrations and randomized scripted-expert demonstrations in simulation.
In simulation, success improves with more data and updates; a short learning-rate cooldown adds up to 31 success-rate points.
Validation loss and action error are unreliable for selecting checkpoints.
Several rollout-based and reinforcement-learning refinements did not measurably outperform plain behavior cloning in this setting; simulator, expert, and demonstrations are released.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical study of VLA fine-tuning and sim-to-real transfer for precise robotic manipulation with language-specified goals.
papers.title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
papers.tldr: A robotic chess case study shows that simulated demonstrations can improve VLA fine-tuning when real data is scarce, while checkpoint selection requires success-based evaluation rather than common loss metrics.

papers.abstract: Interpretability tools are usually built for one model at a time: a refusal direction, a truthfulness probe, or a steering vector is found with labeled data inside the model it explains. We ask whether such tools can be carried to other models through a map between residual streams fit only on unlabeled prompts. We transfer a refusal direction, tested causally by addition and ablation, and two read-out tools, a correctness direction and a sentiment probe, across 110 pairs of models from five families and 1B to 72B parameters and between base and instruction-tuned models, with controls for specificity and five seeds. How much transfers depends on what the map was fit on. A map fit on ordinary questions recovers 54\% of the target's own refusal steering and 16\% to 77\% of its correctness gain; adding unlabeled prompts from the region where the tool operates raises these to 102\% and 88\% to 98\%, while control directions recover at most 1\%. We prove that a linear map behaves this way whenever two models correspond linearly on the data it covers, and a label-free coverage score derived from this result tracks recovery across more than 16,000 runs and explains earlier reports that maps between models fail across domains. Carried read-out tools outperform anything the target's unlabeled representations yield. Interpretability results, once found, can be reused across models at the cost of a few unlabeled prompts.
bullets: Tests refusal steering, correctness directions, and sentiment probes across 110 model pairs spanning five families, 1B–72B parameters, and base/instruction-tuned variants.
Transfer quality depends on whether mapping data covers the tool’s operating region; targeted prompts substantially improve recovery over ordinary questions.
A coverage score predicts transfer success across more than 16,000 runs and explains failures when mappings are fit outside the relevant domain.
Transferred read-out tools outperform tools learned solely from the target model’s unlabeled representations.
Scope: results concern linear residual-stream maps and the tested interpretability tools, model pairs, and prompt coverage settings.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates the transferability of interpretability tools (refusal steering, correctness probes) across different LLMs using linear maps, contributing to LLM understanding and robustness.
papers.title: Interpretability Is Not Model-Specific
papers.tldr: Interpretability tools can transfer across models using linear residual-stream maps fit on a small number of targeted unlabeled prompts.

papers.abstract: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare nine dense detectors, eight YOLO models of four generations and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.
bullets: The study evaluates nine dense detectors, including eight YOLO models and FCOS, on VisDrone and DOTA with controlled tuning and held-out testing.

On VisDrone, training a single detector at higher resolution outperforms tiled inference with box fusion whenever that resolution is feasible; higher resolution also beats a larger model at equal compute.
SCAHI combines dense outputs from tiles using coverage-aware weighting and a fine peak grid, avoiding information loss from decoded-box fusion.
With identical tiles, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS.
On DOTA, where full-image resolution is infeasible, SCAHI improves over the best single pass and replacing SAHI's merge step yields substantial gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview. One detector processes a whole-image pass at its training size and overlapping tiles. The baseline merges decoded boxes across passes (orange). SCAHI accumulates the dense outputs of all passes in a global volume over position and object size, weights them so that every position receives the same total weight, and extracts one peak per object. For YOLOv10 and YOLO26, SCAHI uses the one-to-many head.

YOLOv10s, the detector of the main study, is reported in Sec. 10.

Figure 2. Why dense fusion removes tile-border fragments. (a) Box fusion sees two decoded boxes for one object that straddles a tile seam: the fragment predicted by tile A overlaps the full box from tile B too little to be suppressed. (b) Dense fusion weights every prediction by a raised-cosine taper bt over the overlap; the tapers of overlapping tiles sum to one (Eq. 2), so a prediction near a tile border carries little weight and the cluster around the object yields one detection. The fusion must also keep adjacent objects apart: its peak search has to be fine relative to object size (Sec. 5.2). Schematic, not to scale.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces SCAHI, a method for efficient small object detection using dense fusion and coverage-aware inference, which is relevant for perception in embodied systems.
papers.title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
papers.tldr: Slicing helps mainly when full-image resolution is insufficient, and SCAHI improves tile fusion by preserving dense, complementary predictions.

papers.abstract: We examine what plan validation and execution reports establish in natural-language robot fleet control. Commands are traced through typed plans, deterministic corrections, fleet coordination and outcome checks in a three-level Robot Operating System 2 implementation with twenty simulated robots. An offline benchmark of 44 cases checks plan structure and selected command requirements. Across five local configurations without a response schema, 70.0-87.3% of responses pass. All runs in a selected 18-run simulation series meet their pose-based task conditions. This series includes two successful repeats that replaced incomplete runs after a software change. Saved plans and logs document duplicate pickup assignments and goal adjustments within the original task zones. Separate formation traces show a structurally accepted plan with the wrong formation shape and a rejected route, and an arrival report that omitted a requested robot after replanning. Carry completion records pickup and subsequent drop-off zone presence for the same robot. The cases distinguish changes to executable actions from changes to the requirements covered by a completion report. They motivate checking the effective assignments, goals and reported outcome against the original command.
bullets: The study examines what validation and execution reports actually establish in robot fleet control.
Commands are traced through typed plans, deterministic corrections, coordination, and outcome checks in a three-level ROS 2 implementation with 20 simulated robots.
An offline 44-case benchmark found 70.0–87.3% of responses passed across five local configurations without a response schema.
Simulation cases exposed duplicate pickup assignments, adjusted goals, an incorrect formation shape, a rejected route, and an arrival report omitting a requested robot after replanning.
The findings motivate checking effective assignments, goals, and reported outcomes against the original command.
