papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms often rely on data collected from a target environment, which can be expensive and noisy. Although simulators can generate large amounts of additional data, standard simulation mixing approaches, which directly combine simulated and real experience, can degrade performance due to simulator inaccuracies, especially when they bias the solution away from the optimal policy. We propose a conservative simulation-aided learning method based on control variates, where simulated data is used solely to reduce variance in the learning process rather than directly shaping the learning target. We develop our approach for Policy-Evaluation, which is a fundamental building block of RL algorithms. Then we combine it within the actor-critic framework towards policy improvement, as well as extend it towards offline RL scenarios. Experiments on multiple MuJoCo benchmark tasks demonstrate improvements over standard simulation mixing approaches, highlighting control variates as an effective tool for simulation-aided reinforcement learning.
bullets: Motivated by the high cost and noise of collecting real-environment data.
Develops a control-variate method for policy evaluation that uses simulation only for variance reduction.
Extends the approach to actor–critic policy improvement and offline RL.
Experiments across multiple MuJoCo tasks show improvements over standard simulation-mixing methods.
The approach is designed to mitigate inaccuracies in imperfect simulators.:

papers.abstract: Urban traffic flow prediction is a cornerstone of intelligent transportation systems, yet accurate forecasting under adverse weather conditions remains a significant challenge. Existing data-driven models, while effective for routine patterns, often struggle with the sparse data and complex non-linear shifts associated with rare meteorological events. These methods typically treat environmental contexts as shallow numerical features, failing to capture the underlying semantic reasoning-why and how specific adverse conditions alter mobility behaviors across regions with different functional compositions. To address this limitation, we propose Multi-STG, a unified framework that integrates Large Language Model (LLM)-derived semantic priors with graph-based spatiotemporal learning. Multi-STG introduces an LLM-empowered semantic enhancement module that transforms comprehensive context descriptions such as weather, POIs, and holidays into high-level semantic embeddings, effectively providing a knowledge-driven complement to data scarcity. Furthermore, we design a multimodal attentional fusion mechanism to dynamically weigh heterogeneous inputs and a semantic-enhanced prediction head with gated residual calibration to robustly adjust forecasts based on semantic guidance. Extensive experiments on real-world multi-city private car datasets demonstrate that Multi-STG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, reducing MAE by 11.82\% on average relative to the strongest baseline across three cities, while maintaining stable performance under sparse and non-stationary conditions.
bullets: Targets sparse data and nonlinear traffic shifts during rare adverse weather events.
Converts weather, points of interest, and holiday descriptions into semantic embeddings using an LLM.
Fuses heterogeneous inputs with multimodal attention and calibrates predictions through a gated residual head.
Outperforms the strongest baseline by an average 11.82% MAE across three cities, with stable performance under sparse, non-stationary conditions.

papers.abstract: Serving systems choose a weight format for each model and deployment. A low-cost screen predicts the resulting KL divergence from the unquantized model's Fisher information using $\tfrac12Δ^\top FΔ$, the expansion underlying Hessian-aware and second-order post-training quantizers. We assess the reliability of this screen in GPU batches with channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8 and group-wise int4 on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, OLMo-2-7B, Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Relative predictions hold across a 16-fold range of perturbation scales, int4 group sizes and rounding modes, while absolute predictions are heavy-tailed. A trimmed average brings 10 of 12 cells on Qwen3-4B and OLMo-2 within 15% of measured KL. The MoE model exhibits nonquadratic response at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as $α^{0.63}$. Computing per-sequence gradients in bf16 can cause fourfold prediction errors. We trace these errors to arithmetic in the lower half of the backward pass and eliminate them by using fp32 there. Batch-invariant kernels run at 0.55 times the throughput, while changes in reduction order introduce a floor of 0.17-0.22 nats per sequence. We build a screener with one streamed fp32 Fisher pass, trimmed tensor-block predictions with a band, a flag for aligned tensors and per-layer format allocation. On the unseen Mistral-7B-v0.3 family, all six predictions fall within the band, all three KL budgets are met, and vLLM throughput is predicted within 0.4%.
bullets: The study evaluates the approximation ½ΔᵀFΔ for channel-wise int8, per-tensor fp8, and group-wise int4 quantization across five language models and varied perturbation settings.
Relative predictions remain consistent across scales, group sizes, and rounding modes, while absolute errors are heavy-tailed; trimmed averaging improves calibration in most tested cells.
The MoE model shows nonquadratic behavior at small perturbations, with int8 KL scaling as α^0.63 rather than quadratically.
bf16 per-sequence gradients can produce fourfold prediction errors; fp32 computation in the lower backward pass removes these errors, at 0.55× throughput for batch-invariant kernels.
A proposed screener accurately predicts all six held-out Mistral-7B-v0.3 cases, meets three KL budgets, and predicts vLLM throughput within 0.4%.

papers.abstract: Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.
bullets: Addresses the gap between likelihood convergence and parameter recovery in POMDPs.
Bounds parameter error using the likelihood gap, observation/transition-kernel conditioning, and the behavior policy.
Covers both undercomplete and overcomplete POMDP regimes.
Applies to maximum-likelihood estimators and any method producing a sufficiently good likelihood candidate.
Separates model and behavior-policy effects, including action coverage and mixing, to guide data collection.

papers.abstract: As vision-language models (VLMs) move toward interpreting medical images directly, their outputs increasingly include not just a label but a stated confidence and a written justification. Yet the field still predominantly evaluates VLMs using just accuracy. We evaluate the coherence between answer, confidence, and explanation across four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization, using two mammography datasets. We perform controlled perturbations of the question, multiple choice option orders, and the images and assess changes in the three outputs. Our results suggest confidence does not decrease even as the mammography image is changed. Shuffling the options also changes most VLMs' answers. Notably, there are cases where a model's own stated reasoning contradicts its final answer, a distinction accuracy alone cannot capture but one that governs whether an AI-generated answer can be trusted.
bullets: Evaluates four VLMs on breast density and BI-RADS categorization using two mammography datasets.
Tests robustness with controlled changes to questions, answer-option order, and images.
Models often retain confidence when the mammography image changes.
Shuffling answer options changes the answers of most evaluated VLMs.
Some explanations contradict the models’ final answers, raising trust concerns.

papers.abstract: Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation in learned composition while avoiding the rigidity of fully hardcoded classical estimators.
Uses an exact group-law operation, learned edge increments, and a zero-initialized correction for unknown deviations.
A pre-training criterion predicts whether the task is exactly representable by the imposed law.
On SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter model approaches the Bayes floor and uses 27× fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline.

On real robot arms, the correction achieves 1.12–1.14 mm error versus 1.29–1.33 mm for Gauss–Newton at N ≥ 60, transferring across vendors and protocols; performance declines when the imposed law is mismatched.

papers.selection_reason: Group-law layer learns residual deviations in transformation composition for robot and navigation tasks.
papers.title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
papers.tldr: LawKAN embeds a known non-commutative group law into a learnable layer, learning only local increments and deviations, and achieves accurate, parameter-efficient composition when the law matches the task.

papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) encode substantial expert knowledge within their weights, yet their direct application to specialised classification domains such as benthic imagery remains limited. Meanwhile, vision transformers trained on these tasks rely predominantly on low-level visual latents (colours, textures, and shapes) that lack the higher-level reasoning humans employ for identification. We propose Guided Hierarchical Multi-Label (GHiML) learning, a pipeline that extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM conditioned on training data, generates sample-relevant captions grounded in those variables, and fuses the resulting textual embeddings with image embeddings via cross-attention and a per-node gated router. We also introduce the inverted HML score ($d_{\mathrm{inv}}$), a similarity score that evaluates hierarchical multi-label predictions through graph traversal distance and a cardinality penalty, providing an interpretable alternative to existing measures, which are insensitive to realistic degradations in sparse, deep hierarchies. Experiments on BenthicNet, FathomNet and iNaturalist show that the router improves macro $F_1$ over the vision-only baseline by up to 6.7 pp and $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ by up to 21.1 pp on in-domain benthic data, with gains persisting under distribution shift. Ablations locate the contribution of the text itself: on the multi-label biotic hierarchies, removing the per-sample text signal degrades $d_{\mathrm{inv}}$ while leaving macro $F_1$ unchanged, consistent with text acting through prediction cardinality rather than node discrimination, whereas iNaturalist, whose annotations are single-label, loses 18.7% of macro $F_1$. Our results support the hypothesis that VLMs contain exploitable specialised knowledge that, when appropriately elicited, can augment classification in domains where direct visual learning is insufficient.
bullets: Extracts conceptual latent variables from a VLM and generates captions grounded in each image’s relevant concepts.
Fuses text and image embeddings using cross-attention and a per-node gated router for hierarchical multi-label prediction.
Introduces the interpretable inverted HML score (d_inv), combining graph-traversal distance with a cardinality penalty.
On benthic datasets, improves macro F1 by up to 6.7 percentage points and d_inv by up to 21.1 points over vision-only models, with gains under distribution shift.
Ablations suggest text mainly improves prediction cardinality in multi-label hierarchies, while single-label iNaturalist loses 18.7% macro F1 without it.

papers.abstract: Video world models conditioned on an input video make it possible to explore real, recorded dynamic scenes, enabling re-shooting of footage, free-viewpoint replay, and real-to-sim environments for embodied agents. Such uses require the generated rollout to stay faithful to the recorded world, yet existing benchmarks start from a single image or a text prompt, and video-conditioned generation is evaluated mainly on perceptual quality and camera following. These evaluations do not directly assess whether exploration preserves subject identity, event progression, and scene consistency upon revisiting a location. We introduce WanderBench, a benchmark for exploring dynamic worlds from video. It comprises 745 single-shot source videos of real and AI-generated content in three difficulty tiers (3-25 s), paired with camera routes given as keyboard actions, and evaluates six dimensions with 24 human-validated sub-metrics. Benchmarking eight models, we find that as clips grow longer, models keep the static scene and visual quality but lose camera control and the source dynamics, and that none keeps revisited places consistent. We further propose WanderLand, a training-free framework that conditions each frame of a frozen model on the same-instant source and, on revisits, on its own earlier static content. WanderLand improves five models on every dimension, by up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 745 real and AI-generated single-shot videos across three difficulty tiers, paired with keyboard-action camera routes.
Evaluates six dimensions through 24 human-validated sub-metrics, including identity, event progression, camera control, and consistency when revisiting locations.
Across eight models, longer rollouts preserve static appearance and visual quality but degrade camera control and source dynamics.
No evaluated model maintains consistency when revisiting previously seen places.
Proposes WanderLand, a training-free conditioning framework that improves all dimensions across five models, with up to 8.3 points in source-dynamics fidelity.

papers.abstract: We propose SciMARS, a framework for recursive task-local adaptation of multi-agent harnesses in closed-loop scientific discovery. Multi-agent systems coordinate analysis, experimental design, and verification as scientific evidence evolves. However, two problems limit their effectiveness: (i) without shared memory, agents lose observations and repeat work; (ii) fixed role procedures, handoffs, and memory policies perpetuate mistakes despite retained evidence. We address these problems with a shared evidence graph and separate component editors. SciMARS adapts roles and coordination; SciMARS + Memory adds a third editor for how agents record, retrieve, and receive evidence. Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next harness. We evaluate scientific discovery through experimental-data replay and a digital twin. SciMARS + Memory resolves 12/18 GPT-6-Astra and 2/18 GLM-5.3 attempts on Autonomous Science Bench, compared with 8/18 and 1/18 for the base multi-agent team. On ScienceAgentBench and AppWorld, it solves 14/38 and 11/20 tasks, compared with 11/38 and 5/20 for the base team. These results support combining shared memory with harness adaptation across scientific and interactive tasks.
bullets: Targets repeated work caused by missing shared memory and persistent errors from fixed agent procedures.
Uses a shared evidence graph and separate editors for roles/coordination and, in SciMARS + Memory, evidence recording and retrieval.
Candidate probes guide composition and selection of the next multi-agent harness.
Evaluated with experimental-data replay, a digital twin, Autonomous Science Bench, ScienceAgentBench, and AppWorld.
SciMARS + Memory outperformed the base team across the reported benchmarks, though results varied by model and task.

papers.title: SciMARS: Multi-Agent Recursive Self-Improvement for Closed-Loop Scientific Discovery

papers.abstract: Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.
bullets: Targets the high cost of solving coupled alternating-minimization subproblems exactly or iteratively.
Uses learned networks to approximate each subproblem solution and trains them greedily according to a derived per-iteration error bound.
For convex problems with quadratic coupling and quadratic growth, combines worst-case analysis with PAC-Bayes to bound expected optimality gaps with high probability.
In robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction, achieves 5×–13× speedups at matched accuracy versus an inexact first-order baseline.
Brief end-to-end fine-tuning increases the speedup to 30× and outperforms other learned schemes.

papers.abstract: Self-recurrence represents an important component for temporal processing in neural networks, both artificial and biological, where it appears naturally in the form of leaky integration. However, due to the complex temporal dependencies of the gradient, an efficient and effective method of online training is still lacking. Here we propose K-prop, a novel online learning method for leaky neural networks. It dramatically reduces the computational and memory cost of real time recurrent learning (RTRL) by propagating kernel gains. K-prop also outperforms existing RTRL approximations and achieves performance comparable to backpropagation through time in sequence learning, classification, and reinforcement learning tasks. We further analyze how its sole approximation affects gradient quality and identify conditions under which K-prop remains accurate and effective.
bullets: Addresses the high computational and memory cost of online recurrent learning caused by complex temporal gradient dependencies.
Propagates kernel gains to reduce the cost of real-time recurrent learning (RTRL).
Outperforms existing RTRL approximations and performs comparably to backpropagation through time across several task types.
Analyzes the method’s single approximation and identifies conditions where its gradients remain accurate and effective.

figures.caption: Figure 4: N-sum task evaluated with various online learning methods. ProspE only considers prospective errors ϵ̆ in GLE [Ellenberger et al., 2025], without further augmentations. (a) Training loss over time. K-prop achieves substantially lower error than other approximation methods and closely matches RTRL. (b) Temporal response of hidden neurons to a step input before and after learning. K-prop develops more structured and contrastive temporal kernels. (c) Example input and corresponding outputs. Before learning, all models produce non-informative outputs. After learning, K-prop and RTRL closely align with the target sequence, while other methods deviate in both timing and amplitude.

Figure 1: Kernel propagation. (a) Calculating gradients involves hierarchical filters along paths of neuron connections. (b) Illustration of kernel decomposition. The complicated temporal structure in the true gradient can be approximated by a sum over ζ weighted by τ -dependent coefficients K. Every ζ (solid) is weighted by corresponding K as a component (dashed in the same color). The sum of all components aligns well with the exact term computed by RTRL.

Figure 7: Compare the cost under multi-layer architecture. Left: Memory cost Middle: Computational cost per time step. GLE has O(n) memory and O(n2) computational cost. All costs are computed in optimal layer-wise implementations instead of directly from scaling law. Experiments were conducted on a local machine equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4060 Laptop GPU (8 GB). Overall running time reflects additional latency introduced by temporal loop overhead.

Dissimilarity ranges from 0 to 2 with 0 indicating complete alignment, 1 orthogonality, and 2 complete anti-alignment. Error bars show median, 1st, and 3rd quartiles. Figure 5: Sequential Classification Benchmark learning. (a) Mean, minimum, and maximum validation accuracy during training on GSC Warden [2018] 20-command task. papers.abstract: Answer accuracy alone does not distinguish failures in acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application. AuDiR (Audio Diagnostic Reasoning) examines these distinctions through controlled input interventions. Each item contains an audio clip, a multiple-choice question, a task-general rule, and a textual description of the acoustic observations needed to answer. Three conditions progressively supply the rule and observations; a fourth removes the audio while retaining the question and rule. The first correct diagnostic condition assigns an operational response label, without identifying a unique internal cause. The current benchmark contains 201 items in 18 families drawn from 9 sources, with answer references documented separately from percept extraction. In a preliminary evaluation of Gemini-3.8-flash, accuracy is 29.3% without supplied information, 31.3% with the rule, and 98.5% with the observations also supplied. No-audio accuracy is 23.9%, with a confidence interval containing the 25.0% chance rate. A family-level knowledge probe associates incomplete rule recall with larger gains from rule provision. These results show the benefit of supplying acoustic observations as text, while incomplete validation, possible recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit stronger failure-attribution claims.
bullets: Targets three stages of audio reasoning: acoustic perception, rule knowledge, and rule application.
Uses four controlled conditions that progressively provide rules, textual acoustic observations, or no audio.
The benchmark has 201 items across 18 families from 9 sources, with answers separated from percept extraction.
In a preliminary Gemini-3.8-flash evaluation, accuracy rose from 29.3% unaided to 98.5% when observations were supplied; no-audio accuracy was near chance at 23.9%.
Incomplete validation, recognition shortcuts, and non-monotonic responses limit definitive attribution of internal failure causes.

papers.abstract: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between foundation-model accuracy and per-input query cost.
Introduces a fixed-query method that combines outputs with non-query features, and an adaptive method using Q-learning to select models and stop querying.
Shows that multiple individually inaccurate models can jointly outperform the best single model.
Provides minimax-rate guarantees for fixed querying and finite-sample risk/cost bounds for adaptive querying.
Simulations and a multimodal laptop-price application show both methods outperform existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoders raise throughput by banking more target tokens per forward pass, and Medusa, EAGLE-3, DFlash and DSpark all do it the same way: more candidates that survive verification. All of them draft in the target's own vocabulary, so one node of the candidate tree is one target token, and the tokenizer makes that unit look like a constant. It is not. BPE's pretokenizer splits on whitespace before merges are learned, so no multi-word string can ever become a single token: in Qwen3-4B, "United States of America" is four tokens and no adjacent pair of them exists as one entry, so a phrase is out of reach of any method drafting in the target's vocabulary. We change the unit. A small MLP head reads the frozen target's hidden state and predicts a one- to three-word phrase as one entry in a separate draft vocabulary; greedy longest-match expansion maps it back into the target's own tokens, and N candidates are verified in one forward pass behind a prefix-tree mask, so the change is orthogonal to tree depth and width. The target and its tokenizer stay frozen and a candidate is accepted only while it matches the target's own argmax, so the served output is identical to greedy decoding up to floating-point tie-breaking. On one A5000 at batch 1, against HuggingFace generate(), a 21.94M head (0.545% of Qwen3-4B) reaches 2.391x on GSM8K, 2.444x on MATH-500 and 1.544x on MT-Bench. Because the head's output layer is one row of 257 parameters per entry, the draft vocabulary size is the parameter budget: an 8,000-entry head is 3.434M parameters, 0.0854% of the target and 64x smaller than EAGLE-3's drafter, and keeps 92.3% of the larger head's GSM8K tokens per pass. With EAGLE-3 run on same prompts and baseline, our 21.94M head is ahead of tree-16 on both maths sets and behind tree-60 on every set.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that target-vocabulary drafting cannot represent multi-word phrases as single candidate units.
A small MLP predicts one- to three-word entries from a separate draft vocabulary, expands them into target tokens, and verifies candidates in one prefix-tree-masked pass.
Accepted tokens exactly match the target model’s greedy output, aside from floating-point tie-breaking.
On an A5000 at batch 1, it achieves 2.391× on GSM8K, 2.444× on MATH-500, and 1.544× on MT-Bench versus HuggingFace generate().
An 8,000-entry head uses 3.434M parameters and retains 92.3% of the larger head’s GSM8K tokens per pass; performance is ahead of EAGLE-3 tree-16 but behind tree-60.

papers.abstract: To address unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence feed-forward dense SLAM, this letter presents V3DSAM, an open-vocabulary semantic dense SLAM system that establishes physical correspondences at both the scene and object levels. The system combines feed-forward geometric estimates from VGGT-SLAM 2.0 with open-vocabulary semantic observations from SAM3. We introduce semantic-geometric dual-scale loop verification, which identifies false loop closures using pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D spatial correspondences, without accessing backbone-internal features. We further propose geometry-anchored persistent instance mapping, which defines physical instances through class-constrained 3D connectivity in an optimized global coordinate system and assigns global IDs without inter-frame identity propagation. The proposed verifier rejects all four false loop candidates in our TUM RGB-D evaluation, while long-sequence ScanNet experiments show improved instance identity consistency. Thus, V3DSAM reduces dependence on internal backbone features and temporal ID propagation for robust long-term cross-view association.
bullets: Targets unreliable cross-view association in long-sequence dense SLAM.
Combines VGGT-SLAM 2.0 geometric estimates with SAM3 open-vocabulary semantic observations.
Uses pixel-level bidirectional reprojection and object-level 3D correspondences to reject false loop closures.
Maps persistent instances via class-constrained 3D connectivity in a globally optimized coordinate system, avoiding temporal ID propagation.
Rejected all four false loop candidates in TUM RGB-D evaluation and improved instance identity consistency on long-sequence ScanNet experiments.

papers.abstract: Video out-painting is an important problem, yet existing research focuses primarily on short clips, leaving long video out-painting largely underexplored. Extending video out-painting to long videos poses substantial challenges. A natural solution is iterative out-painting, i.e., generating videos chunk by chunk, but this introduces two major issues: generation instability or even failure caused by inter-chunk inconsistencies and error accumulation, and semantic drift over long temporal horizons. In this paper, we propose LongSCOP, short for Semantically Consistent long Video Out-Painting. First, we introduce a training recipe with three components for smooth and stable long-horizon generation: self-forcing training, latent calibration, and future references. Beyond generation stability, we recognize that the rich temporal context of long videos provides valuable references for maintaining semantic consistency. We therefore develop a VLM-based agent that automatically selects the most informative reference frames from the entire video to maintain consistent subjects, scenes, and backgrounds throughout long-horizon generation. We also construct a high-quality training dataset of 62K video clips. To facilitate research on this underexplored problem, we introduce LVO-Bench, a benchmark curated by human experts to assess long-horizon stability and semantic consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms existing approaches in both generation stability and semantic coherence.
bullets: Addresses instability, error accumulation, and semantic drift in iterative long-video out-painting.
Uses self-forcing training, latent calibration, and future references for smoother long-horizon generation.
Employs a VLM-based agent to select informative frames that preserve subjects, scenes, and backgrounds.
Introduces a 62K-clip training dataset and the human-curated LVO-Bench benchmark.
Experiments show improved generation stability and semantic coherence over existing approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Illustration of key reference frame retrieval framework. Specifically, we calculate the registration maps and scores for all query-candidate pairs, and then input them into a VLM, Qwen3.5-VL-27B [32]. The VLM is requested to understand the whole video, speculate the missing contents (i.e., contents to out-paint like the two women and the indoor background), analyze which candidate frames may contain such missing contents, finally select the most suitable reference frames.

Figure 1: Illustration of the two main challenges in long video out-painting: (a) unstable generation including abrupt transitions, brightness flickering, and even complete generation collapse caused by accumulated errors, and (b) semantic drift like changed scene layouts, unstable object identities, or inconsistent subject appearances over long time. papers.abstract: Generalizable deepfake video detection remains challenging because forgery artifacts vary substantially across manipulation types and often combine diverse spatial and temporal inconsistencies. Existing parameter-efficient adaptation methods typically rely on a single shared representation, rendering them prone to manipulation-specific bias and limiting transfer to unseen forgeries. To address this challenge, we propose Mixture Of Spatio-Temporal Experts (MoSTE), an adaptation framework that enables conditional specialization of forensic representations. Instead of forcing one adapter to model all forgery patterns, MoSTE decomposes adaptation into parallel spatial and temporal expert pools and dynamically routes tokens to the most relevant experts through an unsupervised token-level routing mechanism. This allows experts to naturally specialize in complementary forgery cues without requiring explicit manipulation labels or multi-stage training, while effectively transferring representations from CLIP to the video domain. Extensive experiments across cross-dataset and cross-manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that MoSTE sets a new state of the art in average generalization while preserving strong performance across diverse manipulation families. Additional analysis of expert routing and attention behavior reveals the emergence of expert diversity, suggesting that MoSTE learns complementary spatio-temporal forensic features. Code is available at https://github.com/charbelyah/MoSTE
bullets: Deepfake artifacts vary across manipulation types and involve both spatial and temporal inconsistencies, making transfer to unseen forgeries difficult.
MoSTE uses parallel spatial and temporal expert pools with unsupervised, token-level dynamic routing.
The framework adapts CLIP representations to video without explicit manipulation labels or multi-stage training.
Experiments on cross-dataset and cross-manipulation benchmarks report state-of-the-art average generalization and strong performance across manipulation families.
Routing and attention analyses indicate that experts learn complementary forensic features.

papers.abstract: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.
bullets: Addresses whether a finite discrete vocabulary can represent the richness of visual content.
Uses a frozen pretrained encoder with lightweight residual modulation and a dual-branch reconstruction-aware objective.
Applies grouped product quantization to expand discrete capacity without increasing spatial sequence length.
Provides unified visual encoding and high-fidelity image decoding across downstream tasks.
Matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 understanding, 4 generation, and 1 image-editing benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 6 Overview of the code-conditioned Refiner. Code embeddings condition a flow decoder through global context tokens and time-conditioned spatial residuals. A multi-step teacher is distilled into an efficient one-step student with adversarial supervision. The timestep t in the diagram corresponds to τ in the equations. Increasing the quantization group count (G64) improves reconstruction fidelity, whereas combining fewer groups (G16) with the one-step Refiner preserves fidelity while enhancing perceptual quality.

Figure 3 Overview of dNaViT. (a) A frozen representation encoder handles arbitrary resolutions, with ResMod injecting multi-level information before group-wise product quantization. The shared discrete codes are decoded by individual ViT decoders into pixel and semantic reconstructions. (b) ResMod fuses intermediate features and predicts a zeroinitialized scale-and-shift residual. (c) Pixel and semantic branches are optimized with image and feature reconstruction losses, respectively.

Figure 4 Tokenization and Unified Codes for Downstream Tasks. (a) At spatial position t, the modulated feature zt is split into G channel groups and quantized with group-specific codebooks E(g), yielding indices (k (1) t , . . . , k (G) t ) and their embeddings. (b) Understanding supplies only code indices to the language model (LM) through newly initialized group-wise embedding tables {W(g)}Gg=1, trained jointly with the LM. (c) Reconstruction concatenates the indexed embeddings from the frozen tokenizer codebooks and feeds them to the pixel decoder Dpix. (d) Generation and editing use a multi-sub-token head atop the LM to predict each position’s multi-level indices, optionally conditioned on a reference image, then decode through the same frozen codebooks and pixel decoder.

papers.abstract: While modern video generative models achieve remarkable visual fidelity, they remain noticeably brittle when generating physically plausible dynamics and complex interactions. Targeted post-training is crucial, yet supervised fine-tuning suffers from offline state mismatch, and reinforcement learning is hindered by sparse, ill-defined physical reward functions. On-Policy (Self-)Distillation (OPSD) reconciles on-policy rollouts with dense corrective feedback, shifting the core challenge to designing effective privileged context. However, conventional modalities fall short: text prompts are inherently declarative, whereas real reference videos heavily entangle physical laws with visual appearance without parametric control. To this end, we propose PhysOPSD, introducing executable code as privileged physical context for video generation. Unlike static visual observations, executable code instantiates an editable physical world with intrinsic abstraction and controllability. Powered by PhysOPSD-Engine, we translate real-world physical scenarios into verifiable simulation programs. PhysOPSD then incorporates (i) dual-level physical privilege to bridge the information gap via an intermediate bottleneck, alongside (ii) controlled physical variations under shared rollout noise to expose causal dynamic shifts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PhysOPSD substantially improves physical plausibility across diverse backbones, outperforming SFT and RL baselines with only $3$K samples, while preserving general video generation quality.
bullets: Addresses brittle physical dynamics and interactions in video generation, where SFT faces state mismatch and RL lacks dense physical rewards.
Translates real-world scenarios into verifiable simulation programs with PhysOPSD-Engine.
Uses dual-level physical privilege and controlled physical variations with shared rollout noise to expose causal dynamics.
Improves physical plausibility across diverse backbones, outperforming SFT and RL baselines with 3K samples while preserving general video quality.

papers.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to execute natural-language manipulation tasks in real-world environments. This is particularly relevant in household assistance and logistics, where clutter requires reasoning about both task objectives and execution feasibility. This challenge becomes even more pronounced for bimanual humanoid platforms, where coordinating two manipulators introduces additional interaction and kinematic constraints. We present a zero-shot vision-language framework for execution-aware bimanual manipulation that jointly reasons about task objectives and physical feasibility. Planning is grounded in a structured scene representation that combines semantic object relations with execution constraints, enabling the selection of obstacle relocations and execution choices while preserving task semantics. Compatible actions are organised into parallel bimanual stages with explicit pre- and post-conditions. A hierarchical validator evaluates these conditions under perceptual uncertainty and uses stage-level execution history to support local recovery or targeted replanning. Experiments on the CENTAURO hybrid wheeled-legged humanoid robot across nine language-conditioned manipulation scenarios show higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline. In dedicated failure scenarios, hierarchical validation recovers from execution failures with fewer model queries than always replanning. These results demonstrate the benefits of combining execution reasoning directly into task planning. Videos and additional material are available on the Project Webpage: https://advrhumanoids.github.io/bridging-planning-execution/.
bullets: Targets household and logistics tasks where clutter, bimanual coordination, and kinematic constraints complicate execution.
Uses a structured scene representation combining semantic object relations with execution constraints to choose relocations and actions.

A hierarchical validator handles perceptual uncertainty and supports local recovery or targeted replanning using execution history.
On the CENTAURO robot, it achieves higher task success than a non-execution-aware baseline and recovers failures with fewer model queries than always replanning.

papers.abstract: Modern visuotactile sensors primarily sense contact by imaging the deformation of a compliant interface. Using techniques such as photometric stereo, they can recover detailed contact geometry, often represented as surface normals or depth. However, force-related information typically still needs to be inferred indirectly through calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings. Mechanochromic photonic-crystal (PC) materials offer an alternative physical encoding mechanism: contact loading changes their periodic microstructure and spectral response, directly transforming local stress into a spatially resolved structural-color field. Despite this potential, PC materials have rarely been explored as visuotactile sensors for closed-loop robot learning. We present PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic PC fingertip that uses a dense hue field as its tactile observation. Loading characterization demonstrates a repeatable relationship between the applied normal load and the observed hue response. We further integrate this representation directly into a Diffusion Policy and evaluate it on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Across 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68 successes (75.6\%), compared with 60 (66.7\%) for PCTac RGB, 57 (63.3\%) for Wedge RGB, and 29 (32.2\%) for vision-only. PCTac Hue also achieves the highest observed success rate on each evaluated task, including Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, where it achieves 16/30 successes versus 13/30 for tactile RGB baselines and 1/30 for vision-only. These results demonstrate the potential of mechanochromic structural color as a compact, load-sensitive tactile representation for robot learning and closed-loop manipulation. Project page: https://bey0ndt1me.github.io/PCTac-page/.
bullets: Encodes local contact load as a spatially resolved hue field through structural-color changes.

Integrates the hue representation directly into a Diffusion Policy for real-robot learning.
Across 90 rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 75.6% success, outperforming its RGB variant, another tactile sensor, and vision-only control.
Demonstrates potential as a compact tactile representation for dexterous manipulation, though evaluation is limited to three real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between action-oriented driving instructions and direct continuous ego-trajectory prediction.
Introduces TrajCond, a discrete 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory for conditioning VLA planning.
Uses two-stage training, followed by simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories.
Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show consistent gains in open- and closed-loop trajectory prediction.
Discrete trajectories are more effective as conditioning signals than as final planning outputs.

papers.abstract: Control barrier function (CBF) filters depend on dynamic models that can be inaccurate when their parameters and external forces are uncertain. This paper investigates a radial basis function (RBF) neural network compensator whose output is shared by a Cartesian tracking controller and a joint-space CBF filter. An auxiliary state driven by the difference between requested and applied torques corrects the learning signal, reducing the direct influence of filter intervention on adaptation. A two-link manipulator is evaluated through constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbance trials, and operating-range and timing studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed controller improves tracking while maintaining joint, velocity, and torque limits under parameter uncertainty, and that both the shared compensation and the auxiliary correction contribute to this improvement.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate CBF-filter dynamics caused by uncertain parameters and external forces.
Uses one RBF neural-network compensator shared by Cartesian tracking and a joint-space CBF filter.
Adds an auxiliary state based on requested-versus-applied torque differences to reduce filter-intervention effects on learning.
Experiments cover constrained regulation, ablations, matched uncertainty and disturbances, operating range, and timing.
Reported results maintain joint, velocity, and torque limits while improving tracking; both compensation and correction contribute.

papers.abstract: Correlation Matrix Memories (CMMs) store associations as sums of rank-one outer products, providing closed-form addressability, exact deletion, and linear attribution. While classical analyses assume random, orthogonal keys, semantic encoders produce correlated representations. We analyse CMMs under correlated keys using frame-theoretic coherence: (i) capacity bounds yielding an encoder-independent limit $n \le d(1+\varepsilon^2)$ for mean squared crosstalk $\varepsilon^2$; (ii) an exact characterisation of the collateral effect of deleting an association, guaranteeing that deletion never invalidates certified associations; and (iii) a geometric transparency bound demonstrating why attribution requires candidate sets of centred keys. On this basis, we introduce Topology-Aware Neuro-Symbolic Associative Retrieval (TANSAR). TANSAR traverses a directed acyclic association graph, prunes invalid paths via sound ground Horn constraints, and injects a representation derived strictly from the verified path into the residual stream of a frozen language model, guarded by a Clopper--Pearson selective-risk gate. Controlled experiments confirm all theoretical bounds. In multi-hop knowledge editing, Horn pruning reduces answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5%, whereas Hopfield retrieval incurs 24% contradictions when stale associations remain stored (and 0% if stale associations are removed). An end-to-end edit transaction requires 13.6 ms on a standard CPU and 2.37 ms on GPU. The symbolic component matches gold labels across all 600 ProofWriter theories and achieves 94.0% agreement on FOLIO, demonstrating sound and efficient multi-hop associative retrieval with exact unlearning.
bullets: Analyzes CMMs with correlated keys, deriving capacity, deletion-collateral, and attribution-transparency guarantees.
Traverses directed acyclic association graphs and prunes invalid paths using sound ground Horn constraints.
Injects only verified-path representations into a frozen language model, with a Clopper–Pearson selective-risk gate.
Reports reductions in multi-hop answer contradictions from 25.1% to 0.5% with Horn pruning, plus millisecond-scale edit transactions.
Matches gold labels on 600 ProofWriter theories and reaches 94.0% agreement on FOLIO.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding speeds up language models by having a lightweight drafter propose future tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. Block diffusion drafters such as DFlash predict an entire block in one forward pass, and DDTree builds draft trees directly from their per-position distributions. Each distribution implicitly assumes that the drafter's own greedy continuation is accepted, whereas a draft tree improves over a chain only on branches that leave this greedy path. Once a path forks, the drafter's top-1 accuracy drops from 89% to 18% and its top candidates often miss the true token. Re-running the drafter from the fork token largely restores its accuracy, showing that the errors stem from conditioning on an outdated prefix rather than from limited model capacity. In this paper, we introduce DForkTree, a training-free method that re-anchors each branch on its own tokens. It adjusts the drafter's scores with pointwise mutual information from target-generated n-grams, weighted more heavily after a fork, and a layer-wise GPU search recovers the exact optimal tree under these scores. On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all baselines on every benchmark, by up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree, with average speedups of up to 4.75x over autoregressive decoding.
bullets: Problem: Block-diffusion drafters become inaccurate after a tree branch because they condition on an outdated prefix.
Method: Re-anchor each branch using its own tokens, adjust scores with target-generated n-gram PMI, and emphasize corrections after forks.
The method is training-free and uses a layer-wise GPU search to recover the exact optimal tree under its scoring function.
On Qwen3.5-4B and 9B, DForkTree outperforms all reported baselines across benchmarks.
It achieves up to 4.75× speedup over autoregressive decoding, with gains of up to 41.5% over DFlash and 15.1% over DDTree.

papers.abstract: A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation. Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions. On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking high-dimensional visual observations, action-conditioned macro-state prediction, and future image generation.
Uses action responses and causal abstraction to aggregate local visual features into spatially corresponding macro-nodes.
A shared reference quotient measurement and motion-based appearance transport constrain recursive state and visual prediction.
Node-level visual errors are mapped back to spatial regions to correct generated observations and improve consistency.
On US-VLA, it reports 0.01861 ROI-MSE for four-step prediction and reduced LPIPS versus the best horizon-specific baseline for four-, eight-, and sixteen-step prediction.

The model then reads back the current generation under the same quotient measurement and maps the remaining node-level errors to the corresponding spatial locations to obtain future observations. The reference quotient mapping connects node construction, macro-state prediction, and spatial generation.

papers.abstract: Achieving generalizable and well-aligned multimodal representations remains a core challenge in robot learning. While recent approaches have attempted to align modalities by modeling conditional or higher-order statistical dependencies, they do not explicitly consider the structural coherence across modalities. In this work, we propose a novel multimodal alignment method that augments existing contrastive losses with a geometry-aware Gromov--Wasserstein (GW) distance-based regularization. To this end, we encode intra-modal geometry for each modality and reduce cross-modal structural discrepancies through a dynamically learned GW barycenter, thereby encouraging structural consistency in addition to instance-level contrastive alignment. We apply this optimal-transport-based alignment strategy to robot perception tasks involving underexplored modalities such as force and tactile signals, where modality data often exhibit varying sample densities. Extensive experiments on five robotic benchmarks show that our method improves structural alignment and downstream performance over state-of-the-art multimodal contrastive baselines across a wide range of downstream tasks, including robot and environment state prediction. Moreover, our GW-based regularization can be seamlessly integrated into most InfoNCE-like objectives.
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit cross-modal structural coherence in existing multimodal representation methods.
Encodes intra-modal geometry and uses a dynamically learned Gromov–Wasserstein barycenter to reduce structural discrepancies.
Supports challenging modalities such as force and tactile signals with differing sample densities.
Evaluated on five robotic benchmarks, improving structural alignment and downstream performance over multimodal contrastive baselines.
The GW regularizer integrates with most InfoNCE-like objectives.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP achieve strong performance across computer vision tasks, yet their image-text alignment is less reliable for infrared (IR) imagery because large-scale pre-training is dominated by visible-spectrum data. Due to the high cost of the infrared-text labeling, we investigate adapting CLIP to IR through only paired infrared-visible images, which requires considering modality-specific knowledge while preserving scene content and CLIP's image-text alignment. To achieve this, we propose TMT (Text-Derived Modality Knowledge Transfer), which adapts CLIP's image encoder through a text-defined infrared-to-visible direction and supervision from paired IR-visible images. First, we found that modality discrepancy can be described by corresponding text embeddings, thus using the direction of text embedding differences to guide the knowledge transfer between visible and infrared modalities without erasing infrared-specific information. To enhance the representation of semantics and details of infrared images, we introduce Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision that combines semantic alignment from CLIP visible image encoder with diffusion noise-prediction feedbacks. On four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks, TMT achieves the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among the compared methods (48.92%). It also achieves the best IR-text retrieval results among the compared methods without infrared-text supervision during adaptation and the highest open-vocabulary segmentation mIoU on both CART and SemanticRT among the CLIP-like methods.
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s weaker infrared image-text alignment caused by visible-spectrum-dominated pretraining.
Uses text-embedding differences to guide infrared-to-visible knowledge transfer while preserving infrared-specific information.
Introduces Generative-Perceptual Co-Supervision, combining CLIP semantic alignment with diffusion noise-prediction feedback.
Reports the highest mean zero-shot accuracy among compared methods on four source-disjoint IR classification benchmarks (48.92%).
Also achieves the best IR-text retrieval and strongest open-vocabulary segmentation among compared CLIP-like methods on the reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Raw radar spectra are widely viewed as too cluttered and noisy for direct representation learning, motivating handcrafted reductions, sparse point clouds, or compact Doppler descriptors in radar perception. We challenge this assumption and argue that the main limitation lies not in the raw representation itself, but in the absence of a learning objective that separates structured signal from noise. Handcrafted reductions partially address this problem but impose rigid assumptions about what constitutes signal, discarding weak yet informative structure while retaining artifacts that fit the reduction model. Once removed, such information cannot be recovered by supervised learning. We propose an alternative: structure is the component of a radar spectrum that remains reconstructable under localized corruption, while noise is the component that does not. This perspective motivates self-supervised masked modeling for dense radar spectra without predefined signal-noise separation. We instantiate it with Leakage-aware Spectral MAE, a masked autoencoder for raw radar cubes using a corruption strategy inspired by cross-bin energy spreading caused by spectral leakage. We also demonstrate the importance of Doppler organization: treating Doppler as a primary spatial dimension in an x-y-D representation, with height encoded as features, substantially outperforms naive channel stacking and enables effective learning from dense 4D spectra. Without handcrafted reductions, our approach consistently outperforms state-of-the-art radar-based detectors and point-cloud-based self-supervised learning (SSL) counterparts. These results establish raw radar spectra as an effective representation for 3D perception when paired with an appropriate pretraining objective.
bullets: Handcrafted reductions and sparse representations may discard weak but informative structure and preserve reduction-specific artifacts.
The paper defines structure as spectrum content recoverable after localized corruption, distinguishing it from unreconstructable noise.
Leakage-aware Spectral MAE pretrains on raw radar cubes using masking and corruption inspired by spectral leakage.
Organizing Doppler as a primary x-y-D dimension, with height as features, improves learning over naive channel stacking.
The approach consistently outperforms radar detectors and point-cloud SSL counterparts without handcrafted reductions.

papers.abstract: World models enable agents to plan and learn from imagined experience, but in an unfamiliar environment they must learn its mechanics from limited interaction. A mechanic is a rule for how an action or an interaction changes part of the environment. Each occurrence of a mechanic that the model observes is one exposure. We ask how many exposures a world model needs to predict the effects of a new environment's mechanics. We address this question on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark of interactive games defined by their programs. We introduce MechEval, which labels 69 recurring mechanics across 20 games from these programs. It scores each prediction on the cells the mechanic changes at each exposure. As a test bed, we build WARC (World model for ARC-AGI-3), a 35M-parameter vision transformer that is pretrained on other games and updates all of its parameters after each transition. On held-out games, WARC learns to predict four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy on the cells they change and keeps that accuracy to the end of the recordings. Half of them reach that accuracy within about 80 exposures, in a single play of the game, and without updates only one in seven does at all. In closed-loop play on the public games, WARC-Agent, which pairs WARC with a fixed graph explorer, triples the explorer's official efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, mostly through test-time training. On the hidden games of the Kaggle leaderboard, our entry scores 0.20.
bullets: Studies how many observations are needed to predict mechanics—rules governing how actions alter an environment—in unfamiliar games.
Introduces MechEval, covering 69 recurring mechanics across 20 ARC-AGI-3 games and scoring predictions on changed cells.
Builds WARC, a 35M-parameter vision transformer that updates all parameters after each observed transition.
On held-out games, WARC predicts four in five mechanics with at least 80% accuracy; about half reach that level within roughly 80 exposures.
Pairing WARC with a fixed graph explorer triples the public-game efficiency score from 0.15 to 0.46, while the hidden-game leaderboard score is 0.20.

papers.abstract: Recurrent latent reasoning in large lanugage models (LLMs) scales test-time computation by increasing recurrent depth, naturally framing inference as a problem of deciding when to stop. We identify a previously overlooked limitation of this single-depth view through systematic preliminary analysis: deeper recurrence can lose correct solutions found at shallower depths, while depth-specific success sets remain broadly non-nested even after controlling for marginal accuracy. This suggests that depth determines not only computation cost, but also access to distinct candidate solutions. Motivated by this finding, we propose Depth Portfolio Allocation (DPA), which reformulates recurrent test-time scaling as budgeted allocation across depth-specific candidate sources. DPA supports both fixed portfolios and feedback-guided sequential allocation under a shared inference budget. Experiments on GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, and MBPP show that mixed-depth portfolios expand oracle coverage under matched candidate counts and nominal costs, while feedback-guided allocation generally matches or improves uniform allocation and can reduce computation in high-budget settings. Code and data are avaible at : https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LLM-latent-B7BC/.

papers.abstract: Speech comprehension in the human brain is an incremental process that begins with acoustic processing and advances to linguistic processing. While recent studies have revealed that the hierarchy of deep neural networks (DNNs) correlates with the ascending auditory pathway, the exact nature of this DNN-brain alignment remains underexplored. In this study, we investigate how DNN representations align with the brain's acoustic-to-linguistic processing. Specifically, we employed neural encoding models to simulate neural responses to acoustic (i.e., speech and noise envelope) and linguistic features (i.e., word onset and surprisal). By applying representational similarity analysis (RSA), we quantified the similarity between these neural responses and the DNN embeddings generated by a pre-trained automatic speech recognition (ASR) model, both before and after fine-tuning on audiovisual noisy data. Our results demonstrate significant DNN-brain alignment: embeddings from shallow layers exhibit higher similarity to neural responses associated with acoustic features, while those from deeper layers align more closely with neural responses related to linguistic features. Importantly, the fine-tuning process enhances this alignment by improving noise processing in shallower layers and refining linguistic representations in deeper layers. These results suggest that fine-tuned DNN models can naturally develop human-like processing patterns in noisy environments, highlighting a functional alignment between the human brain and DNNs in speech representation.
bullets: The study examines how DNN representations align with the brain’s acoustic-to-linguistic speech-processing hierarchy under audiovisual noise.
Neural encoding models represent acoustic features (speech/noise envelopes) and linguistic features (word onset and surprisal).
Representational similarity analysis compares these neural responses with embeddings from a pre-trained ASR model before and after fine-tuning.
Shallow DNN layers align more with acoustic neural responses, while deeper layers align more with linguistic responses.
Fine-tuning improves noise processing in shallow layers and linguistic representations in deeper layers.ﬁ

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of analysis framework for computing representational similarity between DNNs embeddings and neural responses. For transformer-based DNNs (top panel), the model is fine-tuned on speech data with congruent audiovisual noise, starting from a pre-trained initialization. Then, embedding vectors of stimulus input are extracted from 12 transformer hidden layers, and utilized to calculate representational dissimilarity matrixs (RDMs). For neural encoding model (bottom panel), the EEG data in each EEG channel is predicted based on a linear combination of time-shifted stimulus features (speech envelope, noise envelope, word onset, and word surprisal). The encoder weights (temporal response functions) are estimated by maximizing the correlation between the actual neural responses and simulated neural responses. The simulated neural responses to stimulus features are utilized to calculate RDMs. Representational similarity is index through Spearman correlation between the RDMs of model embeddings and simulated neural responses.

papers.abstract: LLM-driven time series forecasting has become increasingly promising by leveraging contextual features to generate future values directly or refine forecast priors. However, incorporating contextual features alone does not ensure that models can identify which features matter for forecasting and understand what they suggest about future dynamics. We argue that the fundamental challenge is how to extract predictive evidence from contextual features and when and how to leverage it to guide forecasting decisions. In this paper, we propose CastReasoner, an evidence-grounded reasoning model for context-aware time series forecasting. Specifically, CastReasoner uses a structured chain of thought (CoT) to extract predictive evidence from contextual features, infer the future dynamics suggested by this evidence, and assess these dynamics against the forecast prior to guide adaptive forecasting decisions. To enable this capability, we design a reasoning-centric two-stage post-training framework including supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). First, we synthesize reasoning trajectories through controllable multi-teacher guidance and select high-quality ones using a novel student-aware difficulty metric. Second, we design fine-grained multi-objective rewards to further improve reasoning and forecasting. To address heterogeneous learning needs across domains in both stages, we introduce a convergence-guided data balancing strategy. Through this two-stage training, CastReasoner improves both reasoning quality and predictive accuracy. Extensive experiments across multi-domain forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that CastReasoner achieves superior forecasting performance.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of determining which contextual features matter and how they indicate future dynamics.
Uses structured chain-of-thought to extract evidence, infer dynamics, and compare them with a forecast prior.
Trains the model with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning using multi-objective rewards.
Employs multi-teacher trajectory synthesis, student-aware difficulty selection, and convergence-guided data balancing.
Experiments across multi-domain benchmarks show improved reasoning quality and predictive accuracy, with superior forecasting performance.

papers.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets provide a natural testbed for autonomous AI agents because they are digital-native, high-frequency, and machine-speed environments, yet existing methods often struggle with non-stationary market regimes, opaque decisions, and fixed aggregation rules. In this paper, we propose Agent4Crypto, a dual-reflective and market-feedback-aligned multi-agent system. The framework coordinates specialized agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading, synthesizing heterogeneous signals from prices, indicators, news, and charts in an interpretable decision pipeline. Our central design is a trader-centric decision mechanism: three style-specific trader agents, Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative, generate candidate actions and natural-language rationales from the same market context, while their influence is learned rather than manually fixed. A PPO-based gating policy dynamically allocates trader weights through a dual-reflective feedback process. One reflection stream evaluates post-trade decision quality from realized portfolio outcomes and distills reusable lessons into a Financial ReasoningBank for retrieval in subsequent trader prompts, while the other estimates trader-level counterfactual contribution, indicating which style has recently aligned better with market movements. The PPO state combines Counterfactual Contribution Memory with market features, previous trader weights, and current trader actions, so trader influence adapts across bull, sideways, and bear regimes. Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP show that Agent4Crypto improves total return and Sharpe ratio over traditional strategies, machine learning and reinforcement learning baselines, and existing LLM-based trading systems, demonstrating the value of interpretable trader competition and market-feedback-driven adaptation in volatile cryptocurrency markets.
bullets: Targets non-stationary crypto markets, opaque decisions, and fixed signal-aggregation rules.
Coordinates agents for data collection, analysis, risk assessment, reflection, and trading across prices, indicators, news, and charts.
Uses Aggressive, Neutral, and Conservative trader agents whose influence is learned by a PPO-based gating policy.
Combines post-trade reflection via a Financial ReasoningBank with counterfactual trader-contribution estimates to adapt across market regimes.
Experiments on BTC, ETH, and XRP report higher total return and Sharpe ratio than traditional, ML, RL, and existing LLM-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Foundation models increasingly combine geometry, semantics, and spatial context for three-dimensional scene understanding, but their suitability for forensic crime scene reconstruction remains unclear. This study presents a structured forensic evaluation framework for egocentric foundation models and demonstrates it using the Egocentric Foundation Model for 3D (EFM3D). Four simulated indoor crime scenes were recorded with Meta Project Aria Gen~1 at Robert Gordon University's East Lodge House forensic training facility. The framework evaluates room-scale reconstruction, semantic scene understanding, computational performance, and forensic suitability. Across the four scenes, EFM3D generated meshes averaging $12{,}668\pm2{,}430$ vertices and $24{,}838\pm4{,}903$ faces, with 39,529 recorded semantic predictions spanning 21--24 categories at a mean confidence of 0.40. Because reference meshes and expert-labelled 3D ground truth were unavailable, these statistics are treated as descriptive outputs rather than measures of geometric or detection accuracy. Final inference runs processed $1{,}388\pm203$ snippets per scene at $0.69\pm0.01$ samples/s and required $50.77\pm6.12$ minutes per recording. A seven-criterion capability profile indicated stronger support for room geometry, furniture localisation, scene context, and spatial relationships than for fine-scale forensic evidence. The results position EFM3D as a complementary tool for contextual documentation and scene review rather than a replacement for high-fidelity forensic capture. The framework provides a reproducible basis for evaluating future egocentric foundation models in specialised forensic settings.
bullets: Addresses the unclear suitability of egocentric foundation models for crime scene reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) methods update models online using a stream of unlabeled data to overcome distribution shifts encountered at test time. However, CTTA is often unstable, as it can reinforce biases in early predictions and increasingly predict only a few classes, resulting in drift or even collapse. In this paper, we identify narrowing pseudo-label class usage as an indicator of CTTA instability and quantify this behavior. Most existing methods have attempted to address this issue by either selecting reliable adaptation samples or re-weighting the loss to encourage diverse pseudo-labels, but they do not explicitly enforce a class marginal over a temporal window. Instead, we propose Sinkhorn Class-Marginal Regularization (SCALAR), a simple plug-and-play module that controls the pseudo-label distribution over a short temporal window. SCALAR works by maintaining recent predictions in a buffer, balancing their class distribution via the Sinkhorn algorithm to match a specified target distribution, and using the balanced soft targets for adaptation. Without changing the model architecture, SCALAR maintains the per-step runtime and increases the peak allocated GPU memory by only 10 MB on ImageNet-C. Our method is particularly effective on skewed, non-stationary data with severe distribution shifts, where SCALAR significantly alleviates drift and collapse when combined with existing stabilization methods based on entropy or diversity.
bullets: CTTA can become unstable when early prediction biases narrow pseudo-label usage and cause class collapse.
SCALAR stores recent predictions and uses Sinkhorn balancing to match their class marginals to a specified target distribution.
The plug-and-play module uses balanced soft targets without changing model architecture.
It is especially effective on skewed, non-stationary data and complements entropy- or diversity-based stabilization methods.
On ImageNet-C, it adds only 10 MB of peak GPU memory while maintaining per-step runtime.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the SCALAR framework. White blocks denote the baseline teacher–student CTTA pipeline; green blocks denote the added SCALAR module. Given an input view xu for the teacher branch and an augmented view xv for the student branch, the teacher produces logits zu and probabilities qu = softmax(zu). Recent teacher logits are stored in a FIFO window and converted to probabilities P , which are balanced toward a target prior π via Sinkhorn to produce balanced targets q̃u. The student produces logits sv and probabilities pv, and is optimized using a mixture of the baseline consistency loss and the SCALAR loss based on q̃u. Gradients are stopped through teacher-derived targets, marked by sg, and teacher parameters are updated via EMA. Here Lcons ≡ Lconsistency and Lbal = CE(sg[q̃u], pv).

Figure 2: Temporal contraction across adaptation regimes. Here, Ceff denotes the effective number of classes in the teacher pseudo-label distribution. Left: Balanced stream (no skew) exhibits gradual contraction and late-stage drift. Middle: Fixed skew with rotating dominant classes (medium adaptation) results in stronger drift. Right: Dynamic skew with fast adaptation induces rapid contraction leading to collapse.
