papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.
bullets: The study compares REAP expert pruning with REAM expert merging across five web-hosting production tasks and two 30B-parameter MoE models.
At 25% expert removal, REAP preserves 93.6% of Qwen3-30B’s generative quality, versus 62.5% for REAM.
Across 20 matched comparisons, REAP performs significantly better in 16, while REAM does so in 2.
Most quality loss in email generation comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts, and runaway generation—not loss of content.
Cross-perplexity, logit divergence, and repetition-loop rates track production quality; n-gram diversity does not.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates expert compression methods for MoE LLMs, directly relevant to LLM efficiency and memory optimization.
papers.title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
papers.tldr: On multilingual production tasks, one-shot expert pruning substantially outperforms expert merging for compressing MoE LLMs, mainly by preserving required output formats and behavior.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation lets a language agent act as its own Teacher by conditioning on privileged context such as skills written from its own trajectories. Its guidance, however, is weighted by how much this context shifts token likelihoods rather than by whether it improves behavior, so errors in self-written skills return through later updates. We propose environment-calibrated on-policy self-distillation, which uses environmental outcomes to decide how much to trust the Teacher's current guidance and which self-written skills to reinforce. Command-level advantages, estimated by comparing commands executed at similar observations, scale each Teacher preference and reward reflections and skills whose induced preferences favor higher-advantage commands. Without skills at inference, 3B and 7B agents reach 90.5% and 93.3% macro success on seen ALFWorld tasks and 75.5% and 80.5% success on WebShop. On unseen ALFWorld tasks, they outperform GRPO under the same protocol by 11.0 and 7.6 percentage points, respectively. In an ablation study, supervising only executable commands rather than the Actor's full response raises 3B WebShop success from 52.3% to 75.0%.
bullets: Self-written skills can propagate errors when guidance is weighted by token-likelihood shifts instead of behavioral improvement.
ECOS estimates command-level advantages by comparing commands taken in similar observations.
These advantages weight Teacher preferences and reinforce skills that favor higher-advantage commands.
Without inference-time skills, ECOS achieves strong performance on seen ALFWorld and WebShop tasks and outperforms GRPO on unseen ALFWorld tasks.
An ablation shows that supervising only executable commands substantially improves 3B WebShop success over supervising the full response.

papers.title: ECOS: Environment-Calibrated On-Policy Self-Distillation for Language Agents
papers.tldr: ECOS improves on-policy self-distillation for language agents by using environment outcomes to calibrate which self-generated guidance and skills to trust.

papers.abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
bullets: Targets multi-drone coordination in both cooperative and adversarial settings.
Combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints, and trajectory-tracking interfaces.
Compares cooperative game solvers for finding feasible conflict-resolving trajectories.
Evaluates how drone count, prediction horizon, and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance.
PyBullet simulations and a physical-drone flight validate the planner and tracking interfaces; timing tests identify practical real-time limits.

papers.abstract: A worked solution can make self-generated training targets shorter and cheaper, but accuracy on the practiced operation may hide how well a model can reuse newly learned rules. We study this choice in a 2B-parameter reasoning model learning two invented quantitative rules. The model generates targets from a rule sheet alone or from the sheet plus a program-written worked solution; targets are accepted for final-answer correctness, and the support is removed for fine-tuning and evaluation. Training questions request forward use in one segment; composition requires sequential reuse of the same rule across two segments. After six passes, using a program-checked numerical signature, sheet-only targets lead by 24.3 percentage points (95% item-bootstrap CI 14.6-34.0) on composition in a prospective test. On unseen argument values, observed forward accuracy is identical (87.5% each), but composition accuracy is 58.3% versus 23.6%, a 34.7-point gap (25.7-43.8). An independently sampled second target-bank pair repeats the direction (+14.6 points, 2.1-26.0). Ten passes on the shorter worked-solution targets, approximately matching the domain tokens of six sheet-only passes while changing other training quantities, narrow the gap to 16.3 points (6.3-26.7) in the first bank pair and 6.2 points (-6.3 to 18.8) in the second, where the pre-specified test does not hold. At six passes each, the worked-solution policy uses fewer capture tokens and less update time, yet the trained models use 2.6 times as many generated tokens per composition success under the numerical signature (2.1 times in the second bank pair). Choosing a capture context therefore requires testing how the new rules are reused, alongside the inference cost of those uses, rather than relying on forward accuracy alone.
bullets: The study compares rule-sheet-only targets with targets generated using rule sheets plus program-written worked solutions.
With six training passes, sheet-only targets improve composition accuracy by 24.3 percentage points in a prospective test.
On unseen arguments, forward accuracy is identical at 87.5%, while composition accuracy is 58.3% for sheet-only versus 23.6% with worked solutions.
More passes with shorter worked-solution targets narrow the gap, but do not consistently eliminate it across target-bank pairs.
Worked solutions reduce capture tokens and update time, yet require 2.1–2.6× more generated tokens per successful composition.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates training data generation and compositional rule reuse in a reasoning model, relevant to LLM training and continual learning.
papers.title: A Cost That Practice Accuracy Hides: Worked Solutions in Self-Generated Training Data and the Compositional Use of New Rules
papers.tldr: Worked solutions make self-generated training targets cheaper but can substantially impair a model’s ability to compose newly learned rules, despite equal forward accuracy.

papers.abstract: Systematic literature reviews (SRs) remain slow and labor-intensive, and most automation tools address single stages of the workflow. We present PARIS (PRISMA Agentic Research Intelligence System), an open-source framework in which a conductor agent running in Claude Code orchestrates 15 specialized large language model (LLM) agents, from scoping a research question to exporting a manuscript draft. Agents are specified declaratively, coordinate exclusively through persisted artifacts that the conductor validates before every transition, and delegate retrieval, bibliometric analysis and scoring to deterministic Python utilities. Three human checkpoints gate study inclusion, corpus adequacy and the synthesis outline. We also introduce QualityScore, a pre-synthesis index that aggregates normalized network, bibliometric, semantic and process sub-scores into a 0-100 grade. Two case studies illustrate both: AI chatbots and university students' learning (388 records, 100 included) and AI-assisted SR methods (131 records, 123 included, QualityScore 69.1 recomputed with a proxy network sub-score). They show end-to-end feasibility across domains and the diagnostic use of QualityScore: in the first run, corpus improvements chosen at the corpus-adequacy checkpoint raised the score from 74.6 to 81.9 and the number of pre-2023 studies from 1 to 19. Audits of both runs exposed failure modes: incomplete retrieval, counts that drifted between agents, unrecorded or delegated checkpoint decisions and a grade that depends on how citation data are handled. PARIS fully supports 8 of the 27 PRISMA 2020 items and partially supports 11. Output quality has so far been judged only by an internal reviewer agent; independent validation against human reviews is the next step.
bullets: Orchestrates 15 specialized LLM agents through persisted, validated artifacts and deterministic Python utilities.
Includes three human checkpoints for study inclusion, corpus adequacy, and synthesis-outline approval.
Introduces QualityScore, a 0–100 index combining network, bibliometric, semantic, and process measures.
Two case studies demonstrate end-to-end feasibility and show that corpus improvements can raise the quality score and increase coverage of older studies.
Audits found incomplete retrieval, inconsistent counts, undocumented checkpoint decisions, and sensitivity to citation-data handling; independent human validation remains pending.

papers.abstract: Transformers are built with continuous symmetries in the attention mechanism. We derive $ρ$, a scalar invariant that measures each head's capacity to couple to rotary positional encodings. This framework allows us to analyze heads without forward passes, opening a new research direction into data-independent analysis of modern LLMs. Empirically, we find that $ρ$ predicts induction heads, the most-studied circuit type in mechanistic interpretability, with Spearman correlation between $-0.55$ and $-0.74$ across four bias-free RoPE models spanning $135$M to $7$B parameters. As a preliminary proof of concept, we use $ρ$ to apply YaRN to only the top-50% positional heads, which degrades perplexity less than uniform application. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/rho-invariant.
bullets: ρ measures each attention head’s capacity to couple with rotary positional encodings.
Across four bias-free RoPE models (135M–7B parameters), ρ predicts induction heads with Spearman correlations from −0.55 to −0.74.
Applying YaRN only to the top 50% of positional heads causes less perplexity degradation than applying it uniformly.
The study focuses on bias-free RoPE models and presents targeted YaRN application as a preliminary proof of concept.

papers.title: A Geometric Invariant of Attention Predicts Head Specialization from Weights Alone
papers.tldr: A weight-only geometric invariant, ρ, predicts induction-head specialization and helps target positional adaptations without forward passes.

papers.abstract: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.
bullets: Targets fleet management with minimized completion time and priority-dependent tardiness.
Combines current-aware grid path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based RL.
Uses a Feasible Transition Graph to encode temporally feasible rendezvous events and transitions.
Reduces the average objective by 10.5% versus greedy, 3.5% versus MLP-RL, and 1.5% versus 2-step lookahead greedy.
Requires about 1/35 the computation time of 2-step lookahead greedy and retains advantages under unseen priority tiers, especially for larger fleets.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation has advanced rapidly in mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions. However, reliable manipulation in open-world environments requires robust spatial understanding: the ability to identify targets in complex layouts (spatial reasoning) and adapt to scenes that continuously evolve through interaction (spatial memory). Yet existing embodied benchmarks fall short in evaluating spatial understanding: they often introduce strong visual cues that bypass spatial reasoning, and focus on static scenes that offer little insight into an agent's capacity for spatial memory. To address this gap, we introduce GeoMind, a systematic benchmark for structured spatial understanding through tabletop manipulation. GeoMind comprises 54 evaluated task variants organized around spatial reasoning and spatial memory. It also incorporates a scalable pipeline that automates the generation and annotation of task instances with verified targets and executable interactions. Extensive evaluations across diverse embodied agents reveal their consistent weaknesses in spatial understanding. Our findings highlight that these agents struggle to track identities after spatial changes and convert relational or geometric constraints into executable actions. We release the GeoMind benchmark at https://github.com/Notfound-JH/GEOMIND-benchmark.git.
bullets: Targets gaps in existing benchmarks, including shortcut visual cues and predominantly static scenes.
Covers 54 task variants spanning spatial reasoning and spatial memory.
Uses an automated pipeline to generate and annotate tasks with verified targets and executable interactions.
Evaluations show consistent weaknesses in tracking object identities after spatial changes and translating relational or geometric constraints into actions.
The benchmark is publicly released on GitHub.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for spatial reasoning and spatial memory in robotic manipulation, directly relevant to embodied manipulation, embodied memory, and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: GeoMind: A Benchmark for Spatial Understanding in Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: GeoMind benchmarks whether robotic agents can reason about and remember spatial relationships during evolving tabletop manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation propagates derivatives through a physics simulator, turning animation, system identification, control, and computational design into gradient-based optimization. Engines differ in the physics they model and, less visibly, in which mathematical object they differentiate. We separate two questions the literature conflates. The referent is which object the returned derivative belongs to: the finite computation that executed, the converged equation it approximates, or the continuous dynamics. The realization describes the organization of the backward pass: automatically generated differentiation, an equation-level adjoint solve, or a custom adjoint. The referent defines the target against which exactness is assessed; the implementation determines how accurately that target is approximated. Cost depends on the realization together with how the states needed by the backward pass are retained or recovered. Crossing the axes places every method and engine we classify in a cell, separates claims the literature merges, and shows that the apparent trade-off between exactness and memory follows from how methods have been built rather than from a constraint. A second, orthogonal taxonomy covers contact, where the map is non-smooth. We then ask whether a correct gradient helps. Four mechanisms by which useful gradients are lost are cataloged and measured on one testbed, where the advantage of the exact derivative over the equation-level adjoint depends on where the fitting target comes from as much as on the solver budget, and we review the evidence that zeroth-order methods can outperform simulator gradients in the regimes where those mechanisms act. The model classes, systems techniques and applications are surveyed through this lens, and we close with a reporting checklist, a released diagnostic that computes it, and a research agenda.
bullets: Separates the gradient’s referent—executed computation, converged equations, or continuous dynamics—from the backward-pass realization.
Classifies methods and engines by automatic differentiation, equation-level adjoints, or custom adjoints, including state-storage and recovery costs.
Provides a separate taxonomy for non-smooth contact dynamics.
Identifies and measures four mechanisms that can degrade useful gradients, finding that exact derivatives do not always improve fitting.
Reviews cases where zeroth-order optimization can outperform simulator gradients and proposes a reporting checklist, diagnostic tool, and research agenda.

figures.caption: Figure 3: The two model families where the choice of referent bites hardest, and why. Left, deformables at the scale the field now works at: every one of these bodies is soft, they are in sustained mutual contact, and the solver is truncated to a fixed iteration budget, which is the regime where the converged equation and the executed computation stop agreeing (Section 6.2). Right, the same smoke plume under four schemes. The differences are large and come from the numerics rather than from the physics being modeled, which is the sense in which a fluid solver’s structure decides what its adjoint can be (Section 6.4). Images reproduced, cropped but otherwise unaltered, from [CLYY24, LHB∗25].

Figure 5: Mechanism 1 measured. A mass-spring chain is stepped with implicit Euler and solved by K Gauss–Seidel sweeps of per-vertex Newton updates, a one-dimensional instance of vertex block descent [CLYY24]; the parameter is the vector of per-spring stiffnesses. We compare the exact derivative of the K sweeps that actually executed, referent A1, against the equation-level adjoint, referent A2, evaluated as an implementation evaluates it: at the iterate the K sweeps reached, as if the residual there had vanished. (a) how far the truncated solve is from convergence. (b) the norm of the difference between the two gradients, relative to the gradient of the same solve run to convergence; above the dashed line the discrepancy is larger than the quantity being estimated. (c) the cosine of the angle between them, which indicates whether the negative returned vector is a local descent direction for the executed objective. Actual progress also depends on step size, curvature, and the optimizer. The shaded band marks the one to ten sweeps a real-time deformable solver actually runs. Within that band the two derivatives agree well for compliant material from two sweeps on, but for the stiffest material (k = 2×105) the equation-level adjoint is nearly orthogonal to the true derivative of the executed computation, and agreement is recovered only after hundreds of sweeps; at k = 2×104 a few dozen suffice. The forward sensitivity was differentiated by hand through the executed arithmetic and checked against central differences of the same pipeline to a relative error below 4×10−6.

Figure 4: The report’s running example, one implicit step followed from what is computed to what it costs. Two mass-spring chains stepped with implicit Euler and solved by K Gauss–Seidel sweeps; panels (a) to (c) take one step at k = 2×105, panel (d) fits random stiffness fields near 6×103 on a shorter, pinned chain over twelve steps. (a) what ran: the residual falls with the budget but does not vanish, so the iterate the sweeps reached (A1) and the root they approach (A2) are two different objects to differentiate. (b) the relative norm of the vector difference between the two gradients is of order one across the plotted range. (c) they disagree in direction too, the cosine sitting between 0.1 and 0.55, so the two are nearly orthogonal. (d) and, for a target the same solver generated, it makes almost no difference to the optimization: from two sweeps onward no stable advantage is separable, median and interquartile range over forty seeds. Panels (b) and (c) are large at the stiff setting; (d) shows no separation between A1 and A2 for its fitting problem from two sweeps on. For this reason the report separates which derivative a method returns from whether it helps.

Table 4: Representative methods grouped by physical model. Ref.: A1 executed computation, A2 converged equation, A3 continuous dynamics (Section 4.1). Real.: B1 framework-generated reverse; B2 equation-level adjoint, including a discretized continuous adjoint; B3 custom operator-level adjoint composition (Section 4.2). For hybrid engines these labels identify the main documented backward construction; custom solves and recorded remainders are noted and do not imply exactness of the full engine. A1* treats an internal linear solve as exact; finite primal and adjoint tolerances still cause error. A2a marks an additional approximation in the derivative system. surr. marks a returned direction that need not differentiate the forward objective; it can still have a specified surrogate target. State describes recovery: tape, recorded reverse-pass intermediates; trajectory, states and required auxiliary data per step; checkpoint, selected states with recomputation; recompute, per-step intermediates regenerated from saved states; final state, converged state of each step plus required auxiliary data, not just the rollout endpoint; replay, sweeps rerun from saved inputs; reverse, state recovered by reversing the map. These choices do not specify a unique memory cost. none and not stated indicate no reverse-state store or an unreported strategy. Contact follows Table 3 where applicable. Alternatives are noted in the final column. The realization is n/a when there is no backward pass, including forward sensitivities; shooting alone does not determine the realization. Methods that only consume a simulator appear in Sections 7 and 9.

Figure 2: What a contact solver is asked to resolve, and why contact modes matter. Left, two elastic beams twisted around one another, 97 thousand vertices between them, in sustained frictional contact along the whole interface while they buckle. The active pairs change along the trajectory. Local branch derivatives can remain valid despite these temporal changes, but may poorly predict finite parameter updates that change the contact sequence. Right, an elastic cube released on an incline at four friction coefficients. Whether it sticks or slides is decided by the friction cone. At a regular stick–slip transition, the branch derivatives can differ (Section 5.1). Images reproduced, cropped but otherwise unaltered, from [CLYY24] under the authors’ CC BY 4.0 license.

Figure 8: Three uses of a simulator gradient, as their authors report them. Left, material parameters recovered from observed cloth motion by optimizing through the simulator, the inverse problem of Section 9.1. Middle, a trajectory optimized through frictional contact; the loss curve beneath compares the analytic gradient against two zeroth-order optimizers on the same task, which is the comparison item 7 of our checklist asks every paper to report. Right, smoke steered from one silhouette through fixed obstacles into another, by optimizing the forces with an adjoint taken on the flow map. Keyframe control of fluids is an early application of differentiable simulation. The illustrated result uses the recent continuous-adjoint flow-map method [LHB∗25], corresponding to referent A3 in Section 4.1. None of the three results is ours. Images reproduced, cropped or letterboxed but otherwise unaltered, from [LDW∗23, LHB∗25].

Figure 6: Mechanism 2 measured, on the mass-spring chain of Figure 5 stepped with implicit Euler and eight Gauss–Seidel sweeps. Per-spring stiffnesses are the parameters and the sensitivity is propagated forward through the executed arithmetic, so the experiment tests sensitivity to the forward states and arithmetic precision without introducing a reverse-mode implementation. (a), the accumulated sensitivity ∥dxT /dk∥ varies by a factor of fifteen over three hundred steps: it does not explode, and the loss-gradient norm, not shown, rises by less than three orders of magnitude while the loss rises by eight and a half, so neither would alarm a monitor. (b), the cosine between derivatives obtained from the same sensitivity recurrence in double and in single precision, with two controls that separate the two places rounding can enter. With state and sensitivity both in single, agreement holds to four figures out to twenty steps and three at forty, and then falls: 0.79 at eighty, 0.64 at a hundred and sixty, 0.48 at three hundred and twenty (the last two vary with hardware; see text). With the trajectory in double and only the sensitivity recurrence in single, the cosine stays above 0.999 throughout. With the trajectory in single and the sensitivity in double, the fall is reproduced to within 0.003 in cosine. The disagreement therefore comes from the single-precision trajectory, which differs from the double one by a relative 10−4 at eighty steps while the loss differs by about two parts in ten thousand (at most 2.2×10−4): the gradient is far more sensitive to the trajectory than the objective is. The final contraction of the sensitivity with the loss gradient is done in double in every variant, so that it does not enter the comparison.

Figure 7: Contact-gradient support and sensitivity amplification in the massspring contact testbed (k = 2×104, eight sweeps, no gravity, wall stiffness 2×105), with launch velocity as the single parameter and accumulated contact energy as the objective. Panel (a) uses a 120-step rollout; panel (b) varies the horizon. (a) the derivative against launch velocity: below the velocity at which a vertex reaches the wall within the horizon (shaded), no contact occurs and the derivative is zero; gradients can be nonzero in the active-contact region. This is a derivative-support diagnostic, not evidence that minimizing contact energy fails in the zero-contact region. (b) spread (standard deviation) of the same derivative over an ensemble of launches perturbed by 10−6. Between two walls, repeated bounces are associated with roughly seventy-fold growth in spread over the tested horizons. With one wall, the chain bounces once and the spread remains approximately flat. These observations do not establish chaos or show that repeated contact is necessary for sensitivity amplification.

Table 2: The two axes crossed. Rows identify derivative targets; columns are operational categories for the organization of the backward pass. Exactness must be assessed against the row’s target and the implementation’s numerical qualifications. Construction may be automatic, manual, or hybrid within these categories. Memory depends on retained states, recomputation, checkpointing, and solver workspace, not on the column alone. Discrete custom adjoints can exploit forward operator or block structure without necessarily eliminating trajectory storage. A3 includes both equation-level solves and custom continuousadjoint operators. Empty entries reflect the labeling convention and the examples selected, not impossibility claims. Entries are representative, not exhaustive.

Table 7: Differentiable simulation systems viewed as software, complementing Tables 4 and 5. Backward construction describes how derivative computations are implemented. Backward memory lists principal retained information, not a complete allocation bound: forward states, contact data, and linear-solver data may also be required or recomputed. The absence of an inner-iteration tape does not imply constant rollout memory. Backend and AD coverage depend on the solver and version. Entries summarize the cited descriptions and supported derivative paths.
Table 5: Table 4 continued: deformables, cloth and fluids. Columns are as in Table 4.

Table 3: Treatments of contact discontinuity. This axis is orthogonal to both axes of Table 2: an engine can combine a cell there with one or more treatments here. “Obstacle addressed” refers to the enumeration in Section 5.1.
Table 1: Notation used throughout this report.

Table 8: Task benchmarks and a cross-engine survey for differentiable simulation. The task evaluations combine gradient behavior with the optimizer, policy class, and physical model; the Newbury et al. row summarizes engine features. Together they provide useful comparisons, but not a shared cross-engine protocol for reference-Jacobian accuracy at matched solver settings.

Table 9: The reporting checklist computed by the released diagnostic for the chain under both referents. Item (i) is split into an implementation part and a convergence part. The A1 zero in (i-b) denotes its finite-program target, not equality with the converged-equation derivative. Item (iii) uses two query budgets with wall-clock beside them. (v) uses this four-sweep configuration, distinct from Figure 6, and is reported for A1 only because the A2 engine provides no single-precision path; (vi) is the diagnostic’s generic flat fraction, which is zero on this chain; the chain has no contact, so this says nothing about contact-induced flatness. Absence of contact does not rule out other flat directions.

Table 6: What the equation-level referent costs an optimizer, and how much that depends on where the target came from. Loss remaining after 120 gradientdescent steps, as a fraction of the initial loss, median over 40 random instances of the fitting problem (a 16-vertex chain over twelve steps), with the fraction of instances on which A2 finished lower; lower is better. Three constructions of the target, everything else identical: the endpoint the same solver at the same K produces from the true stiffness field, so that the fit can reach it exactly; the endpoint a solve run to convergence (2000 sweeps) produces, fitted with K sweeps; and the rest configuration, which no stiffness field reaches under gravity. Within-row comparisons isolate the choice of gradient for each target construction. Across-budget comparisons for same-K targets also change the target-generating solver; comparisons for converged or external targets isolate the budget only if instances and target data are held fixed.

papers.selection_reason: Taxonomy and analysis of differentiable physics simulation, a core tool for gradient-based robot learning, control, and manipulation.
papers.title: Same Physics, Different Gradients: A State-of-the-Art Report on Differentiable Physics Simulation
papers.tldr: This report disentangles what differentiable physics methods differentiate from how they compute gradients, showing that gradient usefulness depends on both implementation and problem-specific failure modes.

papers.abstract: Egocentric auto-labeling requires depth, camera pose, object, and human-pose estimates to agree across independently developed models. Differences in units, coordinate conventions, and scale can make individually plausible predictions geometrically inconsistent. We present \textbf{EgoLabel}, a zero-shot pipeline that combines off-the-shelf models without target-domain labeled training and provides explicit cross-modal registration and consistency diagnostics. The pipeline integrates MonST3R for geometry, LocateAnything with GMC-BoT-SORT and SAM~2 for objects, and V-HPOT for hands; FisheyeViT provides a separate whole-body compatibility demonstration. Our main hand evaluation uses H2O sensor depth. Across 20 sequences, per-hand depth anchoring reduces the mean of per-sequence median hand--depth residuals by $23\%$ relative to a single global scale, yielding a pooled median of $84.6\,\mathrm{mm}$ against a $20.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ ground-truth reference. Hand PA-MPJPE is $14.53\pm1.29\,\mathrm{mm}$, whereas absolute MPJPE is $119.1\pm31.3\,\mathrm{mm}$, revealing a substantial gap between aligned and metric accuracy. On three RGB-only sequences, camera ATE is $1.40\pm0.29\,\mathrm{cm}$ after $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ alignment. We also identify a sliding-window implementation issue that allows sensor-initialized depth to change during optimization. Because hand anchoring and its residual share the same depth map, the residual measures internal consistency rather than independent accuracy. These results characterize both the utility and the current limits of the registration pipeline.
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies from differing units, coordinate conventions, and scales across independently developed models.
Combines MonST3R, LocateAnything, GMC-BoT-SORT, SAM 2, and V-HPOT, with FisheyeViT used for whole-body compatibility.
Per-hand depth anchoring reduces median hand–depth residuals by 23% versus a single global scale; pooled residual is 84.6 mm against a 20.5 mm reference.
Hand pose reaches 14.53 ± 1.29 mm PA-MPJPE but 119.1 ± 31.3 mm absolute MPJPE, showing a large aligned-versus-metric accuracy gap.
The hand–depth residual is only an internal-consistency measure because anchoring and evaluation use the same depth map; a sliding-window optimization issue is also identified.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of EgoLabel. Off-the-shelf models produce geometry (MonST3R), object annotations (LocateAnything + GMC-BoT-SORT + SAM 2), and hand poses (V-HPOT). Unit conversion, coordinate alignment, and per-hand depth anchoring connect these streams for joint inspection. Hand–depth residuals, object-trajectory smoothness, and control experiments assess their consistency. FisheyeViT is demonstrated on separate fisheye recordings, and structured manipulation captioning is a downstream application. Metric-scale limitations are detailed in Section 3.4.

Figure 4: Final end-to-end output of EgoLabel on H2O h1/0, as rendered in the Rerun viewer at four stages of the manipulation: (a) lifting the box to examine it, (b) peeling the top flaps, (c) removing the flaps, and (d) pulling the box sides. Each panel is one screenshot of the integrated viewer and simultaneously shows the object stream (LocateAnything detections, GMC-BoT-SORT track IDs, and SAM 2 masks, drawn as colored boxes on the overlay video), the 3D hand prediction (left/right V-HPOT skeletons and the camera+wrist trajectory in 3D), and the ASID task caption (bottom panel: hand usage, manipulated object, and action). Object, hand, and camera annotations are produced by independent zero-shot models; the ASID caption (bottom panel) is a GT-assisted downstream consumer (Section 3.5).

Figure 3: Qualitative whole-body results from the FisheyeViT stream. Each panel pairs a head-mounted fisheye frame (left) with the reconstructed 3D skeleton in the shared metric frame (right); predicted skeletons are orange and, where available, ground-truth skeletons are red. (a) Prediction only; (b)–(d) prediction overlaid with ground truth. The skeleton is mapped into the shared frame by the camera-to-world transform (Section 3.2.4); this is a compatibility demonstration on separate recordings, not a joint H2O result.

Figure 5: Cross-modal consistency of the V-HPOT hand stream against the depth map on H2O h1/0. (a) Distribution of the per-joint hand–depth residual; the solid line is the median. (b) Median residual for a single global scale, our per-hand anchoring, and the reprojected ground-truth hands. The figure shows a representative sequence; across the 20 sequences the per-sequence median ranges from 64.2 to 119.7mm, and the pooled medians are in Table 6. The residual is a consistency check (does the fused skeleton lie on the reconstructed surface?), not an independent accuracy metric.

Figure 6: Camera trajectory on H2O k1/0 for the sensor-depth-injection ablation (the RGB-only trajectory, which we take as the main camera result, is summarized in Table 5), in the first-frame camera frame. (a) Top view: ground-truth (gray) and MonST3R trajectory after 7-DoF Sim(3) alignment (blue). (b) Per-frame ATE (blue) with the mean as a dashed line. The injected run recovers the trajectory shape well, with the residual global-scale error left by the injection acting only as an initialization rather than a constraint (recomputed with the released estimator: Sim(3) ATE 1.76 cm, fitted scale 0.45, strict SE(3) 3.12 cm).

Figure 8: Fused 3D scene on H2O (frame 225), in the first-frame camera frame. Gray: ground-truth camera trajectory; blue: predicted camera trajectory (Sim(3)-aligned); green: the V-HPOT hand skeleton after metric-scale anchoring; colored lines: 3D trajectories of the tracked objects lifted through the depth map and the camera pose (start points marked). The independently estimated hand, object, and camera streams are drawn in one coordinate system for inspection.

Figure 7: V-HPOT hand accuracy on H2O h1/0. (a) Summary bars: scale-invariant PA-MPJPE (14.13mm), scalealigned MPJPE (22.0mm), and absolute (metric) MPJPE (63.7mm) over 900 hand samples. (b) Per-frame PA-MPJPE over time (light) with a 15-frame smoothed curve and the sequence mean (dashed). The per-frame PA-MPJPE is broadly stable over the sequence. 20 sequences: 14.53±1.29 PA-MPJPE, 26.46±4.40 scale-aligned (mean±std).

Figure 2: Object tracking and segmentation on H2O h1/0 (frames 0, 225, 449). LocateAnything detects the prompted objects, GMC-BoT-SORT assigns identity-preserving track IDs (colored boxes), and SAM 2 produces per-instance masks overlaid on the frames. The identities are maintained across head motion and partial hand occlusion by the objects.

Table 4: Per-module accuracy measured with the pipeline on H2O with off-the-shelf models, reported as a component sanity check rather than a new benchmark claim. Camera ATE is averaged over three sequences (h1/0, k1/0, o1/0; 1,233 frames); hand metrics over 20 sequences (h1/0–h1/7, h2/0–h2/7, o1/0–o1/3; 12,032 frames, 21,876 hand samples). Hand metrics are means over hand samples within a sequence, then averaged across sequences; ± denotes sample standard deviation across sequences, not across samples. V-HPOT is run frozen (no test-time optimization); the source paper’s 71% figure is for its TTO variant and is not reproduced here.

Table 3: Coverage of the quantitative results in Section 4. Hand accuracy and hand–depth consistency are measured on 20 sequences; camera ATE on three; object-trajectory smoothness requires the full tracking run and is validated on h1/0. RGB-only variants are listed separately.

Table 1: Provenance of the geometry behind each reported quantity. “Sensor depth” is the dataset’s depth map converted to meters and resampled to 320×176 (nearest neighbor); it never passes through MonST3R. “Window-optimized” is the depth after the sliding-window alignment of Section 3.2.1.
Table 2: Annotation coverage and role of the datasets. ✓ = ground truth available; — = not available. “Quant.” indicates whether the dataset yields quantitative results in this work.

Table 5: Camera ATE (cm) on the three H2O ATE sequences, paired on the same sequences and frame sets and computed with the same evaluation script (scripts/eval_ate.py), using similarity or rigid alignment of camera translations. “Inj.” is the sensor-depth initialization (the released sensor-assisted mode) with the focal either optimized (free) or initialized from the dataset intrinsics (focal-init, not pinned); “RGB-only” uses MonST3R’s predicted depth and is the main camera result. Fitted Sim(3) scale in parentheses.

Table 6: Cross-modal consistency on H2O. Hand–depth residual: pooled median over 20 sequences (429,896 joints), with the per-sequence mean±std of the medians below it. Object-trajectory smoothness: median on h1/0. “Naive” applies no unit conversion; “Const-scale” applies one global scale; “Per-hand” is our anchoring (Eq. (11)); “GT” reprojects the dataset’s ground-truth hands onto the same depth map as a GT reference residual. Aggregation differs by row: the residual is a pooled median over all joint samples, with the distribution of per-sequence medians underneath, and the smoothness is a median over object-frame samples at H2O’s fixed 30 fps. Lower is better.

Table 7: Sensor-depth-free (RGB-only) hand–depth residual on the two sequences that have V-HPOT tracks. MonST3R’s predicted depth is defined only up to a scale, so the residual is normalized by the wrist depth (dimensionless); “per-hand” uses the per-frame box-median ratio and “const” a single per-sequence ratio. These values must not be compared with the millimeter residuals of Table 6.

papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot egocentric auto-labeling pipeline with cross-modal consistency, relevant to generating embodied training data from human egocentric video.
papers.title: EgoLabel: Zero-Shot Egocentric Auto-Labeling with Cross-Modal Consistency
papers.tldr: EgoLabel is a zero-shot pipeline that registers off-the-shelf egocentric geometry, object, and pose models, improving internal hand–depth consistency while exposing substantial metric-accuracy and evaluation limitations.

papers.abstract: General-purpose vision-language models struggle with crisis imagery due to its inherent noise, ambiguity, and high variability across disaster events - yet timely, accurate scene understanding is critical for humanitarian response. To address this, we introduce DisasterVLG, a large-scale multi-task dataset containing 1.24 million disaster images from 142 countries paired with 33 million structured annotations spanning dense captioning with localization, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded visual question answering (VQA) across diverse hazard types and scene contexts worldwide. Unlike prior disaster benchmarks that focus narrowly on classification, DisasterVLG unifies recognition, grounded reasoning, and uncertainty-aware interpretation. A distinguishing feature is its evidence-grounded annotation design: each VQA instance includes supporting evidence text that links visual observations to answers, alongside positive and negative question pairs, multiple answer formats, and difficulty labels. Visual grounding layer links caption phrases to image regions and relationship statements to subject-object boxes, with explicit labels for visual supports and clues. To support rigorous evaluation, we construct a human-verified test set of 38K images (1.15M annotations) spanning broad geographic regions and disaster types. Experiments with domain-adapted vision-language models demonstrate strong performance across disaster captioning, incident recognition, and grounded VQA, while also exposing the limitations of general-purpose models in crisis-specific reasoning. DisasterVLG establishes a scalable, reproducible benchmark for vision-language models that must reason reliably under real-world uncertainty. We will publicly release the dataset, trained models, and code.
bullets: Introduces 1.24M disaster images from 142 countries with 33M structured annotations.
Covers localized dense captioning, incident assessment, relational scene descriptions, and crisis-grounded VQA.
Links answers and descriptions to visual regions, supporting evidence, clues, negative pairs, answer formats, and difficulty labels.
Provides a human-verified test set spanning diverse geographic regions and disaster types.
Experiments show domain-adapted models perform strongly but reveal persistent limitations of general-purpose models in crisis reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. DisasterVLG data and annotation pipeline: A curated disaster image dataset is first collected. GPT-5 [42] then generates image-grounded captions and supporting evidence, followed by tailored VQA annotations conditioned on the caption, incident assessment, supporting evidence, relationships, and uncertainties. Finally, a human and Gemini 3.1 Pro [18] work together to create a verified test set.

Figure 6. Left: ROUGE-L across DisasterVLG model variants, showing the effect of model scaling on captioning performance. Right: ROUGE-L as a function of training-data scale for captioning and reasoning VQA, illustrating that both tasks benefit consistently from larger portions of DisasterVLG.
Figure 1. A DisasterVLG sample and its multi-layer annotations: caption, disaster type, evidence, spatial relationships, question-answer pairs, multiple-choice questions, and uncertainty statements.

Figure 5. Distribution of VQA categories in DisasterVLG. Counts are shown on a logarithmic scale. The most frequent categories focus on damage assessment, visual evidence recognition, and reasoning about uncertainty or absence, while lower-frequency categories cover more specialized reasoning dimensions such as text recognition, counting, temporal conditions, and resource needs.

Figure 7. Object true-positive rate by disaster type for the top 50 object terms. Darker cells indicate stronger grounding of the corresponding object term for that disaster category. The heatmap shows that some hazards, such as wildfire, flood, and storm/severe weather, are associated with broad sets of consistently detected object cues, whereas other categories rely on a narrower set of high-signal terms.

Figure 8. Scene true-positive rate by disaster type for the top 50 scene terms. Compared with object terms, scene terms capture broader environmental and situational context, including terrain, weather, and structural conditions. The results show that many disaster types in DisasterVLG are strongly grounded in global scene structure rather than in isolated objects alone.

Figure 3. Category distribution of DisasterVLG across the full set and test set. The full set follows the naturally imbalanced distribution of collected crisis imagery, with categories such as Urban / Structural Damage and Flooding appearing most frequently. In contrast, the test split is constructed to be more balanced across major disaster types, improving the reliability of evaluation across categories. For readability, low-frequency categories are grouped under Others. For better insight and comparison, the Unknown and Not-Crisis categories are removed from the full set distribution.

Figure 9. Comparison of object and scene grounding performance by disaster type. The left panel reports present F1, while the right panel reports state-agreement scores. Scene grounding is often slightly stronger for context-defined hazards, whereas object grounding remains important for disasters with more localized visual evidence. papers.abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining progress across successive goals while producing stable, natural whole-body motion in confined spaces.
Coordinates three asynchronous roles: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body control.
Uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and execution.
Introduces a physics-grounded data engine for collision-aware, route-faithful motion demonstrations paired with visual observations.

In simulation, LHNav improves success and smoothness while reducing collisions and falls; it reaches 75.56% long-horizon success using only single-goal training, and transfers to real-world zero-shot execution on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: External tool calls are a major running cost of an LLM agent, while its training objectives align almost exclusively with task completion. In a step-level diagnosis of Qwen3.5 trajectories at two model sizes on GAIA, a long-horizon tool-use benchmark, we find that most contain removable calls, at a similar rate at both sizes. Some methods add an efficiency reward to the objective to reduce the call count, but introduce problems of their own: the anchor they price calls against is computed from the policy's own rollouts (e.g., the group's shortest correct rollout) and so moves with the policy; training can drift toward a collapsed policy that issues no tool call at all, a degeneracy seen in published reports and in our 27B baseline; and a training run delivers a single operating point, so the user cannot trade efficiency against capability. We present CARE-PO (Controllable Anchored Relative Efficiency Policy Optimization) to mitigate these problems. The efficiency reward prices calls against a reference budget anchored to the task's own difficulty and fixed before training. Injecting a successful trajectory from the training data into each online GRPO rollout group and charging for evidence a trajectory never gathers ease the drift toward a collapsed call count. Shaping the cost curve by an effort tag in the prompt yields an efficiency and a capability operating point from a single training run. On GAIA, five of the six operating points across three model sizes improve on their base model in success rate and call count at once. On four held-out multi-hop benchmarks the result is size-dependent: at 27B and 4B success rate is held or raised at a lower call count, while at 9B both operating points trade success rate for fewer calls. The call count remains well above zero throughout training at all three sizes.
bullets: Tool-call costs are substantial, and many GAIA trajectories contain removable calls across model sizes.
Existing efficiency rewards can drift toward policies that make no tool calls and typically provide only one efficiency–capability setting.
CARE-PO anchors call costs to fixed task difficulty, injects successful trajectories, and penalizes missing evidence to prevent call-collapse.
Prompt effort tags produce multiple efficiency/capability operating points from one training run.
On GAIA, 5 of 6 operating points improve success rate and reduce calls; held-out results vary by model size, with 9B showing a capability–efficiency trade-off.

papers.abstract: AI agent harnesses play the critical role of providing LLMs with an interface to a computing environment. Recent studies show that AI agents' task-execution accuracy depends mostly on the LLM used, while harness-side variances such as system prompts or tools have minimal impact. Rather, such harness-side variances show a larger impact on the cost of agent executions, achieving cost reductions up to 2.6 times on the same model and task. To further explore these harness-side cost optimization opportunities, we analyze the cost accumulation patterns across various agent traces and identify system opportunities to reduce token use and LLM calls without modifying the model or affecting task accuracy. Based on this analysis, we design Agency, a harness interposition platform that provides a unified abstraction and allows easy and portable implementation of harness-side system optimizations on existing off-the-shelf harnesses such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex. Using Agency, we implement proof-of-concept optimization techniques based on our analysis and achieve cost reductions up to 35% across various real-world benchmarks on existing harnesses without compromising accuracy.
bullets: Agent harness choices have limited effect on accuracy but can substantially affect execution cost.
The study analyzes agent traces to identify opportunities to reduce token consumption and LLM calls.
Agency provides a portable interposition layer for implementing optimizations across existing harnesses.
Proof-of-concept optimizations reduce costs by up to 35% on real-world benchmarks without compromising accuracy.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents must continually acquire reusable knowledge from experience without relying on costly large language model (LLM) reasoning for every decision. However, existing experience-based approaches often struggle to transform accumulated observations and reasoning into compact knowledge that lightweight models can independently apply. This paper proposes SCALE, a small-model-first framework that integrates selective LLM reasoning, experience-driven concept abstraction, and knowledge internalization. A lightweight model handles routine predictions, while prediction errors and accumulated cross-episode evidence selectively trigger LLM reflection. The LLM analyzes relevant historical experiences, generates positive and negative counterfactual examples, and proposes reusable concept hypotheses. Independently validated concepts are progressively incorporated into hierarchical neural representations, enabling lightweight models to exploit increasingly abstract knowledge. Meanwhile, mastered experiences are excluded from active memory while their original records remain available in a complete archive. Experiments across ten random seeds show that historical recall improves held-out accuracy from 87.11% to 98.28%, hierarchical concept knowledge increases difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and abstract archiving reduces active experience records from 6,000 to 1,528.
bullets: Targets the costly reliance on LLM reasoning for every autonomous-agent decision.
Uses small-model-first prediction, triggering LLM reflection on errors and cross-episode evidence.
The LLM creates counterfactual examples and concept hypotheses from relevant historical experiences.
Validated concepts are internalized into hierarchical neural representations for lightweight-model use.
Across ten seeds, held-out accuracy rose from 87.11% to 98.28%, difficult-case accuracy from 55.33% to 66.47%, and active records fell from 6,000 to 1,528.

papers.abstract: A robot that works among people must judge what it cannot see: whether an object is still where it was last seen, and whether a pull on a door or drawer is worth its risk. Maps that track object change hold nothing about force, maps of physical properties answer a risk question at a fixed risk level, and vision-language-action models keep no explicit estimate of hidden physics. We propose Motion Belief Action (MBA), a decision layer on the scene map. From how often people move an object and how much force it needs, how much load it holds and whether it is blocked, MBA chooses under a force limit to look again, nudge, open, brace or decline, with its risk set by the task's costs. On real activity in 9 kitchens, it predicts whether an object is still in place better than FreMEn and Perpetua, and decides when to look again at lower cost than these and the persistence filter, because about a quarter of placements end in a pick-up within 30 s. On real pulls of doors and drawers in 17 locations, made by a person with a force-sensing gripper, the map's force estimates decide better than a part-type average. Setting the risk from the costs also beats a published risk rule at its fixed level. In simulation, with the force limit at the training parts' median force, MBA raises SmolVLA's and Octo's scores by declining pulls; most declined door pulls would fail, but on drawers more would have opened, and a part-type average gets about half of this gain. In both, a published risk rule set to the risk these costs imply is MBA's rule for a single pull and decides as well in the main settings. A link between opening and holding force, a probing nudge and an action prior for camera tracking do not help in the main settings, and over the real-pull sweep the nudge costs a little.
bullets: Addresses hidden object persistence and interaction risk in robots operating around people.
Uses motion frequency, required force, load, and blockage to choose among looking again, nudging, opening, bracing, or declining.
On real kitchen activity and door/drawer pulls, it improves persistence estimation and cost-sensitive decisions over several baselines, including part-type averages for force estimation.
In simulation, declining risky pulls improves SmolVLA and Octo scores, especially for doors; gains are smaller for drawers and partly captured by part-type averages.
Additional force-linking, probing, and camera-tracking priors do not help in the main settings; nudging adds slight cost in real-pull tests.

papers.abstract: Dexterous hands enable versatile manipulation, but policies trained in simulation often degrade on hardware owing to non-idealities, and the high-dimensional action space makes real-world adaptation costly. Piano playing, which requires precise and coordinated multifinger motion, offers a representative testbed. We propose GAP (Generalized Adaptation Prior for Dexterous Piano Playing), a sample-efficient adaptation framework that learns how to adapt, rather than how to act, during simulation pretraining and transfers this adaptation prior to hardware. Between repeated executions, GAP uses feedback to adjust the actions of the next one: a gradient guidance network learns from paired executions how adjusting actions affects playing performance, and its gradients guide these adjustments. In simulation, GAP yields approximately 2.4 times the F1 scores improvement of the existing fast-adaptation baseline for dexterous piano playing under the same interaction budget. The learned prior also generalizes to musical pieces held out from pretraining. On a physical dexterous hand, the same simulation-pretrained prior improves F1 scores by 3.6%-23% across three pieces of varying difficulty after approximately 7 min of adaptation each. These results suggest a practical route to reduce the real-world interaction needed to deploy dexterous hands.
bullets: Addresses simulation-to-hardware degradation and costly adaptation in high-dimensional multifinger control.
Uses paired executions and feedback to train a gradient guidance network that adjusts subsequent actions.
Improves simulated F1-score gains by approximately 2.4× over an existing fast-adaptation baseline under the same interaction budget.
Generalizes to musical pieces not seen during pretraining.
On a physical dexterous hand, improves F1 scores by 3.6%–23% across three pieces after approximately 7 minutes of adaptation per piece.

papers.abstract: During reinforcement learning, experience can be both internalized in LLM parameters and retained externally as reusable textual skills. Parameter updates alter the model's behavior and the interaction experience from which new skills are extracted. These skills, in turn, guide the model's subsequent interactions and parameter updates. As the model's capabilities evolve, previously beneficial skills may become redundant or detrimental. We present SkillDuet, a framework that coordinates parameter updates and skill evolution through model response feedback. Skills extracted from on-policy trajectories guide parameter updates through OPD at every step. A response-based score, Strength, ranks candidate skills by the magnitude of the shift they induce in the current model's responses, and the highest-scoring skills are periodically consolidated into a persistent global skill set (Global). The updated model and Global jointly guide subsequent interactions, generating experience for further parameter and skill updates. With Qwen3-4B, SkillDuet achieves success rates of 98.57% on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, exceeding the matched SEED-API baseline by 2.86 and 5.47 percentage points, respectively. Ablations show that response-based skill selection and Global consolidation improve task performance. Further experiments show that the benefits of retained skills depend on both their content and their compatibility with the model. SkillDuet provides a concrete mechanism for model-skill co-evolution and skill-level recursive self-improvement.
bullets: Addresses the challenge that skills can become redundant or harmful as the model changes during reinforcement learning.
Uses on-policy skills to guide parameter updates through OPD, while a response-based Strength score ranks candidate skills.
Periodically consolidates high-impact skills into a persistent Global skill set that guides future interactions and updates.
With Qwen3-4B, reports 98.57% success on ALFWorld and 92.97% on WebShop, outperforming the matched SEED-API baseline.
Ablations indicate that response-based selection and Global consolidation improve performance; retained-skill benefits depend on content and model compatibility.

papers.abstract: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation.
bullets: Foundation-model features often emphasize global semantics rather than the temporal and action-relevant information needed for robotics.
SPARK combines temporal abstraction with patch-level knowledge preservation during post-training.
The method produces compact visual state representations that retain useful semantic information.
Across multiple robotics benchmarks, SPARK improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models.
The improvements also transfer to real-world robot manipulation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge). SPARK encourages temporal abstraction of patch-wise semantics while preserving the foundation model’s pre-trained knowledge. Given a reference scene xt, the SPARK encoder fθ produces a class token as a compact abstraction of xt, from which the decoder predicts target token representations with hints from a few target patches. The Temporal Abstraction Loss LTA aligns these predictions with the target representations of a frozen foundation model fθ0 , while the Knowledge Preservation Loss LKP aligns the target patch tokens of fθ and fθ0 . This encourages the class token to serve as a compact visual state for control while retaining the patch-level semantics of the original foundation model.

Figure 2: Real-world demonstration trajectories. Each row shows the temporal progression of a policy from the initial observation to intermediate interaction states and the final outcome. Across tasks, the SPARK-adapted policy exhibits stable approach, contact, and object manipulation behaviors, illustrating that the adapted visual representations capture control-relevant scene information that transfers reliably to real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a core component of autonomous navigation, yet most vision-based methods operate frame-wise and produce temporally inconsistent predictions. We present SAM-VTP (Video Traversability Prediction), which fine-tunes SAM2's video memory pathway for dense, prompt-free traversability segmentation, conditioning each frame on a persistent memory of prior observations. Rather than inferring terrain geometry from appearance, we measure it: slope, roughness and height are computed from depth and fused into the image features. We also introduce an offline continuous supervision pipeline that generates dense per-pixel traversability targets in [0,1] from depth-derived geometry and semantic priors, requiring no robot deployment and no per-pixel annotation, capturing conditional feasibility that binary labels cannot represent. On TartanGround, a large-scale synthetic ground-robot dataset, SAM-VTP improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924 and binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886 over SAM-TP, a frame-wise SAM2 baseline, against a seed-to-seed spread below 0.001, and cuts frame-to-frame flicker by 31%. In closed-loop trials at two field sites, driving the same planner and controller, the baseline's dropouts leave the planner without a feasible path 3.3x more often on a paved course and 6.9x on rough ground, while SAM-VTP runs at 21.4 FPS on the Orin Nano the robot carries.
bullets: Addresses frame-wise vision models that produce inconsistent traversability predictions for autonomous navigation.
Fine-tunes SAM2’s video-memory pathway and fuses depth-derived slope, roughness, and height with image features.
Generates dense continuous traversability targets without robot deployment or per-pixel annotation.
On TartanGround, improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924, binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886, and reduces flicker by 31% versus SAM-TP.
In closed-loop field trials, reduces planner dropouts and runs at 21.4 FPS on an Orin Nano.

papers.abstract: Wearable Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) enable pervasive Human Activity Recognition (HAR), but traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) suffer from an "arithmetic-latency deadlock" due to dense floating-point MAC operations. While Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer ultra-low power, existing ones face spatial blind spots, rigid neurons, and gradient degradation. To address these, we propose TSFFormer, a purely spiking Fourier Transformer for Green HAR. It introduces two key innovations: (1) a MultiHeadFourier attention that performs frequency-domain global mixing, reducing complexity from \(O(V^2)\) to \(O(V\log V)\), eliminating spatial blind spots, and saving \(\sim\)50% GPU memory; and (2) a dual-compartment Temporal Spiking LIF (TSLIFNode) that utilizes dynamic thresholds to adapt to non-stationary rhythms and mitigate gradient degradation. Extensive experiments on 8 public IMU benchmarks demonstrate that TSFFormer surpasses state-of-the-art SNNs and even the classic DeepConvLSTM, achieving a \(\sim\)3\(\times\) faster training speed with an energy footprint of 0.1 pJ. Ablation studies confirm the synergistic effect of our modules, providing a highly accurate, ultra-low-power event-driven paradigm for wearable sensing.
bullets: Uses frequency-domain global mixing to reduce attention complexity from O(V²) to O(V log V) and address spatial blind spots.
Introduces a dual-compartment temporal spiking LIF neuron with dynamic thresholds for non-stationary motion rhythms and improved gradient behavior.
Evaluated on 8 public IMU benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art SNNs and DeepConvLSTM.
The abstract reports approximately 3× faster training, about 50% lower GPU memory use, and a 0.1 pJ energy footprint.
Ablation studies support the complementary effects of the proposed Fourier attention and temporal neuron modules.

papers.abstract: The motion of an articulated part in cluttered surroundings is constrained not only by an object's intrinsic joint limits but also by extrinsic obstacles. However, existing approaches primarily consider object articulation properties alone. Here we present Motion Constraint Prediction Network (MoCo-Net), a two-stream neural network that jointly predicts the continuous motion ranges of articulated parts and obstacle heatmaps highlighting potential collision regions from partial-view point cloud observation. By capturing both internal and external motion constraints, MoCo-Net produces more accurate feasible motion range prediction and obstacles recognition, improves generalization for novel objects in new scenes, and enables robots to construct a scene configuration space for efficient exploration of rearrangement actions. Our experiments show that MoCo-Net's two-stream design enhances each other to deliver more accurate predictions, which subsequently form a compact configuration space for a customized planner to efficiently rearrange the scene.
bullets: Addresses the gap in methods that model intrinsic joint limits but overlook external obstacles.
Uses a two-stream network to predict continuous feasible motion ranges and obstacle heatmaps.
Combining internal and external constraints improves motion-range and obstacle predictions, including for novel objects and scenes.
The predictions enable a compact scene configuration space for efficient rearrangement planning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Network architecture for feasible range and obstacle heatmap prediction. The obstacle heatmap is displayed using a color gradient, where warmer colors indicate higher collision likelihood. In contrast, sequences shown in blue are produced by the proposed configuration space exploration algorithm, resulting in more efficient rearrangement actions.

Orange lines indicate previously explored configurations, while red lines show newly predicted feasible ranges where collision-free movement is possible. papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers (DiTs) generate realistic videos, but their heavy computational cost limits broader real-world applications. Mixed-resolution generation reduces this cost by generating the visually important region at high resolution (HR) and the rest at low resolution (LR), yet existing methods suffer a severe quality drop on videos and require knowing the HR region in advance. We show that these failures are not inherent to mixed resolution, and propose $\textbf{MPEG-Diffusion}$ to address their three root causes: (1) dual-resolution attention to mitigate the curse of mixed resolution, where each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, (2) a mixed-resolution decoder to blend the HR and LR latents before decoding and resolve distortion, and (3) a self-selected HR region using the DiT's knowledge to find the visually important region without requiring it in advance. Processing only $30\%$ of full-resolution tokens, MPEG-Diffusion speeds up denoising by $4.8\times$ on Wan2.1 14B ($3.8\times$ on 1.3B), outperforming prior methods on nearly every metric. In the user study, we demonstrate the high quality of MPEG-Diffusion, with raters preferring it over prior mixed-resolution methods in over $90\%$ of pairs and rating it close to full resolution.
bullets: Addresses quality degradation and the need to specify high-resolution regions in existing mixed-resolution video generation.
Uses dual-resolution attention, where queries attend to keys and values at their own resolution.
Blends high- and low-resolution latents with a mixed-resolution decoder to reduce distortion.
Automatically selects the visually important high-resolution region using the DiT’s learned knowledge.
Processes 30% of full-resolution tokens, achieving 4.8× speedup on Wan2.1 14B and strong user preference over prior mixed-resolution methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MPEG-Diffusion. The first k of T steps run at LR. At step k, a linear head selects the HR region M (part 2), and the remaining steps denoise M at HR and the rest at LR. In dual-resolution attention (part 1), each query reads the K/V of its own resolution, with missing entries (dashed) filled from the other resolution by linear maps. The mixed-resolution decoder (part 3) merges the HR and LR latents into one HR video. Flames mark trained parts.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.
bullets: Addresses memory loss, unbounded storage, and inefficient retrieval in long-running LLM agents.
Uses six typed memory agents, a provenance hypergraph with n-ary frames, explicit retrieval budgets, and optional AutoDream consolidation and skill distillation.
Leads compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks, including 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S.
Achieves the highest mean success among compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop, and 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench.
Runs with closed or open models, requires no fine-tuning, and is faster than HyperMem across five timed benchmarks when AutoDream is disabled.
