papers.abstract: A model that takes over another model's conversation must normally re-read the whole history; a text hand-off shortens the re-read only by dropping content. KV-cache translation instead maps the source's cache into the target's own format, so the target continues from the full context without re-reading it. It works for grouped-query attention (GQA), but open-weights frontier models now cache compressed latents (MLA), sparse-attention indexer keys and fixed-size linear-attention states. We replicate KV-Lingo on a GQA pair and then give, for each of these objects, where to capture and inject it and a mechanism that reaches native quality. We study two hybrid pairs at 16-48B scale in both directions, Kimi-VL-A3B - Kimi-Linear-48B (MLA - MLA + Kimi Delta Attention) and Qwen3.5-27B - Qwen3.8-27B (Gated DeltaNet hybrids), plus a sparse-attention target (Qwen3.8-27B - Qwen3.8-Flash-Next). MLA latents translate with token-wise linear maps; recurrent states are copied with a closed-form correction or synthesised by replaying the target's own recurrence. Exact long-range recall needs token identity: decoding token ids from the source's layer-0 MLA latent raises needle recall from 0.09 to 0.99 at 2-32K and to 0.83-1.00 at 64K, eight times the longest training prompt. The hybrid full-MLA direction is within the paired confidence interval of native quality on every task metric, and same-shape GDN hybrids reach the native level in both directions (apart from 6% refusals inherited from the source), with time to first token 18.7 and 46.8 times shorter than a re-read at 64K tokens. Segment-wise multi-turn transfer stays at the re-prefill level; naive re-translation collapses. On the sparse-attention target, predicted indexer keys recall the needle as well as the target's own keys (one seed). We state as a hypothesis how the recipes transfer to 300B+ hybrid flagships.
bullets: Extends KV-Lingo beyond GQA to MLA latents, recurrent linear-attention states, and sparse-attention indexer keys.
Uses token-wise linear maps for MLA, corrected or replayed recurrences for linear-attention states, and predicted keys for sparse attention.
Across several 16–48B hybrid model pairs, transfers generally reach native or re-prefill quality in both directions.
Decoding token identities from MLA latents restores long-range needle recall, reaching 0.99 at 2–32K tokens and 0.83–1.00 at 64K.
At 64K context, transfer reduces time to first token by 18.7–46.8× versus re-reading; naive repeated translation fails.

papers.abstract: Large language models offer a promising technique for translating natural-language optimization problems into solver code, but their reliability remains constrained by the quality of template retrieval. While recent structured methods improve over flat prompting through hierarchical taxonomy search, their traversal rules remain fixed or LLM-driven at inference time, leaving retrieval unable to improve from past successes and failures. This motivates treating template retrieval as a policy that can be learned from modeling experience, rather than as a static inference-time rule. We propose COMPASS, a policy-amortized framework for retrieving optimization templates in LLM-based solver modeling, which represents the template library as a directed acyclic graph and formulates retrieval as a sequential decision process over template nodes. A deep Q-network learns a reusable traversal policy from template-level judgments and execution feedback, reducing reliance on fixed heuristic traversal through feedback-driven graph navigation. To support extensible retrieval, COMPASS embeds problem descriptions and template nodes in a shared semantic space, allowing newly inserted templates to be scored from their text descriptions without redefining the action space. Experiments across multiple LLM backbones and optimization-modeling benchmarks demonstrate that COMPASS consistently improves over heuristic structured retrieval, with the largest gains on complex and mixed-category problems.
bullets: Targets unreliable template retrieval in LLM-based optimization modeling.
Models templates as a directed acyclic graph and retrieval as sequential graph navigation.
Trains a deep Q-network using template judgments and execution feedback.
Uses shared semantic embeddings to score newly added templates without changing the action space.
Improves over heuristic structured retrieval across LLM backbones and benchmarks, especially on complex and mixed-category problems.

papers.abstract: Online Conformal Prediction (OCP) sequentially constructs prediction sets whose average empirical coverage converges to a target level over time, for arbitrary, potentially adversarial datasets. In the multi-level setting, prediction sets are produced at $d$ coverage levels at once. Prior work argued for the use of online gradient descent with isotonic projections, which produces sets nested across levels, but with a $\sqrt{d}$ dependence in the per-level coverage convergence rate. Here, we both generalize and improve prior work. First, we show that isotonic projections can be used for the construction of multi-level online conformal prediction sets from \emph{any} online learning algorithm (not just gradient descent). Then, through a black-box reduction, we show that the linearized regret of the online algorithm itself automatically gives control over both per-level coverage and distributional consistency of multi-level predictions via Fenchel duality. Finally, by using the Weighted Interval Score, a standard scoring rule for assessing multi-level interval forecasts, we prove that these projections reduce both the size of the sets and their under-coverage. We study two instantiations of our theory, $p$-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods, both improving the dependence on the number of levels to $\sqrt{\log d}$ for the multi-level OCP problem. Experiments on several datasets show favorable performance compared to baselines.
bullets: Addresses multi-level Online Conformal Prediction with adversarial data and simultaneous coverage targets.
Shows isotonic projections can convert any online learning algorithm into nested prediction sets.
Uses Fenchel duality to derive per-level coverage and distributional-consistency guarantees from linearized regret.
Proves improvements in set size and under-coverage under the Weighted Interval Score.
Instantiations with p-norm Online Mirror Descent and coordinate-wise Universal Portfolio methods achieve √log d dependence; experiments report favorable baseline comparisons.

papers.title: A Black-Box Reduction from Regret to Multi-Level Coverage
papers.tldr: A black-box reduction turns online-learning regret into guarantees for nested, multi-level conformal prediction, improving level dependence from √d to √log d.

papers.abstract: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of dense kernel matrices in large-scale GP training.
Combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction.
Computes the objective and analytic gradients using low-rank factors, diagonal terms, and small dense matrices.
On nine large-scale regression datasets, it substantially reduces training time while reaching reference predictive accuracy; the needed rank varies.
FP16/TF32 offer modest extra speedups but may be unreliable for poorly conditioned reduced systems; single precision can also limit predictive solves.

papers.abstract: Constrained preference-conditioned MORL typically assumes full task observability, treating preferences and safety budgets as stationary task signals. In real-world deployment, however, these signals are often unreliable proxies: intent may drift, safety tolerances may shift with context, and exposed descriptors may be noisy, delayed, or incomplete. We therefore formulate constrained preference-conditioned MORL as a partially observed task-specification problem, where the agent must navigate a fundamental conflict between unreliable external signals and latent interaction dynamics. We propose \textbf{BECON}, a belief-conditioned framework for constrained MORL with drifting preferences and budgets, which infers latent task context from recent histories to estimate preferences and safety budgets. These estimates are fused with the exposed task signal via uncertainty-dependent gates, enabling the policy to defer to observations under high epistemic uncertainty while correcting them when history is informative. The fused context jointly conditions preference optimization and context-adaptive constraint enforcement. Experiments on diverse multi-objective control tasks demonstrate that BECON consistently improves over state-of-the-art MORL baselines, achieving stronger robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.
bullets: Models task specifications as partially observed rather than fully reliable or stationary signals.
Infers preferences and safety budgets from recent histories to capture drift and missing or delayed information.
Uses uncertainty-dependent gates to fuse inferred context with exposed task signals.
Jointly conditions preference optimization and adaptive constraint enforcement on the fused context.
Experiments across diverse multi-objective control tasks show improved robustness and constraint satisfaction under task drift.

papers.abstract: Cross-view image sequence geo-localization aims to determine the geographic location of a sequence of ground images by matching it against geo-tagged satellite imagery. Although sequential observations provide complementary scene information, substantial overlap between adjacent images introduces feature redundancy, while conventional fusion strategies may weaken spatial relationships essential for cross-view matching. Therefore, we propose a cross-view image sequence geo-localization method via Attention-guided Sequence fusion and Metric Learning (ASML). Specifically, a Sequential Content Fusion (SCF) module models cross-image feature correlations to suppress redundant content and adaptively preserve geographically informative non-overlapping regions. Next, a Spatial Feature Aggregation (SFA) module is used to capture and aggregate the spatial and semantic information of local features, so as to maintain the spatial layout of the image sequence. Finally, a Geo-InfoNCE loss function is proposed, which comprehensively considers the feature distance and geographic distance for mixed-space metric learning, thus improving the ability of the model to distinguish hard negative samples. A new cross-view image sequence dataset CrossRoad-66K is established to provide more complex scenarios. Extensive experiments and visualizations on the SeqGeo and CrossRoad-66K datasets demonstrate that compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, the proposed method ASML achieves an improvement of 3.37% and 2.10% at R@1, respectively.
bullets: Addresses feature redundancy from overlapping adjacent ground images and weakened spatial relationships in sequence fusion.
Uses Sequential Content Fusion to suppress redundant content while retaining informative non-overlapping regions.
Uses Spatial Feature Aggregation to combine local spatial and semantic information while maintaining scene layout.
Introduces Geo-InfoNCE loss for mixed-space metric learning that incorporates feature and geographic distances to handle hard negatives.
Reports R@1 improvements of 3.37% on SeqGeo and 2.10% on the newly established CrossRoad-66K dataset versus SOTA methods.

papers.abstract: Generating text-bearing images requires coherent scenes and accurate characters. Large text-to-image models improve both capabilities through repeated denoising, at substantial sampling cost. Few-step distillation reduces this cost but requires the student to organize scenes and refine glyphs within a short trajectory. We present a four-step distillation framework combining local response regularization with teacher-guided text training. Built on distribution matching, the framework distills the GLM-Image DiT while retaining its autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder, and VAE. A path-length penalty promotes consistent local responses of the conditional denoising field. Progressive training combines synthetic strings with teacher-generated imagery to preserve character accuracy and scene-integrated typography. The student achieves GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, compared with 0.81 and 0.1690 for four-step TDM. A coefficient study favors $10^{-5}$, and Qwen-Image experiments show additional gains from response regularization and text supervision. Single-image inference takes 1.742 s, compared with 5.818 s for the teacher, yielding a $3.34\times$ speedup at the same 40 GB GPU memory requirement.
bullets: Addresses the high sampling cost of large text-to-image models and the difficulty of refining typography in few-step generation.
Combines distribution matching, local response regularization, and teacher-guided text training.
Retains the GLM-Image DiT’s autoregressive visual prior, glyph encoder, and VAE.
Reports GenEval Overall 0.84 and CVTG-2K word accuracy 0.5045, outperforming four-step TDM results in the abstract.
Reduces single-image inference time to 1.742 s versus 5.818 s for the teacher, a reported 3.34× speedup at the same 40 GB memory requirement.

papers.selection_reason: Few-step distillation with response regularization and teacher guidance reduces sampling cost of large text-to-image models, fitting efficiency interests.
papers.title: Four-Step Text-Bearing Image Generation via Distillation with Local Response Regularization and Teacher-Guided Training
papers.tldr: A four-step distillation framework accelerates text-bearing image generation while preserving scene coherence and character accuracy.

papers.abstract: Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State-Move-Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens--a $\mathbf{59.3}\times$ reduction and $\mathbf{2.46}\times$ compression. Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from $\mathbf{0.6379}$ to $\mathbf{0.7478}$ and increases 5/5 Pass instances from $\mathbf{138}$ to $\mathbf{164}$, while matching or outperforming rawSkill on $\mathbf{208}$ of $\mathbf{232}$ instances. It also reduces average runtime token consumption by $\mathbf{38.38\%}$. These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.
bullets: Addresses skill collections that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose because they remain isolated text artifacts.
Decomposes skills into procedural bricks linked by Outcome-to-State conditions, reusing validated bricks and creating new ones only for uncovered procedures.
On SkillsBench v1.1, represents 232 skills from 87 tasks with 95 shared bricks and reduces representation tokens by 59.3%.
Improves average task score from 0.6379 to 0.7478, raises 5/5 Pass instances from 138 to 164, and matches or beats raw skills on 208/232 instances.
Reduces average runtime token consumption by 38.38%, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations or scope beyond the reported benchmark.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose CM3AE 2.0, a unified RGB Frame and Event-Voxel/-Frame pre-training framework. By jointly learning multimodal spatiotemporal representations and exploiting latent cross-modal dependencies through cross-modal generation, the framework enhances multimodal information interaction and collaborative modeling capabilities. Specifically, we first propose an Event-aware Spatiotemporal Masked Reconstruction (ESMR) strategy to learn unified multimodal spatiotemporal representations. It leverages event responses to guide masking toward dynamically salient regions. Through spatiotemporal masked reconstruction, it learns spatial structures and their temporal variations from continuous RGB-Event observations. In addition, it incorporates multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to facilitate the modeling of cross-modal complementary information and the learning of shared representations. Building upon this, we further propose a Hierarchical Cross-modal Generation (HCG) strategy to learn latent cross-modal dependencies through visual and language generation. At the visual level, Event-conditioned RGB generation is performed using a pre-trained diffusion model to capture visual associations between the two modalities. At the language level, video-level text description generation based on joint RGB-Event representations establishes connections between multimodal visual features and linguistic semantics, further enriching the learning of cross-modal dependencies. Extensive experiments on four diverse downstream tasks demonstrate that CM3AE 2.0 consistently improves performance, validating the effectiveness and generalization capability of the proposed pre-training framework.
bullets: Uses event responses to mask dynamically salient regions for spatiotemporal masked reconstruction of RGB–event observations.
Combines multimodal fusion reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive learning to capture complementary and shared information.
Learns latent cross-modal dependencies through event-conditioned RGB generation and video-level text description generation.
Experiments across four diverse downstream tasks show consistent performance improvements and support the framework’s generalization.
Scope: the abstract does not specify datasets, quantitative gains, or task-specific limitations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Objects in dynamic motion remain a significant challenge for dense visual SLAM since dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction. Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2. For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while metric depth predicted from completed images initializes provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D datasets. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.
bullets: Addresses tracking and reconstruction errors caused by dynamic objects violating static-scene assumptions.
Uses optical-flow motion discovery and SAM2 mask propagation to identify dynamic regions.
Completes occluded backgrounds with diffusion inpainting and initializes provisional Gaussians from predicted metric depth.
Provenance labels prevent generated content from influencing camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization; generated primitives are removed when real observations appear.
Reports competitive tracking on TUM RGB-D and BONN RGB-D, and a 4.60 dB average PSNR improvement over WildGS-SLAM on StaDy4D using monocular RGB.

Dynamic regions are identified using motion discrepancies revealed by optical flow, with SAM2 [13] providing temporally consistent motion masks, while tracking uses observed static regions and background completion provides provisional representations for mapping.

papers.abstract: Single-view 3D hair reconstruction has progressed rapidly, but many methods optimize for visual plausibility rather than producing strand assets that can be directly used in grooming, editing, or simulation pipelines. We propose SAFE-Hair, a framework that reconstructs explicit strand grooms from a single portrait by decoding hair from persistent follicles in a canonical scalp-UV domain. Given a fitted template head, SAFE-Hair projects self-supervised image features onto the scalp, uses a conditional Rectified Flow model to generate latent scalp fields, and decodes occupancy, segment directions, length allocation, and total length at a fixed set of scalp follicles. This representation enforces scalp-rooted strand identities by construction and enables direct export with follicle IDs and guide-family metadata. We further introduce attachment, collision, and bending priors to improve geometric validity without per-subject test-time optimization. To evaluate both reconstruction fidelity and asset usability, we introduce HairBench-3D, a benchmark built from public 3D hair assets with standardized alignment, rendering, resampling, and metrics for geometry, direction consistency, invisible-region completion, silhouette agreement, and collision. SAFE-Hair improves Chamfer distance from 3.74 mm to 3.28 mm, F-score from 77.9 to 81.7, invisible-region F-score from 66.1 to 69.8, and penetration ratio from 4.8% to 3.9% over the strongest baseline.
bullets: Addresses the gap between visually plausible single-view hair reconstruction and strand assets usable for grooming, editing, and simulation.
Projects self-supervised image features into a canonical scalp-UV domain and generates latent scalp fields with conditional Rectified Flow.
Decodes strand occupancy, directions, length allocation, and total length at fixed follicles, preserving strand identities and export metadata.
Introduces attachment, collision, and bending priors without per-subject test-time optimization.
Presents HairBench-3D and reports improved Chamfer distance, F-score, invisible-region completion, and penetration ratio over the strongest baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of SAFE-Hair. Given a single portrait, we fit a template head and use the recovered camera geometry to project dense image features into a canonical scalp-UV domain, producing a scalp-aligned conditioning map. A conditional Rectified Flow model transforms Gaussian noise into a latent scalp field Z. A shared follicle decoder queries Z at persistent canonical follicles {ur}Rr=1 and predicts occupancy, segment directions, length allocation, total length, and export descriptors. The final strand curves are obtained by forward integration from fixed scalp roots, yielding explicit scalp-rooted strands with stable follicle identities and groom metadata for downstream export.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. For each input image, we show reconstructed hair from multiple viewpoints. SAFE-Hair produces scalp-attached strand geometry with more consistent back-view completion and fewer head-interpenetration artifacts than prior methods.

Figure 2: Motivation. Existing 3D hair generators often produce rendering-oriented representations: Mesh-based hair [39] lacks explicit strands, while Gaussian-based hair (UniHair [41]) lacks persistent follicles and suffers from collisions. Our method reconstructs explicit rooted strands with stable scalp follicles, enabling editable and export-ready hair assets from a single portrait.

Figure 5: Qualitative ablation. Left: SAFE-Hair produces more complete and coherent scalp-rooted strands. Right: removing scalp-UV conditioning or the latent scalp field degrades strand coherence and hairstyle consistency.

Figure 8: Additional qualitative comparison on in-the-wild portrait images. From left to right: input image, SAFE-Hair, Hairstep, and NeuralHDHair. SAFE-Hair produces more coherent and complete strand reconstructions across diverse hairstyles, including short, straight, wavy, spiky, curly, and afro hair. Compared with baselines, our method better preserves the global hair silhouette and local strand flow, while reducing floating strands, sparse regions, and unstable scalp attachment.

Figure 6: Exportable groom structure. SAFE-Hair groups active follicles into guide families in canonical scalp UV space. Each child strand stores a persistent follicle ID, guide ID, control points, and optional physical or groom-control attributes.

Figure 9: Additional qualitative results on in-the-wild portrait images. For each pair, the left image shows the input portrait and the right image shows the reconstructed 3D hair rendered on a neutral template head. papers.abstract: Dexterous grasping in robotics relies on distinct hand configurations depending on object geometry. We introduce BetaGrasp, a 3D diffusion policy that conditions a DP3-style point-cloud policy on a four-class grasp label (crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug), running on a Franka arm with a 16-DoF LEAP hand. We also introduce a climbing-hold benchmark: a spring testbed whose ratchet gives a slip-force reading in newtons. In our analysis the policy's point-cloud encoder did not separate the four holds, so the scan alone gave it little to choose a grasp from. Without the label (a DP3-style baseline), simulated rollouts from the robot's reset pose all end in a jug grasp, whatever the hold (25% correct grasp type, versus 94% for BetaGrasp). The label works as a switch for which grasp the policy performs. On 80 paired hardware trials, BetaGrasp raises average slip force from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, and grasps slipping fully off the hold drop from 44% of trials to 10%.
bullets: Targets geometry-dependent grasping for crimp, sloper, pinch, and jug climbing holds.
Conditions a 3D diffusion, DP3-style point-cloud policy on the grasp label using a Franka arm and 16-DoF LEAP hand.
Introduces a spring-based climbing-hold benchmark that measures slip force in newtons.
Without labels, the policy defaults to jug grasps and achieves 25% correct grasp types; BetaGrasp reaches 94% in simulation.
Across 80 paired hardware trials, average slip force increases from 9.6 N to 14.3 N, while complete slips decrease from 44% to 10%.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. BetaGrasp architecture. Point cloud, proprioception, and grasp-type label are encoded independently and fused into a 512-d conditioning vector z that feature-wise conditions a 1D temporal U-Net diffusion denoiser. The DP3 baseline drops only the grasp-type branch (orange) (37,248 parameters, 0.1% of 34.6 M).

Fig. 2. Spring-testbed benchmark. (a) The LEAP Hand v1 (16-DoF, on a Franka Emika Panda) executes a taxonomy-conditioned grasp on a 3D-printed jug hold seated on the testbed. (b) Top-down view: two extension springs in parallel (top) pull the orange deck back along a single axis directed toward the robot base, a center guide rod keeps the deck on that axis, and a pin through the deck rides over the toothed ratchet strips on both sides, holding the deck at its farthest point; the marked teeth (1–11) show how far the hold traveled before the grasp slipped. Lines drawn on the deck guide the five hold orientations. (c) The four 3D-printed climbing holds: pinch (narrow elongated protrusion), jug (domed body with deep finger pocket), crimp (thin edge with shallow finger ridges), and sloper (convex hemispherical surface)

Fig. 3. Final hand poses of simulated closed-loop rollouts started from the deployment reset pose, projected onto the first two principal components of the demonstrators’ final hand poses (light gray; marker shape = hold). BetaGrasp rollouts (orange) mostly land on the demonstrated grasp for their hold; DP3 rollouts (gray outline) end in the jug grasp on every hold.

papers.abstract: Navigation in dynamic environments requires mobile robots to make progress toward their goals while respecting motion limits and avoiding surrounding obstacles. Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem. This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation. A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints. The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty. Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input. The selected-policy comparison also shows fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.
bullets: Targets the gap between geometrically appropriate subgoals and subgoals that yield successfully solvable control problems.
Combines a Soft Actor–Critic subgoal policy with nonlinear model predictive control, motion and collision constraints, and high-order control barrier functions.
Feeds summarized optimization outcomes from each subgoal interval back to the policy without extra optimization calls.
Across five static and dynamic-obstacle scenarios, OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success and consistently outperforms the same hierarchy without optimization-status input.
Selected-policy comparisons show fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall hierarchical architecture of OASIS. The upper layer uses a Soft ActorCritic (SAC) framework to generate normalized subgoals ηj based on environment observations and execution feedback qj . The lower layer transforms ηj into workspace subgoals gj and solves a Nonlinear Model Predictive Control problem with High-Order Control Barrier Functions (NMPC–HOCBF) to compute low-level control commands u = [a, α]T while returning solver outcomes qj+1 to inform future subgoal generation.

Figure 1: Proposed architecture. A high-level policy generates subgoals from navigation observations and previous optimization outcomes. A low-level predictive controller tracks these subgoals subject to motion, collision-avoidance, and HOCBF constraints, and returns optimization feedback for the next policy decision.

papers.abstract: In this work, we study whether frontier agents can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from $6.82\times$ with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to $19.86\times$. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, our Infrathon framework provides resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions. Code is available at https://github.com/InfrathonX/Infrathon
bullets: Introduces a benchmark covering diverse, multi-level, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks.

papers.abstract: Small multimodal models can misjudge emotion when words, voice, and visual cues conflict. We present EmoHarness, which runs such a model, the frozen student, inside a harness: the prompts, settings, and verification code around its calls. A human-written starting harness, the scaffold, numbers the student's visual observations, transcript, and prosody descriptions as citable evidence and has the student weigh candidate emotions against it. In Meta-Harness Evolving (MHE), a stronger LLM, the Builder, reads the student's errors and execution traces offline and edits the harness; static checks and validation gates decide which edits are kept, and the Builder never sees evaluation items. On 5,507 MME-Emotion items, EmoHarness raises task-macro Recognition by 7.6-13.4 points over a single video-only call for all four students and both Builders. Transcripts and prosody descriptions supply most of this boost (+5.38 to +10.71); the scaffold changes the audio-augmented call by -0.79 to +2.54, partly through extra multi-label predictions, and evolved edits add at most +0.95, although no evolved increment survives Holm correction. The harness's emotion context also transfers to IntentQA, with small gains for three of four students, none of which survives correction. EmoHarness thus boosts small multimodal students chiefly by supplying and organizing audio-derived evidence.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation (MERC) combines lexical, acoustic, visual and conversational cues, but accepting audio and video does not establish their effective or robust use. We audit off-the-shelf Omni models while holding the target transcript and prior textual context fixed and adding, removing or replacing target audio and video. In the primary evaluation of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5 and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and the full five-session six-class IEMOCAP set, T+A improves Accuracy in all six model-dataset pairs, with four gains significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Across three source mappings, unrelated A/V (RandA/V) lowers Accuracy relative to Full in all 18 comparisons; all 18 remain significant under dialogue-cluster inference and BH-FDR correction, both on common-valid pairs and when invalid/OOM outcomes are treated as incorrect. Comparisons with modality-omission baselines further distinguish replacement penalties from mismatch-specific harm. A Qwen/MELD case study finds significantly greater gold-vs-best-candidate margin recovery in Late than Early or Middle under decision-query audio knockout, relative to an edge-count-matched Video-Sham control, using Holm-corrected tests. These results distinguish genuine-modality benefit from sensitivity and vulnerability to misleading input.
bullets: Evaluates Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, Baichuan-Omni-1.5, and MiniCPM-o 2.6 on MELD and IEMOCAP with transcripts and textual context held fixed.
Adding target audio and text improves accuracy across all six model–dataset evaluations, with four gains remaining significant after FDR correction.
Replacing target audio/video with unrelated inputs reduces accuracy in all 18 comparisons, with significance robust to dialogue-cluster and BH-FDR correction.
Omission baselines separate general modality sensitivity from harm caused specifically by mismatched inputs.
A Qwen/MELD case study suggests later-stage audio processing better recovers correct decisions after audio removal than earlier or middle-stage processing.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project website: https://j-x-chen.github.io/Thermo-VLA-web/
bullets: Addresses the limited temperature-aware relational reasoning of VLAs that treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs.
Introduces a ThermoRes Encoder that separates hot and cold representations and applies gated, language-conditioned residual modulation to RGB tokens.
Evaluates six real-world tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1, covering grounding and relational reasoning.
Achieves a 0.86 average success rate on four thermal-dependent tasks, 18 percentage points above the pi_0.5 RGB-thermal baseline.
Maintains a 0.78 average success rate under unseen objects and scene variations; the mechanism also improves color-attribute tasks in simulation and on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Fine-tuning a deployed language model on one task after another can change behaviour that should stay fixed, such as earlier skills, general chat or refusals. Today, such forgetting is found only after training, on the benchmarks someone chose to run. This work bounds, before training, how often its outputs change on chosen prompt distributions. FireGate places each task's update, such as a new LoRA, behind a gate, which is a classifier on the model's frozen lower layers that decides for each prompt whether the update is used. Where no gate fires, the model computes exactly what the old one computes. As a result, on any prompt distribution, every bounded behaviour score changes by at most the gates' firing rate there over a whole task stream. Calibrating each gate on unlabeled prompts of what must not change fixes that rate before training, with a PAC guarantee, whatever weights training produces. Forgetting is thus bounded by the gate's false-alarm rate, and its price is the gate's power: no update, gated or not, that changes as few protected outputs can change new-task outputs more often than the best test of that level tells new-task prompts from protected ones. On reinforcement-learning streams of up to five tasks, gated training keeps the earlier tasks and changes 3.3% of held-out chat responses, whereas ungated training changes 91.8%. Across seven models, the gain kept behind the gate follows its firing rate on new-task prompts, measured before training. The certificate covers the gated model as deployed, on the prompt distributions sampled for calibration, not against an adversary who searches for prompts that fire the gate.
bullets: Addresses forgetting of earlier skills, general chat, and refusals that is typically detected only after training.
Places each task update behind a classifier over frozen lower-layer features; when it does not fire, the original model is unchanged.
PAC calibration on unlabeled protected prompts bounds any protected-behaviour score change by the gate’s firing rate over a task stream.
On streams of up to five RL tasks, gated training changed 3.3% of held-out chat responses versus 91.8% for ungated training.
The guarantee applies to calibrated prompt distributions, not adversarially selected prompts; new-task gains depend on gate firing there.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses continual learning and forgetting in LLMs using a gating mechanism to bound behavior change, directly relevant to Adaptation and Memory and Language Foundation Models.
papers.title: FireGate: Bounding Behaviour Change Before Training in Continual RL Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: FireGate uses pre-training prompt gates to certify and limit behavioural changes during continual RL fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation requires autonomous agents to explore unseen environments and locate target objects without task-specific training, posing challenges in perceptual reliability under observation uncertainty and physically grounded goal termination. Although foundation-model-based approaches improve generalization, they remain vulnerable to unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-induced directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect stopping decisions. To address these limitations, we propose CSG-Nav, a zero-shot navigation framework centered on confidence-aware multimodal information fusion. CSG-Nav integrates three complementary fusion mechanisms. First, semantic-source fusion integrates open-vocabulary detection results, detection confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning to produce more reliable direction-level semantic scores and suppress hallucination-induced directional bias. Second, spatial-confidence fusion weights multi-view semantic evidence using a Gaussian decay function, suppressing unreliable distant observations while accumulating spatially consistent exploration preferences. Third, semantic-geometric decision fusion combines semantic target detection with depth-based 3D localization to support physically grounded stopping decisions. Experiments on HM3Dv1, HM3Dv2, and MP3D demonstrate competitive zero-shot performance, achieving success rates of 58.9%, 71.6%, and 44.3%. Fusion-level ablations and real-world deployments in indoor and outdoor environments further verify the effectiveness and practicality of CSG-Nav for robust navigation under uncertain perception. Code is available at https://xr-ui.github.io/CSGNav.github.io/
bullets: Targets unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-driven directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect termination.
Fuses open-vocabulary detections, confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning for more reliable directional guidance.
Uses Gaussian spatial-confidence weighting to downweight distant observations and accumulate consistent exploration preferences.
Combines semantic detection with depth-based 3D localization for physically grounded goal stopping.
Reports success rates of 58.9% on HM3Dv1, 71.6% on HM3Dv2, and 44.3% on MP3D, with ablations and real-world deployments supporting practicality.

papers.abstract: Sequence-to-function models such as AlphaGenome and Borzoi read up to a megabase of DNA and score a genetic variant by comparing their predictions for the reference and alternate sequences. Insertions and deletions (indels) are costly to score, because an indel usually shifts the unchanged DNA after it onto a different pooling grid, which prevents direct reuse of the reference's encoder activations. The AlphaGenome Atlas scored more than 100 million indels with three full model passes each, although the DNA after an indel matches the reference shifted by the indel's length. We present ShiftCache, an exact reuse system that encodes each shifted reference once and shares it among all variants scored in the same window with the same shift. ShiftCache copies every encoder output a variant can reuse and recomputes the rest in batched tiles. On held-out AlphaGenome windows shared by many indels, in strict fp32 on one A6000, ShiftCache is 3.5 to 6.5$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6 to 2.7$\times$ faster than our adaptation of layer-by-layer reuse to indels. It is 3.5 to 4.1$\times$ faster than dense reimplementations of two published analyses with Borzoi and AlphaGenome, and 2.6$\times$ faster than dense execution with Enformer. Scoring each variant in its own centered 131 kb window makes ShiftCache only 1.36$\times$ faster than deduplicated dense execution, and highly diverse insertion lengths or many dispersed edits can make it slower than layer-by-layer reuse or dense execution. For encoders that meet our conditions, ShiftCache computes the same predictions as dense execution in exact arithmetic. On an A6000, every checked output of the default AlphaGenome and Borzoi runs matches dense execution within an absolute and relative tolerance of $10^{-5}$. With larger tile batches, with Enformer or on an H100, a small fraction of values exceeds this tolerance.
bullets: Indels disrupt pooling-grid alignment, making conventional reuse of reference encodings difficult and costly.
ShiftCache encodes each shifted reference once, shares it across variants with the same shift, and recomputes only non-reusable outputs in batched tiles.
On shared AlphaGenome windows, it is 3.5–6.5× faster than deduplicated dense execution and 1.6–2.7× faster than layer-by-layer reuse.
It also outperforms dense Borzoi, AlphaGenome, and Enformer analyses by 3.5–4.1×, 3.5–4.1×, and 2.6×, respectively.
Speedups are smaller for independently centered windows or diverse/dispersed edits; outputs generally match dense execution within 1e-5 tolerance, with occasional deviations under other settings.

papers.abstract: Quantization reduces LLM deployment costs, but effective strategies must balance model quality and storage. LLM-driven search can automate strategy design through repeated proposal and evaluation. This process must identify useful strategies within a limited evaluation budget. The key challenge is that \textit{actual quantization is expensive, while inexpensive proxies may not reflect quantized-model performance.} To address this challenge, we present AutoQS, an \textbf{Auto}mated \textbf{Q}uantization \textbf{S}trategy Design with LLMs. AutoQS keeps weight precision fixed and searches group-size allocations across layers and operators under deployment constraints. Evaluation history guides coordinated LLM proposals, while deterministic validation ensures compatible allocations. An inexpensive quality proxy evaluates candidates, and an candidate repository retains alternative allocations to inform subsequent proposals. Periodic actual quantization complements these proxy evaluations with measured quality and checkpoint storage, providing feedback for further search within the evaluation budget. Experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct show that AutoQS improves seven-task average accuracy over uniform-group GPTQ and AWQ by 0.70 and 1.12 percentage points, respectively, at four-bit weight precision.
bullets: Addresses the costly, potentially unreliable evaluation of quantization strategies.
Searches layer- and operator-specific group-size allocations while keeping weight precision fixed.
Uses evaluation history, deterministic validation, and a repository of alternative candidates to guide proposals.
Combines inexpensive proxy scoring with periodic actual quantization and checkpoint storage.
On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, improves seven-task average accuracy by 0.70 points over uniform-group GPTQ and 1.12 points over AWQ.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the AutoQS framework. AutoQS first defines a structured quantization policy space under a fixed weight bit-width, where layer- and operator-wise group sizes are searched. An LLM-guided search procedure generates constrained policy modifications, which are validated and evaluated using a low-cost proxy while a diversity-preserving candidate records maintains previously explored allocation patterns. Every K = 5 search iterations, the procedure selects the latest eligible candidate in the current five-iteration window for fresh GPTQ quantization. This target selection is independent of the proxy-score ordering. The resulting checkpoint is evaluated for task accuracy and storage, providing measured outcomes for subsequent policy selection.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction models have demonstrated strong generalization under large-scale pre-training, yet they struggle in long-tail scenarios such as low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation. We observe relational attention structure collapse, manifested as the failure of cross-view correspondences, as a primary cause of these limitations. While adaptation offers a practical way to bridge this gap, existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches mainly perform channel-wise feature adjustment and lack mechanisms to explicitly adapt relational structures, leaving correspondence failures unresolved. In this work, we formulate adaptation of 3D reconstruction models as a problem of correspondence recovery under domain shift and propose 3R-Adapter, a PEFT paradigm for long-tail 3D reconstruction scenarios. Our method consists of three components: Deformable Retrieval for task-adaptive relation candidate retrieval, Relational Rewiring for reconstructing cross-view relational structures, and Consistency Refinement for injecting the rewired relations into stable predictions. Extensive experiments on low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation demonstrate that our approach significantly improves robustness over existing PEFT methods while maintaining efficient lightweight adaptation. Our code is released at https://github.com/PKU-OV3-LAB/3R-Adapter.
bullets: Targets long-tail settings including low-light reconstruction, joint human-scene reconstruction, and test-time adaptation.
Attributes failures to collapsed relational attention and disrupted cross-view correspondences.
Introduces three components: Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement.
Experiments report improved robustness over existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods while preserving lightweight adaptation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The data scaling bottleneck in 3D pre-training and our relational adaptation paradigm. (a) While foundation models thrive on massive data, they struggle to generalize to long-tail 3D domains due to the high cost of dense 3D ground truth. (b) Conventional PEFT methods (e.g., LoRA, Adapter) rely on implicit, channel-wise feature adjustment, which struggle to model the correspondence relationship in data-scarce scenarios. In contrast, our 3R-Adapter shifts the paradigm to explicit relational adaptation via Deformable Retrieval, Relational Rewiring, and Consistency Refinement, effectively establishing robust cross-view correspondences without destroying pretrained priors.

Figure 3: The overall pipeline of the proposed 3R-Adapter. To enable efficient adaptation for complex long-tail scenes, our 3R-Adapter modulates the network via three cohesive modules: Deformable Retrieval extracts view-specific anchors and estimates spatial offsets alongside routing weights; Relational Rewiring establishes explicit geometric correspondences across views through deformable spatial sampling; and Consistency Refinement integrates the relational features back into the main stream via a learned gating mechanism, effectively enforcing cross-view consistency.

Figure 2: Relational attention structure collapse in long-tail scenarios. (a) In data-rich daytime scenes, the pre-trained 3D reconstruction model produces concentrated cross-view attention, allowing a selected query token to attend to consistent physical counterparts across reference views. (b) For selected low-light queries, the attention distribution becomes diffuse and fragmented, indicating degraded relational routing and unreliable correspondence modeling. This observation suggests that long-tail adaptation requires explicitly restoring cross-view relational structures, motivating the design of 3R-Adapter.
Figure 4: Qualitative results on joint human-scene reconstruction. 3R-Adapter produces more consistent human mesh recovery and cleaner scene geometry under complex human-scene interactions.
Figure 5: Ablation on the hyperparameters of 3R-Adapter on the Oxford Day&Night [39] test dataset for scene reconstruction.

papers.abstract: We present UltraVoxelGS, a 3D ultrasound reconstruction method that achieves both fast reconstruction and physically faithful rendering for the first time, bringing live spatial feedback during 2D ultrasound scanning within reach. This is made possible by a feed-forward design that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed ultrasound images directly, entirely bypassing the per-scene optimization bottleneck that has confined prior methods to offline use. Realising such feed-forward prediction in this setting is non-trivial: unlike natural images, ultrasound slices share at most one-dimensional intersections and exhibit view-dependent appearance due to acoustic propagation and attenuation, violating the dense overlap and photometric consistency assumed by existing feed-forward Gaussian methods. Hence, to achieve fast reconstruction, we introduce a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass that decouples representation size from input count by lifting all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicting Gaussian parameters directly. For faithful rendering, we propose ultrasound-aware appearance rendering strategy factorize reflection from cumulative attenuation during training and exploit appearance continuity among spatially adjacent slices for efficient Render-time Appearance Adaptation. On both real-world and simulated datasets, UltraVoxelGS achieves best PSNR/SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines while reducing inference from 10-20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds (over 35 times faster) and scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames. Code is available at https://github.com/YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready.
bullets: Addresses the slow, offline nature of existing 3D ultrasound reconstruction methods and the sparse overlap and view-dependent appearance of ultrasound images.
Uses a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pipeline that lifts all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support, decoupling representation size from input count.
Models ultrasound appearance by separating reflection from cumulative attenuation and adapting rendering using continuity across neighboring slices.
Achieves the best reported PSNR/SSIM against per-scene optimization baselines on real and simulated datasets.
Reduces inference time from 10–20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds and supports sequences longer than 1,000 frames.

papers.abstract: Video reasoning hinges on a small number of visually decisive tokens embedded in otherwise largely language-driven chains of thought. Yet prevailing post-training methods such as GRPO overlook this structure, assigning coarse trajectory-level rewards while requiring multiple rollouts and often costly external judges. We introduce Visually-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (VIOS), a post-training framework that identifies where a model under-utilizes visual evidence and concentrates learning at those positions. Our key insight is that a model can audit its own visual reliance: the divergence between its next-token distributions with and without the video reveals how strongly each prediction depends on the visual input. Measuring this reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged teacher exposes a per-token reliance gap, identifying positions where the teacher exploits visual evidence that the student overlooks. VIOS translates this signal into dense, targeted supervision through three complementary components: an exponential moving average (EMA) teacher that co-evolves with the student, a contrastive objective that encourages predictions to depend on the video, and a reliance-gap gate that focuses learning on visually under-utilized tokens. Crucially, VIOS requires only a single on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers. Across 12 benchmarks spanning general, temporal, spatial, knowledge-intensive, and long-video understanding, VIOS consistently improves three model backbones and outperforms contemporary video-reasoning systems, while training in over 9x fewer steps, 60x fewer FLOPs, and 111x fewer generated tokens. Project page: https://vision.cs.utexas.edu/projects/VIOS/
bullets: Targets a limitation of GRPO-style post-training: coarse trajectory rewards, multiple rollouts, and costly external evaluation overlook token-level visual reliance.
Measures how predictions change with versus without video to estimate visual reliance for both a student and an answer-privileged EMA teacher.
Uses a contrastive visual-dependence objective and a reliance-gap gate to focus supervision on visually under-utilized tokens.
Requires one on-policy rollout from a single model, without external rewards, judges, or larger teachers.
Across 12 benchmarks and three backbones, it consistently improves performance while using over 9× fewer steps, 60× fewer FLOPs, and 111× fewer generated tokens than contemporary approaches.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of VIOS. papers.abstract: Robot demonstration datasets combine demonstrations from teleoperators of uneven experience, so collection teams need to know how many demonstrations from one group match those from another. We measure this with a data multiple: the ratio of the numbers of demonstrations two groups need for their policies to reach the same success rate. On robomimic's simulated Square and Can tasks, we train behavior-cloning policies on demonstrations from the two teleoperators robomimic labels Better and the two it labels Worse, varying dataset size and the share of Worse demonstrations. On Square, within robomimic's 25-second time limit, an all-Worse training set needs 1.55 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. Most of this difference is late completion: policies trained on Worse demonstrations finish later, as the Worse teleoperators do, and with a 100-second limit the multiple falls to 1.11. On Can, most of the difference remains at 100 seconds. If each Worse demonstration were worth 1/1.55 of a Better one, as in an all-Worse set, a half-Better, half-Worse set on Square would need 1.22 times as many demonstrations as an all-Better set. In fact, it needs 13% more than that, and this excess persists at every time limit from 20 to 200 seconds. The excess remains when training draws demonstrations uniformly instead of in proportion to their length. On Square, within the 25-second limit, switching to these Worse teleoperators is cheaper at equal success only if they earn less than a third of the Better teleoperators' hourly pay, because Worse demonstrations also take longer to record.
bullets: The study defines a data multiple: how many demonstrations from one teleoperator group are needed to match another group’s policy success.
Using robomimic Square and Can simulations, it compares demonstrations from groups labeled Better and Worse while varying dataset size and mixture.
On Square with a 25-second limit, all-Worse data requires 1.55× as many demonstrations as all-Better data; this falls to 1.11× with a 100-second limit.
On Can, much of the disadvantage persists even with a 100-second limit, indicating task-dependent effects.

On Square, mixed Better/Worse data performs worse than predicted by a simple weighted-value model, and Worse teleoperators are cost-effective only below roughly one-third of Better operators’ hourly pay.

papers.abstract: Flipping is a fundamental robotic manipulation skill that requires reorienting a target object in a stable pose on a planar support surface by rotating it 180$^\circ$ about an axis parallel to the support surface -- think of flipping a coin from heads to tails. Although flipping is a common objective in industrial tasks such as parts inspection, mechanical assembly, and tool use, coding a bimanual robot with grippers to flip diverse objects is a significant challenge. In this paper, we show that a coding agent can autonomously develop and refine object-flipping strategies through iterative learning in physics simulations across diverse object geometries. Progressive skill acquisition, from basic handover to toppling and pushing, robust grasping and sensing, and thin-object manipulation with recovery, improves task success from 24.7% to 95.0%. The resulting graph-based code integrates high-level strategy selection with reactive control, enabling multi-stage flipping on physical robots.
bullets: Flipping objects requires stable 180° reorientation on a planar surface and is difficult to program across varied geometries.
The coding agent iteratively develops skills in physics simulation, progressing from handover to toppling, pushing, grasping, sensing, and recovery.
A graph-based controller combines high-level strategy selection with reactive control for multi-stage flips.
The approach supports thin-object manipulation and transfers to physical robots.
Reported results are based on iterative simulation learning; the abstract does not specify datasets or broader limitations.

papers.abstract: Underwater leader-follower formation control requires continuous relative-pose estimation despite degraded sensing conditions and limited onboard computation. This paper presents a reliability-adaptive multimodal perception framework for six-degree-of-freedom relative-pose tracking between two moving underwater robots. The framework integrates complementary visual, acoustic-ranging, and hydrodynamic measurements while accounting for their distinct physical characteristics and time-varying reliability. It adaptively weights modality contributions and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity, enabling efficient pose estimation on embedded hardware. Extensive experiments were conducted using a custom-built AUV platform, with 648 pool trials spanning two leader vehicle types, three illumination conditions, and nine trajectory patterns. Evaluation yields an average translational error of 3.8 cm and an average orientation error of 2.4°. On an onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the fusion network achieves an inference latency of 17.62 ms, providing a 2.69-fold speedup over the evaluated Transformer-based fusion baseline. Closed-loop experiments further demonstrate stable formation maintenance with a moving leader under onboard computational constraints. A multimodal dataset containing measurements from all 648 trials will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses continuous pose estimation under degraded underwater sensing and limited onboard computation.
Adaptively weights modalities according to their time-varying reliability and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity.
Across 648 pool trials, achieves 3.8 cm average translational error and 2.4° average orientation error.
Runs at 17.62 ms inference latency on a Jetson AGX Orin, reported as 2.69× faster than the evaluated Transformer-based baseline.
Closed-loop tests show stable formation maintenance; a dataset from all trials is planned for public release.

The system combines information-bottleneck visual encoding via IB-VE, physics-aware acoustic temporal encoding via PA-GATE, and hydrodynamic wake encoding with distributional regularization via KLD-WE to estimate the leader’s relative pose. The modality-specific encoders incorporate relevant physical and statistical structure, while the fusion module adjusts modality contributions according to their estimated reliability. The fused relative-pose estimate is provided to a sliding mode controller, supporting real-time formation control on resource-constrained AUV hardware.

papers.abstract: Attention scores candidate supports of an answer, which we call witnesses, and reads the scores at a temperature. We build a higher-order attention layer whose state lives on pairs of items: for a pair (a, b), each third item k is a witness judged through its legs (a, k) and (k, b). It reads witnesses at zero temperature, keeping the best and the number tied with it, passes on only bits comparing such counts, rebuilds its pair state from the input and these bits at every loop, and is trained from answers alone. Each choice removes one way soft attention fails at size: dispersed weight, unresolved gaps between learned scores, and a drifting soft state. In maximum retrieval it is right on at least 99.95% of sets 1,000 times larger than in training, on all ten seeds; trained with a soft count, the same network falls to 42% at 4,096 items. On CLRS-30 without hints, a general form of the layer (half its channels read at zero temperature, numbers embedded, state carried) beats the best published model, which uses hints on some tasks; the full cold layer is exact on every test input of 9 of the 12 tasks whose answers depend on numbers only through comparisons. From yes-or-no answers it decides 2-SAT and two-colouring exactly at 500 variables and, as our theory predicts, not parity equations. Beside a frozen 7B language model it chains family relations exactly at 1,000 statements after training on 16, where the model alone falls to 44%; finite checks on the weights prove every block that learned correct at every size, on acyclic contexts and given what the model reads. On CLUTRR it is right on every story of five to ten relations given the graphs, learning the 62 rules exactly; from text, with the model frozen, no hand-written rule and only a small read-in trained, it lifts an open 7B model from 33% to 65%, above every system we found without hand-written rules except frontier reasoning models.
bullets: Scores candidate witnesses between item pairs at zero temperature, retaining the best score and tie count rather than dispersed soft weights.
Rebuilds pair states from the input and comparison bits at each loop, avoiding unresolved score gaps and drifting soft states.
Achieves at least 99.95% accuracy on maximum retrieval sets 1,000× larger than training; a soft-count variant drops to 42% at 4,096 items.
On CLRS-30, the generalized layer beats the best published hinted model; the full cold layer is exact on 9 of 12 comparison-based tasks.
Supports exact 2-SAT, two-colouring, family chaining, and CLUTRR reasoning, while improving frozen language-model performance on text-based relational tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 4 | One block, run K times, and the four kinds of block we train. Cobalt: the yes-or-no tests, exact counts and verdict bits (cold); rose: real numbers, which a block carries from loop to loop. a, The network keeps one vector of 128 numbers for every ordered pair of items, its pair state. In the general setting the input’s items, facts and numbers enter it once, through a learned embedding. One block then reads the state and writes back to it, with the same weights in every loop. It reads through two learned tests per channel, A(i, k) and B(k, j). Half of its 128 channels count, for every pair, the middle items k that pass both tests (the witnesses) and hand on only two verdict bits per pair of channels: is one count larger, and are the two equal? The other half keep the strongest witness and hand on its strength, a number between 0 and 1. A gated mix of the bits and strengths is added to each cell, then the output of a small network applied to each pair. After the last loop a read-out takes the answer from the pair state: here, for shortest routes, each node points to the one before it. The block has 146,552 parameters, shared by every loop, and one loop costs n3 per channel. b, The four kinds of block in one grammar: the pair state (small square; rose tints, real numbers; cobalt cells, bits), the block (box, naming the channels it holds: count, the count-and-compare channels of a; best, the best-witness channels; or the general and the cold half), what one loop hands to the next (the arrow back; rose, a carried real state; cobalt, bits from which the state is rebuilt), and where numbers enter (into the state through an embedding, rose; into the block as comparisons only, cobalt; from a frozen language model, grey box). General: the general block of a, 97.04% on CLRS-30 with one block per task and 97.20% with one block for all thirty tasks. Cold: the cold block, into which numbers enter only as comparisons made inside the layer, its state rebuilt from bits every loop (kept bits, which only turn on, or free bits; with kept bits it rebuilds twice, and its comparison channels read a state without the bits their learned tests made); right on every test input, on every seed, on 9 of the 12 tasks whose answer depends on the numbers only through comparisons. General and cold halves: the general-and-cold block, one block for all thirty tasks, 96.55% at its registered read (weight-averaged parameters, K(n) loops) and 96.40% read like the general block (final parameters, eight loops), a loss of 0.46 points against our first general block for all thirty read the same way. Beside a language model: three kept bits per pair of mentions, monotone tests, tied legs and a read-out that can only say yes, reading relations from a frozen model; exact to 1,000 statements. Schematic, not data: everything in b (the icons and their cell patterns are drawn, not read from a model); in a, the tests drawn in the block are set by hand, as in Extended Data Fig. 1, and the tints of the pair state and of the bit and strength columns are illustrative.

papers.abstract: Constrained reinforcement learning in hybrid action spaces must coordinate discrete modes and mode-conditioned continuous controls under long-horizon cost constraints. Existing constrained hybrid-action methods typically optimize factorized policies directly in parameter space, whereas Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (CVPO) separates nonparametric improvement from parametric projection in its original continuous-action formulation. We introduce Hybrid Constrained Variational Policy Optimization (H-CVPO), extending this variational framework to hybrid action spaces. Under boundedness and strict feasibility, its constrained E-step has zero duality gap and, when the dual optimum is attained at positive temperature, yields a closed-form joint target distribution over hybrid actions through exponential reward-cost reweighting. Using the exact hybrid KL decomposition, we formulate a factorized M-step that fits both policy components to this target under separate discrete and conditional-continuous trust regions. For exact E/M updates, we prove fixed-reference surrogate improvement and conditional reward-cost bounds with a sufficient feasibility-margin condition. For approximate updates, we establish the existence of a dual minimizer under continuity on a compact domain and use residual-based admissibility to determine whether to project the target. Ablations identify cost-aware reweighting as an important contributor to constraint control. Extensive experiments in simulated hybrid-control environments show that H-CVPO achieves favorable reward-cost trade-offs compared with hybrid-action baselines.
bullets: Targets long-horizon cost constraints while coordinating discrete modes with mode-conditioned continuous controls.
Uses a constrained variational E-step with exponential reward–cost reweighting to form a joint hybrid-action target distribution.
Fits separate discrete and conditional-continuous policy components via an exact hybrid KL decomposition and trust regions.
Provides improvement, feasibility, and dual-optimization guarantees for exact and approximate updates under stated assumptions.
Ablations highlight cost-aware reweighting as important for constraint control; experiments are limited to simulated hybrid-control environments.

papers.tldr: H-CVPO extends variational constrained policy optimization to hybrid discrete–continuous actions, providing theoretically justified updates and favorable reward–cost trade-offs in simulation.

papers.abstract: The wide field of view of fisheye cameras and the simplicity of a monocular setup make monocular fisheye visual odometry (VO) attractive for robotic localization and mapping. Nevertheless, scale drift remains a major challenge over long trajectories. Unsupervised depth learning can help to mitigate this issue, but the pronounced distortion of fisheye images poses challenges for accurate depth estimation. This article presents S$^2$D-FVO, a monocular fisheye VO framework integrating spherical bundle adjustment (SBA)-guided unsupervised depth learning to improve scale consistency and depth estimation accuracy. Given that pixel reprojection residuals do not uniformly reflect angular deviations between viewing rays and that the first-order linearization of a scalar angular reprojection residual is insensitive to perturbations along one tangent direction, SBA employs tangent-space angular reprojection residuals derived from the spherical logarithmic map. These residuals retain sensitivity along both tangent directions, with their norms equal to the corresponding scalar angular residuals. A median depth-based scale regularization term is further integrated into SBA to constrain the reconstruction scale. Building on these formulations, SBA replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised depth learning, providing more reliable relative poses for view synthesis. In turn, depth estimates from the well-trained depth estimation network provide scale references for SBA, improving scale consistency while allowing individual 3-D landmark positions to be refined. Extensive experiments conducted on multiple public datasets, as well as two newly collected large-scale datasets, demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms representative existing approaches in both depth and trajectory estimation accuracy and is applicable to different camera models.
bullets: Addresses long-trajectory scale drift and fisheye distortion challenges in monocular VO.
Uses tangent-space angular reprojection residuals from the spherical logarithmic map to preserve sensitivity in both viewing-ray tangent directions.
Adds median-depth-based scale regularization to constrain reconstruction scale.
Replaces the pose estimation network during unsupervised learning, while learned depth provides scale references for bundle adjustment.
Experiments on public and newly collected datasets show improved depth and trajectory estimation and applicability across camera models.

papers.abstract: In most LLM agents, weights are fixed after deployment, so new information must be retained in external memory. Existing approaches often rely on predefined records and fixed organizational rules, which cannot readily accommodate evolving tasks and interactions. This raises the question: can LLM agents organize their own memory using ordinary documents? We introduce self-organized memory (SoMem), a framework that stores memory in linked documents. The agent decides what to summarize, how to group related information, and when to revise existing topics, and every summary it produces stays linked to the original interactions as evidence. The runtime validates updates and automatically derives temporal, relational, and recent-memory views from the organized content. At query time, the agent chooses what to search and read, following document links and inspecting original evidence as needed. On LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points, respectively. The constructed memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can further improve answer quality. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of agents organizing and using their own persistent memory through ordinary documents. Code is available at: https://github.com/Qi202/SoMem.
bullets: Fixed model weights require agents to store new information in external memory, but predefined records and rules struggle with evolving tasks.
The agent decides what to summarize, how to group information, and when to revise topics, while linking summaries to original interactions as evidence.
Runtime validation and automatically derived temporal, relational, and recent-memory views support flexible retrieval and inspection.
SoMem outperforms the strongest baseline by 2.66, 3.10, and 2.00 percentage points on LoCoMo, BEAM-100K, and LongMemEval-S, respectively.
Organized memory can be reused across models, and additional reasoning effort can improve answer quality.
