papers.abstract: An open-vocabulary segmentation readout silently loses a class deployed beyond its training categories. It still emits masks with high confidence, but the class never wins a single pixel. The training loss falls anyway, and mIoU can even rise while classes die. We show that which classes collapse is written in the class-name list alone. Before any image is seen, we rank each class's collapse risk from its text similarity to the training vocabulary alone. The ranking holds at AUROC 0.69-0.96 across nine model families, twelve backbones and eight pretraining recipes. Two further families, measured only after the predictions were written down, land in the same band. What the list writes, it can rewrite. With identical images and a class's counterpart moved in or out of the training list, retraining flips that class's gain over the frozen baseline by 21 IoU points; swapping in unrelated names changes nothing. We find a vocabulary-distance mechanism behind the collapse. Collapsed classes lose every vote to near-name neighbors, but in the frozen features they survive. Turning down the readout's amplitude, or stopping training early, brings them back, up to +16 points, without retraining; trained with its amplitude held down, the readout never collapses.
bullets: Some classes receive no winning pixels despite high-confidence masks, while training loss and mIoU may improve.
Text similarity to the training vocabulary predicts collapse risk before seeing images, with AUROC 0.69–0.96 across 9 model families, 12 backbones, and 8 pretraining recipes.
Changing whether a class’s near-name counterpart is in the training list can shift its IoU by 21 points, while unrelated names have no effect.
Collapse arises when near-name neighbors take every readout vote; the class remains represented in frozen features.
Reducing readout amplitude or stopping training early can recover collapsed classes by up to 16 IoU points; amplitude-constrained training avoids collapse.

papers.abstract: World models are widely considered to be a potential key component of model-based reinforcement learning and robot planning, but typically require task-specific training on substantial interaction data. We investigate whether a pretrained tabular foundation model (TabFM) can serve as a training-free dynamics model for world modeling by framing next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs, and where such a model helps and where it breaks. Across synthetic dynamical systems and robot locomotion benchmarks, TabFM is more accurate than LSTM and MLP models trained from scratch on the same limited transitions in almost all settings, and among regressors fitted to the same data it is the most accurate on locomotion, while a Gaussian process is more accurate on smooth low-dimensional systems. However, models trained on the full dataset remain substantially better on most systems. When rolled out autoregressively over multiple steps, TabFM's accuracy depends strongly on how much context it is given. With a short context, its rollouts quickly degrade to the level of a trivial baseline, whereas with a long context they improve substantially and, on one locomotion task, exceed a trained LSTM. Inference is also about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM. Overall, in their current state, we find that training-free priors are useful as predictors when data are scarce and enough context is available, but they are not yet a substitute for trained world models in planning.
bullets: Frames next-state prediction as in-context regression over transition pairs using a pretrained TabFM.
Outperforms from-scratch LSTM and MLP models in almost all limited-data settings; performs best among same-data regressors on locomotion.
Gaussian processes are more accurate on smooth, low-dimensional systems, while models trained on full data remain substantially better overall.
Autoregressive rollout quality depends strongly on context length: short contexts degrade quickly, whereas long contexts can outperform a trained LSTM on one locomotion task.
Inference is about three orders of magnitude slower than an LSTM, limiting current use in planning.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates training-free tabular foundation models as dynamics models for next-state prediction in world modeling.
papers.title: An Evaluation of Tabular Foundation Models as Training-Free World Models

papers.abstract: Feature subsampling is used to accelerate gradient-boosted trees, yet standard approaches fix the feature count in advance and largely ignore the split-gain evidence accumulated during training. We introduce CRAFT-GBM (Confidence-Ranked Adaptive Feature Tracking), a native LightGBM extension that uses this evidence to adapt which---and, by default, how many---features are searched each boosting round. CRAFT-GBM transforms root-split gains into bounded observations and constructs joint time-uniform bounds valid under adaptive, non-stationary training histories. In its default endogenous mode, after initialization, CRAFT-GBM retains exactly the features that cannot yet be ruled out as best, letting the selected feature-set size $K_t$ emerge from training history rather than a pre-specified fraction. With probability at least $1-δ$, every feature with the largest expected gain is retained jointly across all rounds after initialization. When a feature fraction $f$ is specified instead, CRAFT-GBM ranks features by their interval point estimates and provides an approximate top-$K$ guarantee for feature budget $K_f$. We implement CRAFT-GBM within LightGBM while preserving its native feature-bundling representation, and evaluate it across 14 public and synthetic dataset families and four noise-augmented settings. In the fully endogenous setting, CRAFT-GBM reduces per-fit training time by 39.74\% with 1.04\% lower test loss in the geometric mean across all 18 RQ1 experiments. Under pre-specified feature fraction $f$, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM also yields aggregate training-time reductions up to 13.52 percentage points larger than random feature subsampling, with no increase in aggregate test loss relative to full-feature LightGBM. Accumulated training evidence can thus support adaptive feature search with statistical guarantees while retaining the practical advantages of native gradient boosting.
bullets: Addresses fixed feature-count subsampling that overlooks split-gain evidence accumulated during training.
Uses time-uniform confidence bounds on root-split gains to track features that may still be best under adaptive, non-stationary histories.
Its default endogenous mode determines the number of searched features from training history; a specified-fraction mode supports approximate top-K selection.
Implemented as a native LightGBM extension while preserving feature bundling.

Across 18 experiments, endogenous CRAFT-GBM reduced geometric-mean training time by 39.74% with 1.04% lower test loss; the fraction-controlled mode improved time savings over random subsampling without increasing aggregate test loss versus full-feature LightGBM.

figures.caption: Figure 2: At f = 0.10, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM substantially reduces training time with essentially unchanged aggregate test loss. Shaded bands show pointwise 95% dataset-resampling intervals, reflecting sensitivity to the composition of the 14 dataset families. At f = 0.10, Exogenous CRAFT-GBM reduces aggregate training time by 62.74% with essentially unchanged test loss (−0.04%). Random subsampling by LightGBM-Fixed saves 49.22% time but raises loss by 4.60%. Thus CRAFT-GBM delivers 13.52 percentage points more time reduction without the aggregate loss increase seen with LightGBM-Fixed. Greedy mean-gain ranking (Mean ablation) and exposure balancing of features (Exposure ablation) save the same training time (63.83% and 64.71%), but incur greater test loss especially at smaller feature fractions (12.69% and 5.71% more test loss at f = 0.10). This contrast is consistent with the expected benefit of combining gain evidence with uncertainty in CRAFT-GBM, especially when the feature budget Kf is restrictive.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive feature subsampling with statistical guarantees reduces gradient-boosting training time, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: CRAFT-GBM: Selecting Best Features for Gradient-Boosted Machine Learning

papers.abstract: Wearables, mobile devices, and IoT platforms generate multimodal time-series data continuously and at scale, making efficient storage and transfer a primary concern. The same recordings are reused after collection by many downstream models, often at different temporal resolutions, so a compressed representation should be small, useful across resolutions, and produced at a bit rate known in advance. Prior work meets parts of this: symbolic and error-bounded compressors reconstruct accurately but fix resolution at compression time, learned codecs target one signal domain, and discrete tokenizers reconstruct without accounting for rate. We introduce CHORD, a coarse-to-fine compressor for heterogeneous multimodal time series. A residual cascade orders each payload from broad to fine temporal scales and synthesizes corrections through learned shapelet-inspired atoms. A shared pathway supplies a reusable synthesis basis across modalities, while private pathways retain capacity for sensor-specific morphology. Finite scalar quantization fixes the bit width of every modality and scale, so payload size is known before encoding, and scale dropout trains each coarse-to-fine prefix to be a valid reconstruction operating point. Across seven wearable-sensing and forecasting benchmarks, CHORD stays within 0.62 points of uncompressed classification accuracy on average at the 8x target, the smallest gap of any compressed method, with all resolutions decoded from one payload.
bullets: Targets efficient storage and transfer for wearable, mobile, and IoT time-series data reused by downstream models.
Uses a coarse-to-fine residual cascade with learned shapelet-inspired atoms to encode broad-to-fine temporal information.
Combines shared synthesis pathways across modalities with private pathways for sensor-specific patterns.
Finite scalar quantization fixes bit width and payload size, while scale dropout makes each prefix a valid reconstruction point.
Across seven benchmarks, it stayed within 0.62 accuracy points of uncompressed classification at 8× compression, with all resolutions decoded from one payload.

papers.abstract: LiDAR point clouds and 3D semantic occupancy represent two distinct modalities capturing fine-grained metric geometry and dense volumetric semantics, respectively, holding natural potential for mutual complementarity. However, existing world models typically forecast these modalities independently or cascade them heuristically, missing the opportunity for reciprocal cross-modal regularization. To address this, we propose \textbf{LO-World}, a unified 4D world model that forecasts both modalities within a shared BEV latent space. This single-stream formulation enables dense semantics and metric geometry to mutually reinforce each other, while eliminating multi-pipeline redundancy. Specifically, LO-World couples an efficient hybrid range-voxel autoencoder with a flow-matching generator that caches historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LO-World outperforms prior state-of-the-art baselines, improving occupancy forecasting IoU by 10.9% and reducing LiDAR Chamfer Distance by 30.1%. Meanwhile, it sustains a real-time throughput exceeding $25$~FPS on a single RTX 4090. Our code is available at https://github.com/lzzzzzm/LO-World.
bullets: Addresses the missed mutual complementarity between semantic occupancy and metric LiDAR geometry.
Uses a unified single-stream BEV latent model with a hybrid range-voxel autoencoder.
Employs flow matching with cached historical context to reduce iterative sampling latency.
Reports 10.9% higher occupancy forecasting IoU and 30.1% lower LiDAR Chamfer Distance than prior state-of-the-art baselines.
Exceeds 25 FPS on a single RTX 4090, though the abstract does not specify broader limitations or evaluation scope.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly plan and run experiments in automated laboratories. These experiments keep running while the model reasons and run on schedules with hard deadlines. If an LLM-generated answer arrives late, the system executes a safe fallback action instead, such as rejecting a sample. This creates a systems problem that standard serving metrics do not capture. An answer that matches the fallback adds no value, and answers that differ from the fallback may require more reasoning time. Reporting answer quality and latency separately can therefore overstate the value of reasoning. We test this on synthetic sample decisions, where the best choice is known exactly and a runtime enforces the deadline. We compare one LLM's fast mode, which answers directly, with its thinking mode, which reasons first. In a prespecified replay of 1,200 new decisions, thinking answers that missed a deadline were worth about five times as much as on-time ones. Multiplying the on-time rate by the mean answer value predicted about twice the value that thinking delivered. This prediction overstated thinking's advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision, and by 0.0191 in a repeat on 300 new decisions. Both 95% confidence intervals excluded zero. In a single-GPU Qwen3-8B experiment using simultaneous request bursts, raising the number of requests from 8 to 56 reduced the share of thinking answers that met a 45 s deadline from 79.2% to 1.4%, although total output tripled. Evaluations of LLM agents for laboratories should therefore measure each answer's value and arrival time together and score the action that actually runs.
bullets: Late reasoning answers can be valuable when they differ from a safe fallback, while on-time answers may add little value if they match it.
In a replay of 1,200 decisions, missed-deadline thinking answers were worth about five times as much as on-time ones.
Estimating value as on-time rate × mean answer value overstated thinking’s advantage over fast mode by 0.0241 per decision; a 300-decision repeat showed a 0.0191 overestimate.
Under burst load on a single-GPU Qwen3-8B setup, meeting a 45-second deadline fell from 79.2% at 8 requests to 1.4% at 56, despite tripled output.
Laboratory-agent evaluations should score the action actually executed, jointly accounting for answer quality and arrival time.

papers.title: Late but Valuable: Why Deadlines Change the Measured Value of LLM Reasoning

papers.abstract: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning (MER) requires perceiving and integrating emotion cues from multiple modalities. Recent advances increasingly leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to enhance reasoning capacity. However, due to the inherent heterogeneity in conveying emotions across modalities, these models often suffer from modality imbalance and confront flawed emotion understanding. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis on MER models and uncover two key empirical insights. (i) In MER, modality imbalance manifests two distinct failure modes: unimodal over-reliance and insufficient cross-modal utilization, which call for different intervention strategies. (ii) MLLM layers exhibit implicit functional hierarchies in multimodal emotion processing, playing separable roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating cross-modal information. Motivated by these observations, we propose a Layer-Aware Modality Rebalancing (LAMR) framework by explicitly aligning intervention strategies with layer roles. Specifically, we first introduce two quantized metrics for adaptive layer role profiling. In each layer, Modality Entropy (ME) measures the dispersion of modality contributions, and Cross-modal Intensity (CMI) captures the strength of cross-modal interactions. Then, we respectively enhance modality equilibrium in stabilization layers and cross-modal propagation in integration layers. Extensive experiments on two comprehensive MER benchmarks demonstrate that LAMR effectively mitigates modality imbalance and improves emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones, without additional training.
bullets: MER imbalance has two failure modes: over-reliance on one modality and inadequate cross-modal use.
MLLM layers serve distinct roles in stabilizing unimodal representations and integrating modalities.
LAMR profiles layers with Modality Entropy and Cross-modal Intensity.
It balances modality contributions in stabilization layers and strengthens cross-modal propagation in integration layers.
Experiments on two MER benchmarks show improved emotion reasoning across diverse MLLM backbones.

papers.abstract: Retinal disease monitoring with optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) relies on segmentation of vessels and the foveal avascular zone (FAZ). Promptable models such as SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) allow click-based refinement, but without adaptation SEEM segments thin vessels poorly and needs many clicks. Fully fine-tuning its 342 million parameters on a few hundred images is costly and risks overfitting, and parameter-efficient methods such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) usually adapt only the encoder. Yet SEEM reads every candidate mask from one feature map at quarter resolution, too coarse for vessels one to three pixels wide. This study introduces the Read-out Basis Adapter (RBA), whose read-out branch generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution. Each candidate accesses them through its own vector and a zero-initialised projection, so the model starts exactly as SEEM. The encoder branch, a standard rank-1 LoRA, supplies the information needed to tell arteries from veins. RBA adds 0.47 million trainable parameters. Under simulated error-driven clicks, with the ground truth used only to place them, RBA outperforms LoRA, Conv-LoRA andAdaptFormer on OCTA-500 3mmlarge vessels. Averaged over three seeds, it reaches an intersection over union (IoU) of 85.16% and a Dice score of 91.93%, 2.90 and 1.72 percentage points above Conv-LoRA. On the 6 mm subset, one run gives margins of 4.35 and 2.76 points. The gain extends to arteries, veins and ROSE-O but not to the FAZ. In SEEM, adaptation capacity pays more at the mask read-out than in the encoder.
bullets: SEEM’s quarter-resolution mask feature map is too coarse for 1–3-pixel vessels and requires many corrective clicks without adaptation.
RBA generates 32 image-specific basis maps at half resolution, with candidate-specific access through a zero-initialized projection so it initially matches SEEM.
A rank-1 LoRA encoder branch helps distinguish arteries from veins; the full adapter adds 0.47 million trainable parameters.
With simulated error-driven clicks, RBA achieves 85.16% IoU and 91.93% Dice on OCTA-500 3 mm large vessels, outperforming Conv-LoRA by 2.90 and 1.72 points.
Improvements extend to arteries, veins, and ROSE-O, but not the FAZ; results suggest adaptation is more valuable in mask read-out than in the encoder.

papers.abstract: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.
bullets: Addresses the overlooked matrix structure of transformer weights in existing unlearning methods.
Combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured, spectral optimization.
Derives the spectral update as the steepest-descent direction for transformers with linear layers and normalized inputs/outputs.
Evaluates memorization, privacy, and utility using their harmonic mean.
Outperforms a broad range of baselines and approaches a retain-trained reference across these measures.

papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) produce explicit chains of thought to improve transparency, but they frequently overthink, generating long yet inefficient reasoning chains that inflate computational costs and risk introducing errors. While numerous reinforcement learning methods struggle to penalize verbosity to achieve conciseness, they typically apply the penalty uniformly across lengthy sequences, which leads to credit confounding, that is, the failure to distinguish essential reasoning steps from superfluous ones. In this paper, we study a measurable proxy for this confounding: high-entropy tokens that often coincide with surface transition points where reasoning re-enters verification. Based on this insight, we propose Adaptive Entropy-Sparing (AES), which selectively spares high-entropy tokens that occur before an efficient in-group reference, while penalizing overlength high-entropy suffix tokens associated with superfluous branching. Our AES thereby navigates the suppression-exploration trade-off, reducing overthinking while preserving average reasoning accuracy. We also present an entropy-length model that motivates why local uncertainty can serve as a proxy for future reasoning cost. Across eight reasoning benchmarks, AES reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% while increasing mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over the base models, consistently outperforming existing efficiency-oriented methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/MobiusDai/AES.
bullets: Addresses overthinking in large reasoning models, where uniformly penalizing long outputs can suppress essential reasoning steps.
Uses high-entropy tokens as a proxy for reasoning transitions and future computational cost.
Spares high-entropy tokens before efficient in-group references, while penalizing high-entropy suffixes linked to unnecessary branching.
Across eight reasoning benchmarks, reduces reasoning length by up to 52.9% and increases mean accuracy by up to 3.8% over base models.
Scope: targets verbosity and efficiency in explicit reasoning chains; the abstract does not specify broader generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Distribution Matching Distillation~(DMD) enables strong few-step diffusion generation by matching the student distribution to a pretrained teacher. Existing improvements to DMD often augment its supervision or modify its optimization machinery. We ask a complementary question: \emph{can DMD diagnose its own updates using signals already produced during training?} DMD inherently computes the discrepancy between a pretrained teacher and a fake model tracking the student distribution, but conventionally uses it primarily to determine the distribution matching direction. We find that the magnitude of this teacher--fake disagreement provides additional diagnostic information. Across extensive experiments, large disagreement in the high-noise regime consistently coincides with substantially higher-energy DMD updates. This reveals a dual role of disagreement: it determines not only \emph{where} the student should move, but also provides an intrinsic signal of \emph{how aggressively} the update should be applied. Based on this observation, we introduce Disagreement-Aware Distribution Matching Distillation (DA-DMD), which activates only in the high-noise regime and continuously modulates the update strength according to teacher--fake disagreement. DA-DMD reuses quantities already available during DMD training and requires no additional model, evaluator, or inference-time modification. We show that it exactly recovers vanilla DMD outside the selected region, reduces update energy only through selected samples, and exhibits redescending influence under extreme disagreement. Across multiple diffusion backbones, DA-DMD consistently improves few-step generation at the same inference cost. On SD3.5-L, DA-DMD improves HPSv2 from $28.23$ to $30.93$, while achieving a $64.4\%$ average win rate over DMD2.
bullets: DMD disagreement indicates both the direction and appropriate aggressiveness of student updates.
Large high-noise disagreement is associated with substantially higher-energy DMD updates.
DA-DMD continuously modulates update strength using signals already available during DMD training.
It leaves vanilla DMD unchanged outside the selected high-noise region and requires no extra model or inference-time changes.
Across multiple backbones, it improves generation at the same inference cost; on SD3.5-L, HPSv2 rises from 28.23 to 30.93.],

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.
bullets: Motivation: Generalist robot policies may fail on a single interpretable step despite otherwise completing the task.
Method: Replays of 21 decisions under reworded instructions identify a misbinding, then copy the rewording’s per-layer effect into language-model MLP weights.
Result: Held-out success increased from 27 to 106 of 128 episodes, with 81 fixes and 2 regressions; random same-size edits had no effect.
Scope: Editing the language model worked best; edits to the action expert or head helped less or not at all, and unrelated failure-targeted edits did not help.
Caveat: Substantial outcome variability motivates paired reruns of the unedited policy and confirmation on held-out seeds.

papers.abstract: Answer probes applied to chain-of-thought hidden states are often read as evidence that a language model has already decided its final response. This reading overlooks a competing signal, the candidate the model is about to mention. We introduce emission-controlled dual-target probing (ECDP), which fits the same low-rank reader family separately to the imminent mention and to the final answer at identical positions, with target-specific nulls and thresholds fixed before any fit. On correct DecisionDepth (DD) rollouts in which a distractor is mentioned before the final answer, Qwen3.5-4B decodes the next mention at .966 (null .234) but the final answer only at .221 (null .186), an emission gap of .696 [.648, .744]; Llama-3.1-8B gives .575 [.514, .632]. This pattern is not universal. In a pre-specified evaluation of Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled on held-out MMLU questions, using a full-prefix attention reader over every thinking position, both targets are decodable and the final answer is read far more strongly (mention-minus-answer lift -.398 [-.459, -.336] at layer 22 over 467 questions). Model, task, positions, and reader change together between these settings, and an attempted matched comparison on DD produced no valid statistics because the imminent-mention probe did not train reliably, so we do not identify what reverses the order. On DD, planted-signal controls show that the reader recovers an injected final-answer signal at one tenth of full dose. Answer-candidate decodability is therefore target-relative and protocol-dependent: a strong answer readout does not by itself establish when a model commits, and a probe that fails to train is not evidence that the information is absent. ECDP is a practical control for distinguishing imminent text emission from evidence of a settled decision.
bullets: ECDP fits separate low-rank probes for the imminent mention and final answer at identical chain-of-thought positions, with pre-fixed target-specific nulls and thresholds.
On correct DD rollouts with an earlier distractor, Qwen3.5-4B strongly decoded the next mention (.966) but weakly decoded the final answer (.221); Llama-3.1-8B showed the same direction.
The pattern is protocol-dependent: on held-out MMLU with Qwen3-8B, both targets were decodable and the final answer was more strongly read at one layer.
Because model, task, positions, and reader changed across settings—and a matched DD comparison failed to train—the study does not explain why the ordering reverses.
Planted-signal controls show the reader can recover an injected final-answer signal at one-tenth of full strength.

papers.abstract: One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.
bullets: Nearest-of-m training selects the closest of m sampled futures, avoiding deterministic mode averaging with one network evaluation.
For frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens and enumerable futures, m=16 outperformed 50-step flow matching, one-step flow generators, and energy-score generators at matched parameter counts.
The method keeps rollouts on the token manifold and improves long-horizon stochastic Push-T error by one third with per-step self-rollout matching.
Increasing m flattens mode probabilities and can cause memorization in nonrepeating contexts; the key factor is expected codebook miss distortion, not merely miss probability.
Continuous high-dimensional outcomes remain under-dispersed, and better risk estimates did not improve planning success.

papers.title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens

papers.abstract: Attention heads in video Transformers vary greatly in functional importance. Understanding their contributions requires examining not only which heads are important, but also how they participate in collective computation within the network. We study this collective computation from two perspectives: the downstream use of head outputs and the composition of interactions across layers. Ablation analyses of four video Transformers show that high-importance heads identified on a single task also support other video understanding tasks and help preserve the representational structure that distinguishes different videos. Representational responses to head ablation correlate weakly with head importance after the attention module, but more strongly after the MLP in the same block. Adapting this downstream processing through MLP-only fine-tuning further improves the use of lower-importance head outputs. Meanwhile, through composition across layers, sets of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances support stronger perturbation responses at distant tokens than sets with longer distances. Their joint ablation causes even greater performance loss than ablating equally sized sets of high-importance heads, revealing collective contributions not fully captured by individual importance rankings. These findings highlight collective computation as a key perspective for understanding attention head function: functional contributions depend on both how head outputs are used downstream and how local interactions compose across layers.
bullets: High-importance heads transfer across video understanding tasks and help preserve distinctions between videos.
Head importance predicts representational effects weakly after attention but more strongly after the block’s MLP.
MLP-only fine-tuning improves the use of outputs from lower-importance heads.
Across layers, groups of heads with shorter spatiotemporal attention distances produce stronger distant-token responses.
Jointly ablating such head groups causes larger performance losses than ablating equally sized individually high-importance groups.

papers.abstract: In modular grounding a frozen detector proposes regions and a vision-language model (VLM) selects one, at lower cost than letting the VLM decode a box, but it is unclear where such systems fail. We hold perception fixed---every trained selector chooses among the same frozen proposals, which contain the referent for at least $99.8\%$ of RefCOCO/+/g queries---and vary the selection interface one factor at a time for two VLMs of one family (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B). On RefCOCOg, what the selector reads matters more than how it is built: the VLM's image-conditioned query encodes the referent's location and beats a text-only query by $0.15$--$0.18$ with every head tested (by less for InternVL3-8B, whose vision encoder differs; one head tested). The remaining errors are rankings among a few top candidates; a cross-attention selector supervised with every valid box reaches the VLM's coordinate decoding on RefCOCOg, and with Qwen2.5-VL on RefCOCO/+ when also trained on their data. Beyond that distribution it does not: on Ref-L4's Objects365 images, mostly of categories outside training, every trained head falls to $0.19$--$0.28$ while Qwen decoding keeps about $0.8$ (InternVL3's drops too), neither a wider detector prompt nor a class-agnostic proposer closes the gap, and on public reasoning benchmarks Ref-Adv-s and RefBench-PRO full-budget heads trail decoding by $0.19$--$0.37$ although proposals cover most referents. A trained verifier reduces to an existence probe on the VLM's query state and does not beat the VLM's yes/no answer on public no-target benchmarks.
bullets: Frozen detector proposals contain the referent for at least 99.8% of RefCOCO/+/g queries, isolating proposal selection as the main bottleneck.
Image-conditioned VLM queries encode location and outperform text-only queries by 0.15–0.18 on RefCOCOg across tested selection heads.
Cross-attention selection can match coordinate decoding in-distribution, especially with supervision on the target data.
Out of distribution, selection accuracy drops to 0.19–0.28 on Ref-L4, while coordinate decoding remains about 0.8; broader proposals and prompts do not fix the gap.
Verifier training mainly probes whether a target exists and does not outperform the VLM’s direct yes/no answers on no-target benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses VLM proposal selection in grounded referring tasks; relevant to multimodal LLMs and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Where Does Proposal Selection Fail? Diagnosing Frozen Vision-Language Queries over Detector Proposals
papers.tldr: Frozen-proposal grounding usually fails at selecting among candidate regions—not at detecting the referent—and selection generalizes poorly beyond training distributions.

papers.abstract: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.
bullets: The study compares matched action representations in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark.
Equivalent interactions described differently can increase data requirements, while omitting peel thickness creates irreducible ambiguity in material-removal predictions.
Surface-relative coordinates improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection when local observations are accurate.

Jointly centering the surface and tool removes sensitivity to their shared translation, but uncertainty in coordinate frames, incorrect contact geometry, and execution deviations cause distinct failures.
The findings support designing representations that preserve outcome-relevant action–state relationships for reuse across spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Exploration in deep reinforcement learning (RL) for continuous control is commonly driven by temporally uncorrelated Gaussian (white) action noise, which leads to jerky motions with locally constrained exploration. In contrast, temporally correlated coloured noise, particularly pink noise, has been shown to support more efficient exploration in RL. Motivated by these findings, we inquire whether scheduling changes to the noise colour over the course of training can outperform white noise for continuous control robotics. We perform a systematic study of 49 linear schedules between white and red noise, together with generalised state-dependent exploration (gSDE), on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks with a Fetch arm and a Shadow Dexterous Hand. We find that the noise colour at the end of training does not affect learning efficiency or end performance, whereas fading towards red noise halves the jerk of exploration in every task. Balancing learning efficiency, end performance and smoothness, red noise emerges as the preferred strategy: it learns as efficiently as pink noise with almost 2-fold less movement jerk. We therefore recommend exploration schedulers that fade towards red noise as the default for off-policy robot learning.
bullets: White action noise causes jerky, locally constrained exploration in continuous-control RL.
The study evaluates 49 white-to-red noise schedules and gSDE on four sparse-reward manipulation tasks.
The final noise colour does not affect learning efficiency or end performance.
Fading toward red noise halves exploration jerk across all tasks.
Red noise matches pink noise’s learning efficiency with nearly 2× less jerk and is recommended as a default for off-policy robot learning.

papers.abstract: Sensory delays create temporal misalignments between the state of the environment and the observations available to an agent, turning Markovian control problems into partially observable ones. In this work, we inquire whether such misalignments can be mitigated during training by using hindsight to recover aligned state-action transitions. We introduce Hindsight Critics, an asymmetric extension of the Soft Actor-Critic for reinforcement learning under partial observability. The critics are trained on hindsight-aligned transitions whereas the actor learns from the resulting privileged value estimates despite only having access to delayed observations. Comparisons against delay-aware and unaware baselines on the DelayBench suite show that Hindsight Critics can partially compensate for observation delays without requiring modifications to the agent's observations during deployment.
bullets: Observation delays misalign environmental states and agent observations, causing partial observability.
The method extends Soft Actor-Critic asymmetrically: critics use hindsight-aligned transitions, while the actor uses their privileged value estimates.
Experiments on DelayBench compare the approach with delay-aware and delay-unaware baselines.
Results show partial compensation for observation delays without modifying observations at deployment.

Sigmoid curves are fitted to those returns and used to compute the AUC scores. SAC achieves high zero-delay performances but is particularly sensitive to delays. Hindsight Critics can partially mitigate this degradation.

Table 2: AUC scores of Hindsight Critics (HC) compared with other common RL algorithms across multiple environments. The highest score for each environment is highlighted in bold.

papers.abstract: Fleets of driving vision-language-action (VLA) models are developed one domain at a time: each operator finetunes a shared base model on private data, producing specialized experts that are costly to consolidate into a single model. Weight merging loses accuracy as heterogeneous domains accumulate, and dense mixture-of-experts routing is prohibitively expensive to combine them. We present DeltaForge, to our knowledge the first post-hoc mixture-of-experts VLA for driving, which consolidates N independently finetuned per-domain models into a single multi-domain model from their weights and a small proxy set alone. When different operators finetune the same base model, their weight updates end up sharing a lot of structure. We exploit this by decomposing all the updates together using singular value decomposition (SVD), splitting each one into a shared part (the same across all domains) and a tiny domain-specific part. The router then only needs to work with those tiny domain-specific pieces, not the full expert weights, which is what keeps the approach efficient. Then two cooperating clip-level blind routers, one over the VLM reasoning experts and one over the flow-matching dynamics experts, are trained from soft labels on the proxy dataset. Across six diverse domains spanning urban, off-road, and highway driving on cars, trucks, and all-terrain vehicles (ATVs), DeltaForge approaches the accuracy of the per-domain experts and surpasses every merging, routing, centralized, and federated baseline at close to single-model parameter and compute cost. Adding a new domain requires only projecting its weight update onto the shared basis with no end-to-end retraining needed. The resulting model also generalizes to domain combinations it was never explicitly trained on.
bullets: Addresses the accuracy loss and computational cost of merging heterogeneous, privately trained driving experts.
Jointly decomposes expert weight updates with SVD into shared components and small domain-specific residuals.
Uses two clip-level blind routers for VLM reasoning and flow-matching dynamics, trained from soft labels on a small proxy set.
Across six diverse driving domains and vehicle types, it approaches per-domain expert accuracy and outperforms reported baselines near single-model cost.
New domains can be added by projecting their updates onto the shared basis, without end-to-end retraining; the model also generalizes to unseen domain combinations.

Composition is trained on a small proxy set, and a new domain opts in by projecting its delta onto the frozen basis.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
bullets: Addresses stale observations and reduced control rates caused by placing large VLA backbones in the closed-loop control path.
Runs a slow vision-language model and fast flow-matching action head asynchronously via LCM.
Fuses stale semantic features with fresh visual input and uses desynchronized training plus adaptive temporal aggregation to handle latency.
Maintains 20 Hz control from 0.8B to 8B backbones, while the synchronous pipeline drops from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz on RoboTwin.
Achieves higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline on a real humanoid with dexterous hands.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. DASH architecture. The policy is split into a slow VLM (System 2) and a fast action head (System 1), deployed as three concurrent processes (environment, VLM server, and action server) coupled by a decentralized, non-blocking latest-value bus (LCM). The VLM runs off the control loop and publishes a context (the hidden states of the routed VLM layers) that the action head reads with latest-value semantics, so the control rate is set by the action head alone.

Fig. 7. Matched simulation episodes, synchronous inference (top) vs. DASH (bottom). Frames are sampled at equal intervals of simulated time up to the completion time of the successful run; done marks completion, and still running marks the run that later times out.

Fig. 2. (a) Uncertainty grows along the prediction horizon: the early portion of an action chunk is reliable, while its distant tail admits increasingly different future actions. (b) Frequent chunk updates curb divergence: synchronous inference executes the long, uncertain tail of each chunk, so a new prediction can trigger a large correction; DASH refreshes chunks often and stays on the reliable early portion.

Fig. 4. Desynchronized training data. The two visual channels are sampled at different times so the training inputs reproduce the staleness met at deployment, while the supervision target remains anchored at the action head’s timestamp.

Fig. 5. Adaptive interpolation for temporal aggregation. The fractional offset measured from the true chunk arrival interval is split into a whole-tick shift and a linear interpolation between adjacent entries, with the residual fractions accumulated so the alignment tracks elapsed execution time.

papers.abstract: Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.
bullets: Introduces 350 deterministic scenarios across seven evidence-update regimes, each with normative posterior references at every evidence prefix.
Tests nine representation conditions to separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata effects.
Finds entity grounding is a major source of weak-model errors, while removing semantic relations reduces strict belief-state accuracy by 15.3 points on relation-dependent cases.
Structured lists can outperform full graphs, and graph shuffling causes no consistent harm, suggesting graph serialization alone provides no reliable benefit.
Belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic, revealing mid-trajectory failures missed by endpoint-only evaluation; resources support offline, hardware-free reproduction.

papers.abstract: An answer can match the reference for a complete agent history even when the reader's visible history does not determine it. We study this distinction using executable device logs. Our protocol separates reference agreement, certified evidence sufficiency, and context-appropriate behavior. Insufficiency requires two legal histories yielding byte-identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology and query cutoffs certify sufficient prefixes. On 80 confirmation histories, Qwen3-32B matches 87 hidden references among 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, with only seven appropriate abstentions. A fixed-input DeepSeek-V4-Flash replication matches 85 and abstains on 21 of the same 203 instances. Each reader makes 1,600 requests. Compact CSV's estimated appropriateness effects remain inconclusive: +3.16 percentage points, clustered 95% interval [0.00,6.57], for Qwen and +2.46, [-1.84,6.94], for DeepSeek. A separate held-out judge study achieves 99.38% correctness but retains support errors and truncations; a deterministic baseline solves all constructed cases. These results support an evaluation diagnosis across two hosted reader configurations, not gains for a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.
bullets: Using executable device logs, the protocol tests whether visible histories uniquely determine the reference answer.
Insufficiency is certified by finding two legal histories with identical visible contexts but different answers; public chronology certifies sufficient prefixes.
On 203 insufficient raw-prefix instances, Qwen3-32B matched 87 hidden references and abstained appropriately only seven times; DeepSeek-V4-Flash matched 85 and abstained 21 times.
Compact CSV’s estimated appropriateness effects were inconclusive for both readers, and a separate judge study still showed support errors and truncations.
The findings diagnose evaluation issues across two hosted configurations, not improvements to a general memory system or natural-language evidence assessment.

papers.abstract: While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Visuomotor policies rely heavily on visual inputs, yet images provide an inherently ambiguous signal under viewpoint change: similar scenes may appear markedly different across viewpoints, while distinct states may share certain visual overlaps. A policy must therefore infer not only the task-relevant state, but also how it is visually projected under a particular camera configuration. This entanglement of viewpoint-dependent appearance and task-relevant state can make learning inefficient and limit generalization to unseen viewpoints. Recent work has begun to address this challenge through camera-ray conditioning and representation learning using geometric cues to induce invariance. However, providing camera information as additional context does not by itself ground visual representations in how the task scene is visually projected, while geometric alignment without camera context can introduce spurious correspondences by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection. We propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework that aligns joint image-ray representations using robot proprioception. PAIR encourages observations with similar robot states to remain close in representation space across viewpoints, providing a structured grounding signal for learning viewpoint-robust features. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train Diffusion Policy (DP) or post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. In simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks with camera variation, PAIR consistently outperforms the behavior cloning baseline without ray conditioning by 12.7% and 26.7% points, respectively, demonstrating stronger generalization to unseen viewpoints. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io.
bullets: Viewpoint changes entangle task-relevant state with camera-dependent visual appearance, hindering imitation-learning generalization.
The method applies contrastive learning to bring joint image-ray representations with similar robot states closer across viewpoints.
PAIR can train Diffusion Policies or post-train vision-language-action models.
On simulated and real-world camera-variation benchmarks, it improves over behavior cloning without ray conditioning by 12.7 and 26.7 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Robots are typically evaluated in episodes that begin from a reset, while industrial work consists of repeated jobs whose outcomes affect subsequent operations. Evaluating such work at scale requires simulation of task-critical physical interactions, construction of industrial environments, and measurements of performance as scene state persists. We present HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0, a framework for simulating, generating, and evaluating industrial robot work. Given a human-specified workplace and task, the framework defines a world pairing a scenario of scene variants and process logic with an evaluation defining a job, metrics, and a rubric. HOLIDAYFACTORY 1.0 comprises three components. HOLIDAY-SIM extends Newton's SDF-based hydroelastic contact with additional constitutive laws and a semi-implicit primal-dual solver, couples stateful actuator dynamics to articulated motion, and derives tactile and joint observations from simulated states. Agentic world construction generates simulation-ready assets and scene variants using geometric and interaction checks, and proposes task-conditioned evaluations for human confirmation and executable checks. 24/7-BENCH introduces seven industrial tasks in which jobs are evaluated without resetting the scene, measuring completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy. Controlled studies characterize the proposed contact, actuator, and tactile models and examine the effectiveness of verification-guided world construction. Experiments on scene and evaluation generation further reveal the limitations of model critics and the difficulty of ensuring that generated evaluations faithfully capture task requirements. We examine job-level evaluations with scripted trajectories (e.g., code-as-policy) but have not yet compared policies over persistent runs.
bullets: Targets the gap between reset-based robot benchmarks and real industrial workflows, where each job changes the state for subsequent jobs.
Combines HOLIDAY-SIM for contact, actuator, articulated-motion, tactile, and joint-state simulation with agentic construction of verified workplace assets and scene variants.
Introduces 24/7-BENCH with seven industrial tasks evaluated using completed, failed, and unfinished jobs, throughput, latency, and motor energy.
Controlled studies assess the simulation models and verification-guided world construction, while generation experiments expose weaknesses in model critics and evaluation fidelity.
Evaluations currently use scripted trajectories; policies have not yet been compared over persistent runs.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have demonstrated remarkable effectiveness in mitigating hallucinations by incorporating external knowledge. However, the retrieval process inevitably introduces noise, posing significant challenges to RAG robustness. Fundamentally, noise robustness is a composite competency encompassing noise identification, retrieval filtering, and robust reasoning. Unfortunately, existing methods often fail to capture this holistic nature, typically restricted to single-dimensional enhancements or hampered by noise-induced optimization interference. To address these limitations, we decompose RAG robustness into three sub-tasks: knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning. Accordingly, we propose ARMOR, an Adaptive Curriculum Meta-Learning for Noise Robust RAG Reasoning. Inspired by the teaching process, ARMOR introduces an adaptive task scheduler as a teacher to curate training plans according to the absolute learning progress of RAG generators (Student). Distinct from GRPO, ARMOR utilizes inter-group advantage estimation during learning to effectively mitigate mode collapse caused by limited output spaces. Experiments on three complex reasoning datasets (2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA) indicate that ARMOR achieves synergistic improvements in retrieval noise robustness, significantly outperforming baselines in output quality.
bullets: Decomposes noise robustness into knowledge boundary perception, retrieval verification, and robust reasoning.
Uses an adaptive task scheduler to tailor the training curriculum to the generator’s learning progress.
Applies inter-group advantage estimation to reduce mode collapse under limited output spaces.
Evaluated on 2WikiMultiHopQA, MusiQue, and HotPotQA, with reported improvements in noise robustness and output quality over baselines.

(Right) The RAG Generator (Student) generates multiple rollouts to learn the selected task. (Bottom Right) Inter-Group Advantage Estimation computes reward advantages across the global batch scope rather than within groups, effectively mitigating mode collapse and stabilizing the decoupled training process.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth estimation has advanced through large-scale pretraining and strong visual backbones, yet metric depth remains sensitive to scene-level scale. Indoor rooms and outdoor driving scenes occupy very different depth ranges, but most depth decoders infer this global structure implicitly from visual features. We ask whether scene-level semantic structure can instead act as an upstream prior that shapes the metric output space before dense prediction. We present LangDepth (SemanticBins), a monocular depth architecture that couples strong visual features with a scene-conditioned output space. A frozen CLIP encoder and a learnable bank of scene- and geometry-oriented concept keys convert image features into a compact scene descriptor, without requiring per-image text or an external captioner. A Scene Prior Module (SPM) maps this descriptor to a scene-conditioned metric depth interval, providing a global range anchor before dense decoding. In parallel, a DINOv2-L backbone with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features, and a Per-Pixel Assignment Network (PPAN) assigns pixels to the scene-prescribed bin structure. A confidence gate fuses the dense visual estimate with the SPM prior. We train LangDepth jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI under a modest supervised depth budget, without web-scale depth supervision or pseudo-labelled depth data. A single model achieves delta_1 = 0.960 on NYU, 0.960 on KITTI, 0.887 on DIODE indoor, 0.946 on iBims-1, and 0.861 on SUN RGB-D. Beyond aggregate accuracy, the SPM predicts compact indoor ranges and much wider outdoor KITTI ranges, the gate becomes SPM-dominant on outdoor scenes, and perturbing the routed scene context causes large drops on KITTI and iBims-1. These results support scene-conditioned output spaces as a practical and interpretable mechanism for cross-domain monocular depth estimation.
bullets: Addresses scene-scale variation between indoor and outdoor environments, which can make metric depth estimation sensitive to global range.
Uses a frozen CLIP encoder and learned scene/geometry concept keys to form a compact scene descriptor without per-image text or captioning.
A Scene Prior Module predicts a scene-conditioned depth interval, while DINOv2-L, an FPN, and PPAN perform dense depth decoding with confidence-gated fusion.
Trained jointly on NYU Depth V2 and KITTI with modest supervised depth data, the single model reports strong results across NYU, KITTI, DIODE, iBims-1, and SUN RGB-D.
Scene priors adapt to compact indoor versus wider outdoor ranges; disrupting routed scene context substantially harms performance on KITTI and iBims-1.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: LangDepth (SemanticBins) pipeline. The input image is encoded by a frozen CLIP ViT-B/32, whose image features are routed through learnable scene and geometry concept keys to produce a compact scene descriptor z. The Scene Prior Module (SPM) uses only z to predict a scene-conditioned range (dmin, dmax), ordered bin centres {ck}Kk=1, and a global prior over those centres. In parallel, DINOv2-L with a lightweight FPN extracts dense visual features. PPAN conditions these features on z and predicts per-pixel bin weights {Wk}Kk=1 and a gate map g. Depth fusion forms the visual estimate dvis = ∑ k Wkck and the SPM prior dSPM = ∑ k πkck, then outputs d̂ = g ⊙ dvis + (1− g)⊙ dSPM.

Table 4: Confidence gate statistics. KITTI is strongly SPM-dominant, while indoor datasets are more balanced or slightly vision-dominant.

papers.abstract: LLM inference has two phases with different bottlenecks: LLM prefill runs once per request and is compute-intensive. Decoding repeats for every output token and is limited by memory bandwidth. To address the challenges associated with this issue, different solutions have been proposed. All of these solutions use the same model for both prefill and decode phases. We propose BridgeKV, which uses a larger model for prefill and a smaller model of the same family for decoding. A lightweight KV-stitching module translates the larger model's prompt cache into the smaller model's cache layout. It handles differences in cache shape and representation through learned local layer mixing and separate nonlinear maps for keys and values. With both models frozen, we train the module to align their caches and make the smaller model follow the larger model's next-token predictions. A second training stage adds low-rank adapters when further task adaptation is needed. Across six model pairs and five datasets, BridgeKV outperforms fine-tuned small-model baselines with matched trainable parameter budgets in all 30 settings. It closes up to 80% of the quality gap to using the larger model for both phases. On one A40 GPU, Llama-3.1-Instruct-8B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B achieves 3.0X faster requests than the larger model alone, with latency close to the smaller model alone. BridgeKV can improve the hardware and system solutions that separate prefill and decode phases across GPUs. A separate serving simulation models request arrivals, queues, and cache transfer. For Llama-3.1-Instruct-70B to Llama-3.2-Instruct-1B, it predicts up to 33.86X faster requests and 27.5X lower energy use than using the larger model for both prefill and decode phases.
bullets: Targets the compute-heavy prefill phase and memory-bandwidth-limited decoding phase with different model sizes.
Uses a lightweight KV-stitching module with local layer mixing and separate nonlinear key/value mappings to reconcile cache differences.
Trains the translation module with both models frozen; optional low-rank adapters support further task adaptation.
Across six model pairs and five datasets, it outperformed matched-budget fine-tuned small-model baselines in all 30 settings and closed up to 80% of the quality gap to the large model.
Reported serving gains include 3.0× faster requests for an 8B-to-1B pair and simulated gains up to 33.86× faster with 27.5% lower energy for a 70B-to-1B pair.

papers.abstract: Language-model post-training modifies weights through cumulative updates and successive displacements, yet existing studies report seemingly conflicting spectral properties: nearly full-rank updates and low stable-rank changes. We show these observations are compatible and characterize update directions during training. For singular values following $σ_i \propto i^{-α}$ with $0 < α\leq 1/2$, we prove that stable rank becomes negligible relative to fixed-energy rank as dimension increases. Full singular value decompositions of selected OLMo-2-7B updates confirm this separation: three proximal policy optimization (PPO) attention updates have stable ranks of 9.6-18.3 but require 532-1,222 singular components to capture 80% of their energy. We next compute consecutive checkpoint-displacement cosines from full-model inner products. Across nine publicly released reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) stages, all 131 adjacent pairs have negative cosines on their native checkpoint grids, including PPO and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) trajectories. Supervised fine-tuning comparisons across four model families show configuration-dependent alignment, including negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama. Finally, a controlled OLMo-2-1B study with three paired seeds and a 2,048-token response cap compares group-relative advantages against a learned critic with generalized advantage estimation (GAE). At matched 60-rollout windows, late-training mean cosines are +0.259 and +0.012, respectively; the paired critic-minus-group difference is -0.247 (seed-level 95% interval [-0.358, -0.137]). These findings distinguish spectral concentration, energy coverage, and trajectory direction, and demonstrate that the advantage system influences directional alignment under matched training conditions.
bullets: Stable rank and fixed-energy rank measure different properties; power-law spectra can make stable rank small even when many singular components capture most energy.
Full SVDs of selected OLMo-2-7B PPO attention updates found stable ranks of 9.6–18.3, while 532–1,222 components were needed for 80% energy.
All 131 adjacent checkpoint pairs across nine RLVR stages had negative displacement cosines on their native grids, including PPO and GRPO.
SFT direction alignment was configuration-dependent, with negative late-training cosines for Mistral and FP32 Llama.
In a controlled OLMo-2-1B comparison, critic-based GAE produced less aligned late-training directions than group-relative advantages, with a paired cosine difference of -0.247.

papers.selection_reason: Spectral and directional analysis of LLM post-training; relevant to LLM architecture understanding.
papers.title: Spectral Rank and Step-Direction Dynamics in Language-Model Post-Training
papers.tldr: Language-model post-training can produce updates that are nearly full-rank yet energy-concentrated, while successive update directions often reverse—an effect influenced by the advantage-estimation system.

papers.abstract: Optical flow requires reliable matching from sufficient visual context and precise motion at every pixel. Existing methods such as WAFT match and estimate flow on the same coarse grids, then recover dense flow through learned upsampling, without explicitly linking visual support for matching to dense flow reconstruction. Our key insight is that dense pixel-level flow does not require equally dense matching. We decouple correspondence scale from flow resolution by adapting the size and shape of spatial supports to image structure for reliable matching, while reusing these supports for precise dense flow reconstruction. We realize this in Flow from Adaptive Token Estimation (FATE), whose token supports expand within coherent regions and contract near motion boundaries. Shared pixel-to-token associations pool features for matching and reconstruct pixel flow from token motions. Flow supervision jointly trains pixel grouping, token matching, and flow estimation without grouping labels, allowing FATE to anticipate which pixels are likely to move together from appearance alone. Trained on FlyingChairs/FlyingThings3D, FATE achieves the highest zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, a critical setting given scarce real-world flow labels. For visible pixels, FATE improves accuracy within coherent regions, and more near motion boundaries. Its largest gains occur where direct matches are unavailable: Occluded or out-of-frame pixels account for roughly 10% of valid pixels but 50% of WAFT's total error. Experiments show that adaptive correspondence through pixel-to-token grouping enables reliable matching and precise pixel-level flow, improving generalization to unseen real scenes.
bullets: Decouples correspondence density from flow resolution, avoiding uniformly dense matching.
Adapts token supports to image structure: larger in coherent regions and smaller near motion boundaries.
Shares pixel-to-token associations for feature pooling, token matching, and dense flow reconstruction.
Joint flow supervision learns pixel grouping without grouping labels and helps infer shared motion from appearance.
Trained only on synthetic data, FATE achieves the best zero-shot accuracy on Sintel Final and KITTI, with notable gains near boundaries and for occluded or out-of-frame pixels.

papers.abstract: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.
bullets: Addresses partially observed robotics, where uncertainty about state can hinder control.
Maintains competing state-history hypotheses using particles generated by one pretrained diffusion model.
Reweights particles by agreement between predicted and observed measurements.
Uses these weights for both state estimation and action selection, without modifying the model or adding test-time information.
Simulation results in navigation and vision-based manipulation show improved estimation and task performance over unfiltered action generation.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) requires large amounts of interaction data or a reliable simulator, both hard to obtain for nonlinear soft robotic hardware. Recent work shows that a time-scale separation inherent to soft robot dynamics justifies their reduction to low-dimensional invariant manifolds, known as adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs). We demonstrate that an aSSM-reduced model, a simple polynomial ordinary differential equation learned purely from pre-collected data, can serve as an RL training environment. On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, we train a trajectory-tracking policy in 3 hours on a six-dimensional aSSM-reduced model and deploy it without fine-tuning, whereas reproducing this policy training extrapolates to 3 years of hardware interaction. Our policy tracks dynamic targets with 40% lower error than otherwise identical policies trained on a 4.8-million-parameter recurrent neural network (RNN) or a 1.7-million-parameter transformer, which take 13 and 100 hours to identify, against 5 minutes for our mathematically justified 6,924-parameter model.
bullets: Soft-robot RL is hindered by costly hardware interactions and unreliable or unavailable simulators.
A time-scale separation reduces the robot dynamics to a low-dimensional adiabatic spectral submanifold (aSSM).
A 6,924-parameter polynomial ODE learned from pre-collected data provides the RL training environment.
On a pneumatically actuated soft arm, the policy trained in 3 hours deployed without fine-tuning and achieved 40% lower tracking error than comparable RNN- and transformer-based approaches.
The approach remains demonstrated on one soft-arm trajectory-tracking task and depends on the validity of the aSSM reduction.
