papers.abstract: Unlike the brain, artificial neural networks (ANNs) suffer from "catastrophic forgetting": complete overwriting of solutions when re-training on new functions ("concept shift") or on a disjoint domain of the current function ("domain shift"). ANNs require each batch of data to be roughly representative of the complete distribution, a typically expensive and impractical requirement. In this paper, we introduce Functional Task Networks (FTNs), a method of continual learning and knowledge transfer modeled after several properties of the mammalian neocortex. FTN is formulated as a distributed, stochastic mixture of experts in which a sparse, binary routing mask is computed at inference time using a small support sample of input-output pairs. Per-batch reconfiguration of the router during training, together with mask-overlap-filtered replay, shapes a basis of overlapping, partially trained subnetworks. Unrelated tasks route through mostly separate assemblies, related tasks overlap on shared components. On block-sequentially trained continual learning and knowledge transfer tasks FTN retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and attains the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators. The learned mask-overlap geometry tracks the known concept-sharing structure where available. We show experimentally that under correlated concept shift, support-set mask reconfiguration is necessary even for retention. Under domain shift, the distributed bank with replay is sufficient to handle retention without the configurer. Forward transfer, or head-start, and backward transfer, are also contributed by support-set mask configuration.
bullets: Targets catastrophic forgetting under concept shift and domain shift without requiring each batch to represent the full data distribution.
Uses a distributed stochastic mixture of experts with sparse binary routing masks computed from a small support set of input-output pairs.
Combines training-time router reconfiguration with mask-overlap-filtered replay to form overlapping subnetworks for related tasks and separate assemblies for unrelated tasks.
Retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and achieves the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators.

Support-set reconfiguration is necessary for retention under correlated concept shift, while replay alone suffices for retention under domain shift; configuration also supports forward and backward transfer.

papers.abstract: A purely data-driven method grounded in the theory of adiabatic spectral submanifolds (aSSMs) was recently used to model and control nonlinear soft robotic simulators. Here, we extend the methodology to learn aSSM-reduced models from data collected from hardware soft robotic platforms. Specifically, we learn a five dimensional (5D) aSSM-reduced nonlinear ordinary differential equation (ODE) that accurately models the dynamics of a soft-helicoid trunk robot. We then use this ODE in a model predictive control scheme to demonstrate real-time precision control across various challenging closed-loop trajectory-tracking tasks, ranging from 2D to 3D trajectories with static and dynamic constraints. We find that our methodology enhances accuracy and precision across all control tasks compared to available data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning. While we focus here on a soft-helicoid trunk robot, our methodology relies solely on hardware data and is therefore applicable to a broader class of soft robotic systems.
bullets: Learns a nonlinear reduced-order ODE directly from hardware data.
Integrates the learned model into a model predictive control scheme.
Demonstrates closed-loop tracking with static and dynamic constraints.
Reports improved accuracy and precision over data-driven linear methods and model-free reinforcement learning.
The hardware-data-based approach is intended to generalize to other soft robotic systems.

papers.abstract: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. Homepage: https://wrld.github.io/surgtap-3d/
bullets: Addresses limited scale, diversity, and interaction-aware 3D supervision in existing surgical datasets.
Provides 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from robotic and manual surgeries.
Uses contact-region prompting, tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement to convert monocular videos into structured annotations.
Includes temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks despite occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and fast motion.
Benchmarks instrument and tissue tracking, displacement estimation, deformable reconstruction, and surgical action understanding.

papers.abstract: Energy claims for efficient neural networks are often inferred from operation counts. We report direct GPU energy measurements on two workloads that batch very differently, recurrent policies in GPU-vectorised multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) and mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, and ask one question of both: can the rows of a batch be made to share computation, across the batch and over time, at a measured saving? On recurrent policies the answer so far is no. Shared activity patterns exist but rarely last one step, masking a frozen policy fails, and trained-in masks succeed only because a fixed mask is equivalent to a narrow GRU, at 11x the energy of a small dense policy in our implementation. Test-time steering adds nothing beyond re-picking on either workload. On MoE models the answer is yes, and granularity decides how much: on Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware routing reads 25-31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05, with benchmark changes within noise at 500 items, and uses 12-18% less energy per token on a fused forward. We also introduce persistence-aware OEA, a one-parameter rule that keeps the batch-aware cut with about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch 32-64, though its energy has not yet been measured. These are pilot measurements on one GPU type, and we state their limits.
bullets: The study tests whether batch rows can share computation across examples and over time, using direct GPU energy measurements rather than operation counts.
For recurrent MARL policies, shared patterns are too short-lived; masking and test-time steering do not provide useful savings, while trained-in masks reduce the model to a narrow GRU.
For Qwen3-30B-A3B, batch-aware MoE routing reads 25–31% fewer expert weights within KL 0.05 and reduces fused-forward energy per token by 12–18%.
Persistence-aware OEA achieves about 40% fewer new experts per step than native routing at batch sizes 32–64, but its energy impact remains unmeasured.
Results are pilot measurements on one GPU type and are limited to the studied workloads and implementation.

papers.abstract: Compression can preserve a language model's average accuracy while selectively degrading individual capabilities. Whether these losses follow method-specific patterns or a transferable order is unclear. We applied seven perturbation and compression methods to eight instruction-tuned models, scoring 16 tasks in four answer formats against preregistered predictions. Short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order under four random perturbations with different mechanisms (median correlation 0.90) and, within each model, under pruning and quantization (0.875). Intact answer margin, answer frequency and answer format predicted this order. Fragility profiles measured under random perturbation predicted which tasks and facts compression removes first and, after four-task calibration, held-out task accuracy (median absolute error 0.11-0.12, against 0.20-0.21 for uniform decline); profiles borrowed from other model families did almost as well. The order did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization or hold for long-form tasks. Within short answers, what compression removes is predictable before deployment.
bullets: Across four random perturbations, short-answer capabilities failed in nearly the same order (median correlation 0.90).
Within individual models, pruning and quantization produced similarly ordered failures (correlation 0.875).
Answer margin, answer frequency, and answer format predicted which capabilities degraded first.
Random-perturbation fragility profiles predicted compression-related task loss and held-out accuracy after four-task calibration.
The ordering did not transfer across models under GPTQ quantization and did not apply to long-form tasks.

Top, the answer of Qwen2.5-7B to one item as the noise dose rises. b, Every damage removes the same capabilities first, each at its own dose. c, Three separable axes: how securely the task is held, how familiar the answer is and how much of it must be produced. Because the effects add, the failure front is a plane, and more damage moves it towards the robust corner; the fact axis was measured within recall tasks only. d, Measured once under random damage, in the model itself or in other models, the profile predicts what compression removes first and how much accuracy it leaves. papers.selection_reason: Analysis of LLM capability ordering under compression.
papers.title: Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation
papers.tldr: Language-model capabilities tend to fail in a predictable, shared order under many perturbations and compression methods, but this predictability is limited across model families and long-form tasks.

papers.abstract: Textured 3D meshes specify object geometry and appearance, making them a natural query for finding a particular asset in an image. We introduce LocateAnyMesh, a vision-language model that uses the mesh itself as part of its prompt. A frozen 3D encoder maps colored surface points to a compact token sequence, which a learned connector places alongside image and instruction tokens. We evaluate two grounding models with PPAT mesh tokens: LAM-Select selects image-region proposals, while LAM-Direct predicts coordinates directly. Neither requires rendered query views or view-template matching. New objects require a single encoder pass and no object-specific fine-tuning. LAM-Select improves localization on the reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation. Secondary experiments compare mesh encoders, and a LAM-Direct study isolates surface color. A single-seed LAM-Select continuation supplies pointing and mesh-only description evidence without replacing the reported localization model. The results support mesh tokens as a query representation, with remaining limitations in presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.
bullets: Uses a frozen 3D encoder and learned connector to combine colored mesh tokens with image and instruction tokens.
Introduces LAM-Select for selecting image-region proposals and LAM-Direct for directly predicting coordinates.
Avoids rendered query views and view-template matching; new objects need only one encoder pass without object-specific fine-tuning.
LAM-Select improves localization on reported real-image suites and the official BOP YCB-V evaluation.
Limitations include presence decisions, identity binding, proposal coverage, and descriptive fidelity.

papers.abstract: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.
bullets: Frozen monitors degrade to near-chance failure ranking after task or policy changes.
SFF updates only the monitor’s last linear layer after each episode using its success/failure label; its threshold adapts after successes.
The method runs at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core.
Under unannounced drift, SFF outperformed a frozen monitor on 4 of 5 simulated test suites and a reset strategy on all suites.
Across 434 real-robot runs involving four VLAs, SFF outperformed the frozen monitor after task or policy switches and exceeded a full reset in an exploratory comparison.

papers.abstract: Continual instruction tuning often preserves old skills with task-private modules. Inference still requires selecting the right module from the prompt alone. We introduce Task-Isolated Latent Adapter Continual Training (TILA-CT), a replay-free method that makes each task module self-indexing. Each task receives a latent memory and adapter bank in a frozen LLM. During adaptation, the memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context. For access, its persistent state provides the routing prototype used by a shared prompt-only router. On the 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, TILA-CT achieves 65.19 acquisition and 63.98 final macro score, with 1.38 points of average forgetting. A middle-reversed order gives 65.38 acquisition and 64.17 final macro score. Across 6 backbones, final scores remain within 1.5 points of acquisition. Ablations support memory-derived routing keys and causal gathering. Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9\%, and oracle routing recovers 1.21 final macro points. These results separate preserved task computation from learned access to it.
bullets: Targets the access problem in continual instruction tuning: selecting the correct task module from a prompt alone.
Uses a frozen LLM with task-isolated latent memories and adapter banks; memories gather causal-prefix information and inject task-conditioned context.
The memories’ persistent states serve as routing prototypes for a shared prompt-only router.
On an 8-task CT-Pipeline stream, it reports 65.19 acquisition, 63.98 final macro score, and 1.38 average forgetting; results are similar under reversed task order.
Final macro routing accuracy is 93.9%, while oracle routing adds 1.21 final macro points, highlighting routing as a remaining limitation.

The shared router selects one task-private module using a key derived from the task’s persistent latent memory. The selected memory gathers causal-prefix information and injects task-conditioned context through adapters at each adapted layer. Pink marks frozen backbone computation, green marks learned router and adapter computation, and gray marks stored modules or intermediate representations.

papers.abstract: Creating high-quality 3D content has traditionally required specialist expertise and experience with complex tools. The growing ecosystem of AI-assisted creativity demands accessible and intuitive 3D generation systems. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising directions, yet extending their generative capabilities to 3D remains fundamentally challenging because existing 3D representations are not naturally compatible with language-based reasoning. Current approaches either depend on expensive fine-tuning or impose restrictive structural priors that sacrifice expressiveness and exclude organic shapes. We argue that the mismatch between LLM-native reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations is a core bottleneck of LLM-driven 3D generation. To address this, we introduce the Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), a representation designed around semantically meaningful, interpretable part-level abstractions that are naturally understood by both humans and LLMs, enabling expressive, editable, and open-domain 3D generation without imposing restrictive geometric priors or expensive fine-tuning. Building upon HPS, we introduce SurfScaff3D, an interactive framework for text and image-to-3D generation. HPS inherits the flexibility of B-spline patches, while exposing an interface that leverages open-world capabilities of foundation models to reliably generate 3D. Its hierarchical part-level semantic labels enable targeted, natural-language edits at any level of granularity without re-running generation. Further, HPS offers explicit per-patch control over surface detail, enabling more expressive geometry capable of representing arbitrary objects. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art LLM-based 3D generation methods demonstrate strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between LLM reasoning and conventional 3D parameterizations.
Introduces Hierarchical Patch Scaffold (HPS), built from flexible B-spline patches with interpretable, part-level semantics.
Supports interactive text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation without expensive fine-tuning or restrictive geometric priors.
Enables targeted natural-language edits at multiple granularities and explicit per-patch surface-detail control.
Experiments report strong geometric fidelity, semantic alignment, and flexible editing across diverse object categories.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of SurfScaff3D. SurfScaff3D iteratively constructs an HPS representation by programmatically generating surface geometry and verifying its local geometry through rendered views. HPS organizes geometry as a hierarchical semantic tree of B-spline surface patches with explicit patch-level control over surface variation, enabling both structured mechanical objects and organic shapes. The examples illustrate how frequency and amplitude help in modelling diverse objects. A critic evaluates rendered outputs and provides targeted feedback, forming a closed-loop refinement process that progressively improves prompt alignment and geometric fidelity. The critic loop executes for a fixed number of N iterations unless an early stopping criterion is met.

Figure 2. Qualitative Comparison of SurfScaff3D. We provide qualitative examples of SurfScaff3D against similar works, on the left we represent methods which allow greater geometric flexibility but require fine-tuning, in the middle we show methods which benefit from the zero-shot generalizability of modern LLMs but suffer from restrictive geometric priors. On the right we show SurfScaff3D using the open-source Kimi K2.6 [20] and Claude Sonnet 4.6 [4] as generation backbones, respectively. Each row corresponds to a single object prompt, all methods are generated using the identical prompts to ensure a fair qualitative comparison.
Figure 14. System prompt for SurfScaff3D critic agent.

Figure 12. Editing capabilities of our model. We display the original 3D object alongside the edited result. The corresponding ShapeTalkbased text prompts used to guide the edits are shown on the arrows.
Figure 13. System Prompt for SurfScaff3D Generator Agent.

Figure 4. Surface Variation. An organic broccoli model generated by SurfScaff3D, demonstrating the expressive capacity of the HPS smoothness parameters. By modulating the local smoothness parameters sf and ωf , the model synthesizes complex, highfrequency organic geometry without losing geometric coherence.

Figure 10. Qualitative Samples for text-to-3D generation. We show samples generated by SurfScaff3D from the object categories of ShapeNetCore [8], Toys4K [34] and OmniObject3D [40] datasets. The corresponding MARVEL-40M+ level-3 text prompts are displayed below each result.

Figure 16. Failure cases of SurfScaff3D. The model can misjudge the orientation and relative positioning of object parts (left), and in some cases leaves parts detached from the body, producing visible gaps in the generated surface (right).
Figure 11. Qualitative samples for image-to-3D. We demonstrate the performance of SurfScaff3D on diverse image inputs. The source conditioning images are provided below each resulting 3D asset.

Figure 6. Qualitative Image-to-3D Comparison. We present qualitative comparisons of various organic, synthetic and CAD objects. The source image is provided without any textual description of the object. HPS allows greater flexibility in geometry.
Figure 15. Prompt appended to SurfScaff3D critic agent when an image is provided.

Figure 5. Human-as-the-Critic Refinement. SurfScaff3D allows integration of the user as a real-time critic within the generative loop. By providing natural language feedback, the human critic can drive targeted and personalized refinements.
Figure 7. HPS allows more intuitive editing, consuming fewer tokens.
Figure 9. Prompt for editing existing HPS representations.

Table 6. Comparison of capabilities and representations of related 3D generation and editing frameworks. TF = training-free; PS = decomposition into explicitly labelled semantic parts; IR = inference-time iterative/interactive refinement; PE = part-level/local editing without regenerating the complete object; TG-Gen = text-to-3D generation from scratch; TG-Edit = text-guided editing of an existing asset; IM = image-conditioned input. 1CAD-Coder’s text input is a fixed instruction template rather than an object description, and all its reported results are image-conditioned. 2Neither method trains a task-specific model, but both rely on per-instance test-time optimization (ShapeCraft uses score distillation for texturing, and MvDrag3D uses deformation and score distillation). 3The Articraft paper describes only local edits made during generation, though its released code also supports text-guided editing of a completed asset. 4Prox-E’s superquadric primitives carry only a numeric index and colour rather than semantic part labels. 5Neither method supports editing natively. For Table 3 of the main paper, we provide the source shape in each model’s own format along with the edit instruction.
Figure 8. Critic score plateaus for SurfScaff3D (Claude Sonnet 4.6) after 2-3 iterations.

Table 1. Evaluation of Text-to-3D Generation. We evaluate the prompt fidelity using CLIP, ULIP scores, and VQA pass rate and 3D quality using FPD [32] and an Elo scoring based on GPT-5.4-mini [26] preferences (GPT represents an independent LLM family which was not a part of any of the evaluated pipelines). We evaluate generation across three 3D datasets on captions from MARVEL-40M+ [33]. The zero-failure rate of SurfScaff3D across different backbone variants demonstrates the reliability of HPS as an intermediate representation.

Table 2. Image-to-3D. We evaluate image-conditioned 3D generation on OmniObject3D and DeepCAD, reporting geometric accuracy (Chamfer, F@0.05), conditioning fidelity (CLIP-I), and novel-view reconstruction quality (LPIPS).

Table 3. Editing. We evaluate the editing capability of various LLM-based text-to-3D models. We employ CLIP, ULIP and VQA scores along with FPD to evaluate the quality of the edited 3D assets and utilise edit prompts from ShapeTalk [1].

Table 5. Isolating Impact of HPS. In Cloud, the agent outputs a point cloud without additional structure. In Control, each patch is specified by control points instead of surface points. HPS is far more effective than both. All settings are evaluated without critic iterations and with the same set of in-context objects, to isolate the impact of the representations.

Table 4. Impact of Surface Variation. Pairwise preference (GPT5.4-mini [26], same protocol as the Elo scores in Table 1) between the HPS output and the same output exported without surface variation (w/o SV), per dataset, across two open-source backbones. For each backbone, the two columns add up to the number of objects in the dataset (55, 105 and 71). Higher is better ↑.

Table 7. SurfScaff3D with other backbones. SurfScaff3D with each backbone, evaluated on OmniObject3D under the same protocol as Table 1 of the main paper. The MiMo and DeepSeek runs use three critic iterations, with Gemini 2.5 Pro [11] as the critic. Active parameter counts are reported since all three backbones are mixture-of-experts models.

papers.abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
bullets: Latent-action assignments vary drastically across training runs and numerical precision, despite similar robot motion inputs.
The method adds a straight-through similarity loss to align a video-trained tokenizer’s code geometry with macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv) activity.
On held-out shape categories, PMv alignment reaches 0.52 versus 0.20–0.26 for released or no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for random kinematic encoders.
Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer, but a hand-designed initial-stroke-direction descriptor scores higher (0.65).
A shuffled-PMv control still scores 0.41, and downstream manipulation effects are specified for future testing rather than reported.

Dashed (0.42): the kinematic yardstick, each session’s 95th percentile of 100 random nonlinear encoders of pen motion (mean 0.26), averaged over sessions (Section A); only the PMv tokenizer exceeds it. The 95th percentile of the encoders’ four-session means is lower (0.39), and the shuffled tokenizer also exceeds that. Dotted (0.65): a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke’s initial direction, which exceeds every tokenizer. (B) The same score at every scored checkpoint (mean over sessions); PMv and shuffled PMv are emphasized, and the dashed line is the same yardstick. Single checkpoints are noisy because each session’s score is a rank correlation over ten distances, which is why the final checkpoint was fixed as the read-out in advance.

Every targeted tokenizer raises reconstruction error, to 1.35–2.05× the no-prior level; the PMv tokenizer reaches the highest alignment, at the second-highest cost.

papers.title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have achieved significant progress in locomotion and manipulation, enabling traversal over rough terrain and richer interaction with the environment, such as moving obstacles. However, most traditional navigation methods assume non-interactive environments and focus only on traversal. While Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches relax this assumption, prior efforts have largely focused on flat environments and reactive interaction, rather than predicting object movability and planning ahead. These limitations become critical in outdoor rough-terrain scenarios, where robots must jointly reason about terrain traversability and object movability. In this work, we address NAMO for humanoid robots in cluttered outdoor rough terrain by proposing a hybrid planning framework that combines semantic priors from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) with embodied robot interaction data through a Gaussian process (GP) residual model. The GP corrects the VLM-derived movability prior to produce embodiment-grounded probabilistic movability estimates, which are then incorporated into hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning. The proposed approach allows humanoids to jointly leverage locomotion and manipulation for efficient and safe navigation, representing the first solution to NAMO in rough terrain through predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.
bullets: Addresses Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) for humanoids in cluttered outdoor rough terrain.
Combines VLM semantic priors with a Gaussian process residual model trained from embodied interaction data.
Produces probabilistic estimates of whether objects can be moved, while accounting for robot-specific capabilities.
Uses hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning to jointly coordinate locomotion and manipulation.
The abstract presents it as the first rough-terrain NAMO approach based on predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.

papers.abstract: A deployed language model does not merely answer questions. It spends computation, consumes time, consults evidence, exposes memory, invites or avoids human review, and sometimes makes mistakes whose consequences are radically unequal. Yet LLM systems are still commonly compared as if the relevant object were a single model and the relevant outcome were a single benchmark score. This paper argues that the unit of analysis should instead be the deployment policy: the mechanism that decides when to retrieve, when to remember, when to call a larger model, when to verify, and when not to answer at all. We introduce risk-adjusted deployment efficiency (RADE), a system-level objective that scores the utility a deployment delivers net of inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected failure cost, while treating harms that cannot be priced as hard budgets alongside constraints on latency, privacy, and resources. The framework brings selective routing, retrieval and governed memory, efficient specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and human escalation into a common account. We then examine five deployment regimes in which the same nominal LLM capability leads to different rational architectures, and propose a reporting protocol based on risk-coverage behavior, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load. The central claim is modest but consequential: frontier capability should be treated as a resource to allocate, not a default state to maintain. A safe and sustainable system is not the one that always uses the strongest model; it is the one that spends capability where the reduction in risk or increase in utility justifies the cost.
bullets: Argues that deployment policy—not a standalone model or benchmark score—is the proper unit of analysis.
Defines risk-adjusted deployment efficiency as utility minus inference, retry, oversight, and priced expected-failure costs.
Treats unpriced harms, latency, privacy, and resource use as constraints or hard budgets.
Unifies routing, retrieval, governed memory, specialization, uncertainty estimation, abstention, and escalation.
Proposes reporting risk-coverage, end-to-end cost, update drift, memory exposure, evidence quality, and escalation load across five deployment regimes.

papers.abstract: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of assessing pretrained model fit to a new deployment and estimating remaining adaptation-data needs.
Introduces training-free metrics based on the flow-matching objective and predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations.
Distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across four embodied foundation model families in real and simulated manipulation.
On 17 RoboCasa365 tasks, FlowEval correlates with success-rate gains from additional adaptation data for Pi-0.5 and GR00T.
Provides a lightweight diagnostic, though its demonstrated scope is manipulation deployments and the evaluated model families.

papers.abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
bullets: Models environmental ground truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior as distinct components.
Integrates model-predictive and learning-based exploration, safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive guidance.
Simulation studies show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion.
Supervisory task allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D detection (Mono3D) hinges on recovering depth from a single image, for which the geometric formulation $z \approx f \cdot H / h_{2D}$ is widely adopted due to its simplicity and direct grounding in projective geometry. We show that this formulation harbors a systematic, projection-induced bias: substituting the 2D bounding-box height $h_{2D}$ recovers the depth of an object's visible front surface rather than its center, causing size-dependent underestimation that persists even under ground-truth inputs. We address this front-surface bias with MonoPCA, a unified framework built on a projection-consistent reformulation. At its core, PCDepth retains the measurable $h_{2D}$ and closes the gap to center depth through an orientation- and size-aware correction derived from perspective geometry, eliminating the bias without introducing ill-posed regression targets. Because PCDepth couples depth to predicted object size and orientation, attribute perception becomes essential. We therefore introduce GeoAlign, a teacher-student framework that transfers geometric representations from Vision Foundation Models into a lightweight student, strengthening attribute perception at no inference cost. Across four challenging benchmarks, MonoPCA achieves SoTA performance, including a +1.44% AP$_{3D}$ gain on the KITTI leaderboard and +2.80% on Omni3D$_{OUT}$. Code is available at https://github.com/alanzhangcs/MonoPCA.
bullets: The common depth estimate based on 2D box height systematically underestimates object-center depth, even with ground-truth inputs.
PCDepth retains measurable 2D height and applies an orientation- and size-aware perspective correction without ill-posed regression targets.
GeoAlign transfers geometric representations from vision foundation models to a lightweight student at no inference cost.
MonoPCA reports state-of-the-art results across four challenging benchmarks, with gains of 1.44 AP3D on KITTI and 2.80 on Omni3D_OUT.
The approach depends on accurately perceiving object size and orientation because these attributes are coupled to depth estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of MonoPCA. The conventional geometric depth z = f ·H/h2D recovers the visible front surface rather than the object center, causing a systematic projection bias. PCDepth corrects this bias analytically by adding an orientation- and size-aware offset, making depth an explicit function of the predicted 3D size and yaw. This shifts the bottleneck onto attribute accuracy, which GeoAlign strengthens by distilling representations from a Mixture-of-Backbone (MoB) teacher into a ResNet student via Hierarchical Feature Alignment (HFA).

Figure 2: Geometric basis of PCDepth. (a) Source of the front-surface bias. Under perspective projection, the 3D bottom center (red) is self-occluded by a nearer surface point (green) that projects higher on the image plane, while the visible bottom of the box corresponds to a still-closer point (yellow), giving h′ 2D < h2D. The conventional estimate z = f ·H/h2D therefore recovers the frontsurface depth rather than the center depth. (b) h′ 2D is depth-dependent. As the center depth changes from z1 to z2, the surface point defining h′ 2D shifts (green to purple), so h′ 2D is not directly observable and its regression is ill-posed. (c) Recovering center depth via an optical-axis correction. zgeo recovers the front-surface depth, displaced from the object center by an offset ∆ along the optical axis: ∆ ≈ W/2 at γ = 0◦ (Left), ∆ ≈ L/2 at γ = 90◦ (Middle), and ∆ ≈ L 2 | sin γ| + W 2 | cos γ| for arbitrary yaw (Right), giving z = zgeo +∆.

Figure 1: (a) Depth error under ideal inputs. We evaluate the GeoDepth formulation [69] using ground-truth f , H , and h2D. Even with these oracle inputs, GeoDepth incurs a non-trivial error that grows with object scale, revealing a structural rather than statistical bias. Our PCDepth substantially mitigates this bias across all categories. (b) Geometric origin of the bias. Under perspective projection, the 3D bottom center (red) is self-occluded by a nearer surface point (green) that projects higher on the image plane, while the visible bottom in the image corresponds to a still-closer surface point (yellow). The commonly adopted formulation z = f ·H/h2D therefore recovers the depth of the visible front surface rather than that of the object center, systematically underestimating depth.

Figure 7: PCDepth generalizes across detectors. Replacing only the depth head with PCDepth yields consistent gains, indicating that the improvement stems from correcting the projection bias rather than architectural interactions.
Figure 5: Details of Mixture-of-Backbone. MoB adaptively fuses a convolutional pyramid with a single-scale VFM branch at every scale.

Figure 4: GeoAlign reduces depth error through the attributes PCDepth depends on. Per-distance errors on KITTI Val for 3D size (Left), orientation (Middle), and depth (Right). GeoAlign consistently lowers size and orientation errors across all ranges, and since PCDepth computes depth analytically from these two attributes, the improvements propagate directly to depth.
Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on Omni3DOUT. 3D predictions overlaid on the image (Left) and the corresponding bird’s-eye view with a 1m×1m grid (Right).

papers.selection_reason: Reformulates geometric depth for monocular 3D detection, correcting projection-induced bias; fits 3D vision and geometric perception.
papers.title: Rethinking Geometric Depth in Monocular 3D Object Detection: A Projection-Consistent Reformulation
papers.tldr: MonoPCA corrects projection-induced front-surface depth bias in monocular 3D detection using geometry-aware depth reformulation and stronger attribute perception.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: Controlled acquisition setups are widely used for high-accuracy multi-view 3D surface reconstruction, as they allow sensor configuration, image resolution, viewpoint distribution, and illumination to be specified. Yet benchmarking remains difficult, since reconstruction accuracy depends jointly on the reconstruction paradigm, object properties, and acquisition regime. Existing benchmarks often restrict viewpoint coverage, resolution, or illumination, which can bias comparisons towards methods suited to the chosen setting. Others lack accurate 3D ground truth or quantified image-to-geometry alignment, limiting their use for metric surface evaluation. We introduce Martine, a benchmark for controlled 3D object surface reconstruction. Martine comprises 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at 9568 x 6376 pixels from 84 views over a spherical cap under both single-light and multi-light regimes. It provides object-independent camera calibration, accurate 3D ground-truth scans, calibration and image-to-geometry accuracy quantified on test images, and 3D property masks for analysing errors by material properties, visibility, curvature and fine structures. Experiments across photogrammetry, classical multi-view stereo, neural implicit surfaces, Gaussian-splatting-based reconstruction, and multi-view photometric stereo show that Martine enables regime-aware evaluation with explicit control over reference-data accuracy. The benchmark resolves sub-millimetric reconstruction differences, with a best observed Chamfer distance of 0.058 mm over the evaluated visible surface.
bullets: Includes 28 objects, including transparent materials and fine structures, captured at high resolution from 84 spherical-cap views under single- and multi-light settings.
Provides accurate 3D ground-truth scans, object-independent camera calibration, quantified image-to-geometry alignment, and property-based 3D masks.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation trains a student language model to match a teacher's predictions on the training text. We ask whether learning the teacher's behavior beyond the training text can further improve the student. We investigate this using three input perturbations: additive token noise, blending two documents, and blending neighboring tokens. Specifically, for an early part of pretraining we perturb the inputs and train the student to match the teacher on them, and we spend the rest of the same token budget on ordinary distillation. When pretraining from scratch, the best method improves on standard distillation at both scales we tried, by 0.025 nats at 135M parameters and by 0.020 nats at 0.5B (mean of three seeds). At 135M this is 1.45 times the gain that distillation itself provides over next-token training. We also observe promising downstream transfer: at 0.5B, the best variant improves average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks. It also retains its validation-loss advantage after low-bit weight quantization. We also test a data-limited setting in which training data must be reused, and find that the gains persist. Finally, ablations suggest that, for additive noise, perturbing the teacher's inputs contributes most of the gain, while perturbing only the student's inputs yields much less.
bullets: Studies additive token noise, document blending, and neighboring-token blending during an early distillation phase.
The best perturbation method improves validation loss at both tested scales: 135M and 0.5B parameters.
At 0.5B, it increases average zero-shot accuracy by about one percentage point across seven tasks.
Benefits persist when training data is reused and after low-bit weight quantization.
Ablations indicate that perturbing the teacher’s inputs is more beneficial than perturbing only the student’s inputs.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview. (a) In standard distillation, teacher and student read the same clean text and the student is trained to match the teacher’s prediction on it. In the early stage of our method, both read a perturbed version of the text, and the student matches the teacher’s prediction on that perturbed input: the inputs on which the teacher supervises the student change, not only the student’s input. The bars under each token sketch its input vector over a toy vocabulary, one-hot for clean text and spread over several vocabulary items when perturbed (Fig. 2). The rest of training is standard distillation on clean text. (b) Clean validation loss of two 0.5B students trained from the same initialization on the same data order, one with standard distillation and one with adjacent blending (λ=0.5) for the first 30% of training, and their difference (symmetric log scale). While its inputs are perturbed, the blended student lags by about one nat. After the switch it recovers quickly, overtakes the baseline at about 47% of training and finishes 0.020 nats below it.

Figure 3: Change in final validation loss against standard distillation (below zero is better). (a–c) 135M student with the SmolLM2-1.7B teacher, 4.2B tokens. The dashed line is next-token prediction without a teacher. (a) Noise size, with a 50% perturbed stage. The open markers in (a) are Gaussian noise added to each model’s input embedding; their σ is relative to the embedding’s rootmean-square value, so it is not in the same units as token noise. (b) Blend weight for both blends, with a 30% perturbed stage. (c) Length of the perturbed stage at each family’s best size. (d–f) 0.5B student with the Qwen2.5-1.5B teacher, 10B tokens, scored on the full validation split. Error bars are ±2 paired standard errors. (d) Noise size and (e) blend weight, with the same perturbed-stage lengths as in (a, b). (f) Length of the perturbed stage at each family’s best size.

Figure 4: Ablations (135M, SmolLM2-1.7B teacher; difference in final validation loss, lower is better). Bars show the mean over initialization seeds and dots the individual seeds, each compared with standard distillation from the same seed. (a) Each family at its best setting, with and without the teacher, each compared with its own unperturbed baseline (standard distillation or next-token prediction). (b) Token noise given to both models, to the teacher only, or to the student only. The grey bar is the sum of the two one-sided gains. (c) Clean inputs, with the teacher’s target softened instead, either by a temperature τ (τ=1.15 matches the entropy of the teacher’s prediction on σ=0.4 inputs) or by label smoothing to the same entropy. (d) Clean inputs for the first half of training, distilled from a weaker model (an early checkpoint of the teacher, or a smaller model) instead of the teacher. (e) Adjacent blending at λ=0.8, as in the main runs and on the same raw tokens as the baseline, and the overlapping variant described in the text (one seed).

Figure 5: Data-constrained pretraining at 135M: 16 epochs over 262M unique tokens, same 4.2Btoken budget. (a) Final validation loss of standard distillation with and without noise (token noise σ=0.4 for the first 50% of training) as a function of AdamW weight decay. Black dots are two initialization seeds at weight decay 1, and dotted lines show the same 4.2B-token budget without repeated data (weight decay 0.1). Weight decay 10 diverges. (b) The gain from the same noise with and without a teacher. Dotted lines again show the gain without repeated data. Exact values in Table 4 (Appendix B).

papers.abstract: Recent progress on contrastive audio-language models can be attributed mainly to the scale and quality of their training data. Larger training datasets expose models to a broader range of sounds and corresponding audio captions. To exploit this, we collect 1.48 billion audio samples from academic datasets, internet datasets, web collections, Common Crawl, and YouTube, and process them with a multi-stage curation pipeline. Furthermore, we generate short and long captions for samples in our corpus that lack them. We use our dataset to study the scaling behavior of contrastive audio-language models based on the NaFlex architecture for the audio encoder. Our experiments identify trade-offs between model size and training data for a given compute budget. Moreover, our resulting models, CLAP2, outperform prior audio-text models of comparable size on the MAEB and HEAR benchmarks. We release our dataset, captions, model checkpoints, and code.
bullets: Addresses the need for larger, broader, and higher-quality audio-caption training data.
Aggregates audio from academic, internet, web, Common Crawl, and YouTube sources using multi-stage curation.
Generates short and long captions for samples without existing captions.
Studies model-size versus training-data trade-offs for NaFlex-based contrastive audio-language models.
Releases the corpus, captions, CLAP2 checkpoints, and code; CLAP2 outperforms similarly sized prior models on MAEB and HEAR.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the LAION-Audio-XL dataset curation pipeline. We collected 1.48B audio samples from online platforms, of which 1.47B entered deduplication. Removing silent audio, duplicates (including SemDeDup [59]), and evaluation data leaves 1.28B audio samples. We then selected 500M audio samples based on categorical taxonomy annotations. The same annotations were used to prompt Qwen3-Omni [61] and MOSS-Audio [42] to generate short and long captions for 471M audio samples without textual descriptions, resulting in 500M captioned audio samples in total (the 500M selection). The 365M audio samples that are up to 30 seconds long form LAIONAudio-XL.

Left: the compute-Pareto-optimal runs (solid points) of all warmup-stable-decay and cosine learning-rate-scheduled runs, with our fitted scaling function and its 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples). papers.abstract: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop FastGRT, which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. FastGRT further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement FastGRT in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9$\times$ to 4.97$\times$, while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open source.
bullets: 3D Gaussian ray tracing offers capabilities beyond rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting but has substantially higher training costs.
FastGRT decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses forward-pass computations during backpropagation.
It adds fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to address other training bottlenecks.
Implemented in Vulkan, FastGRT supports both training and rendering while preserving the original rendering formulation.
The reported training speedup over 3DGRT is 1.9× to 4.97×; the code is open source.

papers.title: FastGRT: Accelerating Training of 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing
papers.tldr: FastGRT accelerates 3D Gaussian ray-tracing training by reorganizing GPU computation and reusing forward-pass work, achieving 1.9×–4.97× faster training than 3DGRT.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles use pedestrian crossing intention prediction (PCIP) to participate safely in traffic. Existing models are largely trained under favourable daytime conditions with sufficient daylight. Little is known about the robustness of these models under night-time and low-light conditions, due to the lack of datasets containing night-time footage. This paper investigates how a dataset, named NightSteps, can be constructed and evaluated as a baseline benchmark. The dataset is based on nighttime dashcam footage collected from six different cities around the world, capturing a wide variety of road conditions. The dataset consists of dashcam-recorded point-of-view footage, raw data of pedestrians' locations with corresponding 'track ids' and ground-truth labels containing accurate information about pedestrian crossing behaviour, resulting in a diverse dataset. Gemini, ChatGPT, and human assessment are used to demonstrate the usability of the dataset by predicting crossings in clips from the dataset and comparing the results with the initial ground-truth labels. These results show that human input achieves an accuracy of 88.17% and an F1-score of 80.21%. Predictions from Gemini and ChatGPT perform lower, with accuracies of 60% and 79.13% respectively, and F1-scores of 42.50% and 63.64%. The evaluation demonstrates that the NightSteps dataset can be used for future model evaluation to test the performance of PCIP, with the aim of improving road safety at night.
bullets: Addresses the lack of nighttime data for robust pedestrian crossing intention prediction.
Uses dashcam footage from six cities with varied road conditions, pedestrian locations, track IDs, and crossing labels.
Evaluates dataset usability with human assessment, Gemini, and ChatGPT predictions against ground truth.
Humans achieved 88.17% accuracy and an 80.21% F1-score; Gemini and ChatGPT performed lower.
Supports future evaluation and improvement of nighttime PCIP systems for road safety.

papers.abstract: Hybrid quantum reinforcement learning has been explored for robotic decision-making, but evaluations often emphasize task success, return, or convergence, leaving unresolved whether quantum circuit outputs influence constrained actions and remain traceable through robot execution. We present \texttt{Qubit-to-Motion}, an evidence-centered framework for support-constrained sequencing and simulated robotic placement. Four Pauli-$Z$ readouts provide the sole learned input to the actor and critic, while a support mask enforces admissible object selection. Each decision is recorded and linked via step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints to a sealed route, deterministic Cartesian and inverse-kinematics waypoints, prescribed joint motion, and MuJoCo contact replay. A frozen checkpoint is evaluated across five deterministic 30-object scene variants. All 150 placements satisfy support, containment, and settling criteria. A fixed-state zero-readout intervention changes $90.0\pm0.0\%$ of decisions, demonstrating dependence on the joint circuit representation. Mean macro travel is $34.537\pm0.206$~m, inference requires $8.60\pm1.27$~ms per route, and replay achieves $8.764\pm0.220~μ$m mean final position error with 0.356~mm maximum interpenetration. These results establish reproducible decision-to-contact traceability. The implementation is available at \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Qubit-to-Motion-Quantum-Reinforcement-Learning-F7DC}{\textcolor{linkpink}{the anonymous repository}}.
bullets: Addresses whether quantum circuit outputs truly influence constrained actions and remain traceable during execution.
Uses four Pauli-Z readouts as the actor–critic input, with a support mask enforcing admissible object choices.
Links each decision to sealed routes, deterministic waypoints, joint motions, and MuJoCo contact replay using step indices and SHA-256 fingerprints.
Across five deterministic 30-object scenes, all 150 placements met support, containment, and settling criteria.
A zero-readout intervention changed 90.0% of decisions, while replay achieved 8.764 μm mean final-position error and 0.356 mm maximum interpenetration.

papers.abstract: Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.
bullets: Benchmarks can overestimate acoustic understanding because many tasks are answerable from the transcript or question alone.
The study separates lexical tasks from global-attribute tasks (e.g., speaker, emotion) and within-recording structure tasks (e.g., stress, intonation).
Across 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro, open-model deficits are especially large on attribute and structure tasks, with much of the gap tied to recording-specific information.
Linear probes show relevant acoustic information is often readable in early layers but becomes less accessible in later layers.
LoRA adapters trained in these layers, using a content anchor, improve attribute and structure accuracy while keeping lexical accuracy nearly unchanged.

papers.title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
papers.tldr: Audio language models often encode useful acoustic cues but fail to use them; targeted intermediate-layer training substantially improves non-lexical audio understanding while preserving transcript-based performance.

papers.abstract: LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. These credits adjust the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions. During the final episodes, EARN directly replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded context and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation. We evaluate performance at the end of the interaction budget using the average score over the final four episodes. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best score on this metric in 31 of 33 task--budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties. Across the evaluated Jericho budgets, replay bypasses 78.9--86.3\% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.
bullets: Addresses stagnation from repeatedly rewarding actions that achieve the same score and the risk of harmful exploration in final attempts.
Uses experience-based credits: repeated-score outcomes receive less credit, while action segments reaching higher scores receive more.
Adjusts probabilities of LLM-proposed actions using these credits to guide further progress.
Conditionally replays stored actions when the context matches and actions remain available, bypassing new candidate generation.
Achieves the best final-four-episode average score in 31 of 33 task–budget settings, including ties; replay bypasses 78.9–86.3% of candidate-generation calls across evaluated Jericho budgets.

papers.abstract: As long-video understanding gains increasing attention, augmented reality (AR) devices are emerging as a compelling deployment platform. However, egocentric videos exhibit significant temporal redundancy, imposing substantial memory and computational burdens on resource-constrained AR hardware. To address this challenge, we introduce UTOPI, a plug-and-play pre-compression module designed specifically for egocentric long videos on AR platforms. First, we leverage user motion signals to estimate inter-frame overlap and propose a viewpoint-shift-invariant pruning algorithm. Second, we exploit eye-tracking sensors to identify user fixations, enabling the separation of attended foreground content from background and its preferential retention via a fine-tuned neural network-based adjustment mechanism. Across multiple benchmarks and model backbones, UTOPI achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance. Code and project page are available at https://sai-lab-nyu.github.io/utopi/.
bullets: Addresses the memory and computation costs of temporally redundant egocentric videos on resource-constrained AR hardware.
Uses user motion to estimate inter-frame overlap and perform viewpoint-shift-invariant token pruning.
Uses eye tracking to distinguish attended foreground content from background and preferentially retain it.
Works as a plug-and-play pre-compression module across multiple benchmarks and model backbones.
Achieves up to 95% compression while preserving performance, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents acting across web applications and online services often need multi-turn corrections to align their work with users' underspecified goals and preferences. In practice, users may identify problems in the current outcome without specifying the desired result, so learning user intentions requires interpreting each correction against the agent's preceding and revised outcomes. These expectations are often connected to a particular context, making it hard to know when they apply and how to ensure the agent later acts as the user expects. To this end, we propose LiveAsset, an intent harness that learns reusable intent assets from corrective interactions and uses them for runtime control of agent execution. LiveAsset jointly interprets each correction with the agent's original and revised results to infer user intent, incrementally updating the assets while preserving earlier requirements that remain applicable. The learned requirements guide agent execution from task entry and provide criteria for runtime verification, which uses the explanations to assess applicability before each reply is delivered and directs the agent to revise the result to address unmet requirements while preserving those already satisfied. Following a learning phase in which simulated users progressively reveal requirements through multi-turn corrections, we evaluate LiveAsset using same-task replay of the original requests on π-Bench, PERMA, and Vita and cross-task transfer on PAST-Bench and SkillEvolBench. Experiments show that LiveAsset better fulfills requirements learned from corrective interactions and improves performance on these benchmarks compared with memory, skill, and rule-based harness baselines. Code is available at github.com/landian60/LiveAsset.
bullets: Addresses underspecified goals where users correct outcomes without explicitly stating the desired result.
Interprets each correction alongside the agent’s original and revised outputs to infer and incrementally update intent assets.
Guides execution from task entry and verifies each response, prompting revisions while preserving already satisfied requirements.
Evaluated through same-task replay and cross-task transfer across five benchmarks after simulated multi-turn requirement learning.
Outperforms memory-, skill-, and rule-based harness baselines in fulfilling requirements learned from corrections.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.
bullets: Problem: Existing vision-language-action and world-action priors may not adequately capture humanoid robot motion structure.
Method: Kinematic Action Models pretrain directly on whole-body motion and condition generation on tasks, visual observations, and execution feedback.
Architecture: Kimodo-Policy combines a frozen text-to-motion backbone, lightweight ControlNet visual conditioning, hierarchical root-body-hand coordination, and motion-history-based action chunks.
Results: It reports 72.14% overall success on HumanoidArena, competitive SIMPLE performance, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks.
Scope: Results provide initial evidence that motion generation can complement foundation models for humanoid action learning.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: llama.cpp's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against llama.cpp and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.
bullets: Existing CPU-GPU MoE engines trade off fast prefill against fast decode, causing multi-second waits after tool outputs.
Ostinato routes stable, frequently used experts to GPUs while sending only a small remainder to the CPU; long prefills upload each cold expert once.
Each decode step uses a fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU without changing the model’s computation.
On coding and customer-service sessions, Ostinato was fastest in both phases and completed sessions 1.4–2.5× sooner than llama.cpp and KTransformers.
It reduced median post-tool-output waits by 22–55% against those baselines on four RTX 4090D GPUs.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of OSTINATO. The resident experts run on the GPU in every forward pass; only where the cold experts run changes. Slate: hot experts and GPU; teal: cold experts and CPU; charcoal: uploads over PCIe; black numbers: the steps of Section 3.1. (a) Offline, development sessions rank the experts (❶), a capacity test fixes the expert slots of each GPU (❷), and the highest-ranked experts fill them (❸); during decode, the buffers reserved for prefill hold borrowed experts. (b) In a decode step, the router selects k = 6 experts, two of them cold (❹). Inside the CUDA graph of the GPU (dashed), the index table passes all k IDs to the GPU branch and maps the cold ones to all-zero slots, so every step keeps the same shapes. The graph writes the cold IDs and the token’s input into mapped host memory, a resident CPU thread pool outside the graph computes only the r = 2 cold experts (❺), and a wait kernel joins the two branches before the next layer (❻). The timeline is drawn to measured scale for r = 2. (c) A prefill forward pass of fewer than Np = 512 tokens splits its routes between the two branches, which run in turn; a larger one uploads each of its distinct cold experts once (❼).

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.
