papers.abstract: The CoRL 2026 RoboEval challenge has eight bimanual tasks, and it ranks a policy not only on whether it succeeds but on how: every stage of the task, done safely, efficiently and with both arms in coordination, scored against human demonstrations. My solution has two parts. The generic part, carried over from my LeHome challenge solution, is off-policy RL on a $π_{0.5}$-based policy that is also its own value function. It is trained with AWR and RECAP on advantages of the exact official score, in a loop where every rollout is at the same time a Thompson-sampling trial of about 20 inference parameters. Out of the box, it took the policy to 0.85 RDS on held-out seeds in two days (and it was still very far from convergence). The competition-specific part adds data that local exploration cannot find: generated demonstrations that reach the full reward, and recovery episodes that start from the policy's own failures. The submitted policy reaches 0.990 RDS on held-out seeds and 0.987 on the official seeds.
bullets: Targets eight bimanual tasks scored on safe, efficient, coordinated execution against human demonstrations.
Uses AWR and RECAP to train a π₀.₅-based policy/value function on advantages from the official score.
Treats each rollout as a Thompson-sampling trial over roughly 20 inference parameters.
Adds generated full-reward demonstrations and recovery episodes from the policy’s failures to address exploration gaps.
The generic method reached 0.85 RDS in two days but remained far from convergence; the submitted system improved substantially.

papers.abstract: Agentic autoregressive video generation combines semantic planning, sequential generation, and visual verification for controllable synthesis. Growing visual histories enlarge the key-value (KV) cache, increasing memory use and attention costs across candidate rollouts. Existing compression methods primarily optimize individual generators without the planner's semantic constraints, risking low priority for states supporting requested attributes or actions. We introduce SemanticKV, a training-free method for semantically aligned KV cache compression. To our knowledge, SemanticKV is the first KV cache compression method for agentic autoregressive video generation that explicitly uses planner-extracted semantic constraints to guide retention. Text cross-attention identifies constraint-related video positions, whose self-attention queries are collected into separate groups. Attention weights are averaged within each group and maximized across groups, giving each cached entry a high score when strongly used by any represented constraint. A single top-k selection retains high-scoring entries under the memory budget, leaving their keys, values, and positions unchanged. For fixed query groups and equal entry costs, this selection minimizes an additive upper bound on worst-group discarded attention. The method operates independently within each candidate without retraining or additional video generations. We evaluate four AR video backbones on three benchmarks for 5-, 30-, and 60-second generation. On Causal Forcing at a compression ratio of 0.7, SemanticKV obtains a VBench Total Score of 84.10, compared with 84.05 for the strongest compressed baseline and 83.99 for Full KV. It achieves a 1.22x speedup over Full KV and reduces KV-cache memory from 6.04 GB to 1.81 GB, a 3.35x reduction.

Uses planner-extracted constraints and text cross-attention to group relevant queries, then selects a single top-k set of high-value cache entries.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model on its own responses, guided by a fixed teacher. Generating these responses is expensive, so systems use quantized inference and asynchronous rollouts to reduce the cost. Both, however, introduce training-inference mismatch between the rollout engine and the model being trained. Such mismatch can destabilize reinforcement learning (RL), but its effects on OPD remain unclear. This paper investigates how much mismatch OPD tolerates, where its effects arise, and how training systems can use this tolerance. Measuring all mismatch sources on one scale, we examine quantization across three student-teacher pairs, with additional tests of weight staleness and injected noise on one pair. OPD tolerates substantial mismatch without meaningful loss of training quality but degrades at higher levels, revealing an empirical mismatch budget. Both the quality cost of mismatch and the mismatch introduced by quantization depend on the model, with some layers particularly sensitive to reduced precision. In controlled comparisons, OPD remains stable under rollout configurations that destabilize RL methods. Under weight noise, mismatch also shifts the prefixes reached during generation, introducing errors that per-token corrections cannot address. To put these findings into practice, we introduce a lightweight admission check that screens rollout configurations against a calibrated budget without requiring a full training run for each candidate. Model-specific FP8 recipes preserve training quality while providing capacity for at least $1.93\times$ as many KV-cache tokens as BF16. Combining FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches the same training quality $1.62\times$ sooner than synchronous BF16 training. Code is available at https://github.com/benyucong/train-inference-mismatch-opd
bullets: Quantization, weight staleness, and injected noise introduce mismatch, but OPD quality degrades meaningfully only beyond an empirical mismatch budget.
Mismatch tolerance and quantization sensitivity vary across models and layers, with some layers especially vulnerable to reduced precision.
OPD stays stable under rollout settings that destabilize reinforcement-learning methods.
Weight noise can alter generated prefixes, causing errors that per-token corrections cannot fix.

A lightweight admission check screens rollout configurations; model-specific FP8 recipes support at least 1.93× more KV-cache tokens, while FP8 with asynchronous rollouts reaches equivalent quality 1.62× sooner than synchronous BF16.

papers.selection_reason: Studies quantization and rollout mismatch in LLM distillation, with FP8 KV-cache capacity gains and efficiency-oriented training configurations.
papers.title: How Much Training-Inference Mismatch Can On-Policy Distillation Tolerate?
papers.tldr: On-policy distillation remains robust to substantial training–inference mismatch, enabling faster and more memory-efficient rollout systems until a model-specific tolerance budget is exceeded.

papers.abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.
bullets: Zero-shot, end-to-end robot control gives coding agents capabilities beyond earlier VLA and WAM systems.
Digital threats such as indirect prompt injection can propagate from webpages or emails to physical robot behavior.
ArmedAgent evaluates robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios.
The benchmark is tested in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm across several frontier models and agent frameworks.
Results indicate substantial safety risks in current coding-agent robot-control systems.

papers.abstract: Evaluating general-purpose multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for surgical scene understanding remains limited due to scarce surgical data and fragmented evaluation protocols. We address these challenges through a two-stage evaluation framework for surgical scene understanding. In Stage I, we introduce SurgKnowBench, a diagnostic benchmark that harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks and evaluates proprietary and open-source MLLMs to map the boundary of pretrained surgical competence. SurgKnowBench reveals that current models retain partial visual priors but remain weak on relational and procedural understanding and workflow assessment. Building on this failure frontier and motivated by the scaffolded nature of surgical training, we introduce SurgAgentGym, an agentic environment where general-purpose MLLM agents can use bounded knowledge search over SurgWiki and general-purpose visual grounding for surgical tasks. SurgAgentGym evaluates whether generalist agents can improve surgical understanding at inference time through tool-mediated evidence use, without additional surgical training. Our results show that agentic inference narrows the gap mainly for perception-heavy tasks, while fine-grained localization and expert-style assessment remain persistent bottlenecks. This opens a path toward future studies of agentic surgical understanding.
bullets: SurgKnowBench harmonizes public surgical datasets across procedures and tasks to evaluate proprietary and open-source multimodal models.
Current models show partial visual knowledge but weak relational, procedural, and workflow understanding.
SurgAgentGym enables agents to use bounded SurgWiki searches and general-purpose visual grounding without additional surgical training.
Tool-mediated inference mainly improves perception-heavy tasks; fine-grained localization and expert assessment remain bottlenecks.
The framework supports future research on agentic approaches to surgical understanding.

papers.abstract: Aligning video generation models with human preference depends critically on the quality of the reward model that scores generated videos. Current video reward models, however, source their reward signal from a model's representational rather than generative capacity: they either repurpose vision-language models as pixel-space scorers, or train auxiliary scoring heads on top of frozen generator features. The generator's actual ability to predict velocities, denoise latents, and produce videos plays no role in scoring its own generations. We argue that this overlooks a structural property of offline preference learning. Any preference optimization objective that approximates an offline preference dataset mathematically targets a strictly defined KL-constrained optimal policy. By isolating the reward term from this analytical solution and mapping the exact generation log-likelihood to its flow-matching surrogate, the empirical reward emerges deterministically as the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors. We formalize this equivalence into GenRM-Flow, a framework where a preference-tuned video generator inherently operates as a process-aware reward model directly in the noisy latent space. We further show theoretically that distinct fine-tuning objectives, whether contrastive like DPO and IPO or non-contrastive like RWR, are alternative optimization pathways toward the same optimal policy, each inducing a reward readout from the generator's velocity-prediction errors. Furthermore, the extracted process reward seamlessly substitutes external VLM scorers in FlowAWR. Operating purely on native latent outputs without auxiliary reward networks, this generative reward drives measurable improvements in downstream video generation.
bullets: Current video reward models score representations or add scoring heads, ignoring the generator’s denoising and video-generation capabilities.
GenRM-Flow derives an empirical reward from the relative difference in continuous-time velocity-prediction errors in noisy latent space.
The framework links preference objectives such as DPO, IPO, and RWR to the same KL-constrained optimal policy and reward readout.
The process reward can replace external vision-language-model scorers in FlowAWR.
Using native latent outputs, the approach yields measurable downstream improvements in video generation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The pipeline of GenRM-Flow. (Panel A) Traditional paradigms rely on representational capacity, utilizing a frozen backbone (e.g., a VLM or base generator) as a feature extractor coupled with an auxiliary discriminative head. (Panel B) The proposed framework sources the reward directly from generative capacity. Following preference optimization, the implicit reward RD(x, c) is algebraically extracted from the velocity-prediction errors. The scalar score is computed natively by contrasting the active policy (flame, θ⋆) against a frozen reference (snowflake, θref ), requiring no architectural modifications or auxiliary heads.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison between PAVRM and GenRM-Flow as the per-step reward signal in FlowAWR with a 1.3B backbone. Both runs use FlowAWR with the same configuration, differing only in the reward signal. Red boxes mark localized structural deformations, spatial inconsistencies, and temporal artifacts produced by PAVRM. Across scenes, our reward yields visibly fewer geometric defects and better spatial and temporal continuity.

Table 1: Three preference fine-tuning objectives as optimization pathways to obtain the trained weights θ⋆. While their loss formulations LF (θ) vary significantly—ranging from bounded contrastive margins to reference-free likelihood maximization—they all structurally aim to approximate the optimal offline policy π∗. Consequently, during the evaluation phase, they implicitly define reward readouts corresponding to their theoretical likelihood shifts: the relative readout of Eq. (6) for contrastive objectives and a reference-free readout for RWR.

papers.abstract: What if a face recognition system could learn from every encounter without a single gradient update? We present Gallery Self-Evolution (GSE), a training-free framework where the gallery itself adapts at test time. The core mechanism---dedup-FIFO curation---archives novel appearance samples after successful recognition while permanently locking the enrollment template, bounded at 30 embeddings per identity. On CFP-FP and IJB-C benchmarks, GSE closes the side-view gap by +23 points at 45° yaw and boosts TAR@FAR=0.001 by +9.4 points, all at CPU-level cost. No retraining. No GPU. Just a gallery that grows smarter every time it meets you.
bullets: Addresses the performance gap caused by side-view faces.
Uses dedup-FIFO curation to archive novel samples after successful recognition.
Keeps enrollment templates permanently locked and limits each identity to 30 embeddings.
Improves 45° yaw performance by 23 points and TAR@FAR=0.001 by 9.4 points on CFP-FP and IJB-C.
Operates at CPU-level cost without gradient updates or retraining.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have demonstrated the effectiveness of score-based objectives for generative modeling, yet their potential for self-supervised representation learning remains underexplored. We introduce Entropy-Based Regularization (EBReg), a framework that uses latent score estimation to regularize the latent distribution during self-supervised training. EBReg jointly learns an encoder and a latent score model, and utilizes the learned score to provide a diversity-preserving signal that prevents representational collapse. Motivated by a mutual-information lower bound, we formulate the objective as view alignment with smoothed marginal entropy maximization and optimize the marginal entropy without explicit density evaluation. The same score model can additionally be used at test time to refine corrupted representations toward the training latent distribution. Empirically, EBReg learns competitive representations on ImageNet-1K, achieving 75.57% linear-probe accuracy with ViT-L. Across diverse architectures, score-guided test-time adaptation further improves robustness on ImageNet-C, yielding an average relative accuracy gain of approximately 5%.
bullets: Addresses representation collapse and underuse of score-based objectives in self-supervised learning.
Jointly trains an encoder and latent score model to align views while maximizing smoothed marginal entropy.
Optimizes entropy without explicit density evaluation, motivated by a mutual-information lower bound.
Achieves 75.57% ImageNet-1K linear-probe accuracy with ViT-L.
Score-guided test-time adaptation improves robustness on ImageNet-C by approximately 5% relative on average.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EBReg: training and test-time adaptation. (a) Two augmented views are encoded into normalized embeddings. The encoder minimizes a view-alignment loss and an entropy regularizer, LEBReg, using a detached estimate of the score of the noise-smoothed embedding distribution. (b). The latent score is parameterized by a noise-prediction network fitted on detached embeddings, with Kscore updates per encoder step; it predicts the injected Gaussian noise, giving the score estimate sψ,σ(h̃) = −ϵ̂ψ(h̃)/σ. (c) At test time, the learned score is reused as a test-time adaptation signal. The score model and remaining encoder–projector parameters are frozen, while only normalization parameters α are updated by minimizing LTTA, guiding corrupted embeddings toward higher-density regions of the learned source distribution.

Figure 1: Illustration of the EBReg anti-collapse mechanism. Top: (a) Representations lie near a one-dimensional subspace of R2. (b) EBReg alone spreads them across both dimensions. (c) Alignment alone contracts them, resulting in dimensional collapse. (d) Alignment + EBReg yields compact, separated classes while preventing dimensional collapse. Bottom: Evolution of the latent distribution under EBReg. Samples are moved away from the diagonal and populate both dimensions, ultimately forming an isotropic Gaussian distribution.

Table 5: ImageNet-C accuracy (%) before and after five adaptation steps. Seven corruptions with gains for every model are selected by mean gain across models; the final row averages all 15 corruptions. Bold indicates higher accuracy within each model.

Table 2: Linear-probe performance and effective rank on ImageNet-1K. Results are grouped by pretraining setup. ResNet-50, ViT-L, and ViT-H use the setups from Bardes et al. Within each setup, EBReg and the corresponding baselines use the same backbone, data augmentations, optimization settings, training schedule, and evaluation procedure. papers.abstract: Block-diffusion drafters propose a whole block of tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees built from their position-wise marginals increase the expected accepted length of speculative decoding. Every tree node occupies a query row in target verification, so under concurrent serving low-yield branches compete with other requests for verification capacity. Existing tree methods select verified nodes by draft probability under a fixed or cost-selected per-request budget, and thus always retain a prefix of the drafter's ranking. We present D3Tree, which learns which nodes of a block-diffusion draft tree are worth verifying. A tree-size head with 2H+2 parameters predicts each candidate's conditional survival from the draft state, the candidate embedding, and its draft log-probability. Thresholding the product of these scores along parent chains yields an ancestor-closed subtree whose size adapts to each request and decoding round. The head is trained on a frozen drafter with conditional labels on the full candidate tree; an optional joint mode also steers the drafter toward the retained reference path. At serving time, D3Tree verifies whole trees under light load and, under heavy load, allocates one batch-wide node budget by predicted survival, sized to the target's matrix-multiplication tiles. Retained trees share one ancestor-masked target pass, while construction, pruning, and scheduling run on the GPU and overlap with the host. Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, D3Tree is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings, with 3.2-4.0x speedup over autoregressive decoding for one request and 1.3-1.8x at 64 concurrent requests, where fixed-budget trees fall below autoregressive speed. Under a time-varying arrival trace, it has the lowest mean end-to-end latency in every arrival phase.
bullets: Fixed probability-ranked trees waste verification capacity on low-yield branches when requests compete for resources.
D3Tree predicts each candidate’s conditional survival and retains an ancestor-closed subtree with request- and round-adaptive size.
It supports whole-tree verification under light load and batch-wide, tile-aligned node budgeting under heavy load.
Across six vision-language verifiers and 17 benchmarks, it is fastest in 70 of 72 load settings.
Reported speedups are 3.2–4.0× for one request and 1.3–1.8× at 64 concurrent requests; it also achieves the lowest latency across all phases of a time-varying arrival trace.

papers.title: D3Tree: Learning to Prune Block-Diffusion Draft Trees for Efficient Verification

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models, while having become a powerful backbone for generative synthesis, suffer from high inference cost on generating high-resolution images. Diffusion caching has emerged as a promising acceleration technique to reduce inference cost. However, existing caching strategies fail to accurately identify the varying importance of different computational modules and rarely coordinate cache reusing across the timestep and layer granularities, making it difficult to control error accumulation. To address these limitations, we propose multi-granularity caching (MG-Cache) for DiTs, a novel and fully training-free approach to exploit computational redundancy both on timesteps and Transformer layers. Our core innovation contains a two-stage caching strategy: an offline timestep profiling analysis that identifies redundant timesteps for cache reuse, followed by an adaptive layer-wise caching strategy that combines input stability with importance of each Transformer layer to selectively cache stable Attention and MLP submodules. Extensive experiments on mainstream open-source DiT models validate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant acceleration while maintaining high fidelity to the uncached output, with up to a 4.18x acceleration on HunyuanVideo.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of DiT-based high-resolution image generation.
Coordinates cache reuse across both diffusion timesteps and Transformer layers to limit error accumulation.
Uses offline timestep profiling to identify redundant timesteps for reuse.
Adaptively caches stable Attention and MLP submodules based on input stability and layer importance.
Reports up to 4.18× acceleration on HunyuanVideo while maintaining high output fidelity.

Stage 1 performs a static offline analysis to identify and preserve critical timesteps based on a timestep feature table [M̂t ] constructed from a small batch of calibration dataset. Stage 2 introduces a dynamic layer-wise caching mechanism that computes layer importance scores and input stability to adaptively determine whether to reuse cached features.

papers.abstract: Offloading model state to host memory and streaming layer weights let a single multi-GPU node train large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. GPU memory then becomes a performance budget, shared by resident expert state, retained activations, and execution worksets. The best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size, and sequence length. We present OOM (Offload-Optimized MoE), a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation. For expert-parallel execution, OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies. For local execution, OOM bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models, it also retains attention results on the host to avoid costly recomputation and selectively regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers to make room. Calibrated cost models guide joint configuration within GPU and host budgets to minimize step time; OOM selects among the configured paths through short executions. On four H100s, OOM trains with 1M-token contexts, whereas FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload, and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K. It also trains a 122B-parameter MoE model, on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s, it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Across matched-global-batch comparisons, OOM delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms while using the least host memory among the evaluated systems -- as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's.
bullets: Targets GPU-memory bottlenecks caused by resident experts, retained activations, and execution worksets during host-offloaded MoE training.
Jointly plans expert residency, activation retention, workset partitioning, recomputation, and host retention across expert-parallel, local, and hybrid execution paths.
Uses calibrated cost models and short trial executions to select configurations that minimize training step time within GPU and host-memory budgets.
On four H100s, supports 1M-token contexts and a 122B-parameter MoE model; on four RTX 4090s, supports 512K-token contexts and 1,024 sequences per step without gradient accumulation.
Achieves 1.58× and 4.08× geometric-mean throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms, while using as little as one-third of its host memory.

papers.abstract: Spatial reasoning requires understanding how objects and observers are arranged in a scene and how their relations change with viewpoint or movement. Vision-language models (VLMs) typically perform both steps through model-internal reasoning, forming an implicit scene interpretation from partial views and imagining the consequences of spatial transformations. A misread scene can lead to a wrong answer, while even a correct interpretation does not ensure that imagined transformations satisfy spatial constraints. We introduce Spatial Harness, which represents scenes as explicit and executable world states to ground spatial reasoning in physics-engine feedback. A Perceiver integrates scene constraints extracted from the question with specialized visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame. The resulting state is instantiated in a physics engine, where a Reasoner executes viewpoint changes and uses computed measurements and rendered views to guide reasoning. We evaluate on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs. On MindCube, Spatial Harness improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%, surpassing pySpatial by 7.52 percentage points. Given identical annotated object and camera poses, it reaches 98.25% versus 71.81% for model-internal reasoning. Code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/Spatial-Harness
bullets: VLMs can fail when they misinterpret scenes or mentally simulate transformations that violate spatial constraints.
A Perceiver combines question-derived constraints with visual estimates to place objects and cameras in a shared coordinate frame.
A physics engine executes viewpoint changes and provides measurements and rendered views to guide a Reasoner.
Evaluated on MindCube, SAT, MMSI-Bench, and SpatialRGPT-Bench with open- and closed-weight VLMs.
On MindCube, it improves Qwen3.5-27B from 52.70% to 71.14%; with identical annotated poses, it achieves 98.25% versus 71.81% for internal reasoning.

papers.abstract: Modern state-space models owe much of their computational efficiency to their linear, often diagonal, dynamics. Classical recurrent neural networks instead allow nonlinear state-to-state interactions, which can be beneficial when memory updates need to depend on the past context. In this paper, we ask whether state feedback through a simple gate regulating memory updates can enhance the expressivity of diagonal state-space models. To investigate this question, we compare gates that depend on the current input, the recurrent state, or both. We establish a strict expressivity separation: for scalar models, state gating solves induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary size and sequence length, whereas input gating fails on a finite instance under standard stability assumptions on the state transition matrix. Experiments show that state gating retains its advantage on induction-head tasks in higher-dimensional models, whereas input gating performs better on selective copying tasks. Together, our results show that even a simple, diagonal form of state-feedback gating can unlock capabilities unavailable to input-controlled models, while input and state gating offer complementary strengths and achieve the strongest overall performance when combined.
bullets: The paper compares gates driven by the current input, recurrent state, or both in diagonal state-space models.
State gating strictly increases expressivity: scalar models solve induction-head tasks for arbitrary vocabulary sizes and sequence lengths.
Under standard stability assumptions, input gating fails on a finite induction-head instance.
Experiments confirm state-gating advantages on induction tasks and input-gating advantages on selective copying.
The two gating mechanisms provide complementary capabilities when combined.

papers.abstract: 3D visual grounding (3DVG) localizes language-referred objects in 3D scenes, with broad applicability in both indoor and outdoor environments. However, existing 3DVG research focuses on static indoor objects, limiting its use in dynamic outdoor autonomous driving. Motion descriptions, which capture the temporal dynamics of moving objects, offer a promising way to address this challenge. We therefore introduce MoT3DVG, a large-scale dataset for dynamic-aware outdoor 3DVG with temporally evolving motion descriptions. It contains 850 scenarios with 31,128 frames from nuScenes dataset, and provides 144,568 language prompts with motion-aware descriptions for dynamic objects across time. We further propose DynaVG, a novel framework that effectively leverages temporal cues for outdoor 3DVG. In addition to the standard modality-specific encoders, DynaVG introduces a Short-Long Integrated Dynamic Encoding (SLIDE) module before the language-point cloud alignment. SLIDE models both local motion cues and global temporal context via short-term window encoding and long-term window shifting. Extensive experiments demonstrate its state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG, validating the effectiveness of motion-aware encoding. Our work reveals open challenges and promising directions for future research in outdoor 3DVG.
bullets: Targets the gap between static indoor 3D visual grounding and dynamic outdoor autonomous-driving scenarios.
Provides 850 nuScenes scenarios, 31,128 frames, and 144,568 temporally evolving motion-aware prompts.
DynaVG uses the SLIDE module to capture both short-term local motion and long-term temporal context before language–point cloud alignment.
Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on MoT3DVG and support the value of motion-aware encoding.
The benchmark also highlights open challenges for future outdoor 3D visual grounding research.

papers.title: MoT3DVG: A Benchmark for Outdoor 3D Visual Grounding with Motion-Aware Descriptions and Temporal Cues

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains language models through multi-turn tool interactions, yet their reasoning performance and tool-calling ability can decline during training. We trace this degradation to three coupled mechanisms: (1) tool-token imbalance produces negative overall tool credit when incorrect trajectories contain more tool tokens per turn than correct ones; (2) aggregation amplification can further strengthen this negative signal as token-mean aggregation gives longer incorrect trajectories greater weight in policy updates; and (3) failure-driven retries prolong trajectories as models tend to call tools again after execution errors, extending potential negative credit to recovery attempts. To counter this suppression, we propose Transition-Aware Credit Assignment (TACA), which targets the transition from reasoning to tool use through supervision of both call initiation and generation. Specifically, TACA uses Advantage Projection to enforce a nonnegative mean advantage on tool-call tokens within each prompt group through a minimal uniform shift. Additionally, TACA guides tool-use decisions with Decision Contrast, comparing rewards for tool-assisted and direct answers to the same prompt. Through Supervised Replay, it reinforces tool-call generation using calls from previously sampled correct trajectories. Across models and tasks, TACA improves performance and sustains more reliable tool interaction during training, raising mean accuracy over MT-GRPO on six reasoning benchmarks by 4.61 percentage points for Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 for Qwen2.5-3B. Our code is available at https://github.com/tmlr-group/TACA.
bullets: Identifies three causes of tool-use degradation: tool-token imbalance, length-amplified credit aggregation, and failure-driven retries.
Uses Advantage Projection to ensure tool-call tokens receive nonnegative mean advantage within each prompt group.
Applies Decision Contrast to compare tool-assisted and direct answers, plus Supervised Replay from correct trajectories.
Improves mean accuracy over MT-GRPO by 4.61 points on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 3.61 points on Qwen2.5-3B across six reasoning benchmarks.
Scope: targets multi-turn tool interactions trained with verifiable rewards.

papers.tldr: TACA prevents tool-use suppression in agentic RL by correcting negative credit around reasoning-to-tool transitions, improving reasoning accuracy and tool reliability.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, yet their computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on mobile devices. Data-free quantization (DFQ) enables the compression of ViTs without access to their original training data. Existing DFQ methods often synthesize calibration samples by maximizing the entropy of patch similarity. However, similarity entropy describes the dispersion of similarity values without ensuring that the generated samples cover diverse feature directions, potentially limiting their effectiveness for quantization calibration. To address this limitation, we propose RankQ-ViT, a rank-guided DFQ framework for ViTs. We first observe that patch similarity matrices derived from Gaussian noise tend to have lower ranks than those derived from real images. Motivated by this observation, we introduce a block-aware self-contrastive objective that promotes feature diversity during synthetic data generation without explicitly computing matrix rank at each optimization step. We then select calibration samples based on their rank and semantic consistency and use them for block-wise reconstruction of the quantized model. Experiments on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet demonstrate the effectiveness of RankQ-ViT across multiple architectures and tasks, particularly under low-bit quantization. The code is available at https://github.com/Runqing-forMost/rankq-vit.git
bullets: Addresses the limited feature-direction diversity of calibration samples generated by similarity-entropy-based DFQ methods.
Uses a block-aware self-contrastive objective to promote feature diversity without explicitly computing matrix rank during optimization.
Selects synthetic calibration samples using rank and semantic consistency, then applies them to block-wise quantized-model reconstruction.
Evaluations on ImageNet, COCO, ModelNet40, and ShapeNet show effectiveness across architectures and tasks, particularly at low bit widths.
Scope: performance depends on synthetic calibration data and is evaluated across the listed vision tasks and architectures.

papers.abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(ε, δ)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.
bullets: Targets long-context inference where the KV cache exceeds GPU HBM and host-memory transfers dominate latency.
Keeps query-agnostic pivotal tokens and a token-level sketch on the GPU, while storing the full cache in CPU memory.
Uses PoissonComp for pivotal-token sampling and KVFetch to verify attention error against a user-specified $(ε, δ)$ tolerance.
Fetches additional CPU-resident tokens only when the tolerance cannot be met locally.
Reports 90–100% of dense quality at 32K context, with 8–32× lower GPU memory use and 2–23% cache fetched per generated token across the evaluated models and benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of VERKV. The GPU holds query-agnostic pivotal tokens (deterministic and stochastic) and a sparse attention indexer (sketch), while the full KV cache resides in CPU memory. An error-estimation module uses the pivotal tokens and sketch to decide whether the approximation already meets a user tolerance (ϵ, δ); if not, a query-aware fetch recovers additional tokens from the host so that the final attention is guaranteed to have error (ϵ, δ).

Figure 3. Quality vs. compression rate. Average quality of different compression setups across the RULER and LOFT benchmarks at context lengths of 32K and 128K for three models. We observe that (1) POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) consistently outperforms KVzip, and (2) VERKV(C=KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) = POISSONCOMP(C=KVzip) + KVFETCH improves upon POISSONCOMP under all settings. (3) Relative to dense attention, quality is better preserved at shorter context lengths for a given compression rate, for the Qwen family compared to Ministral, and on RULER compared to LOFT. In particular, VERKV recovers near-dense quality on RULER-32K across all three models. Our algorithm currently uses a naive 2-bit sketch to bootstrap its estimates; improving sketch accuracy is a promising direction for further quality gains as can be seen with VERKV(C=KVzip, A=perfect sketch) which matches Dense in nearly every setting. Host traffic for these runs is reported per generated token in Table 1 and per forward pass in Table 2.

Figure 7. Decode throughput, time per output token and time to first token vs. batch size in vLLM (Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K and RULER-128K, 16×, δ = 0.05). At 32K, VERKV stays ahead of Dense (offload) at every batch size, and its throughput grows from 13.8 to 20.6 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.05 and from 26.8 to 42.4 tokens/s at ε0 = 0.5, while Dense (offload) is bound by PCIe and stays near 9 tokens/s. The gain from batching is small because the decide kernel saturates shared memory and runs the requests of a batch one after another. At 128K, VERKV at ε0 = 0.05 approaches Dense (offload) as the batch grows, whereas ε0 = 0.5 keeps a 4–5× advantage. Fast KVzip is fastest throughout but loses most of its quality (Table 1).

Figure 6. Quality vs. speed in vLLM. VERKV(C=Fast KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K at 16×, sweeping ε0 at δ = 0.1 against dense attention with the cache offloaded to host memory. At the default ε0 = 0.05, VERKV decodes 1.6× faster and cuts end-to-end latency by 5 s at near-dense quality; larger ε0 trades a few points of quality for up to 3× throughput, with gains flattening once fetching becomes negligible.

Figure 2. Binary shrinkage. In practice we apply a simpler bound, with λi ∈ {1, ri}. The figure shows the MSE of the denominator estimate for one query row (Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×) as more tokens of L are switched from λi = 1 to λi = ri, relative to the unbiased estimator. Shrinking a few tokens cuts the MSE nearly in half, while shrinking all of them makes it worse (1.62×); the deployed sketch finds a slightly earlier, shallower minimum than exact weights. See Appendix A.2.

Figure 5. Error adherence of VERKV(C=KVzip) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×, δ = 0.1 (about one million attention decisions per setting). With a perfect sketch, under 1% of decisions exceed ε0, far below δ at every tolerance. The naive 2-bit sketch stays within δ only at ε0 = 0.3, but remains far below the failure rate without fetching. Sketch error, not the certificate, is what limits adherence.

Figure 4. Effect of the tolerance ε0 and failure probability δ. VERKV(C=KVzip, A=2-bit sketch) on Qwen3-4B, RULER-32K, 16×: KV read from host per decode step (a) and score change relative to Dense (b). ε0 controls traffic, which falls about 43× from ε0 = 0.01 to 0.3, while δ changes it by less than 2×. Quality stays within one point of Dense up to ε0 = 0.05, the default (circled), and degrades slightly beyond it.

Figure 8. GPU kernel time per decode step, split by phase (Qwen34B, RULER-32K, 16×, batch size 1, δ = 0.05). Dense (offload) spends almost all of its step fetching the cache over PCIe. VERKV spends most of its step in the decide kernel that computes the certificate and the fetch set, and only 1–37 ms fetching; at the default ε0 = 0.05, fetching takes 8 ms against 107 ms for Dense (offload). Faster decide kernels are therefore the main lever for further speedups.

Figure 9. Host-to-GPU PCIe utilization during decode (Qwen34B, RULER-32K, 16×, batch size 1, δ = 0.05; measured link bandwidth 55.5 GB/s). Dense (offload) saturates the link at 92%, while VERKV uses 2–16% of it (4.4% at the default ε0 = 0.05), leaving bandwidth for other requests or larger contexts.

Table 2. Fetch statistics of VERKV(C=KVzip, 16×, RULER-32K, δ = 0.1). Decisions that fetch: share of decisions (one query head in one layer at one forward pass) that fetch at least one token. KV-head steps that fetch: the same per KV head, after merging the query heads that share it. Tokens per fetch: tokens fetched by a fetching decision, as % of the context. KV read: fetched keys and values plus shortlist keys over all forward passes, as % of the full cache. At the default ε0 = 0.05, three quarters of decisions fetch, yet each fetches only 4–6% of the context and the overall read is 10.8% of the cache. [Top] Detailed statistics for Qwen3-4B [Bottom] 2-bit sketch fetches across models.

Table 1. Quality, GPU-resident memory and host traffic of dense attention, KVzip, Fast KVzip and VERKV on three models. Quality is the mean fraction of dense performance across 18 tasks spanning RULER (multi-key and multi-value needle retrieval, common-word extraction, question answering) and LOFT (NQ, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, QAMPARI, QUEST) at 32K and 128K context (C = Fast KVzip, A = 2-bit sketch, ε0 = 0.05, δ = 0.1). VERKV delivers a score comparable to dense attention, while keeping a low GPU-resident memory and simultaneously fetching a fraction of the full cache per generated token.

papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression with bounded-error attention and reduced CPU-to-GPU transfer for LLM inference.
papers.title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
papers.tldr: VerKV provides error-bounded KV-cache compression that avoids unnecessary CPU-to-GPU transfers while preserving near-dense LLM attention quality.

papers.abstract: High-resolution weather prediction is important for resolving local atmospheric patterns missed by coarse global forecasts. Large pretrained weather backbones have improved global forecasting, but adapting them to produce future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states remains challenging and costly. We formulate this setting as Predictive Spatiotemporal Weather Downscaling (PSWD), a task that jointly refines spatial and temporal resolution while predicting future high-resolution trajectories. To this end, we propose a framework that decomposes prediction into spatial and temporal stages using a shared pretrained backbone, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads. For backbone adaptation, we introduce PROLA (PRincipal-Orthogonal Low-rank Adaptation), which allocates a fixed low-rank budget between pretrained weights' principal directions and their orthogonal complement. PROLA further rescales rank-1 optimizer updates using gradient signals, improving adaptation without increasing trainable rank. Experiments in the PSWD setting show that PROLA outperforms representative low-rank adaptation baselines. Further experiments across diverse datasets and tasks support the broader applicability of PROLA, showing that its benefits extend beyond the primary weather downscaling setting.
bullets: Addresses predictive spatiotemporal weather downscaling: forecasting future high-resolution fields from recent coarse states.
Uses a shared pretrained backbone with separate spatial and temporal stages, fixed numerical scaffolds, and lightweight residual heads.
Introduces PROLA, which splits a fixed low-rank budget between principal weight directions and their orthogonal complement.
Rescales rank-1 optimizer updates according to gradient signals without increasing trainable rank.
Experiments report improvements over representative low-rank adaptation baselines, with benefits also observed across diverse datasets and tasks.

The effective weight combines the frozen residual weight and the two trainable branches as W eff = W res +∆Wp +∆Wo. papers.abstract: We evaluate AI agents in an online setting where tasks arrive sequentially and, before running each task, we construct an upper predictive bound on its \emph{time-to-success}---the number of interactions until the task is completed successfully. Under a limited budget, some runs are stopped early, so their time-to-success is unobserved (right-censored), and the correctness of the bound may be unknown. We introduce \emph{\textbf{PR}edictive Bounds for \textbf{O}nline \textbf{B}udget \textbf{E}fficiency} (\texttt{PROBE}), a method for constructing calibrated upper predictive bounds while adaptively allocating a limited budget across agent tasks to reduce the anticipated coverage deficit. Our method calibrates the bounds online using inverse-probability-weighted feedback together with a correction designed to minimize coverage deficit while remaining unbiased. We prove that \texttt{PROBE} provides a coverage guarantee for any finite time horizon while satisfying the budget constraint. Experiments on software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show that \texttt{PROBE} attains a coverage rate closer to the target level with tighter predictive bounds than a calibrated baseline.
bullets: Addresses online agent evaluation when tasks arrive sequentially and early stopping leaves completion times unobserved.
Constructs upper predictive bounds for the number of interactions needed to complete each task successfully.
Uses inverse-probability-weighted feedback and an unbiased correction to reduce anticipated coverage deficit.
Provides finite-horizon coverage guarantees while respecting the budget constraint.
Experiments across software engineering, retrieval-augmented generation, and instruction following show coverage closer to target with tighter bounds than a calibrated baseline.

Both outcomes are integrated via a coverage-aware update (6) (Theorem 3) consisting of (6a) online calibration to adjust predictive upper bounds (τt+1) and (6b) a budget strategy to optimize future budget allocation (πt+1).

papers.abstract: Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width. Under this unified weight-traffic metric, our 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent models establish a new accuracy-traffic Pareto frontier: the 2.5-bit-equivalent models match dense 3-bit QAT accuracy, while the 1.5-bit-equivalent models approach dense 2-bit models and outperform dense ternary models by 1.3 pp on average. These results establish native-gate training as a practical approach for combining high FFN sparsity with low-bit weights.
bullets: Problem: Native-gate routing performs poorly at high sparsity in pretrained SwiGLU models, and inactive FFN weights must be avoided early to reduce decoding traffic.
Method: End-to-end sparsity-aware training turns the existing gate projection into a fixed-budget top-k router without adding auxiliary router parameters or changing the SwiGLU activation.
Result: After approximately 30B tokens, 1B–8B LLaMA models retain average zero-shot accuracy within 0.2–2.7 percentage points of dense checkpoints at 75–85% sparsity.
Quantization: Continued-QAT helps recover accuracy at 4-bit weights, while joint-QAT is more effective below 4 bits.
Contribution: Under a unified weight-traffic metric, the approach reaches 2.5- and 1.5-bit-equivalent trade-offs, matching dense 3-bit QAT and approaching dense 2-bit performance.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc explanation methods for video action recognition typically conflate spatial appearance and temporal dynamics into a single saliency or importance map. We propose a perturbation-based framework that disentangles these contributions into a spatial appearance mask ($M_a$) and a temporal motion mask ($M_m$). The two masks are jointly optimized against a frozen action recognition model through factored perturbation architecture, with nearest frame replacement to identify important temporal dynamics. A separation penalty discourages the appearance mask from spending budget on frames that the motion mask has already discarded. A ReLU-based area constraint penalizes explanations larger than an assigned budget. To evaluate these explanations, we introduce a separation protocol that sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames independently, backed by proofs characterizing the proposed method. Across EPIC-Kitchens-55, EGTEA Gaze+, and Something-Something V2, our method attains the lowest deletion AUC against leading baselines while producing masks roughly five times sparser.
bullets: Addresses the conflation of spatial appearance and temporal dynamics in existing video explanations.
Jointly learns an appearance mask and a motion mask against a frozen recognition model.
Uses nearest-frame replacement, separation penalties, and area constraints to isolate temporal and spatial importance.
Introduces a protocol that independently sweeps spatial pixels and temporal frames to evaluate explanations.
Across three video datasets, achieves the lowest deletion AUC among compared baselines with masks about five times sparser.

papers.abstract: Visual chain-of-thought (visual-CoT), also known as "thinking with images", equips LVLMs with the ability to locate and use key visual evidence for reasoning. However, acquiring such visual-CoT capabilities requires costly post-training and tightly couples them to a specific backbone, making transfer to other LVLMs difficult. Existing cross-model transfer methods typically treat visual-CoT as a monolithic capability, using a unified representation that ignores the functional distinction between grounding and reasoning and introduces stage-irrelevant interventions. To address this problem, we propose Viscot-steer, a training-free activation steering framework for transferring visual-CoT capabilities across heterogeneous LVLMs. Specifically, Viscot-steer first disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning vectors and extracts them from the source-model layers associated with the corresponding capabilities. It then aligns the vectors with the activation space of the target model and steers the grounding and reasoning layers during bounding-box prediction and reasoning-trace generation, respectively. Across benchmarks covering high-resolution visual understanding, general visual perception and reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning, Viscot-steer transfers capabilities from different visual-CoT models to architecturally diverse LVLMs and outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on the primary evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses costly, backbone-specific post-training for visual-CoT capabilities.
Disentangles visual-CoT into grounding and reasoning components rather than treating it as one capability.
Extracts source-model capability vectors, aligns them to the target activation space, and steers relevant layers at different stages.
Works across heterogeneous LVLMs and benchmarks spanning high-resolution understanding, perception/reasoning, and mathematical visual reasoning.
Outperforms the strongest capability-transfer baseline by an average of 1.86 percentage points on primary metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our Viscot-steer framework. (a) Disentangled vector extraction. Disentangled reasoning and grounding vectors are extracted from capability-specific contrastive prompts. (b) Phase-aware activation steering. The reasoning and grounding vectors are routed only to their corresponding generation phases and injected at capability-specific target layers.

Figure 1: Disentangling and transferring visual-CoT with our Viscot-steer. (a) Existing methods extract a unified visual-CoT vector, whereas our Viscot-steer extracts separate grounding and reasoning vectors using capability-specific contrastive prompts. (b) Existing methods inject a unified vector at a fixed layer, whereas our Viscot-steer steers each vector at its corresponding layer and generation phase. (c) Activation distributions and strengths of grounding, reasoning, and undisentangled visual-CoT at the early (12th) and later (22nd) layers during the grounding and reasoning stages. (d) Our Viscot-steer outperforms the existing baselines by a substantial margin.

papers.abstract: We study prompted chain-of-thought (CoT) with self-consistency (SC), i.e. sampling N traces and plurality-voting, on small language models, a regime where per-query compute budgets are tight yet SC is commonly applied with a fixed sample budget inherited from large-model practice, regardless of instance difficulty. Across two model families (Qwen-2.5-0.5B, Gemma-3-1B) at FP16 and MLX-Q4 (4-bit quantisation in Apple's MLX framework), on GSM8K and MATH-500, we run 8 per-task and 4 task-pooled experiments at n=200-400 with 1,000x paired-bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). Our first result is an upper bound: an oracle gate deciding per prompt whether to invoke SC reaches 109-174% of always-SC's accuracy at 23-30% of its compute in all 12/12 cases, so at N=5 always-SC is dominated everywhere on our grid. That margin is exactly the rate at which SC flips correct greedy answers to wrong, here 3-10.5% of prompts, which on Qwen-Q4 x MATH-500 exceeds the wrong-to-right rate and leaves always-SC 3 pt worse than always-greedy. Our second result is a deployable approximation: a gate over greedy-pass signals skips 45-99% of SC calls, with bootstrap CI half-widths under 5 pt, removing 36-79% of always-SC compute. Accuracy retention at those operating points has point estimates of 98.1-98.8%, which we report as point estimates because their CIs are wide (lower bounds 76-86%) over an SC accuracy of only 15-36%. The evidence covers N=5 on two <=1B families and two math benchmarks, which is the scope we claim. Code is available at https://github.com/heywanrong/SiftSC.
bullets: Across Qwen-2.5-0.5B and Gemma-3-1B on GSM8K and MATH-500, always using self-consistency with N=5 was dominated by an oracle that selectively invoked it.
Self-consistency flipped correct greedy answers to wrong on 3–10.5% of prompts; on Qwen-Q4/MATH-500, it made accuracy 3 points worse than greedy decoding.
A deployable gate using greedy-pass signals skipped 45–99% of self-consistency calls and reduced compute by 36–79% versus always using it.
Gated accuracy point estimates retained 98.1–98.8% of always-self-consistency accuracy, though confidence intervals were wide.
Results are scoped to N=5, two sub-billion-parameter model families, two math benchmarks, and FP16/MLX-Q4 inference.

papers.selection_reason: Gating self-consistency to reduce inference compute is an efficiency method for language models.

papers.tldr: Fixed-budget self-consistency can hurt small language models, while difficulty-aware gating preserves most accuracy and substantially reduces compute.

papers.abstract: Random perturbations around a shared checkpoint can produce experts for distinct tasks, but shared origin does not ensure that their gains survive composition. We formulate expert-pair selection for joint base-relative retention, measured by strict joint success and worst-task gain with unconditional abstention accounting. An exact finite-difference decomposition and an arbitrarily small orthogonal counterexample show why proximity and orthogonality alone are insufficient. We instantiate this formulation with quality-constrained spectral selection, a fixed-budget framework combining cross-task screening, layerwise pair geometry, separate validation, and Base fallback. Across six checkpoints, 21 task pairs, and five independent perturbation pools, the procedure improves strict joint success over Top-1 averaging throughout and leads the four-method model-scale comparison on four of six checkpoints. For the five models with at least 1.5B parameters, matched quality-only, global-cosine, and spectral ranking attain 49.1%, 50.5%, and 53.1% joint success. Under this matched protocol, the spectral selector also yields the highest worst-task gain and Weak Pareto rate and the lowest regression rate. Mean worst-task gain reaches +0.61 percentage points, while 17.1% regression and 13.0% abstention show that composability remains conditional. papers.title: When Are Nearby Experts Composable? Cross-Task Model Merging in Neural Thickets
papers.tldr: Nearby experts are not automatically composable; a quality-constrained spectral selector improves joint task success while showing that merging remains conditional.

papers.abstract: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/.
bullets: Addresses drift accumulation because streaming model predictions are fixed after emission and cannot be corrected by loop closures.
Uses causal streaming inference for frame tracking, while selecting keyframes to write into persistent SLAM state.
An asynchronous back end re-observes past frames with fresh context to verify loops, correct trajectories, and refine dense geometry.
Shares one frame-encoder pass across invocations; cached features also support loop retrieval without extra encoding cost.
Reports state-of-the-art results on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, with over 40% lower mean ATE than the best uncalibrated baselines and tracking above 28 FPS at 518×154 on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline. Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
bullets: Learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from depth, hand geometry, and demonstrations.
Predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, including occluded finger dynamics and scene changes.
Aligns policy queries with world-model predictions, then freezes the world model and transfers its dynamics into policy latents.
At deployment, the policy uses only RGB observations, language, and robot state.
Improves success from 49.4% to 60.5% on 11 DexJoCo tasks and achieves 58.3% versus 50.0% for the strongest baseline on three real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: Test-time reinforcement learning with majority-vote rewards trains a language model on unlabeled questions by rewarding the samples that agree with its most frequent answer. During training, each question locks into one answer, on hard questions often a wrong one, but which answer it locks into is known only after training. In this paper, we show that this outcome is decided early, in a short race driven by sampling noise between the answers that are close at the start, and we derive the probability of each outcome. With a separate logit for each answer, the runner-up wins with a normal tail probability of the initial gap, scaled by an explicit noise constant. In a network, however, the answer logits depend on shared parameters, and through the kernel of these parameters the updates of the trailing answers also change the gap of the two leaders. This spillover shifts the boundary between the starts won by each leader, and a closed form computes the shifted probability from a kernel probe and the start logits. In LoRA experiments with three models from two families, predictions made before training with the kernel frozen at its start value forecast which answer each question locks into better than a logistic model refitted on the outcomes, although they use no fitted constants. The closed form matches these predictions on the runs in which a check before training finds that the two leaders stay above the other answers, and it explains why a law that ignores the spillover needs a strongly inflated step.
bullets: Lock-in is decided early by sampling noise between the initially closest answer logits, often causing hard questions to settle on wrong answers.
For independent answer logits, the runner-up’s win probability follows a normal-tail law determined by the initial gap and an explicit noise constant.
In neural networks, shared parameters couple answer logits; a parameter kernel captures how trailing-answer updates alter the leaders’ gap.
A closed-form kernel probe predicts lock-in outcomes before training without fitted constants, outperforming a refitted logistic model in LoRA experiments across three models.
The closed form agrees when the two leading answers remain ahead of the others; ignoring spillover requires an inflated step-size parameter.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes test-time reinforcement learning dynamics for language models with majority-vote rewards.
papers.title: The Race Is Decided Early! A Kernel Law Predicts Lock-In in Majority-Vote Test-Time RL
papers.tldr: A kernel-based law predicts early which answer majority-vote test-time RL will lock into, including how shared-parameter spillover shifts the outcome boundary.

papers.abstract: Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. Project website: https://jinggm.github.io/mosu2/
bullets: Addresses evolving outdoor interactions involving pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, signals, terrain, and temporary restrictions.
Uses two-stage trajectory selection: contextual reasoning decides when and what additional evidence to retrieve.
Retrieves and aligns geometric and dynamic information only for unresolved interactions to support real-time decisions.
Follows GPS-planned routes and filters candidate trajectories through multimodal traversability analysis.
Real-world success increased from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4%, with about 2.2× higher mean decision latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the MOSU2 architecture. Building on MOSU’s routing and traversability framework, GPS-based routing provides subgoals, while LiDAR and robot-velocity observations support candidate trajectory generation. RGB-based semantic segmentation provides complementary traversability assessments. MOSU2 introduces a VLM-retrievable local map and two-stage trajectory selection: the first stage screens the current scene and determines if more analysis is required, and the second stage, when invoked, combines recent images with retrieved geometric and dynamic information to select a trajectory and velocity mode. The motion planner converts the selected motion into linear and angular velocity commands (v, ω).

Figure 7. Qualitative Evaluation: Each column illustrates one of the three components in our trajectory generation pipeline, (a) CVAE-based multiple trajectory generation, (b) semantic segmentation for traversability analysis, and (c) VLM-based trajectory ranking in the outdoor scenarios with various social conditions. In (a) and (b), lighter colors indicate higher scores, confidence scores in (a) and traversability scores in (b). In (c), the VLM ranks trajectories based on social cues. The top example shows a ranking of [3, 0, 1, 2, 4]. The bottom example shows a ranking of [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3].

Figure 1. MOSU2 supports long-range outdoor navigation across wheeled-legged, wheeled, and legged robot platforms (bottom row). The satellite view illustrates a route from the start (yellow star) to the goal (green circle). The left-side examples highlight traversability challenges: (a) distinguishing sidewalks from off-road terrain, (b) accounting for differences in robot mobility, and (c) identifying crosswalks for street crossing. The right-side examples highlight social and traffic challenges: (d) interacting with moving agents, such as pedestrians, (e) interpreting traffic signals, including pedestrian signals with countdown displays, and (f) resolving conflicting traffic cues when vehicles violate traffic rules and obstruct the robot’s path. MOSU2 combines global route guidance and robot-specific traversability assessment with two-stage reasoning that retrieves local geometric and dynamic information to interpret these conditions and select appropriate motion.

Figure 6. Geometric and Semantic Analysis: Both geometric trajectory generation and semantic segmentation perform well in most cases, but there are also failure cases, as marked in yellow circles in (c) and (d). When the elevations of the lawn and sidewalk are similar, the geometric model struggles to perform accurately. Additionally, segmentation fails in out-of-distribution scenarios.

Figure 3. Routing and subgoal transformation. OpenRouteService routing uses the robot’s GPS location and the destination to obtain a global route, from which an intermediate GPS waypoint ĝ is selected. The waypoint is converted to the odometry frame with metric coordinates by aligning the GPS and robot motion, yielding the subgoal g. This subgoal provides directional guidance for trajectory selection.

Figure 8. Representative social, traffic, and irregular navigation scenarios used to evaluate MOSU2: (a) responding to a pedestrian’s stop gesture, (b) navigating a construction area with warning and directional signs, (c) crossing at a signalized intersection, (d) sharing the road with moving agents, illustrated by a cyclist, (e) intersecting with a vehicle, requiring the robot to analyze the car’s velocity to determine if it is yielding, and (f) navigating in sidewalk baseline without any social or traffic situation. Panels (d) and (e) both belong to the shared-road group (Road + Vehicles/Bikes/Peds) in Table 2. These scenarios require interpreting contextual cues and, where relevant, considering the geometry and motion of surrounding road users to determine appropriate robot behavior.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient image-to-video transfer adapts frozen image foundation models to video via lightweight trainable adapters. Existing methods insert the same adapter at every transformer layer, implicitly assuming all layers require equal temporal modeling. A layer-wise sensitivity analysis across four video-native model families and two pretraining paradigms reveals that this assumption is wrong: temporal sensitivity increases with depth, and the pretraining paradigm determines its growth profile. Vision-only models exhibit a gradual rise, while vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery. This finding motivates STRAP, a training-free adapter placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model. Spatial adapters are assigned before this boundary and temporal adapters after it, without modifying the adapter architecture itself. On four fine-grained action recognition benchmarks, STRAP improves accuracy by up to 11.8% over uniform placement, reduces trainable parameters by 29 to 48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%. On standard benchmarks, it matches accuracy with fewer parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/th-nesh/STRAP.
bullets: Temporal sensitivity generally increases with transformer depth, but its pattern depends on the model’s pretraining paradigm.
Vision-only models show a gradual sensitivity increase; vision-language models show early suppression followed by late recovery.
STRAP is a training-free placement rule that derives a spatial-to-temporal transition boundary from a paradigm-matched video model.
Across four fine-grained action-recognition benchmarks, it improves accuracy by up to 11.8%, reduces trainable parameters by 29–48%, and lowers inference time by up to 10%.
On standard benchmarks, STRAP matches accuracy with fewer parameters.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning have made verifiable rewards a central post-training paradigm for improving multimodal reasoning. However, methods such as GRPO remain data- and compute-inefficient, spending rollout and annotation budget on prompts that provide little learning signal. We propose DISCOVER, an online data-discovery framework for budgeted multimodal GRPO that enables vision-language models to dynamically identify prompts that are most useful for the current policy. DISCOVER first organizes the multimodal sample pool into semantic clusters and queries a small set of density-diverse representative samples to obtain initial reward observations. During training, it estimates the utility of unannotated samples by transferring sparse reward feedback from queried samples. Since sample utility changes as the policy evolves, DISCOVER dynamically updates these estimates with recency-weighted rollout observations. It then selects only high-utility prompts for annotation using a policy-conditioned score that accounts for reward variance and difficulty. Once the discovery budget is exhausted, DISCOVER continues with utility-based replay. Experiments on ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B show that DISCOVER substantially improves multimodal mathematical reasoning under a strict 10% unique-sample budget, outperforming budget-matched random selection, hard-example sampling, full-pool GRPO under the same training-step budget, and online selection baselines. Ablations further validate the importance of semantic coverage, online reward transfer, and stable discovery cadence, establishing DISCOVER as a practical framework for data-efficient multimodal RL post-training.
bullets: Targets wasted rollout and annotation costs from low-signal prompts in verifiable-reward multimodal RL.
Clusters samples semantically, queries diverse representatives, and transfers sparse reward feedback to estimate unannotated-sample utility.
Continuously updates utility using recency-weighted rollouts and selects prompts based on reward variance and difficulty.
Uses utility-based replay after the discovery budget is exhausted.
On ViRL39K and VLAA-Thinking with Qwen3-VL-2B, improves mathematical reasoning under a 10% unique-sample budget; ablations support its key design components.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Cluster-balanced online discovery and frozen-pool reweighting. Once the unique-prompt budget is exhausted, the pool is frozen and subsequent GRPO steps reweight replay from the buffer; intensity encodes recency.

Figure 1: DISCOVER pipeline. Offline (green, left): prompts are embedded, clustered via spherical k-means, and seeded with REPR samples.
