papers.abstract: Surgical procedures are inherently partially observable, requiring surgeons to continuously infer evolving anatomical dynamics and future surgical states beyond the current observation. However, existing self-supervised learning methods primarily learn from observed surgical videos through masked reconstruction or predicting representations within the camera's current field of view, lacking the capability to explicitly model the out-of-sight surgical dynamics. Inspired by latent predictive world models, we introduce SurgWorld, a video-native, self-supervised framework for surgical representation learning, which treats a specified spatial or temporal shift as a pseudo-action and learns to predict the target latent representation from a partial observation. Specifically, we propose Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling (OSDM) as the pretraining objective for predicting representations conditioned on relative spatio-temporal shifts. We further regularize the learned latent dynamics from OSDM with a Geometric Visual Similarity (GVS) objective by aligning patch-level relational structures between predicted and target representations, preserving spatial geometry and local visual coherence for dense perception. These two objectives are integrated through an agglomerative training framework that consolidates complementary supervisory signals from multiple teachers to learn a unified latent representation of surgical dynamics and visual geometry. Extensive transfer learning experiments on 17 surgical benchmarks show that SurgWorld consistently outperforms existing vision foundation models across surgical workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense visual perception. We further conduct tailored qualitative and quantitative analyses, demonstrating that SurgWorld effectively captures surgical dynamics beyond the directly observed context through latent prediction.
bullets: Addresses the partial observability of surgery, which limits methods focused only on visible content.
Uses spatial or temporal shifts as pseudo-actions and introduces Out-of-Sight Dynamics Modeling to predict target latent representations.
Adds Geometric Visual Similarity regularization to preserve patch-level spatial relationships and local visual coherence.
Combines complementary supervisory signals through an agglomerative training framework for unified dynamics and geometry representations.
Transfers effectively across 17 surgical benchmarks spanning workflow recognition, fine-grained action understanding, and dense perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the SurgWorld framework. For clarity, the framework is presented in a simplified form to highlight its key methodological innovations.

(c) SurgWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated surgical benchmarks.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes Graphene, a lightweight image super-resolution architecture with two complementary feature refinement mechanisms: Ising-model-inspired local feature refinement using an Ising Refinement Block (IRB) and stage-history-based feature refinement using a History Attention (HistAttn) module. The IRB reuses attention output features and pre-softmax attention logits to construct signed pairwise token couplings within each local window, applies unrolled mean-field updates, and refines features through a gated residual correction. These signed couplings allow alignment and opposition between latent spins to modulate local feature refinement. HistAttn attends over the current stage output and earlier representations at the same token position and adaptively blends the current stage output with a history-weighted feature aggregate without adding spatial pairwise attention. On Urban100 at $\times4$, Graphene and Graphene-light improve over IET and IET-light by 0.24 dB and 0.38 dB, respectively, with 34.3%/13.7% fewer parameters, 44.8%/44.4% fewer FLOPs, 83.9%/95.9% lower latency, and 63.7%/92.0% lower peak memory. Real-world SR comparisons further show that Graphene recovers fine details and preserves textures across diverse degradations. Code and reference checkpoints are available at https://github.com/skethz/Graphene
bullets: Targets efficient image super-resolution while preserving fine textures and details.
Uses an Ising Refinement Block with signed local token couplings and unrolled mean-field updates for gated feature refinement.
Uses History Attention to blend current features with earlier stage representations without spatial pairwise attention.
On Urban100 at ×4, it improves over IET/IET-light by 0.24/0.38 dB while substantially reducing parameters, FLOPs, latency, and peak memory.
Real-world comparisons indicate improved detail recovery and texture preservation across diverse degradations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of Graphene. Top: Given an LR input, Graphene applies shallow feature extraction with a convolutional stem, deep feature extraction through six Graphene stages, each containing six Graphene Blocks (GBLKs), followed by a trunk convolution, and HR reconstruction with a PixelShuffle head (Shi et al., 2016) and a long residual connection. Bottom-left: Each GBLK applies LayerNorm, PSA (Zhou et al., 2023), an Ising Refinement Block (IRB), and a residual LayerNorm–ConvFFN branch. The IRB takes the PSA output features y and pre-softmax logits L as inputs: each token feature yi is projected to a scalar field hi and an initial magnetization m(0) i , while the logits L are mapped to a signed, symmetric window-level coupling matrix J with a zero diagonal. Thus, the resulting couplings define a window-local, undirected spin interaction graph. The IRB then performs Kmf mean-field updates to obtain magnetizations m, which gate a lightweight residual MLP correction. The final magnetizations modulate token-wise residual corrections through their gates. Bottom-right: HistAttn connects successive Graphene stages by matching a learnable stagehistory probe ηs with LayerNorm-normalized stored features, producing dynamic history selection weights w(s) r over the stage history {z(0), . . . , z(s)}, where r indexes the stored feature. The selected history is then fused with the current stage output z(s) using a learnable history fusion strength λs: ẑ(s) = z(s) + λs( ∑s r=0 w (s) r z(r) − z(s)). This update refines the current stage output by adaptively blending it with a history-weighted feature aggregate.

papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay in Minecraft and Roblox, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting gameplay demonstrations for vision-language-action models.
An LLM agent builds executable game environments and skill-targeted tasks.
Programmatic experts use privileged simulator state to produce instructions, visual observations, and keyboard/mouse actions.
Script2Play is behavior-cloned on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay.
It performs effectively on multiple public benchmarks and generalizes across game engines.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview. Generate: a coding agent turns each specification into a game with scenes s0, tasks (g, V ), and a scripted teacher π∗; a game must pass five audit gates, and a failing game is repaired (up to three rounds) or discarded. Demonstrate: the teacher plans on privileged engine state but acts only through keyboard and mouse; the piano roll shows its recorded keys (W: forward,←: camera left,→: camera right, E: object interaction) in one rollout, which the verifier accepts (V = 1). Only verified rollouts enter D. Play: behavior cloning on D turns a pretrained VLM into the policy πθ , which writes each 200 ms action chunk as text. It is evaluated on OpenHA in Minecraft, a training engine, and zero-shot on OmniGameArena (UE5) and ViZDoom.

papers.abstract: High-fidelity LiDAR simulation remains a bottleneck for scalable development and validation of autonomous systems. Existing generators can synthesize realistic scans, but they are typically constrained to a single sensor configuration, offer limited control over structure and geometry, and drift in long-horizon 4D generation. We present CrossLiDAR, a unified transformer-based framework capable of generating controllable and spatio-temporally consistent multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. Our approach leverages a rectified flow objective with a Multi-Modal Diffusion Transformer (MM-DiT) backbone, within a compact latent space of range images. To support multiple LiDAR sensors, an Inter-sensor Module enables interaction across sensors, while a ControlNet-style branch provides structural conditioning (e.g., BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes). For modeling the temporal consistency, CrossLiDAR generates short $N$-frame sequences and extends them autoregressively to improve long-horizon coherence. Our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving an average improvement of 29.56\% in JSD and 15.36\% in MMD evaluated on nuScenes and the Waymo Dataset. CrossLiDAR bridges the gap to modern autonomous-driving simulation by enabling calibration-consistent multi-sensor LiDAR rollouts over long horizons for controllable, scenario-based testing.
bullets: Addresses single-sensor limitations, weak structural control, and long-horizon drift in LiDAR generation.
Uses a rectified-flow objective with an MM-DiT transformer operating in a compact range-image latent space.
Models cross-sensor interactions and supports conditioning from BEV priors or 3D bounding boxes.
Generates short sequences and extends them autoregressively for longer temporal consistency.
Improves JSD by 29.56% and MMD by 15.36% over state-of-the-art baselines on nuScenes and Waymo.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of CrossLiDAR Framework. Our framework utilizes a latent rectified-flow [26] formulation to generate synchronized multi-sensor LiDAR sequences. (Left) A frozen VAE encoder first maps range images into a compact latent space zt. (Right) These latents are processed by an MM-DiT [9] backbone, which incorporates two different attention mechanisms: an Inter-sensor Module for crosssensor alignment and a LiDAR Sequence Module for temporal consistency. The generation is guided by a dedicated ControlNet [70] branch for BEV and 3D layout control. Finally, a frozen VAE decoder transforms the denoised latents back into high-fidelity temporal point clouds.

Figure 1. CrossLiDAR jointly generates synchronized LiDAR sequences for multi-sensor setups. Top: given multiple sensors mounted around the ego vehicle, CrossLiDAR synthesizes geometrically aligned per-sensor views (front/rear/left/right) that can be fused into a consistent ego-frame point cloud, while supporting structural conditions such as 3D bounding boxes. Bottom: our pipeline operates in a VAE-compressed range-image latent space; a rectified-flow module integrates an Inter-sensor Module for sensor-aware generation and a ControlNet branch for structural conditioning using BEV maps with projected 3D bounding boxes, yielding controllable multi-sensor LiDAR sequences.

The bottom row demonstrates multi-sensor Waymo generation, where a single unified scene is reconstructed by synchronizing outputs from four distinct generated sensors. papers.abstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. The final policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of a 43-second routine, a 46-second performance with automatic handoff, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance composed from the captured motion. In a live handover, a single remote request let the robot start from and return to the manufacturer's walking controller on stage, with a measured torque-free window of 45-140 ms. We report the training dynamics and hardware outcomes and discuss failure boundaries involving compliant flooring and occlusion in monocular capture.
bullets: Combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, simulated reinforcement-learning motion tracking, and ONNX onboard deployment.
An eleven-version hardware ladder addresses deployment-artifact corruption, state-estimator drift, and reference-motion edits for stable completion.
The robot completed the routine three consecutive times without a rope, performed a 46-second automatic-handoff demonstration, and sustained a 9.7-minute composed performance.
A live remote handoff returned control between the dance policy and the manufacturer's walking controller, with a measured torque-free window of 45–140 ms.
Failure boundaries include compliant flooring and occlusions in monocular video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real humanoid dance learning from monocular human video via RL and retargeting; directly fits embodied robot learning and human-video transfer.
papers.title: From Festival Video to the Stage: A Sim-to-Real Ladder for Long-Horizon Expressive Whole-Body Dance on a Commercial Humanoid
papers.tldr: A sim-to-real pipeline transfers a 43-second Awa Odori dance from monocular video to a Unitree G1 EDU, enabling repeated and extended hardware performances with automatic controller handoff.

papers.abstract: Describing hours of audio requires accurate event timing and sustained descriptive detail throughout the recording. We present LongCap, a framework for timestamped audio captioning (TAC), with the human-annotated LongCapBench and three diarization-inspired metrics: Timeline Error Rate (TER), Granularity Error Rate (GER), and Caption Similarity (tcpCapSim). LongCap interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and retained context to support length extrapolation within a 1M-token inference context window. Event-level reannotation restores caption detail, while systematic studies examine model scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation. LongCap-Diar achieves strong benchmark results and extrapolates to 16 hours of concatenated audio despite training on recordings no longer than 40 minutes. Our TAC models are competitive with Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus on short clips, outperform evaluated baselines in caption similarity and timeline accuracy in segment-level comparisons on LongCapBench-TAC-Long, and caption full recordings approaching two hours. On LongCapBench-TAC, 9B and 35B-A3B offer favorable size-performance tradeoffs, while 122B-A10B substantially improves event-dependency recovery. These findings support long-horizon general audio understanding and provide a foundation for always-on voice agents.
bullets: Introduces LongCapBench and three metrics for timeline accuracy, granularity, and caption similarity.
Interleaves audio chunks with structured event captions, using relative timestamps and context retention for length extrapolation.
Event-level reannotation restores descriptive detail, while studies examine scaling, dependency supervision, and self-distillation.
LongCap-Diar extrapolates to 16 hours despite training on recordings up to 40 minutes and can caption recordings approaching two hours.
Models are competitive on short clips and outperform evaluated baselines in segment-level caption similarity and timeline accuracy.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.
bullets: Models human activity as part of the manipulation task rather than background variation.
Covers four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence, with paired human-present task variants.
Includes a demonstration-generation pipeline and evaluates VLA, imitation-learning, and heuristic policies.
Human presence challenges current policies; manipulation and recovery are the dominant failure sources, and success does not consistently imply better safety.
HARP-Bench demonstrations improve simulated performance and help on real-world human contribution, but transfer to interruption remains limited.

papers.abstract: Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.
bullets: Addresses the exponential sample complexity of black-box safety certification methods for complex systems.
Uses monotone inductive barrier certificates to characterize safety when unsafe sets are upper-closed.
Reduces continuous-space certificate verification to localized checks on finitely many boundary cells.
Introduces Max-Monotone Networks, which universally approximate monotone functions, plus a training and refinement procedure.
The method can require only O(n) simulator queries under mild partition assumptions and certifies systems with up to 13,659 states in reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-stage large language model (LLM) cascades balance accuracy and inference cost, but reliable deployment also requires controlling error risk and identifying its sources across stages. We propose Compositional Conformal Risk Control (CompCRC), a risk-control framework for pre-specified multi-stage LLM cascades. We decompose the risk of accepting incorrect answers into additive stage-wise contributions over the full query population, linking local risk budgets to a system-level guarantee. CompCRC constructs and freezes candidate budget allocations and acceptance thresholds, selects one candidate on independent data, and certifies its stage-wise risk contributions on separate held-out data. Under conditional exchangeability, we establish a finite-sample guarantee: the marginal expected accepted-error risk of the complete deployment procedure does not exceed the global risk budget. At the reported comparison budget of $α=0.45$, all three stages of CompCRC pass their local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag. Compared with Global-CRC, which passes system-level risk certification at the same budget, CompCRC reduces observed accepted-error risk by 1.33--2.00 percentage points, improves final accuracy by 0.67--2.00 percentage points, and reduces weighted inference cost by 30.37\% on HellaSwag. The selected cost-based budget allocation also improves accuracy per unit cost by 10.6\%--46.7\% over uniform allocation. Further experiments show that stage-wise statistics identify stages that fail local certification checks, providing diagnostic information alongside system-level risk control.
bullets: Decomposes accepted-error risk into additive contributions from individual cascade stages.
Pre-specifies budget allocations and thresholds, selects among candidates on independent data, and certifies the choice on held-out data.
Under conditional exchangeability, guarantees that the complete deployment procedure stays within a global marginal expected accepted-error budget.
At α=0.45, all stages pass local checks on MMLU, GSM8K, and HellaSwag; compared with Global-CRC, it lowers observed risk and improves accuracy.
Stage-wise diagnostics reveal which stages fail local certification, while cost-based allocation improves accuracy per unit cost over uniform allocation.

papers.abstract: In edge intelligence systems, computation offloading and dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) are widely used to improve energy efficiency. However, as applications like deep neural network (DNN) inference evolve in complexity, their demands for memory resources have progressively increased, establishing memory as a critical bottleneck that impacts both latency and energy consumption. In this paper, we propose a joint optimization scheme integrating memory, computing and offloading for energy-efficient DNN inference. We formulate the energy minimization problem under deadline constraints as a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem, where the main challenge arises from the coupling between offloading and resource optimization. To address this issue, we decompose the original problem into two subproblems under a fixed offloading policy. The local subproblem is transformed into an equivalent geometric programming (GP) problem to derive the optimal memory frequency and computing frequency, while the edge subproblem is solved via convex optimization. An efficient coordinate descent (CD) algorithm is further developed to jointly optimize all variables. Simulation results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm achieves near-optimal performance with the gap from the optimal policy being at most 9.3%, and reduces the energy consumption of devices by up to 16.1% compared with benchmarks without memory frequency optimization.
bullets: Memory frequency is treated as a critical resource alongside computation and offloading.
The energy-minimization problem is formulated as a mixed-integer nonlinear program.
The approach decomposes the problem into local geometric programming and edge convex optimization subproblems.
A coordinate descent algorithm jointly optimizes offloading, memory frequency, and computing frequency.
Simulations show at most a 9.3% gap from the optimum and up to 16.1% device-energy reduction versus benchmarks without memory-frequency optimization.

papers.abstract: Mathematical performance depends on how a language model receives information, uses generated text and submits an answer. We study these dependencies through paired comparisons that separate submission requirements, draft reuse and candidate availability. On 65 development problems, an instruction permitting continued derivation produced no valid final answers in 390 short-output calls; a single-line submission instruction produced 390 format-valid outputs, including 389 parseable answers. Under the fixed submission protocol, 198 problems with failed initial submissions were answered correctly in 9.09p of cases with the question alone, 33.84p with its draft, 46.46p with candidates, and 59.60p with both. Drafts added 13.13 percentage points with candidates fixed, and candidates added 25.76 points with drafts fixed; both effects were significant after Holm correction and were subadditive on the accuracy scale. Retaining a trailing excerpt outperformed retaining a leading excerpt of similar average length by 10.10 points Holm-adjusted p 0.027. A second completion model showed the same directions of input effects on the fixed materials. In a cohort with parseable initial submissions, candidates added no correct answers when the previous draft was supplied, but added 27 points when it was absent. These results establish a conditional value of generated text: a failed submission can leave useful material, whose contribution depends on what else is supplied and what is retained.
bullets: A single-line submission instruction yielded format-valid outputs, whereas allowing continued derivation produced none in the short-output calls.
For failed initial submissions, accuracy rose from 9.09p with only the question to 59.60p with both the draft and candidate answers.
Drafts and candidates each improved accuracy, but their combined effects were subadditive.
Retaining trailing draft excerpts outperformed similarly sized leading excerpts by 10.10 points.
Candidate benefits depended on draft availability and were directionally replicated with a second completion model.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms. In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.
bullets: Targets the high latency of autoregressive action generation on resource-constrained robots.
Uses a lightweight retrieval-augmented draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without an additional neural draft model.
Reduces verification overhead through kinematics-guided action acceptance and KV-cache-sharing attention.
Introduces the Zora core to accelerate irregular memory access during retrieval.
On four VLA models using LIBERO, it retains comparable accuracy and achieves up to 3.4× software-only and 7.6× hardware-supported speedup over GPUs.

papers.abstract: Compressing continuous human motion into a finite vocabulary of discrete tokens is now the first stage of many motion understanding and generation pipelines. Vector quantization partitions a latent space into Voronoi cells around a finite codebook, but the geometry of that latent space is inherited from the input pose encoding, and it is unclear which encoding admits an efficient discretization. We study four encodings that place skeletal motion in different geometric spaces: Gaussian joint heatmaps on the pixel lattice, which we show to be a morphological dilation of the joint point set by a quadratic structuring function; root-relative joint positions in Euclidean space; local joint rotations on $\SO$ through a continuous 6D embedding; and a redundant full kinematic encoding. For each, we train VQ-VAE tokenizers whose codebooks lie on the unit hypersphere, varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension. Beyond reconstruction, we measure codebook utilization and the effective vocabulary size, i.e., the number of equiprobable spherical Voronoi cells with the same entropy as the observed token distribution. Rotation and position encodings keep converting additional codewords into effective vocabulary, whereas the full kinematic encoding saturates at a few hundred effective cells and heatmaps at fewer than sixty. The smallest code dimension gives the highest utilization for three of the four encodings, and the effect of temporal stride depends on the encoding. Encodings of the same pose family can thus yield effective vocabularies differing by an order of magnitude, a difference that reconstruction loss alone does not reveal, which points to input geometry as a first-order design choice in motion tokenization.
bullets: Compares four pose geometries: joint heatmaps, root-relative positions, local rotations, and full kinematic features.
Trains VQ-VAE tokenizers while varying codebook size, temporal stride, and code dimension.
Evaluates reconstruction alongside codebook utilization and entropy-based effective vocabulary size.
Rotation and position encodings continue benefiting from larger codebooks; full kinematic features saturate at a few hundred effective cells, while heatmaps remain below 60.
Small code dimensions generally maximize utilization, and temporal-stride effects depend on the encoding.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis of pose encodings for discrete motion vocabulary learning, relevant to motion representation and understanding.
papers.title: Does Pose Encoding Matter? Analyzing Geometric Representations for Discrete Motion Vocabulary Learning
papers.tldr: Pose encoding strongly determines how efficiently continuous motion can be converted into discrete tokens, with rotation and position representations supporting much larger effective vocabularies than heatmaps or redundant kinematic encodings.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning from limited feedback (RLLF), only a small fraction of an offline dataset can be labeled with rewards, and the central question is which samples should be labeled to learn a high-performing policy from the resulting partially labeled dataset. Prior work formalized this as a reward-selection problem by focusing on the selection stage while treating downstream policy learning as a black box, in a regime where queried rewards are not retained for reward-model training. We instead study the retained-label setting, where queried rewards can be stored and used to fit a reward model before policy learning. We bound the suboptimality of the learned policy in terms of two sources of error: one arising from offline RL on a fixed, offline dataset, and the other from uncertainty in the reward model. Since reward selection cannot change the offline dataset, the limited labeling budget must be used to strategically reduce reward uncertainty. Motivated by RLLF's observation that useful rewards tend to keep the agent on high-return trajectories, we introduce Successor-Guided Uncertainty REduction (SURE), a novel method that uses successor features to select rewards that are both uncertain and associated with states from which high-valued states are reachable. We formally derive SURE from a bound-induced design objective and characterize its exact one-step marginal gain. Empirically, SURE reaches near full-feedback performance with few reward labels across a variety of domains and offline-RL backbones, yielding an effective method for feedback-efficient reinforcement learning.
bullets: Addresses reward selection in retained-label reinforcement learning from limited feedback, where queried rewards train a reward model.
Decomposes policy suboptimality into offline-RL error and reward-model uncertainty.
Uses successor features to prioritize samples that are both uncertain and connected to reachable high-value states.
Derives SURE from a bound-based objective and characterizes its exact one-step marginal gain.
Empirically achieves near full-feedback performance across multiple domains and offline-RL backbones with few labels.

Figure 1: Illustrative retained-label reward-selection example in a navigation task. The agent must reach the goal while avoiding a central obstacle. With the initial reward labels, the policy learned from the current reward model takes a long detour, while a more direct path remains possible. Uncertainty-only selection chooses a state where the reward model is uncertain, but the selected state may be far from trajectories that lead to high return. Reachability-only selection chooses a state that can lead toward regions assigned high value by the current reward model, but this estimate can be misleading when the reward model is inaccurate. SURE combines both signals, selecting for labeling a reward that is uncertain under the current reward model and lies on a reachable path toward currently high-value states, yielding a better policy with fewer reward labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the high action-inference cost that slows vision-based robot execution.
Generates continuous target positions from discontinuous predictions using a tracking-control formulation.
Uses asynchronous inference and variance-based adaptive action skipping to improve execution speed.
Evaluated with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot.
Reports substantial speedups while maintaining high task success rates.

papers.abstract: We present SoftPAT3D, a physics-augmented framework for text-to-3D scene generation in which deformable objects, such as cloth, stuffed toys and ropes, are generated as physically valid, simulation-ready bodies and placed in intersection-free contact with the furniture that supports them, with one another and with themselves. Existing physics-augmented pipelines simulate rigid bodies only and cannot accommodate a generated deformable object, which text-to-3D generation returns as a geometrically invalid mesh, sometimes self-intersecting, that has no rest shape, no material model and no admissible initial state. These are the inputs a deformable simulation requires, and we construct each from information already in the pipeline. The rest shape comes from how the object is manufactured rather than from the generated physically inconsistent deformed configuration, and a material library assigns each deformable object its initial elastic parameters, which can then be optimized. The occluded support is regenerated and converted into a watertight collision mesh, each object is released from an optimizable placement above the supporting part that the prompt specifies, and the complete scene is driven to static equilibrium under one unified contact model, with completion verified by geometric checks and a vision-language model. When a scene fails the prompt, a grid search over placements corrects it, and the adjoint of a differentiable simulation of the same contact energy reaches the targets the grid does not, places several bodies jointly and recovers and optimizes material parameters. Multi-body scenes equilibrate in a single simulation, and the pipeline also runs from the text prompt alone. On all sixty-five prompts, SoftPAT3D produces no undesired interpenetration of any kind, whereas every other system does, and its scenes directly support scene editing and robotic manipulation.
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing physics-augmented text-to-3D systems to handle deformable objects with invalid meshes, missing rest shapes, and absent material models.
Constructs rest shapes, collision meshes, material parameters, and admissible placements from information available in the generation pipeline.
Uses unified differentiable contact simulation to bring multi-body scenes to static equilibrium, with grid search and adjoint optimization for placement and material refinement.
Verifies prompt compliance and geometric validity using checks and a vision-language model.
Across 65 prompts, reports no undesired interpenetration, while every compared system exhibits some; the approach also supports prompt-only scene generation.

papers.abstract: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.
bullets: Introduces 3D full-object flow: dense trajectories over an object’s complete surface, including occluded regions, for rigid and deformable objects.
Provides a 1210-hour dataset combining real-world videos and physical simulations to supervise complete 3D object motion.
Develops a scalable annotation pipeline and quality metrics for recovering and evaluating full-object flow from observations.
Trains a world model that predicts full-object flow from an image and task description over reconstructed object geometry.
Reports reliable annotations, scalable flow prediction, and effective manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Object-centric full-object flow prediction framework. Given an initial RGB-D observation and task instruction, Qwen2.5-VL [39] extracts task-conditioned visual-language features, while a joint PointTransformer V3 [40] (PTv3) encodes reconstructed object and scene geometry. These features are fused into object tokens and refined by self-attention. The object queries attend to scene and language context through a cross-attention decoder, conditioned on noisy flow and time t, before a flow head predicts dense trajectories over the complete object surface.

Fig. 7: Visualization of real-world full-object flow annotations. Examples from AgiBot World [31], EPIC-KITCHENS [22], and Something-Something V2 [25]. Colored trajectories represent the estimated motion of points on the reconstructed complete object surface, with colors progressing from red at earlier timesteps to blue at later timesteps. Each example corresponds to a different manipulation clip processed by our automatic annotation pipeline.

Fig. 2: Automatic data annotation pipeline. Given an in-the-wild manipulation video, a VLM identifies the target object, describes the task, and segments the video into atomic action clips. For each clip, our pipeline extracts the target-object masks, reconstructs the complete object mesh and the point clouds, and aligns the mesh with the point clouds across frames to recover the object motion. The motion is propagated over the complete object surface to produce 3D full-object flow.

papers.selection_reason: Object-centric world model predicting dense 3D object flow for scalable robot manipulation, with a large-scale dataset.
papers.title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset
papers.tldr: ObjectWorld scales object-centric robot world modeling by introducing dense 3D full-object motion supervision that covers both visible and occluded surfaces.

papers.abstract: Video understanding evaluations are intended to measure a model's proficiency in video perception and task solving. However, current VideoQA benchmarks struggle to isolate these capabilities due to their reliance on multiple-choice (MC) answer guidance, language priors, and fragile scoring pipelines. Disentangling these confounding factors reveals how much of a model's score is supplied by the evaluation context rather than earned through faithful perception. Across six VideoQA benchmarks of varying length, we find that accuracy is significantly above chance without any visual input. This is caused by shortcutting and option-prior reliance. We express these effects in the language of faithfulness: option-exploitation and answer-conditioned reasoning traces are unfaithful even when they are correct. Together, our results show that a VideoQA score is jointly determined by language priors, option timing, and how outputs and labels are converted into correctness. We produce a novel Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) mechanism that discloses options at controlled stages of an open-ended (OE) trajectory, to obtain objective MC scores from faithful option-free inference. Our work demonstrates that agentic methods with ODR and faithful inference can match option-exploiting performance. Finally, we formalize our diagnostic collection and ODR as a reproducible evaluation protocol, and we release a human-relabelled edition of LVBench (correcting $20.5\%$ of keys) to remove annotation noise as a confounding variable.
bullets: Across six VideoQA benchmarks, models perform above chance even without visual input, indicating reliance on language priors and answer-option exploitation.
The study identifies option timing, answer-conditioned reasoning, and scoring/label conversion as major confounds in VideoQA evaluation.
Option-Delayed Replay (ODR) reveals answer choices at controlled points during an otherwise open-ended, option-free inference process.
Agentic methods using ODR and faithful inference can match performance achieved through option exploitation.
The authors release a reproducible diagnostic protocol and a human-relabelled LVBench edition correcting 20.5% of answer keys.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The core context variations against direct QA, drawn against each benchmark’s chance baseline and its model-free heuristic. The gap between the blind bars and chance is the accuracy the question and options carry on their own; the No question bars withhold the options along with the question. See more in Table 2.

Figure 8: LVBench, moALQl818ZY.mp4, question 3 (frames sampled inside the annotated time_reference window). Options (A) and (D) are the identical string ‘RACE TO RESCUE’, and only (D) is gold. A model that answers (A) gives a textually identical answer and is scored wrong.

Table 2: How much multiple-choice accuracy survives without the evidence it should require. Each column withholds or perturbs a single input while holding all other settings fixed relative to MC (full). Chance and Heuristic use no model at all (Appendix F). No question hides the question and the options, leaving the video and an instruction to emit a single letter, so it measures the label prior rather than a question-only baseline (§D). As expected, it scores below Heuristic on all six benchmarks. No video hides the video, and Black replaces the video with a blank one. Shuffle permutes the option order. Numeric relabels the options as digits. Splits and scorers are in Table 3, and Appendix E gives confidence intervals for the no-video, MC−OE and replay contrasts. Without video, models retain roughly half of their full MC accuracy on average (51% for direct QA and 50% for the Gaia loop, using flat per-question accuracy throughout). After correcting for random chance, no-video performance retains 29% of the available headroom above chance for direct QA (26% for the Gaia loop), ranging from 45% on EgoSchema to 12% on Perception Test. Shuffling or relabelling options has little effect.

Table 1: Multiple choice, open-ended, and the mechanisms that convert between them. OE scores free-text answers with two judges, claude-sonnet-4-5 and gpt-5.4-mini, against the correct option’s text (Appendix G.7). OE→match maps the prediction back onto the options, with the matcher’s abstention rate in brackets (abst). MC, OE→match and both replay columns are option-label accuracy. The two OE columns report the mean judge rating (0–100) followed in parentheses by the binarised accuracy (the percentage of items rated ≥ 80, corresponding to “mostly correct” in Box 3); all MC−OE differences in the paper use this binarised accuracy (see Table 8 for alternative thresholds). Replay rewinds the rollout and discloses the options at its last step or halfway through. Note: Direct QA has no replay condition because it is never denied the options. Video-MME v2 is reported using flat per-question accuracy with its non-linear group score in parentheses, except in the OE columns where only per-question judge ratings apply. Paired confidence intervals for the MC−OE and MC−replay differences are in Appendix E. Observed evaluator variance is low: over the 77 cells here whose scorer was run three times, the run-to-run standard deviation has median 0.03 and maximum 0.65 accuracy points.

Table 5: Paired 95% confidence intervals on the principal contrasts. Each entry is that row’s multiple-choice score minus the named condition, in accuracy points, with its video-clustered paired bootstrap interval. A positive number means MC scores higher. Per-question correctness is computed using the same evaluators as Tables 1 and 2. Each interval is computed over the intersection of items completed by both conditions. This equals the full split everywhere except LVBench open-ended (1,477 of 1,549 items) and the two QBench-Video Author-AVP replay conditions (622 of 868 items), where differences are taken over the shared subset. The two OE columns take the difference against the judge binarised at ≥ 80 (§G.7), not against the mean rating, so both sides of every entry are per-item correctness on one scale; the bracketed figures in Table 1 are these binarised scores. The two judges still disagree, by as much as 11.9 points on the same generations after binarising, which is why they are reported apart. On Video-MME v2 both OE columns are on the flat per-question scale, because the judges are defined only there, while its no-video and replay columns are the group score over 800 four-question groups. “–” marks a condition that was never run: direct QA is never denied the options, so it has no replay variant, and the two author implementations were not run without video.

Table 4: LVBench accuracy under the published and the corrected keys. Every condition is scored three ways: against the published keys on the full set, against the published keys once the 19 unanswerable items are dropped, and against the corrected keys on that same reduced set. Every cell uses the benchmark’s released scorer, as in Table 1. The middle column isolates the effect of correcting the keys from the effect of removing the items.

Table 6: Paired 95% confidence intervals on the option-channel controls. Each entry is that row’s multiple-choice score minus the same run with its options shuffled or its labels replaced by digits, read as in Table 5. A ±2-point equivalence margin was fixed before the intervals were computed; 9 of the 18 fall inside it, so we read these as descriptive rather than as evidence of invariance. “–” marks a condition that was never run.

Table 3: The evaluated split of each benchmark. Every condition in this paper runs the same split file, so all conditions are paired on identical questions. Chance is the exact analytic baseline over the split’s per-question option counts, which are fixed on three benchmarks and mixed on the rest, and MC acc. is the sighted direct-QA score of Table 2 under the scorer beside it.

Table 7: Run-to-run variance of no-video runs. The standard deviation is broadly smaller on the larger evaluation sets, from 0.16 at n = 3,200 to 1.20 at n = 454, though not monotonically: QBench-Video reaches 0.98 over 868 questions against EgoSchema’s 0.89 over 500. Every value is small enough that run differences remain interpretable. Video-MME v2 follows the paper-wide convention of Table 2: flat per-question accuracy first, group score in brackets.

Table 8: Sensitivity of open-ended accuracy to the judge binarisation threshold. Each row scores an open-ended answer correct when the judge rated it at or above the cut, over the 48 judge-scored cells of Table 1. OE is the mean binarised score, MC−OE its mean difference from the same row’s multiple-choice accuracy, inverted counts cells where open-ended scoring beats multiple choice, and recovery is the share of the MC−OE gap that last-step replay closes on the Gaia loop. The paper reports ≥ 80.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and improves VideoQA evaluation by disentangling genuine video understanding from option exploitation, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: What Does Multiple Choice Actually Measure? Disentangling Video Understanding from Option Exploitation
papers.tldr: Multiple-choice VideoQA scores can substantially reflect language and option shortcuts rather than genuine video understanding, so the paper introduces option-delayed evaluation for more faithful measurement.

papers.abstract: Adaptive tokenization aims to reduce the compute spent on uninformative image regions while preserving accuracy. Existing work relies on (i) fixed or frozen scoring rules, which cannot be trained toward the task loss, or (ii) discrete masks trained with straight-through estimators, which yield noisy gradients, while fully differentiable alternatives instead leave the pre-trained regular grid. We revisit adaptive tokenization from a regular-grid perspective and ask: can a two-scale quadtree be learned end-to-end without deleting a single token during training? We show that one coarse token and its four fine children can be made the two endpoints of a single continuous interpolation. We introduce Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning (\dvsp{}), which keeps four \emph{virtual slots} per $2{\times}2$ region and blends their token features and attention mass with a single weight $α$, exactly reproducing the discrete grid at $α\in \{0,1\}$. On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, \dvsp{} retains $97.9\%$ of dense Box AP while removing $64.2\%$ of visual tokens, giving a $1.61\times$ end-to-end speedup, and it outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution dense adaptation at matched budgets; these gains depend on the conserved attention mass, whose removal costs $1.59$ Box AP. On a frozen Segmenter it also improves Cityscapes mIoU, and on frozen DeiT backbones it exceeds entropy selection at identical per-image token counts.
bullets: Addresses fixed scoring rules, noisy straight-through masks, and differentiable methods that abandon the pre-trained regular grid.
Uses four virtual slots per 2×2 region and a single interpolation weight to blend coarse and fine token features and attention mass.
On COCO detection with EVA-02-B, removes 64.2% of visual tokens while retaining 97.9% of dense Box AP and achieving a 1.61× end-to-end speedup.
Outperforms entropy-based APT, DART, and uniform lower-resolution adaptation at matched token budgets.
Improves Cityscapes mIoU on a frozen Segmenter and exceeds entropy selection on frozen DeiT backbones; conserving attention mass is important.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. DVSP overview. (a) A dense ViT detector processes 9,216 uniform 16×16 tokens. (b) DVSP chooses 16×16 or 32×32 tokens per 2×2 parent with learned continuous weights, keeping fine tokens on the person and bench. (c) On COCO val2017 (EVA-02-B), DVSP retains 97.9% Box AP (58.93→ 57.72) with 3,303 tokens per image (↓ 64.2%) and a measured 1.61× speedup.

Fig. 2. Token allocation paradigms. (a) APT picks coarse/fine regions with a fixed image-entropy rule, so task gradients cannot train the router. (b) Discrete-gate methods (e.g., MSViT) gate in the forward pass and rely on straight-through gradients. (c) DVSP keeps four continuous virtual slots per parent: one router weight α blends token features and attention mass, so exact task gradients reach the router.

Fig. 8. ImageNet-1k classification examples. Five val images from the frozen-backbone router study of Sec. IV-C; in every row DVSP is correct while the entropy control is wrong. (a) DVSP partition; (b) APT entropy partition. Class names under the panels give each method’s Top-1 prediction, and the ground truth tags each row. Fig. 9. Cityscapes semantic segmentation examples. Six fixed 768×768 val windows (rows) under the frozen Segmenter of Sec. IV-C: two non-overlapping windows from each of three val images. Each window compares three methods at the same fine-parent budget: Dense (uniform 16×16 grid, 2,304 tokens), APT entropy (the Table II baseline), and DVSP (1,035/1,098/1,161/1,167/1,146/1,074 tokens). In each of the three columns the left panel is the input with that method’s executed patch assignment and the right panel the resulting segmentation. Entropy places fine patches on textured facades and foliage, while DVSP keeps them along object edges and small pedestrians; flat road and sky become 32×32 tokens in both adaptive rows. The DVSP partitions use the recorded |α|≥0.1 projection of this frozen-scorer study.

Fig. 7. COCO object detection examples. Routing and the coarse-token patch branch add 15.6ms while the transformer drops 98.7 → 25.2ms, so wall time falls 157.5 → 97.6ms (6.35 → 10.24 images/s, 1.61×).

Fig. 4. Token splits on a COCO scene. (a) Dense, (b) APT, (c) DART-Flow, (d) DVSP, with 9,216, 3,303, 3,303, and 3,378 tokens. Boxes with score ≥ 0.5. Of the 35 annotated objects, DVSP matches 21, as many as dense, against 14 for APT and 13 for DART-Flow. More cases in Appendix C.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable adaptive tokenization removes a large fraction of visual tokens in ViTs, directly relevant to token pruning and eviction.
papers.title: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning for Adaptive Tokenization in Vision Transformers
papers.tldr: Differentiable Virtual-Slot Partitioning learns adaptive quadtree tokenization end-to-end while preserving regular-grid training, substantially reducing vision-token compute with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Implementing intelligent learning systems on low- power edge devices is challenging due to the high compu- tational complexity, training latency, and energy demands of traditional Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs). Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), biologically plausible and spike-driven, come as an alternative. However, SNN training commonly relies on backpropagation through time (BPTT), which is computationally expensive, inherently global, and unsuitable for battery-driven devices. This work proposes a novel local learning framework for multi-layered SNNs inspired by Neural Activity Synchronization (NAS). Each layer updates its own weights using locally com- puted gradients. No gradient backpropagation is needed. This significantly reduces computational complexity, training latency, and energy consumption. The proposed SNN model is trained and evaluated on the MNIST dataset, achieving a classification accuracy of 97.78%. The model is also analyzed with Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise, demonstrating robust performance across different noise levels.
bullets: Targets the computational cost, latency, and energy demands of training SNNs on low-power edge devices.
Uses Neural Activity Synchronization to update each layer’s weights with locally computed gradients.
Eliminates global gradient backpropagation through time (BPTT).
Achieves 97.78% classification accuracy on MNIST.
Maintains robust performance under Gaussian and salt-and-pepper noise at different noise levels.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Implementation of the Local Neuronal Synchronous Model. The figure illustrates the formation of the basis matrix using periodic function in the proposed architecture. A distinct spatial frequency fc is assigned to each class c, thus they become class-specific periodic basis vectors. For a layer containing D neurons and C classes, the basis matrix B ∈ RC×D is formed by stacking these basis vectors. The spike count vector SC(ℓ) of the layer, with dimension 1 ×D, is projected onto the transposed basis matrix B⊤ ∈ RD×C to compute the logits, resulting in a logit vector of dimension 1× C.

Fig. 1: Neural Activity Synchronization based Spiking Neural Network architecture. This figure illustrates the processing of image data at a single time-step after Poisson rate encoding. The data is encoded for T time steps. Here, I represents the input vector dimension, Dn denotes the number of neurons in the n-th hidden layer, and C represents the number of classes. The Red Tick mark indicates the firing of a neuron at that instant.
Fig. 3: Results of proposed model on MNIST: (a) training loss curve showing loss decreasing after every epoch, (b) training accuracy plot showing stable learning.
Fig. 4: Results of proposed model on Fashion-MNIST: (a) training loss curve showing loss decreasing after every epoch, (b) training accuracy plot showing fluctuations during training.

papers.selection_reason: Local learning for spiking neural networks reduces training computation and energy, fitting the efficient-AI scope.
papers.title: Neural Activity Synchronization-Based Fast Local Learnable Spiking Neural Network Architecture
papers.tldr: A neural-activity-synchronization-based local-learning SNN avoids backpropagation through time while achieving 97.78% MNIST accuracy and robustness to image noise.

papers.abstract: Multi-task scene understanding models typically rely on modified vision encoders or complex decoders for cross-task interaction, which limits their flexibility and compatibility with off-the-shelf vision foundation models (VFMs). We introduce Virtual Task Prompting (VTP), which frames multi-task prompting as retrieving task-adaptive compositions from a shared virtual state, where both the state and routing process are optimized in an end-to-end manner. Concretely, VTP maintains an expanded set of virtual tasks alongside the backbone. At each layer, learnable routing matrices read task-specific compositions as input to interact with image tokens and write the processed results back, forming explicit pathways that capture the intricacies among tasks outside the encoder. Since VTP keeps the backbone clean, it integrates seamlessly with pretrained VFMs, advancing the state of the art on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2. Stress test on Taskonomy with 13 heterogeneous tasks further shows VTP's robustness in extreme settings. Ablations and analysis indicate that VTP's gains stem from adaptive routing rather than increased capacity. The project page is available at https://jacky1128.github.io/VTP/.
bullets: Addresses the rigidity and incompatibility of conventional modified encoders or complex decoders for multi-task interaction.
Maintains shared virtual tasks and uses learnable routing matrices to compose task-specific prompts at each layer.
Keeps the vision backbone unchanged, allowing seamless integration with pretrained vision foundation models.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2, with robustness across 13 heterogeneous Taskonomy tasks.
Ablations suggest improvements come from adaptive routing rather than simply increasing model capacity.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Qualitative results on Pascal-Context [9]. VTPtimm produces precise fine-grained object segmentation (bags), body-part parsing (human arms) with tighter saliency (suppress the spurious background). Key regions are with red circles. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 and more results on Figure 5.
Figure 3: Qualitative results on Taskonomy [77] with 9 dense tasks. VTPtimm produces apparently more accurate predictions than the baseline. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 and more results on Figure 8.

Figure 5: Qualitative results on Pascal-Context [9]. VTPtimm produces precise fine-grained object segmentation (bags), body-part parsing (human arms) with tighter saliency (suppress the spurious background). VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 further sharpen the details. Key regions are with red circles.

Figure 6: Additional qualitative results on Pascal-Context (Set 1). Two multi-person outdoor scenes that stress-test inter-individual disambiguation. Left: a man holding an infant against a cluttered natural background. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) lets semantic labels bleed across the person with background contour in segmentation, fragments body-part assignments at the overlapping arms in parsing, and over-highlights background clutter in boundary. Right: a crowded group where closely spaced individuals share similar appearance. TaskPrompter’s parsing labels entangle across adjacent persons, with leg assignments bleeding from one individual into the next. In both scenes, VTPtimm recovers coherent per-person segmentation masks, disentangled body-part labels, and tighter saliency focus. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 [57, 52] further resolve fine-grained inter-person boundaries, saliency, and produce geometrically smoother surface normals, approaching the ground-truth.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative results (Set 2). A challenging street scene that stress-tests two orthogonal challenges simultaneously: extremely small and thin semantic objects (distant poles, a tiny person occupying only a handful of pixels) and dense edge structures from road markings, building contours, and lampposts. TaskPrompter [71] (red circles) drops these tiny objects entirely from its segmentation and parsing maps, and produces a large spurious saliency blob on the background sky. VTPtimm begins to recover the thin structures in segmentation and parsing while suppressing the false saliency response. VTPvit-5 and VTPdinov3 further sharpen the objects (the blue and green masks in Semseg) and produce boundaries that capture both macro building contours and micro pole edges.

Figure 8: Qualitative results on Taskonomy [77]. An indoor scene with 9 dense prediction tasks under the extreme 13-task joint training regime. From top to bottom, predictions become progressively finer and more accurate. TaskPrompter [71] produces over-smoothed depth maps, flat curvature, and imprecise edges, while VTPtimm through VTPdinov3 successively recover depth discontinuities, surface details, and region coherence, converging toward the ground truth. This progressive improvement requires no additional computational cost. Only the backbone weights are swapped among VFMs.

Table 5: Comparisons to further ablating VTP’s effectiveness and contribution on PascalContext [9]. We compare VTP against (1) standard PEFT (LoRA) on a frozen ViT, (2) HPS with DINOv3 and task-specific heads, (3) TaskPrompter forcibly adapted to DINOv3, (4) multi-task PEFT methods (Polyhistor, VMT-Adapter, MTLoRA) with their original frozen-backbone setting, (5) the same multi-task PEFT methods extended with a fully tunable ViT-L backbone, and (6) our VTPtimm. ∆p is computed relative to TaskPrompter [71]. The results demonstrate that the effectiveness of VTP is attributed more to its prompting design, rather than the VFMs or the added capacity. Although it shares similar technical formation with those PEFT methods, their goals are different. VTP as a multi-task model architecture jointly trains the base model and the VTP modules, surpassing PEFT methods on both fully and partially fine-tune scenarios.

Table 2: Taskonomy results over 13 tasks. ∆p (%) denotes the average MTL performance gains relative to TaskPrompter [71] baseline (∆p=0). ↑ (↓) indicates the higher (lower) values are better. The best and second-best results for each task are highlighted in bold and underline, respectively.

Table 3: Ablation (left) and efficiency (right) results. Left: ∆pascal and ∆nyu denote the MTL gains ∆p (%) on Pascal-Context and NYUD-v2 relative to TaskPrompter [71]. V : virtual task number. VTPs share similar parameters and FLOPs. Throughput results are measured on a single L40 GPU.

Table 1: State-of-the-art comparison on NYUD-v2 [51] (left) and PASCAL-Context [9] (right). All Transformer-based models use a ViT-L backbone. VTPtimm is with ImageNet-pretrained weights, while VTPdinov3 and VTPvit-5 employ DINOv3 [52] and ViT-5 [57] without any modification. ∆p (%) denotes the average MTL gains relative to TaskPrompter [71] (∆p=0). ↑ (↓) indicates higher (lower) values are better. The best and second-best results per task are in bold and underline, respectively.

Best and second-best results are marked in bold and underline, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Multi-task scene understanding with task-adaptive prompting is directly relevant to spatial scene understanding and transferable to spatial-intelligence models.
papers.title: Virtual Task Prompting for Multi-Task Scene Understanding
papers.tldr: Virtual Task Prompting enables flexible multi-task scene understanding with pretrained vision foundation models by learning adaptive task interactions outside the backbone.

papers.abstract: Language models often abandon a correct answer when a user pushes back without giving a reason, and this behavior is usually studied as sycophancy to be suppressed. The same pushback, however, also leads models to revisit and sometimes repair a wrong answer. We measure both effects on multiple-choice questions from MMLU and ARC-Challenge with four open models from two families (Qwen3 1.7B, 4B and 8B, and OLMo-2 7B), reading the final answer exactly from option logits after a free-form reply. The reply budget changes the verdict. When Qwen3-4B may answer the challenge in at most 96 tokens, pushback leaves accuracy unchanged or slightly lower; with 1,024 tokens, it corrects 43% of its wrong answers and pushback raises accuracy by 5.7 points. Whether pushback helps overall follows a simple break-even rule in the cave and correction rates. Inside the model, caving can be partly predicted before the challenge: hidden states add about 0.04-0.06 AUROC over turn-1 confidence in three of our four probing runs. A probe trained only on self-correction cases predicts caving beyond confidence when replies are truncated, but not when the model can finish its reasoning. Activation steering never reduced caving selectively: where it worked, it suppressed self-correction as well. We conclude that sycophancy evaluations should allow full replies and report self-correction alongside caving.
bullets: Short response limits can hide self-correction; with 1,024 tokens, Qwen3-4B corrected 43% of its wrong answers and gained 5.7 accuracy points after pushback.
Whether pushback helps depends on the balance between answer-changing errors and repaired mistakes.
Hidden states modestly predict caving beyond first-turn confidence in most probing runs.
A probe trained on self-correction cases detected caving under truncation, but not when reasoning could finish.
Activation steering did not selectively reduce caving; it also suppressed self-correction.

Figure 2: Turn-1 accuracy against break-even accuracy for full replies. Points above the diagonal lose accuracy after pushback.

papers.abstract: Reasoning models often continue generating after producing an answer, yet stopping prematurely may interrupt useful verification or revision. In this work, we investigate whether targeted interventions in a model's internal computation can provide a reliable signal for when to stop reasoning. We introduce Prune-to-Probe, an inference-time controller that uses causal activation interventions to probe the stability of a model's current answer. Specifically, we identify late-MLP coordinates that contribute to post-answer continuation while excluding those important for answer completion. Once an answer is stated, Prune-to-Probe temporarily suppresses the selected coordinates and measures the resulting stopping response relative to matched random interventions. Crucially, these interventions serve only as probes: the model either returns its existing answer or resumes generation from an untouched cache. On MATH, Prune-to-Probe reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60%, preserving all naturally correct trajectories while repairing six errors. On MMLU-Pro, it achieves 1.145% pooled savings with no observed harm. Further analysis shows that the intervention captures decision stability rather than correctness (AUROC 0.502). These results demonstrate the potential of causal activation probes for efficient inference-time control without permanent model modification.
bullets: Targets late-MLP coordinates linked to post-answer continuation but not answer completion.
After an answer is stated, temporarily suppresses these coordinates and compares the stopping response with matched random interventions.
Uses interventions only as probes: the model either keeps its answer or resumes from an untouched cache.
Reduces reasoning-token forwards by 2.60% on MATH while preserving naturally correct trajectories and repairing six errors; saves 1.145% on MMLU-Pro with no observed harm.
The probe reflects decision stability rather than correctness, with AUROC 0.502, limiting its use as an accuracy signal.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on a single tokenizer that is chosen at training time and fixed thereafter. Most tokenizers are trained on English-dominant corpora, making them under-serve morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages, where they can produce fragmented representations, longer sequence lengths, and reduced information density during training. We propose Mixture of Tokenizers MoTo, a modular tokenization framework that trains dedicated per-language BPE tokenizers and composes them into a unified superset vocabulary, where tokens shared across languages are deduplicated into a common ID space. Each tokenizer maintains its own normalization policy, pre-tokenization rules, and vocabulary budget. Despite allocating significantly fewer entries to English, MoTo retains English performance while delivering consistent gains across 18 out of 21 typologically diverse languages spanning six scripts, with improvements most pronounced on morphologically complex and non-Latin-script languages that are systematically underserved by English-dominant tokenizer design. Our results suggest that modular subword tokenization is a practical and extensible alternative to monolithic tokenization for multilingual parity.
bullets: English-dominant tokenizers can fragment words and lengthen sequences, especially for morphologically rich and non-Latin-script languages.
MoTo trains separate BPE tokenizers with language-specific normalization, pre-tokenization, and vocabulary budgets.
Their vocabularies are merged into a deduplicated unified token-ID space.
The approach retains English performance and improves results in 18 of 21 diverse languages across six scripts.
Gains are strongest for languages underserved by monolithic English-focused tokenizers.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Left: Superset Vocabulary construction. Language-specific subword tokenizers are trained on their corresponding corpus. Words native to that language tend to be represented with fewer tokens, while non-native words fall back to coarser subwords or byte-level tokens. The superset vocabulary VS is constructed by taking the union of all tokenizer vocabularies, assigning shared tokens a single global index, with |VS | ≤ ∑ i|Ti|. Right: Mixture-of-Tokenizers (MoTo) pipeline. A tokenizer is selected based on the input language ID. The input is encoded into superset indices, processed by the transformer, and decoded back with the tokens from the superset, additionally it can utilize rules from the input tokenizer.

papers.abstract: Extended reasoning can help language models solve complex problems, but long responses often contain both useful computations and redundant checks. Conventional length penalties encourage shorter responses without distinguishing the functions of intermediate steps. We propose Phase-Conditioned Reward Shaping (PCRS), a framework that combines phase identification with training-time reward allocation. We investigate two classification routes: PCRS-H with a hidden-state classifier and PCRS-T with a frozen text classifier. Our main text classifier implementation assigns overlapping reasoning, execution, and revision labels to native chunks, then uses these labels and exact repetition to adjust existing token penalties. We compare the completed configurations on six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks and examine four reward-weight settings with the text classifier. Compared with a baseline using token-level length penalties, the default text classifier configuration reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 is approximately 62.07% for both methods, while oracle Pass@16 rises from 86.08% to 87.67%. These results show how phase-informed penalty allocation can reduce output volume and improve multi-attempt coverage without inference-time classification.
bullets: Targets redundant checks in extended reasoning that conventional length penalties treat the same as useful computation.
Uses phase identification to label chunks as reasoning, execution, or revision, then adjusts existing token penalties during training.
Evaluates hidden-state and frozen text-classifier variants across six mathematical and scientific reasoning benchmarks.
The default text-classifier setup reduces mean response length by 3.13%; sampled Pass@1 remains about 62.07%, while oracle Pass@16 increases from 86.08% to 87.67%.
The approach performs phase classification during training rather than at inference time.
