papers.abstract: Learning predictive models for dynamics is difficult because observations are often sparse and noisy, while the underlying dynamics evolve on nonlinear configuration manifolds and are affected by environmental dissipation and stochastic disturbances. Standard neural dynamics models can fit short-term trajectories but often violate physical structure, accumulate error over long horizons, or rely on parameterizations that introduce singularities such as gimbal lock. We introduce LieSPHGP, a stochastic Gaussian-process framework for learning rigid body dynamics with port-Hamiltonian structure and stability-aware robustness. LieSPHGP represents motion on Lie groups and Lie algebras, enabling coordinate-consistent optimization without singular parameterizations. Learned mass, potential energy, dissipation, and control components retain physical roles and a separate diffusion term represents stochastic forcing. Each component is modeled by Matérn kernel Gaussian processes which capture uncertainty induced by noisy observations. To improve physical validity, Lie group exponential map updates preserve rotational constraints, while positive-definite damping ensures nonnegative deterministic energy dissipation. The implicit-explicit integrator additionally provides unconditional stability for the frozen linear damping subsystem. The resulting model learns predictive dynamics that are robust to noise, respect rigid body geometry, and capture both intrinsic motion and environmental dissipation. Experiments on various noisy rigid body benchmarks show improved prediction accuracy, stronger long-horizon stability, and better satisfaction of manifold constraints compared with neural dynamics baselines. Code, data and interactive results are available on the project website: https://thribhuvanrapolu.github.io/liesphgp/
bullets: Targets sparse, noisy dynamics on nonlinear configuration manifolds, where standard neural models may violate physics or become unstable over long horizons.
Uses Matérn-kernel Gaussian processes for mass, potential energy, dissipation, control, and stochastic forcing components.
Represents motion through Lie groups and Lie algebras to avoid singular parameterizations and preserve rotational geometry.
Combines positive-definite damping with an implicit-explicit integrator for nonnegative dissipation and unconditional stability of frozen linear damping.
Noisy rigid-body benchmarks report improved prediction accuracy, long-horizon stability, and manifold-constraint satisfaction versus neural dynamics baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the proposed framework. Given noisy observations of a dynamical system, we learn a physics-structured model that captures both the underlying dynamics and their uncertainty while preserving the geometric structure of the state space. The learned model is then used to design a controller that drives the true system toward a desired state or trajectory without additional training. We demonstrate the framework on a 3D pendulum evolving on SO(3) and a quadrotor evolving on SE(3).

Figure 2: LieSPHGP framework. Five GP subnetworks (M−1, V , D, G and the diffusion ξ), each a level (constant, or linear for V ) plus a Matérn-kernel random-feature Gaussian process (Section 3.2, Algorithm 5), define a stochastic port-Hamiltonian system on SO(3) or SE(3) (Section 3.1), integrated with the Lie-IMEX solver (Section 3.3, Algorithm 4). At each training step one GP weight sample W ∼ q(W ) is drawn and held fixed throughout each rollout; starting from y0, the solver gives the prediction x̂−k and its Jacobians Ak, Bk, and a Lie-group EKF propagates the covariance P− k = AkPk−1A ⊤ k +BkB ⊤ k , so the diffusion enters only through the process covariance BkB ⊤ k , while the noisy observations yk and the learned measurement-noise scales σobs enter the measurement update. Training minimizes L = Eq(W )[EKF NLL]+βKL ( q(W ) ∥ p(W ) ) , the EKF negative log-likelihood of the noisy windows plus a KL term on the GP weights (Section 3.4, Eq. 21). Each parameter group has its own Prodigy optimizer, so its learning rate ηk(t) is adapted separately during training (Algorithm 1).

Figure 13: Physics Identification in Quadrotor System (Control Matrix): Actuated rows of the learned control map M−1G along a 10-s ground-truth tracking flight (training seed 0). The top row shows body-z thrust (vz), and the next three show body torques (ωx, ωy, ωz), with one column per rotor. The torque rows contain the rotor mixing matrix Bmix. Each row is divided by the magnitude of its nonzero ground-truth entries (37.0, 1658, 1658, and 777, from top to bottom). The normalized ground truth (dashed black) is therefore −1, 0, or 1, and all panels share the same vertical scale. PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) is shown in purple and LieSPHGP in orange. The body-x and body-y force rows are omitted because they are zero in the true model and the controller does not use them.

Figure 14: Physics Identification in Quadrotor System (Dissipation): Comparison of the learned diagonals of M−1 1 Dv for translational damping (top row) and M−1 2 Dω for rotational damping (bottom row) along a 10-s ground-truth tracking flight (training seed 0). The models compared are the ground truth (black, dashed), PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) (purple), and LieSPHGP (orange). LieSPHGP is closer to the ground truth for both translational and rotational damping, while PH-NODE over-estimates both (Table 16).

Figure 11: Physics Identification in Windy Pendulum System: Comparison of the learned diagonals of the matrices M−1G for control (top row) and M−1D for damping (bottom row) along the ground-truth swing-up flight (training seed 0). The models compared are the ground truth (black, dashed), PH-NODE (Duong et al., 2024) (purple), Lie-PH-NN-SDE (blue), and LieSPHGP (orange). Each model supplies the dynamics to the same geometric tracking controller with an IDA-PBC attitude loop. The controller’s commands are allocated to the four rotors of the contact-free PyBullet CF2P plant (Panerati et al., 2021). LieSPHGP (orange) tracks close to the controller using the true dynamics (green), while PH-NODE (purple) deviates during turns. Each model supplies its learned dynamical subnetworks to the same IDA-PBC controller acting in the windy pendulum environment, with the objective of stabilizing the pendulum at the upright configuration. LieSPHGP (orange) closely follows the controller constructed from the true model, which uses ground truth components (green), and reaches the target, whereas PH-NODE (purple) does not reach the upright. The experiment demonstrates that differences in learned physical structure that are modest in open-loop prediction can become consequential for downstream control.

Figure 3: Open-loop prediction on the windy pendulum. Roll, pitch, and yaw (Euler xyz angles of R, as in Figure 4) predicted over 10 s from the true initial state using recorded inputs. Roll = ±π corresponds to the hanging position. Black shows ground truth. Lines show the mean of 32 sampled paths, except for PH-NODE’s single deterministic path. Shading shows ±1σ and ±2σ. The true SDE uses independently sampled wind. We show the held-out trajectory with the largest difference in mean rotation error between Lie-PH-NN-SDE and LieSPHGP (43.1◦ versus 7.0◦). Over all 10 held-out trajectories, Lie-PH-NN-SDE has the larger error on 9. On the shown trajectory, 2σ coverage is 0.97 for both the true SDE and LieSPHGP, and 0.47 for Lie-PH-NN-SDE.

The physics model uses published vehicle parameters. LieSPHGP learns M−1, V , D, and G from training data alone. Figure 5: Control using the learned dynamics. The learned subnetworks M−1, V , D, and G define the IDA-PBC control law. For the quadrotor, IDA-PBC forms the inner attitude loop of an outer position-tracking controller (Appendix A.4).

papers.selection_reason: Learned stochastic dynamics with physical structure constitutes a predictor of environment dynamics, fitting World Models.
papers.title: Stochastic Port-Hamiltonian Gaussian Processes for Learning from Noisy Dynamics on Lie Groups
papers.tldr: LieSPHGP learns uncertainty-aware rigid-body dynamics on Lie groups while preserving physical structure, stability, and manifold constraints under noisy observations.

papers.abstract: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.
bullets: Represents tensors as functions from indices to values and operations as compositions over values, indices, and reductions.
With stacking, the formalism covers dense, jagged, sparse, and factorized tensors, plus many framework operations such as einsum.
Algebraic identities rewrite computations without evaluation; sparse matrix multiplication can thus avoid products involving zero values.
Using index functions as the abstraction could reduce tensor-framework operation complexity from O(mn²) to O(m + k²).
A draft implementation is publicly available; the abstract does not report benchmark results or limitations beyond its stated scope.

papers.abstract: In a multi-turn conversation, the choice of language model at one turn can affect which model should answer the next. The selected model's reply shapes the context for the next query, and its cached prompt prefix can reduce the cost of using that model again. We introduce MultiTurnRoute, a platform for building and evaluating multi-turn LLM routers. A shared interface gives built-in and user-defined routers the current query, dialogue history, and an estimate of each model's reusable prefix length. Our routing algorithm, Chain-of-Route (CoR), uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent dialogue history to predict response quality and estimates cost from each model's reusable prefix. MultiTurnRoute Arena ranks routers on recorded conversations and compares session quality and cost in interactive runs where a simulated user responds to each reply. On a benchmark drawn from WildChat and LMSYS-Chat-1M with per-turn quality annotations for five LLMs, CoR reduces the normalized cost required to match the strongest model's quality by up to 20.3% relative to the strongest routing baseline, while matching or improving peak response quality.
bullets: Multi-turn routing must account for how each model’s response changes future context and reuse opportunities.
The platform exposes the current query, dialogue history, and estimated reusable prefix length to built-in or custom routers.
Chain-of-Route uses a learned gate over recent and recurrent history to predict quality and estimate model-use cost.
Its Arena evaluates routers on recorded conversations and interactive sessions with simulated users.
On WildChat- and LMSYS-Chat-1M-derived benchmarks covering five LLMs, CoR reduced normalized cost by up to 20.3% versus the strongest baseline while matching or improving peak quality.

papers.abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.
bullets: Addresses the cost and manual effort of pragma tuning and repeated synthesis in HLS-based C++-to-RTL generation.
Uses synthesis-grounded data containing C++, Verilog, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives for supervised fine-tuning and GRPO.
Introduces a QoR Prediction Reward Model that estimates latency and resource usage from RTL representations, reducing reliance on repeated synthesis during training.
Reports improved RTL functional pass rates and latency/resource optimization over the base model, HLS optimization methods, and several commercial general-purpose models.

papers.abstract: Iterative neural policies usually spend the same computation on every decision, although the benefit of additional processing varies across states. We introduce Adaptive Internal Computation (AIC), an iterative policy that learns when to stop refining its latent representation and act. In AIC, we train action selection and stopping jointly, an expected-depth penalty values computation and intermediate value predictions provide auxiliary supervision. We show that when only some states benefit from further refinement, an ideal state-dependent allocator outperforms every state-independent stopping schedule at the same expected depth. With at most eight refinement steps per decision, AIC executes 3.3 steps on average across twelve benchmark tasks and lowers per-decision latency by 31--44% relative to a fixed eight-step policy on four control and robotics tasks. Its mean reward exceeds the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four. Ablating adaptive stopping and value supervision separately shows that stopping accounts for most of the reward gain on PickCube and AntMaze, where it also executes more refinement steps and that supervision accounts for most of it on RareEvent.
bullets: The work addresses the inefficiency of using the same number of iterative computations for every decision.
AIC jointly learns action selection and when to stop refining, using an expected-depth penalty and intermediate value predictions.
With up to eight refinement steps, it averages 3.3 steps across twelve benchmark tasks.
On four control and robotics tasks, AIC reduces per-decision latency by 31–44% versus a fixed eight-step policy.
AIC beats the best fixed-depth policy on seven tasks and trails it on four; stopping and value supervision contribute differently across tasks.

papers.abstract: Recent progress in vision foundation models (VFMs) has made automated open-vocabulary 3D bounding box annotation increasingly feasible by jointly leveraging LiDAR point clouds and images. However, partial observations remain a major challenge in sparse driving scenes, where visible LiDAR points often cover only a small fraction of the object's surface and provide insufficient cues for estimating its full spatial extent. As a result, existing methods often produce mislocalized boxes or leave objects unlabeled. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{\Ours{}}, an automated annotation framework that leverages image-generated 3D assets as amodal geometric priors for partially observed objects. By establishing correspondences between input images and rendered views of 3D assets, \Ours{} robustly aligns canonical amodal geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR point clouds. To improve temporal consistency and reduce computational cost, \Ours{} generates a single asset per instance, estimates its metric scale once at a single frame and propagates it across frames for dynamic instances, and aggregates multi-frame observations for static instances. 3D object detectors trained on annotations from \Ours{} improve performance over strong baselines by 14.1 mAP on the nuScenes dataset and by 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for the vehicle class on the Waymo Open Dataset (WOD). Our project page is available at: \href{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}{https://oliver0922.github.io/AmodalBox/}
bullets: Addresses box mislocalization and missed objects caused by sparse, partial LiDAR observations in driving scenes.
Aligns canonical amodal 3D asset geometry with partially observed world-space LiDAR using image-to-rendered-view correspondences.
Improves consistency and efficiency by estimating each instance’s scale once, propagating it across dynamic-object frames, and aggregating observations for static objects.
Detectors trained on AmodalBox annotations improve by 14.1 mAP on nuScenes and 12.45 AP at IoU 0.5 for vehicles on Waymo Open Dataset.

papers.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
bullets: Targets the scalability and resource costs of continuous cooperative perception in multi-agent traffic.
Combines conventional object detection, VLM-based occlusion reasoning, physics-based visibility constraints, and Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Uses real-world connected-vehicle data and evaluates four state-of-the-art VLMs for blind-spot detection and dialogue-based sharing.
Achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind-spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing.
Designed as an interpretable, bandwidth-efficient approach for connected traffic systems.

papers.abstract: Video fusion aims to integrate complementary cues from heterogeneous sources, producing visually informative videos with coherent spatio-temporal structures. Jointly learning cross-modal complementarity and temporal dependencies typically relies on large-scale, high-quality video datasets, whose storage and repeated use during optimization incur substantial costs, making data-efficient learning highly desirable. To address this challenge, we rethink video fusion from the perspective of dataset condensation and propose STAR-VF, the first framework that condenses spatio-temporal representations for data-efficient video fusion. STAR-VF condenses the original training set into a compact set of learnable spatio-temporal representations, which are decoded into synthetic video clips and optimized using feature-level supervision provided by a frozen proxy model. The resulting condensed data preserves fusion-relevant spatial and temporal cues without requiring ground-truth fused videos as supervision. To adapt fusion learning to condensed representations, we equip the final fusion model with flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation, enabling direct temporal interaction and adaptive selection of fusion-relevant information in representation space. Extensive experiments on infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion benchmarks demonstrate that STAR-VF, trained with only approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training set, achieves fusion quality comparable to methods trained on the full data. Further analyses validate the contributions of learned condensation and flow-free temporal modeling, and demonstrate the robustness of the condensed supervision across different proxy encoders and downstream fusion models. Project page: https://zju-xyc.github.io/STAR-VF-Project-Page/.
bullets: Targets the storage and optimization costs of large video-fusion training datasets.
Learns compact spatio-temporal representations, decodes them into synthetic clips, and optimizes them with feature-level supervision from a frozen proxy model.
Uses flow-free inter-frame temporal modeling and query-driven intra-frame aggregation for fusion directly in representation space.
Supports infrared-visible, multi-exposure, multi-focus, and medical video fusion without requiring ground-truth fused videos.
Using approximately 1/16 of the original temporal training data, it achieves fusion quality comparable to full-data training; robustness is shown across proxy encoders and downstream fusion models.

During inference, only the trained fusion model is used, without the condensed set or proxy model.

papers.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.
bullets: The study examines how LLMs interpret identity disclosures in conversations about suicidal ideation and psychological distress.
Using paired counterfactual interventions, it evaluates six LLMs across two datasets, 16 identity/control conditions, and two prompting protocols.
Models often infer identity-related adversity as the cause of distress, especially for marginalized identities.
These assumptions can misrepresent people’s experiences even when responses are otherwise empathetic.
The authors call for interpretations grounded in users’ disclosures rather than unsupported identity-linked explanations.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (H-JEPA) enable long-horizon visual control but rely on costly test-time gradient descent for planning. Our analysis reveals that iterative optimization consumes up to 97.7% of episode runtime and that low predicted rollout costs do not necessarily translate into successful control. We further identify a planning-horizon asymmetry between long-horizon top-level composition and short two-step subordinate planning. To address these challenges, we propose WARP-JEPA, a hierarchical amortized planning framework that replaces online gradient optimization with learned multi-candidate trajectory proposers while keeping the world models frozen. WARP-JEPA combines a lightweight world-model-in-the-loop causal Transformer at the top level with parallel residual MLPs at subordinate levels. The proposers are trained using model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, enabling efficient candidate selection without test-time gradient optimization. Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models on four benchmarks, WARP-JEPA achieves 9.6-18.8x faster episode inference on long-horizon tasks (2.9-3.0x on Cube) and improves task success by up to 33.3 percentage points. These results demonstrate that amortized planning can substantially improve both inference efficiency and control performance without retraining the world models. Code is available at https://github.com/hideinsewer/WARP-JEPA.
bullets: H-JEPA planning can spend up to 97.7% of episode runtime on iterative optimization, and low predicted rollout costs may not ensure successful control.
The method uses a hierarchical planner: a causal Transformer for top-level composition and parallel residual MLPs for short-horizon subordinate planning.
Proposers are trained with model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, while the underlying world models remain frozen.
Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models and four benchmarks, inference is 9.6–18.8× faster on long-horizon tasks and 2.9–3.0× faster on Cube.
Task success improves by up to 33.3 percentage points, demonstrating gains in both efficiency and control without world-model retraining.

papers.abstract: How does Jev compare with other systems on Arabic tasks, and how does its performance change between Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) and dialects? We evaluate 67 systems, including 47 decision models and 20 large language models (LLMs), on 43 tasks across 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol. The Arabic-focused frozen suite includes English controls in three parallel resources, which we also remove in a separate descriptive comparison. Jev 1.14.0 achieves a mean task-primary metric of 69.24 on a scale multiplied by 100, compared with 68.77 for Jev 1.13.0 and 71.81 for Gemma-4-31B, the highest-scoring system on this aggregate. Removing the recorded English controls, repeated cross-task items or both leaves the full system order unchanged. Relative performance and gains between Jev versions vary across task families. In content-matched comparisons within Jev 1.14.0, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from -7.94 to -0.35 percentage points across four datasets; dialect-specific results show larger variation, and SIB-200's source-clustered interval includes zero. Paired contrasts with Jev 1.13.0, Gemma-4-31B and Jais-2-8B show a larger Palestinian banking penalty for Jev 1.14.0 than for either LLM under simultaneous uncertainty; the other gap contrasts remain inconclusive. These descriptive findings show why aggregate scores should be read alongside task-family results, coverage and matched language comparisons. They do not establish a general model ranking for dialect robustness or explain the causes of the observed gaps.
bullets: Evaluates 67 systems—47 decision models and 20 LLMs—across 43 tasks and 9 task families using a shared zero-shot protocol.
Jev 1.14.0 scores 69.24 overall, above Jev 1.13.0 (68.77) but below Gemma-4-31B (71.81), the highest aggregate scorer.
Removing English controls or repeated cross-task items does not change the overall system ordering.
Across four content-matched datasets, pooled dialect-minus-MSA accuracy gaps range from −7.94 to −0.35 percentage points; dialect-specific results vary more.
A larger Palestinian banking penalty is observed for Jev 1.14.0 than for the compared LLMs, while other contrasts are inconclusive.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization estimates descent directions from function values alone, which removes the activation storage required by backpropagation and makes it attractive for memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.
bullets: Targets activation-memory costs of backpropagation using zeroth-order optimization.
Keeps pretrained weights frozen while constraining additive updates to fixed-rank matrix manifolds.
Introduces a tangent-space-projected, scale-normalized Riemannian zeroth-order gradient estimator.
Proposes ZO-RGD and smoothed ZO-RGD-S, with convergence results under trajectory-regularity conditions.
Performs competitively with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, improving results in some settings.

papers.abstract: Variable impedance control enhances the interaction capability of robot manipulators by adapting impedance parameters online. However, time-varying impedance parameters may inject energy into the system and violate passivity, particularly when tasks demand rapid stiffness changes. Existing methods address this by increasing damping or limiting the stiffness profile, which often degrades the dynamic response. In this work, we propose a quadratic programming-based parameter optimization framework that guarantees passivity by modulating the desired inertia to compensate for energy injected by stiffness variations, while preserving a critically damped system. For the case of diagonal impedance matrices, we optimize the rates of change of inertia and stiffness subject to a passivity constraint formulated as a convex quadratic program. We extend the framework to compliance control, where the desired inertia is coupled to the robot's configuration-dependent inertia matrix. We use an eigendecomposition based on Cholesky factorization to optimize the spectral weights while maintaining passivity. Experiments on the Kinova Gen3 7-degree-of-freedom manipulator validate both methods with human interaction perturbations. Comparisons with an energy tank approach and a nonpassivity-based method demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves less conservative stiffness tracking without requiring an energy reservoir or damping overhead.
bullets: Addresses energy injection and passivity violations caused by rapidly changing impedance parameters.
Optimizes inertia and stiffness change rates under a convex passivity constraint while maintaining critical damping.
Extends the approach to compliance control by optimizing spectral weights coupled to configuration-dependent robot inertia.
Validated on a Kinova Gen3 7-DoF manipulator during human interaction perturbations.
Achieves less conservative stiffness tracking than energy-tank and nonpassivity-based methods without an energy reservoir or added damping overhead.

papers.abstract: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.
bullets: Defines world models as history-conditioned dynamical systems that update with actions or interventions and generate coherent observed or counterfactual trajectories.
Organizes evaluation around perceptual grounding, persistent state, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction.
Supports video, 3D/4D, embodied-action, and interactive systems through modality-specific adapters that preserve native execution and evaluation protocols.
Provides discovery, runtime preparation, orchestration, artifact management, visualization, manifests, and evidence-aware scorecards.
Catalogs 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 metric entries, while separating execution readiness from evaluative claims.

papers.abstract: Search allows a robotic policy to evaluate candidate futures before committing to an action. Motivated by test-time planning for vision-language action (VLA) models, we study selective search over action chunks in PushT using a frozen Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy. Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states. Across 50 evaluation episodes, beam search raises task success from 0% to 18% and increases average cumulative reward from 39.44 to 103.2. We introduce One Step Ahead (OSA), a gate that simulates the nominal policy chunk and invokes full search only when its predicted coverage drop exceeds a threshold. In the reported ablations, OSA preserves or improves success while reducing runtime by approximately 3x relative to full beam search. Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work.
bullets: Beam search evaluates perturbed action-chunk candidates using rollouts from cloned simulator states.
Across 50 episodes, success increases from 0% to 18%, and average cumulative reward rises from 39.44 to 103.2.
One Step Ahead (OSA) triggers full search only when the nominal policy predicts a coverage drop.
Search-budget ablations show that larger tree depth, branching, beam width, or replanning frequency do not consistently help.
The study is limited to simulated PushT; language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots are not evaluated.

papers.selection_reason: Test-time search for action-chunking VLA policies, directly fits vision-language-action and robot learning.
papers.title: Look Ahead: Search-Driven Reasoning in Embodied AI
papers.tldr: Selective test-time search over action chunks improves a frozen ACT policy in simulated PushT, while the OSA gate reduces search cost by about 3×.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown promise as interactive agents, yet precise, programmatic 3D graphics editing remains difficult to train because existing systems largely rely on closed-source model APIs and lack deterministic, state-verifiable execution environments. We present BlenderFORGE, a trainable data-environment-optimization framework for open-weight MLLM agents that edit explicit Blender scenes through Blender Python (bpy) code generation. BlenderFORGE targets four fundamental state-verifiable editing task families: object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification. It integrates three components: (1) a scalable perturbation-based data generation pipeline built from curated assets and large-scale 3D scene repositories; (2) an isolated Blender Sandbox for deterministic code execution, structured state export, and closed-loop reward computation; and (3) a two-stage training pipeline that uses offline teacher trajectories for cold-start Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and sandbox-computed rewards for multi-turn tool-agentic Reinforcement Learning (AgentLoop-RL). Experiments across the four task families show that the resulting open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B BlenderFORGE agents substantially improve over their base models and achieve competitive performance with several zero-shot proprietary MLLM baselines on selected metrics. Additional cross-benchmark evaluations and camera-reframing experiments provide evidence of transfer beyond the original training setting.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of training precise 3D-editing agents without closed-source APIs or deterministic execution environments.
Supports object placement, shape-key editing, lighting adjustment, and material modification tasks.
Combines perturbation-based data generation, an isolated Blender Sandbox, offline SFT, and sandbox-rewarded AgentLoop-RL.
Trained Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3.5-9B agents improve over their base models and are competitive with selected zero-shot proprietary baselines.
Cross-benchmark and camera-reframing evaluations suggest transfer beyond the original training setting.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS
bullets: Targets the tension between LLM reasoning flexibility and millisecond-level trajectory-planning requirements.
Grounds LLM outputs in a learned variable-level dynamics model, then verifies them with calibrated predicates and forward rollout.
Consolidates verified decisions into indexed rule memory, enabling O(log n) lookup without repeated LLM calls.
Reported results include 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks.
As memory matures, familiar scenes increasingly bypass the LLM, reducing invocation frequency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The REINS framework. Phase 1 (offline): learn dynamics Ĝ, F̂ and compile rules into initial memory R0. papers.title: REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning

papers.abstract: Lane-level map updating requires temporally consistent, physically valid, and auditable road-scene semantics despite occlusions, ambiguous lane markings, temporary obstacles, and viewpoint changes. We present RoadState, a production-deployed vision-language system that transforms sequential road-scene observations into structured lane-level semantics for Baidu Maps' map-updating pipeline. Its core model, RoadState-VLM, formulates road-scene understanding as autoregressive state estimation, predicting the current structured road state from the previous observation and symbolic state together with the current observation. We introduce Geometric Chain-of-Thought (Geo-CoT), which uses a directed acyclic graph of semantic dependencies as a domain prior to improve semantic consistency and reasoning fidelity across interdependent road-state dimensions. Extensive experiments on a real-world dataset show that RoadState-VLM achieves 94.33% mean accuracy across six road-state dimensions, outperforming the strongest fine-tuned VLM baseline. Ablation studies further demonstrate the complementary effectiveness of Geo-CoT and temporal transition context. A cascaded routing pipeline directs routine cases to lightweight models while reserving complex cases for RoadState-VLM. Since its deployment in March 2025, RoadState has supported lane-level map updating across more than 360 cities and reduced overall production costs by 30%. Together with human-in-the-loop auditing, the system maintains robust performance under stress-test conditions. These results demonstrate how domain-prior-enhanced reasoning, structured state interfaces, selective routing, and human quality control can bridge the gap between VLM-based road-scene understanding and large-scale lane-level map updating.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent and physically invalid road semantics caused by occlusions, ambiguous markings, obstacles, and viewpoint changes.
RoadState-VLM predicts the current structured road state from prior observations, symbolic state, and the current image.
Geo-CoT uses a dependency graph as a domain prior to improve consistency across interdependent road-state dimensions.
Reports 94.33% mean accuracy across six dimensions and complementary benefits from Geo-CoT and temporal context.
Deployed across 360+ cities, the cascaded system reduced production costs by 30% while retaining human-in-the-loop quality control.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the RoadState-VLM framework. The pipeline consists of three main stages covering input and preprocessing for Geo-CoT data construction, the RoadState-VLM training architecture with symbolic feedback injection and a latent reasoning buffer, and autoregressive inference with state evolution for temporally consistent road state estimation.

Figure 2: The RoadState production system. Crowd-sourced and survey imagery is assembled into clips, triaged by complexity, and routed to either lightweight models (∼85% of frames) or RoadState-VLM (∼15%). Both branches emit the same structured road state, which must pass a deterministic constraint check before entering map change fusion; violations and low-confidence outputs are escalated to human auditors, whose corrections are recycled as Geo-CoT training data. Section 3 details the RoadState-VLM component.

Figure 4: Qualitative Case Studies. Representative visualization cases highlighting the complexity of real-world driving scenarios. Red text denotes prediction errors, underscoring the superior reasoning capabilities of our method.

Figure 5: Qualitative Case Studies of Geo-CoT Reasoning. Representative samples illustrating the hierarchical reasoning process of RoadState-VLM across diverse driving environments. Each case demonstrates the model’s logic through Global Observation of static road geometry, Temporal Analysis of ego-motion, and Logical Deduction enforcing axiomatic constraints.
Figure 1: An example of structured road information generated from a crowdsourced front-view image sequence.

papers.title: RoadState: A Domain-Prior-Enhanced Vision-Language System for Industrial-Grade Lane-Level Map Updating
papers.tldr: RoadState combines temporal state estimation, geometric reasoning, selective routing, and human auditing to support scalable, auditable lane-level map updating.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can generate procedures that look convincing on paper, but do they work in practice? In this paper, we propose crochet as an ideal testbed for physically grounded procedural reasoning in VLMs. Crochet cannot be reliably simulated or automated: the only way to know what a pattern produces is to make it by hand, yet verification is tangible and cheap, requiring nothing but a hook and a ball of yarn. We introduce FoundationChain, a deceptively simple test of procedural reasoning: given an image of a basic crochet object, can VLMs infer how it was made and generate a pattern that produces the same result? We crochet 40 patterns generated by four VLMs by hand. Even at this scale, physical execution not only reveals failures that automated proxies cannot detect, but also enables a more precise diagnosis of their causes and consequences: while models write fluent, convincing patterns, only four are free of errors, and our analysis exposes deficiencies in visual, geometric and procedural reasoning.
bullets: Introduces FoundationChain, which asks VLMs to infer a crochet pattern from an object image.
Uses hand-crocheting as a tangible, low-cost way to verify whether generated procedures work.
Evaluates 40 patterns from four VLMs through physical execution.
Only four generated patterns are error-free.
Failures reveal weaknesses in visual, geometric, and procedural reasoning that automated checks may miss.

papers.title: Evaluating Physically Grounded Procedural Reasoning in VLMs through Real-World Execution: Crochet as a Testbed
papers.tldr: Crochet-based real-world testing shows that VLMs often generate fluent but physically incorrect procedures despite appearing convincing on paper.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have made progress in general visual tasks. However, limitations remain in fine-grained visual tasks requiring evidence from minute image regions. Existing methods primarily train models using evidence-related regions while overlooking the influence of extensive background regions, resulting in a limited ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. We propose selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation (SPN-OPSD), which considers both evidence and background regions. Supervision from both views improves the model's ability to resist interference from irrelevant regions. Furthermore, selective token-level distillation provides more informative supervision, improving the model's ability to attend to evidence regions in Fine-Grained Visual Tasks. On Qwen3.5-2B, SPN-OPSD improves accuracy on V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite from 76.44%, 45.92%, and 57.43% to 84.82%, 54.56%, and 59.56%, respectively. Similar gains are also observed on Qwen3.5-0.8B.
bullets: Fine-grained visual tasks require extracting evidence from minute image regions, where background content can distract models.
The method uses selective positive-negative on-policy self-distillation with both evidence and background views.
Selective token-level distillation provides targeted supervision for attending to relevant regions.
On Qwen3.5-2B, accuracy improves across V* Bench, ZoomBench, and MME-RealWorld-Lite; similar gains appear on Qwen3.5-0.8B.

papers.abstract: Few-shot depth completion aims to recover dense metric depth from sparse measurements using only a small number of target-domain annotations, offering a favorable balance between annotation cost and model adaptation. We propose LIFT, a framework that harnesses both depth and feature priors from a frozen pretrained monocular depth estimation (MDE) foundation model for few-shot depth completion. Specifically, LIFT first estimates local scale and shift parameters on a coarse grid and interpolates them into smooth, dense parameter fields, providing a spatially adaptive metric depth initialization. It then progressively refines this initialization through multi-scale depth propagation guided by foundation features. Finally, a lightweight residual decoder combines multi-level foundation features with propagation correction to refine the metric depth. Extensive experiments on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC demonstrate that our proposed method achieves state-of-the-art few-shot performance. The source code will soon be released.
bullets: Addresses dense metric depth recovery when only a small number of target-domain annotations are available.
Estimates spatially varying local scale and shift fields on a coarse grid, then interpolates them for metric depth initialization.
Progressively propagates and refines depth at multiple scales using features from the frozen foundation model.
Uses a lightweight residual decoder to combine foundation features with propagation corrections.
Reports state-of-the-art few-shot performance on NYUv2 and KITTI-DC; code is planned for release.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed LIFT framework. Given an RGB image and sparse depth, the frozen MDE foundation model provides relative depth and multi-level features. The relative depth is first converted into a coarse metric depth by the Grid-based Local Alignment (GLA) module, then refined by the Multi-scale Depth Propagation (MDP) module guided by foundation features, and finally enhanced by a lightweight residual decoder. The final metric depth is obtained by combining the coarse metric depth, propagated depth, and predicted residual.

Fig. 5. Visualization of the outputs throughout the proposed pipeline. From top to bottom: RGB images, sparse depth, relative depth estimated by the MDE model, coarse metric depth aligned by GLA, final depth predictions, and the residual and fusion gate maps predicted by the residual decoder.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison on NYUv2 under 1-shot and 100-shot supervision. The first column shows the RGB image and ground-truth depth; the remaining columns compare BPNet, UniDC, OASIS-DC, and our method. The top and bottom prediction rows correspond to 1-shot and 100-shot training.

papers.abstract: Hazard and Operability (HAZOP) studies safeguard industrial processes against catastrophic accidents. Large language models (LLMs) increasingly assist HAZOP drafting, yet evaluations rely on lexical overlap. Because LLMs internalize human heuristics, prompts may trigger biased judgments. Whether frontier LLMs withstand cognitive perturbations in safety-critical workflows remains unknown. Here we show across 420 trials that three frontier LLMs resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations, rendering overall susceptibility statistically inconclusive. Contrary to assumed broad fragility, models rejected confirmation and availability cues. However, safety-critical risk downgrades emerged under low anchors and gain frames. Thus, automated hazard analysis requires disciplined human-in-the-loop validation.
bullets: HAZOP automation requires evaluation beyond lexical overlap because prompts may induce biased safety judgments.
Across 420 trials, the models resisted 96.8% of cognitive manipulations; overall susceptibility was statistically inconclusive.
Models rejected confirmation and availability cues, contrary to assumptions of broad cognitive fragility.
Low anchors and gain frames nevertheless triggered safety-critical reductions in assessed risk.
Human-in-the-loop validation remains necessary for automated hazard analysis.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.
bullets: Domain shift is structured across image versus text tokens and across model layers, rather than being a single uniform discrepancy.
Activation patching reveals architecture-dependent but dataset-stable layer-wise shift patterns.
MoLaRx estimates a modality-layer shift tensor with the Causal Importance Score and partitions layers into functional zones.
CISR applies zone-specific MMD, LoRA, or freezing operations to match each region’s needs.

Across three VLMs and two cross-city benchmarks, MoLaRx achieves the lowest trajectory-error gap in all six settings, with fewer trainable parameters and lower inference latency; uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses.

papers.abstract: Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that creates AI. Yet public RSI work has so far targeted only post-training, which starts from an existing base model, runs trials costing GPU-hours, and returns verifiable scores. Pre-training breaks all three conditions at orders-of-magnitude higher cost: a run consumes hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours over months and cannot be repeated; its objective, post-training headroom, cannot be read off any single score; and what must improve is not a model but the whole production system, from data pipelines and training infrastructure to the teams that run them. To our knowledge, we are the first to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch and to report it in detail. RSI does not stop at frontier pre-training, but it changes form: since no end-to-end loop can close over a single unrepeatable run, we decompose it into smaller loops that can, each repairing a step the full run breaks. The result is 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a newly formed team. We release it as a base model; the lightweight SFT reported here (6B tokens, no RL) only probes post-training headroom. As a base model, 801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and keeps this position under identical SFT; with lightweight SFT alone, it achieves the highest average on four agentic benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Since post-training RSI presupposes a strong base model, bringing RSI into pre-training acts on the foundation every later stage builds on. We open-source 801-30B-A3B-Base and the lightweight SFT data at https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B .
bullets: Frontier pre-training cannot use ordinary RSI loops because runs are extremely costly, unrepeatable, and require improving an entire production system rather than a single model.
The authors decompose pre-training into smaller closed loops that repair individual steps, enabling RSI from scratch.
This approach produced 801-30B-A3B-Base, a 30B-A3B MoE trained on 11.8T tokens over three months by a new team.
The base model outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B.
The study releases the base model and lightweight SFT data; the reported SFT is only a probe of post-training headroom, not full post-training RSI.

papers.abstract: Image-text alignment models such as CLIP are typically trained with contrastive learning, where unpaired examples are treated as strict negatives. While this assumption introduces noise by penalising semantically related pairs, existing solutions often rely on heuristic similarity thresholds that lack statistical grounding and sensitivity to dataset-specific noise distributions. In this paper, we propose Permute-then-Adapt (PTA), a framework that leverages efficient weak models to identify missed positives while controlling Type-I error relative to a conditional permutation reference, up to calibration approximation error. Unlike standard distillation or arbitrary thresholding, PTA estimates a random-pairing reference distribution from the weak teacher's similarity scores and uses its upper tail, determined by $α$, to select auxiliary positives. The calibrated positive set is then trained against by a single multi-positive contrastive objective: each anchor maximises the total probability mass it assigns to its positive set. Offline calibration with the weak model adds negligible training overhead. Experiments show gains over heuristic soft-label approaches in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency. Project repository: https://github.com/JinhaoLee/Permute-then-Adapt.
bullets: Addresses false negatives in contrastive image-text training, where semantically related pairs may be penalized.
Builds a random-pairing reference distribution from weak-teacher scores and selects auxiliary positives from its upper tail using α-controlled Type-I error.
Trains with a multi-positive contrastive objective that aggregates probability mass over each anchor’s calibrated positive set.
Offline calibration adds negligible training overhead.
Reports improvements over heuristic soft-label methods in object recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and data efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Permute-then-Adapt (PTA). Given paired image–text samples, PTA uses a frozen weak teacher to estimate a permutation null distribution and dataset-adaptive threshold. This threshold selects calibrated off-diagonal auxiliary positives, which join ground-truth diagonal pairs to form positive sets. The student is optimized with a positive-set marginal likelihood objective.

The fixed threshold accepts 12× more false positives from the null on Cars. In contrast, PTA (green solid) estimates a dataset-specific permutation null and adapts its cutoff to control Type-I error relative to that reference at level α, up to calibration approximation error.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs have made remarkable progress in perceiving the physical world, while their perceptual scope remains largely human-centric, focusing on what humans can directly see or hear. This progress raises the prospect of perception beyond human limits, such as extending hearing to sounds that are inaudible to humans. More broadly, the physical world is full of waves, vibrations, and oscillations, only a small fraction of which are directly audible to humans. This invites the extension of multimodal LLMs toward a broader form of machine hearing, which remains largely underexplored. To investigate this direction, we introduce the Machine Hearing Benchmark (MHB), comprising 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains. MHB spans highly heterogeneous input regimes, with sampling rates from approximately $10^{-5}$ to $10^6$ Hz, sequence lengths from $10^1$ to $10^6$ samples, and both single- and multi-channel inputs. Evaluations of current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs (ALLMs) reveal limited zero-shot transfer to machine hearing. Supervised adaptation on machine-hearing data alone does not close this gap, suggesting that the challenge extends beyond data exposure to a systematic mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs. To address this mismatch, we introduce MachEar, a lightweight encoder extension that complements the pretrained Audio LLM for machine-hearing inputs. The results show that MachEar equips a pretrained Audio LLM with stronger machine-hearing capabilities while largely preserving its existing audio understanding performance.
bullets: Introduces MHB, a benchmark with 6,128 instances across 13 tasks and seven domains covering highly varied signals and input regimes.
Current open-source and proprietary Audio LLMs show limited zero-shot transfer to machine-hearing tasks.
Supervised adaptation alone does not resolve the gap, pointing to a mismatch between existing audio front ends and machine-hearing inputs.

papers.abstract: We develop a variational and geometric theory based on statistical physics for the joint evolution of Transformer attention and token representations at fixed model parameters. To this end, we introduce a free energy for the attention and model the evolution of the attention weights by its Fisher--Rao gradient flow. At fixed token representations, we prove that the softmax matrix is the unique free-energy minimiser and that every positive attention trajectory converges to it. For prescribed time-dependent representations, we show that the attention dynamics becomes linear after a change to logit variables. This result yields tracking bounds relative to the instantaneous softmax and sufficient conditions for attention to converge to a fixed matrix. Hamiltonian dynamics for the representations and their momenta are then coupled to the attention relaxation driven by the same energy. This coupling results in an energy-dissipation law. We also develop two alternative Hamiltonians incorporating the attention value map. We prove global well-posedness of the attention flow and all three coupled systems.
bullets: Introduces a free energy for attention and models attention updates via Fisher–Rao gradient flow.
At fixed token representations, the softmax attention matrix is the unique free-energy minimizer, and positive attention trajectories converge to it.
For time-varying representations, attention becomes linear in logit coordinates, enabling tracking bounds and convergence conditions.
Couples attention relaxation with Hamiltonian representation dynamics, yielding an energy-dissipation law.
Proves global well-posedness for the attention flow and three coupled dynamical systems.

papers.abstract: Generating high-fidelity voxels while keeping their lightweight nature remains an open problem in computer vision. Current generators are either high-fidelity but computationally heavy, or lightweight but of lower fidelity. Hierarchical methods keep the lightweight nature of voxels. However, their coarse levels, which decide where all finer cells can appear, are generated with the least information about the shape and are never revisited, so they are often plausible but wrong. Our key insight is to let finer cells take part in deciding coarse cells. To this end, we propose JoVox, a discrete flow matching framework that learns the joint distribution of all levels of the voxel hierarchy, instead of a separate distribution for each level, so that coarse cells can be predicted with finer cells already generated nearby. Within this framework, we further introduce a two-level prediction, which outputs the cells two levels finer at once instead of one level finer, halving the number of levels that the network processes and yielding voxels of higher fidelity. We also introduce an unmasking strategy that revisits early decisions once finer cells are generated and corrects inconsistencies in masked diffusion models. Our framework outperforms the baselines on both unconditional and image-conditioned voxel generation. Compared with the current state-of-the-art TRELLIS.2, we achieve 8x higher training throughput, 1/15 of the FLOPs in a forward pass, train on 4 vs. 32 GPUs, and obtain higher quality with an 11% lower Chamfer distance.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between voxel fidelity and computational efficiency.
Uses discrete flow matching to learn the joint distribution across all voxel hierarchy levels.
Introduces two-level prediction to process half as many hierarchy levels.
Adds unmasking to revise coarse decisions when finer cells reveal inconsistencies.
Outperforms baselines and reports higher quality than TRELLIS.2 with substantially lower compute and training cost.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.
bullets: Public LoRA hubs include adapters with base-model mismatches and near-zero updates that can distort forgetting measurements.
The proposed audit checks base-model compatibility and non-trivial delta norms before evaluation.

On an audited four-adapter set, naive merging reduced GSM8K by 10.5 percentage points and HumanEval by 18.3 points, while Task Arithmetic at λ=0.5 stayed within standard error of the unmerged baseline.
Coordinate search found the math adapter was probe-optimal at λ=-0.5, a setting unavailable to positive-only mergers.
Results replicated on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, though the study focuses on two model families and small audited adapter sets.

papers.abstract: Long-term personalized agents are increasingly expected to answer queries over user histories in which preferences, goals, and constraints evolve across interleaved conversations. Existing retrieval-based and structured-memory systems can surface relevant facts, but often return isolated memory units that do not explain which earlier preference was refined, contradicted, or superseded by later evidence. We introduce TransMem, a transition-aware memory retrieval framework that stores preference updates as explicit retrieval units alongside ordinary factual memories. During memory construction, TransMem routes user interaction history into topic-structured memory graphs, detects shift events, and grounds them as transition records. At inference time, TransMem first retrieves factual anchors and then adaptively expands over transition records, producing a compact context of factual anchors and accepted transition records. Experiments on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones show that TransMem outperforms representative retrieval-based and structured-memory baselines. Controlled analyses further show that transition records and adaptive expansion contribute beyond factual anchoring, chronological expansion, flat transition retrieval, and fixed-hop traversal. These results suggest that preference-update records are useful retrieval units for long-term personalization.
bullets: Addresses the problem of evolving preferences, goals, and constraints that isolated memory retrieval fails to contextualize.
Builds topic-structured memory graphs and records detected preference shifts as explicit transition units.
Retrieves factual anchors first, then adaptively expands to relevant transition records for compact context.
Outperforms representative retrieval and structured-memory baselines on PersonaMem and PersonaBench across two Qwen backbones.
Analyses indicate benefits from transition records and adaptive expansion beyond several alternative retrieval strategies.

papers.abstract: Learning whole-body musculoskeletal control from human motion is important for developing human-like robots, assistive devices, and rehabilitation systems. This task presents two main challenges, namely reference trajectories that are kinematically plausible but difficult to reproduce through muscle-driven dynamics, and a highly redundant 700-dimensional action space in which unstructured exploration can easily disrupt the target motion. In this paper, we propose a motion-to-policy pipeline that exploits muscle redundancy in two complementary stages. First, muscle-aware retargeting (MAR) performs bounded adaptation of kinematic trajectories subject to hard semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints. We motivate the constraint bounds by analyzing how reference-trajectory artifacts affect muscle-driven tracking. Second, null-space exploration (NSE) estimates a one-control-frame mapping from muscle excitations to generalized forces and injects bounded, anatomically structured perturbations along its null space into the actions of a value-guided flow policy. On a 24-clip motion-capture benchmark, MAR and NSE together solve every reference, reach the full horizon with half the samples of the baseline pipeline, and lower joint-center error by 44% without late collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end pipeline that transforms monocular video into a trained whole-body imitation policy controlling 700 muscles.
bullets: Addresses kinematically plausible references that are difficult to reproduce with muscle-driven dynamics and exploration in a 700-dimensional action space.
Muscle-aware retargeting adapts trajectories within semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints.
Null-space exploration adds bounded, anatomically structured perturbations that preserve generalized forces while guiding policy learning.
On 24 motion-capture clips, the combined method solved every reference, used half the baseline samples, and reduced joint-center error by 44%.
Scope: whole-body musculoskeletal control with 700 muscles; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond this benchmark.

papers.abstract: Safe offline reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to learn policies that maximize return while satisfying safety constraints, using a static dataset. To characterize state-wise safety, reachability analysis identifies the feasible region, defined as the set of states from which constraints can be satisfied at every future step. Policies are commonly extracted from learned value functions with advantage-weighted regression (AWR). However, AWR relies on exponentiated weights that amplify value estimation errors, whereas behavior-regularized policy gradient methods directly utilize the action gradient of the value function and often make more effective use of learned critics. We propose Feasibility-Optimized Conditional Actor Learning (FOCAL), a method that incorporates behavior-regularized policy gradients into a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) actor. FOCAL optimizes this policy using a first-order objective partitioned by feasibility, updating the actor to increase return on transitions estimated to be feasible and to reduce constraint violations on transitions estimated to be infeasible. During inference, FOCAL dynamically adjusts the scale of the latent prior according to the estimated feasibility of the state to adjust the conservatism of action sampling. Theoretically, we show that for AWR, the policy update variance depends exponentially on the advantage error, whereas for FOCAL it scales linearly with the variance of the value estimation error. Across the DSRL benchmark, FOCAL satisfies the constraints on all evaluated tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns compared to baselines.
bullets: Targets offline policy learning under state-wise safety constraints using a static dataset.
Uses behavior-regularized policy gradients in a CVAE actor instead of AWR’s error-sensitive exponentiated weights.
Partitions learning by estimated feasibility: improves return in feasible regions and reduces violations in infeasible regions.
Adjusts latent-prior scale during inference to control action-sampling conservatism based on state feasibility.
Provides a variance analysis and satisfies constraints on all evaluated DSRL benchmark tasks while achieving competitive or higher returns.

papers.abstract: This paper presents enhancements to the DINOBot framework for imitation learning of object-object interactions. We introduce two key contributions aimed at improving the accuracy and efficiency of alignment in imitation-based robotic tasks. First, we integrate RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC) for outlier rejection during the alignment phase, effectively mitigating the impact of noisy depth data and spurious feature matches. This improves robustness when transferring demonstrations to real-world applications. Second, we refine the semantic correspondence process by focusing on task-relevant interaction regions, ensuring that the learned representation prioritizes critical object features that influence successful manipulation. We evaluated our approach in a range of real-world manipulation tasks, including picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring, using a robotic system. The experimental results demonstrate an overall improvement of 13.8% in task success rates compared to the baseline, along with faster convergence in the alignment process. These results highlight the effectiveness of our enhancements in improving precision and efficiency for object-object interaction imitation in robotics.
bullets: Targets noisy depth data, spurious feature matches, and irrelevant object regions in imitation-based manipulation.
Uses RANSAC to reject alignment outliers and improve robustness during demonstration transfer.
Prioritizes semantic correspondences in task-relevant interaction regions.
Evaluated on real-world picking, insertion, shaking, and pouring tasks.
Reports a 13.8% overall task-success improvement over the baseline and faster alignment convergence.
