papers.abstract: Latent world models enable visual control by planning action sequences in compact representation spaces, but a gap remains between how latent dynamics are learned and how they are used for planning. First, teacher-forced training does not expose the dynamics model to the recursively predicted latent states encountered during planning. Second, sampling-based planners typically initialize action search from goal-agnostic proposals, without exploiting the action-conditioned dynamics learned by the world model. We introduce Dynamics-Informed Action Learning (DIAL) to bridge these two gaps. During training, rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its own autoregressive latent predictions, while multi-step inverse supervision trains a lightweight inverse dynamics head to infer actions from latent-state transitions. We further apply the inverse head to model-generated transitions with its parameters held fixed, encouraging predicted rollouts to retain action-relevant information. At test time, DIAL autoregressively couples the inverse and forward dynamics to construct a dynamics-informed action sequence toward the goal, which initializes the mean of the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) proposal distribution. The subsequent CEM search then refines this initialization using the standard sampling and updating procedure. Experiments across four visual control benchmarks demonstrate that DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between teacher-forced latent dynamics training and recursive planning, plus goal-agnostic action proposals.
Uses rollout alignment to train on the model’s own predicted latent states.
Adds multi-step inverse dynamics supervision and applies the fixed inverse head to model-generated transitions to preserve action-relevant information.
At test time, couples inverse and forward dynamics to initialize Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planning, which then refines the action sequence.
Outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines across four visual-control benchmarks, including long-horizon settings.

papers.abstract: Driven by increasingly complex real-world applications, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has evolved from textual pipelines to multimodal settings, comprising two complementary dimensions: knowledge organization and retrieval enhancement. However, existing methods still face challenges of high construction cost, context window limitations, and the lack of unified training across offline and online knowledge sources. To address these challenges, we propose MMGraph-Agent, a unified multimodal RAG framework based on cache-inspired multimodal knowledge hypergraphs. MMGraph-Agent enables extremely lightweight hypergraph construction with zero API cost and dynamic memory-based retrieval that alleviates long-context issues. Experiments across offline, online, and joint retrieval settings demonstrate consistent improvements in performance, efficiency, and architectural unification. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/MMGraph-Agent.
bullets: Targets multimodal RAG limitations in knowledge construction cost, context-window constraints, and disconnected offline/online knowledge handling.
Builds lightweight multimodal knowledge hypergraphs with zero API cost.
Uses dynamic, memory-based retrieval to alleviate long-context issues.
Supports offline, online, and joint retrieval within one unified architecture.
Experiments report consistent gains in performance and efficiency across these settings; software and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Continual learning suffers from catastrophic forgetting, leading to the loss of past knowledge and unstable adaptation across task streams. Existing approaches typically address this issue through replay buffers, architectural changes, or additional regularization terms. We argue that forgetting is a consequence of unstable learning dynamics, which may benefit from an optimizer-level solution. The main challenge is that learning dynamics are time-dependent, as demonstrated by empirical phenomena such as the stability gap. First, we formally prove that, for distance-based classifiers, bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion under a local score-stability condition. Based on this insight, we propose STABLE, a primal-dual optimizer with adaptive drift control. STABLE enforces a drift budget by increasing the dual variable when the budget is violated and decreasing it otherwise. This results in high stability without penalizing plasticity. Experiments on long-horizon unimodal streams and CLIP-based multimodal streams show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods. In the multimodal setting, STABLE further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/atlas-luiss/STABLE.
bullets: Targets unstable learning dynamics as a root cause of forgetting, rather than relying on replay, architectural changes, or added regularization.
Proves that bounded parameter drift limits margin erosion for distance-based classifiers under a local score-stability condition.
Uses a primal-dual mechanism that increases or decreases a drift-control dual variable based on budget violations.
On long-horizon unimodal and CLIP-based multimodal streams, vanilla PEFT with STABLE matches or outperforms specialized continual-learning methods.
Preserves zero-shot transfer in multimodal continual learning, matching or exceeding dedicated methods.

papers.abstract: Dense prediction and generative modeling remain challenging in resource-constrained environments, particularly because repeated downsampling can lead to the loss of spatial details and less accurate object boundaries. Although attention mechanisms have been widely adopted to address semantic ambiguity, preserving high-frequency information while maintaining computational efficiency remains an important challenge. To address this issue, we propose Frequency-Guided Depthwise Separable Attention for Efficient Dense Prediction (FG-DSA), a framework that integrates frequency-domain information into lightweight vision architectures for dense visual understanding and generation. Specifically, FG-DSA uses a 2D Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based high-pass filtering module to guide spatial attention, aiming to retain fine-grained features and improve object-boundary representation. Experimental results show that FG-DSA can improve boundary-related performance in semantic segmentation under the evaluated setting. Beyond discriminative tasks, we also examine its application in a generative U-Net for single-step image restoration. The results suggest that incorporating FG-DSA can enhance reconstruction quality and help preserve high-frequency details.
bullets: Targets spatial-detail and boundary loss caused by repeated downsampling in resource-constrained vision systems.
Combines 2D FFT-based high-pass filtering with spatial attention and depthwise-separable design.
Improves boundary-related semantic-segmentation performance in the evaluated setting.
Also enhances reconstruction quality and high-frequency detail preservation in single-step image restoration.
Scope is limited to the tasks and evaluation settings described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis, but deployment budgets vary across devices and network conditions. Most compact methods target one operating point, so another budget requires a separate representation. SHIN is a scalable 3DGS hierarchy with a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers, so each higher-quality operating point extends rather than replaces the decoded representation. Constructing this hierarchy requires deciding which Gaussians each stage adds and how much spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance each retains, because these choices remain fixed in later prefixes. SHIN derives one shared Gaussian order from multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and divides each stage budget between adding Gaussians and retaining SH bands using calibrated gradient-based scores per byte. Lightweight opacity updates adjust compositing while transmitted geometry and SH coefficients remain unchanged. Across three benchmarks, SHIN progressively improves one cumulative representation and achieves the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with the multi-rate and progressive baselines.
bullets: Addresses the need for different 3DGS operating points across devices and network conditions.
Uses a reusable Base plus additive enhancement layers, forming cumulative quality prefixes.
Ranks Gaussian additions using multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and allocates each stage’s byte budget between Gaussians and spherical-harmonic appearance bands.
Applies lightweight opacity updates while keeping transmitted geometry and SH coefficients unchanged.
Across three benchmarks, reports the best PSNR-size efficiency in every overlapping comparison with multi-rate and progressive baselines.

papers.abstract: Weight-activation quantization can reduce the memory and compute cost of neural-network inference, but recent methods often require expensive optimization and architecture-specific propagation of basis transforms across layers. We introduce MACaQ, an MXFP4 W4A4 post-training quantization method that treats every linear layer independently. MACaQ applies a per-channel scale and a block-Hadamard transform online to each layer's activations, while absorbing the corresponding inverse transforms into its weights. Retaining these transforms online avoids cross-layer dependencies and enables a simple streaming implementation of the quantization process, in which only one layer must reside in memory at a time. To improve over round-to-nearest quantization, we introduce Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent procedure that greedily moves individual FP4 codes to adjacent representable values. Despite executing the activation transforms at inference time, MACaQ adds only 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM. MACaQ reaches lower perplexity than DuQuant++ and MR-GPTQ, and already matches their best perplexity on Llama-3-8B in 11 times less quantization time. We further apply MACaQ without architecture-specific modifications to an image diffusion model, illustrating the generality of its layer-local design and show quantization of a 122B parameter model in 64 minutes, using only 32.5GB GPU RAM. Code is available at https://github.com/huawei-csl/MACaQ .
bullets: Targets low-precision weights and activations to reduce neural-network inference memory and compute costs.
Uses per-channel scaling and online block-Hadamard activation transforms, with inverse transforms absorbed into weights.
Introduces Flip-Refinement, a Hessian-aware coordinate-descent method that adjusts individual FP4 codes beyond round-to-nearest quantization.
Adds 2.3% end-to-end overhead over pure MXFP4 on Qwen3-32B in vLLM and matches competing methods’ best Llama-3-8B perplexity using 11× less quantization time.
Its layer-local design supports streaming quantization, diffusion models, and a 122B-parameter model using 32.5 GB GPU RAM in 64 minutes.

papers.abstract: Policies for dexterous manipulation depend on design choices made before training: which sensors enter the observation, where they are placed, and how their readings are arranged for the encoder. These choices are rarely examined. For tactile sensing, simulation studies place taxels uniformly over the hand, and this placement has become a default without being tested. We test this default under a single controlled protocol. The protocol holds the teacher, the training procedure, and the candidate taxels fixed and varies only the sensor configuration and the representation. We evaluate it on in-palm rotation and grasping with three robot hands. A small set of taxels selected from contact statistics matches a far larger uniform set. Taxels at rarely contacted sites are equivalent to no tactile input. With all candidate taxels, their layout in the input tensor does not affect performance, even for a convolutional encoder. Uniform placement therefore overestimates the number of taxels a task requires. We distill these results into lessons for designing tactile policies and into a minimal set of design choices that a tactile policy study should report.
bullets: Uniform taxel placement is tested under a controlled protocol rather than assumed effective.
A small set of taxels chosen from contact statistics matches the performance of a much larger uniform set.
Taxels in rarely contacted locations perform like providing no tactile input.
With all candidate taxels, arranging them in the input tensor does not affect performance, including with convolutional encoders.
Results from in-palm rotation and grasping across three robot hands motivate reporting a minimal set of tactile-policy design choices.

papers.abstract: Transformer-based autoregressive multilingual language models (LMs) are often assumed to store factual knowledge in an interlingua: a language-agnostic latent space. If this assumption holds, a parameter update applied in a source language during knowledge editing should inherently propagate to its semantic equivalents in target languages. However, empirical benchmarks show that cross-lingual propagation of edits often degrades substantially, a degradation that prior work treats largely as an algorithmic symptom rather than a structural bottleneck. In this work, we investigate whether representational anisotropy creates a structural bottleneck for source-only associative-memory editing, and perform a geometric dissection of the cross-lingual propagation gap. Using associative memory-based "locate-then-edit" methods, including ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit, as analytical frameworks, we derive a closed-form decomposition of this gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch. Our empirical findings show that cross-lingual propagation is primarily bottlenecked by a large orthogonal residual component, indicating that source-language edits often fail to span the target-language update directions required for successful transfer. Furthermore, we show that post-hoc correction using only source-language residual statistics encounters a large residual-prediction barrier. Finally, we perform a structural realignment via a targeted contrastive alignment objective and find that it substantially improves key-space propagation and partially improves cross-lingual edit transfer, while leaving value-space mismatch as a remaining bottleneck.
bullets: Challenges the assumption that multilingual models store facts in a fully language-agnostic interlingua.
Decomposes the propagation gap into key-space propagation, parallel residual mismatch, and orthogonal residual mismatch using ROME, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit.
Finds that orthogonal residual mismatch is the primary bottleneck: source edits often do not span target-language update directions.
Shows that source-only residual statistics are insufficient for accurately predicting the needed target updates.
Targeted contrastive alignment improves key-space propagation and partially improves transfer, but value-space mismatch remains.

papers.abstract: AI agents can generate as-built Building Information Models (BIMs) from reality-capture data, but the evidence required for accurate reconstruction remains unclear. This paper presents Agent2BIM, an agent-based Scan-to-BIM framework, and evaluates seven capture configurations in a research laboratory and a mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) scene. Inputs include 360° panoramas, smartphone video, smartphone LiDAR, terrestrial laser scanning (TLS), TLS with posed panoramas, and imagery supplemented by prior IFC models. Outputs are compared against TLS-verified reference models for component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity. In the laboratory, component recall ranged from 84% to 100%, but only 9% of components reconstructed from panoramas were within 20 cm of their reference positions, compared with 86% using smartphone LiDAR. In the MEP scene, scale-free inputs recovered 11 - 43% of components, versus 75 - 93% for metric inputs. Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate inaccuracies. The results highlight the complementary roles of visual and metric evidence in agent-based Scan-to-BIM.
bullets: Evaluates seven reality-capture configurations in laboratory and MEP scenes against TLS-verified reference models.
Assesses component detection, geometric accuracy, and MEP connectivity.
Panorama-based reconstructions detected many components but achieved limited positional accuracy; smartphone LiDAR substantially improved it.
In the MEP scene, metric inputs recovered more components than scale-free imagery.
Prior IFC models improved MEP reconstruction but could propagate existing inaccuracies.

papers.abstract: Visual citations show where an answer is supported, but not how the cited content contributes to it. In scientific document question answering, a model may read a value directly, compress several observations, or combine evidence to infer a conclusion. We study typed visual provenance, where a system generates an answer together with source regions and explicit support relations. We introduce ReViE, a dataset of 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents, with page, section, and region annotations labeled as Quotation, Compression, or Inference. We further propose VisProve, which augments joint answer and provenance generation with differentiable Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback. VisProve conditions next-token prediction on localized visual evidence and its estimated support relation through a gated norm-bounded residual. On the document-disjoint ReViE test set, VisProve improves Typed-F1 from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24 over joint supervised fine-tuning with the same backbone, while Page-F1 changes only marginally. These results suggest that coupling visual grounding with support relation modeling mainly improves fine-grained provenance, while the low absolute Typed-F1 reveals a substantial gap between answer generation and precise visual evidence attribution.
bullets: ReViE contains 3,941 questions over complete scientific documents with page, section, and region annotations.
Annotations classify support as Quotation, Compression, or Inference.
VisProve uses Spatial Evidence Reading and Evidence-Answer Relation Feedback to condition generation on localized evidence and support relations.
On document-disjoint ReViE tests, Typed-F1 rises from 3.52 to 5.48 and Section-F1 from 45.99 to 53.24; Page-F1 changes little.
Low absolute Typed-F1 indicates that precise evidence attribution remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Reliable navigation with a single monocular limited field-of-view camera is challenging because the lack of depth measurements and limited spatial awareness complicate collision checking. Existing approaches to tackle these challenges fall into two categories. Model-based planners can incorporate explicit collision-avoidance guidance which leads to better generalization but are often computationally expensive and require manual tuning of the algorithmic parameters. In contrast, end-to-end approaches trained by imitation learning can be flexible but typically encode safety only implicitly and thus can suffer from high collision rates in novel scenarios. In this paper, we present a middle ground through model-based imitation learning. The model-based part is a learned collision model that can map a sequence of past images and a candidate control sequence to a distribution of worst-case obstacle clearance. This predictive distribution in turn is used to define a collision-risk cost in a trajectory optimization formulation. The imitation component uses human demonstrations to learn scene-dependent balancing of collision risk with other task costs such as goal progress. We also use it to learn the algorithmic parameters (e.g., a warm start) of our optimizer to accelerate the solution process. We show that our approach can demonstrate highly reliable navigation in cluttered environments on robots with different embodiments. We also demonstrate a substantial reduction in collision rate over recent end-to-end and model-based baselines.
bullets: Addresses limited depth and field of view, which make collision avoidance difficult with a single camera.
Learns a model that predicts worst-case obstacle-clearance distributions from image histories and candidate controls.
Uses predicted risk in trajectory optimization, while demonstrations learn how to balance safety with task objectives such as goal progress.
Learns optimizer parameters, including warm starts, to improve solution speed.
Reports highly reliable navigation across different robot embodiments and lower collision rates than end-to-end and model-based baselines.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention accelerates long-context decoding by reading a subset of the KV cache, but existing methods are open-loop: the kernel commits to its selection with no signal indicating whether enough attention mass was preserved and no recovery path when it was not. The needed signal already exists inside the kernel. The fraction of softmax mass on the selected tokens, which we call coverage, satisfies an exact algebraic equality with per-step output error and serves a dual role as the acceptance criterion and the interpolation weight for recovery. Coverage-Verified Sparse Attention (CVSA) turns coverage into a training-free, closed-loop verify-then-correct decode loop that accepts high-coverage drafts and recovers only the heads that fall short, with no sampling, no draft model, and no speculative-decoding infrastructure. Quality varies by only $0.14$ points across the threshold sweep; budget and scheduling ablations characterize the deployed operating point. On LongBench at 7B and 70B, CVSA comes within $1.13$ points of dense attention, statistically matching it at 70B, and it loses $0.8$ points on RULER; measured median decode-step speedup reaches $6.21\times$ at 128K context.
bullets: Addresses the open-loop risk that sparse attention may omit too much attention mass without detecting or correcting the error.
Uses coverage—the softmax mass on selected tokens—as both an exact error-related signal and the acceptance/recovery control.
Implements a training-free verify-then-correct loop without sampling, draft models, or speculative-decoding infrastructure.
Quality changes by only 0.14 points across the threshold sweep; operating points are examined through budget and scheduling ablations.
On LongBench, it comes within 1.13 points of dense attention at 7B and statistically matches it at 70B; median speedup reaches 6.21× at 128K context.

Rejection is concentrated in a few layer-step regions, which is consistent with the static concentrated-failure pattern in Fig. 2 (a).

Figure 3: Closed-loop decode step in CVSA. Unlike open-loop sparse attention, which commits every sparse output without feedback, CVSA interposes a per-head coverage gate between the sparse kernel and the final output. Draft: an off-the-shelf page selector produces Odraft and the LSE statistics from which coverage is computed. Verify: the coverage gate compares each KV head’s coverage against τ ; most heads pass (green) while a small minority fails (red). Correct: accepted heads commit the draft at no additional cost; rejected heads expand the page budget and recompute attention. Page scoring and the coverage check run together every M steps (Section 3.4); sparse attention runs on every step, reusing the selected pages in between.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent-WAM++, a representation-centered World Action Model (WAM) for end-to-end autonomous driving. Existing WAMs are primarily trained to predict future states or final actions, leaving the intermediate world and action representations that connect prediction to planning only indirectly constrained. Latent-WAM++ matches the supervision of each representation to its role in planning. World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilization, and frozen geometric priors to learn a temporally predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation without an EMA target encoder. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals while being optimized with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, enabling one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment further aligns the resulting pre-output action features with a stop-gradient target derived from current visual semantics. Latent-WAM++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2 and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, reaching 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Training the planner end to end costs 190 GPU-hours for Latent-WAM++ versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.
bullets: Addresses weak supervision of intermediate world and action representations in existing World Action Models.

Reports 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, zero-shot results on HUGSIM, and 88.1% lower planner training cost than Latent-WAM.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic diagnosis unfolds over native video, where a single positive finding during traversal of the gastrointestinal tract sets off a multi-minute chain of reasoning over location, morphology, severity and intervention. Existing endoscopy multimodal benchmarks test only static images or single-disease videos, which miss the temporal and clinical reasoning that real-world reporting demands. We introduce EndoSCOP-V, a video-grounded multi-turn evaluation framework for structured endoscopy reporting and clinical reasoning. It contains 1,307 real-world endoscopy and colonoscopy videos (63.2 h; 97% 1080p) averaging about 174 s. Its 20,274 question-answer turns are instantiated deterministically from clinician-filled structured endoscopy-reporting EHRs, so no per-case annotation is synthetic or LLM-rephrased. They come from 1,033 clinician-reviewed templates, about 18 per disease, that span a clinically aligned 9-task x 30-sub-task reporting taxonomy over 54 World Endoscopy Organization (WEO) MST 3.0 diseases. 22% of procedures carry co-existing pathologies, up to six per case. A Markovian context-pruned oracle-forcing protocol evaluates the dialogue turn by turn, injecting the gold answer before each subsequent turn so that per-turn reasoning is isolated from cascading dialogue errors. A panel of 15 board-certified endoscopists sets a 78% strict-accuracy baseline on 1,500 questions. Across 14 open-weight LMMs, the best 27B-class model reaches 59.8% strict accuracy, falling to 53.4% once format-trivial disease-rejection items are excluded. On a between-subjects spot-check, the best of 3 frontier proprietary models trails the clinician panel by 23 pp on strict NDR accuracy. Sub-task analysis reveals consistent gaps in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading and intervention reasoning on long-horizon video. Data: Hugging Face (EndoSCOP-V). Code: GitHub (abhi25t/EndoSCOP-V).
bullets: Addresses the limits of static-image and single-disease benchmarks for temporal, multi-finding endoscopy reasoning.
Includes 1,307 real-world videos, 20,274 deterministic question-answer turns, 54 diseases, and a 9-task, 30-subtask reporting taxonomy.
Uses clinician-derived EHR templates and context-pruned oracle forcing to isolate turn-level reasoning from cascading dialogue errors.
The best 27B open-weight model achieves 59.8% strict accuracy versus 78% for 15 board-certified endoscopists; performance drops to 53.4% after excluding format-trivial items.
Models show persistent weaknesses in quantitative measurement, multi-variable grading, and intervention reasoning over long videos.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity tests whether a model has captured dynamics that remain predictive well beyond the observed history. Prediction quality typically declines as the horizon grows, yet neither short-horizon accuracy nor teacher-forced evaluation, which supplies the true activity preceding each predicted step, reveals how well models sustain predictions from an initial history alone. We compare direct multi-step prediction and autoregressive rollout on spiking recordings across horizons and introduce NeuroHorizon, which pairs event-based spike encoding with a causal decoder for population firing rates. Its hierarchical prediction memory keeps recent predictions at full temporal resolution and compresses earlier ones into segment summaries, giving the decoder both local detail and longer-range context. Under teacher-forced training this memory holds ground-truth activity, whereas during rollout it holds the model's own predictions. To reduce this mismatch, we train with scheduled sampling, progressively exposing the decoder to its own predictions. From 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, NeuroHorizon achieves the highest forward-prediction score among the evaluated autonomous models at all four horizons from 100 to 1000 ms, and its per-bin predictions remain above a mean-firing-rate baseline across nearly the full 1 s window. Complementary experiments on macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region recordings show that performance generally increases with model and data size, alongside improved prediction after cross-subject pretraining and fine-tuning. Together, these results clarify how forecasting performance changes across horizons and offer an effective approach to long-horizon forecasting of neural population activity.
bullets: Addresses the gap between short-horizon or teacher-forced accuracy and sustained forecasting from an initial history alone.
Uses event-based spike encoding, a causal firing-rate decoder, and memory that preserves recent predictions while compressing older context.
Scheduled sampling reduces the mismatch between training with ground-truth activity and rollout using the model’s own predictions.
On 500 ms of macaque motor-cortex activity, it achieved the highest forward-prediction score among evaluated autonomous models from 100–1000 ms.
Additional macaque sensorimotor and mouse multi-region experiments indicate gains with larger models/data and cross-subject pretraining plus fine-tuning.

Figure 2: Per-bin temporal decay of forecasting performance. Panels (a–d) show per-bin fp-bps for prediction horizons of 100, 240, 500, and 1000 ms, respectively, using a 500 ms observation window. Scores use global spike weighting across sessions, neurons, and evaluation windows. All models forecast without additional neural observations, with prediction modes indicated in the legend.

All panels report session means with ±1 SEM for TF and RO fp-bps, using 500 ms observation and prediction windows. Parameter counts are shown in millions and exclude neuron and session embeddings.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a hierarchical memory mechanism for long-horizon forecasting of neural activity, which is highly relevant to spatiotemporal memory and state maintenance in embodied agents.
papers.title: NeuroHorizon: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Neural Population Activity with Hierarchical Memory
papers.tldr: NeuroHorizon improves autonomous long-horizon neural activity forecasting by combining hierarchical prediction memory with scheduled sampling.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.
bullets: Addresses privacy risks from continuous egocentric video capture, where sensitive content varies by user and context.
Converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations for reasoning.
Combines a privacy reasoner with explicit user-specific memory to support personalization and continual adaptation.
Evaluated on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users using a cross-user chronological protocol.
Reports 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming the described baseline systems.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs, enabling parallel generation through iterative denoising. Recent guidance methods improve diffusion LLMs by introducing a weak model to guide the prediction of the base model during denoising. However, the influence of the weak model during denoising remains less clear, and computing its prediction requires an additional forward pass at each denoising step. We present in this paper an in-depth analysis of how diffusion LLMs use contextual information during denoising. Our analysis reveals that diffusion LLMs rely more heavily on local context while often underutilizing global context. Based on this observation, we introduce Global Context Guidance (GCG), a feature-space guidance method that enhances global-context utilization without constructing an explicit weak model. Extensive experiments on LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GCG consistently outperforms existing guidance methods, while incurring much lower inference overhead.
bullets: Diffusion LLMs often rely heavily on local context and underuse global context during denoising.
The authors analyze contextual information usage in diffusion LLMs.
GCG provides feature-space guidance without explicitly constructing a weak model.
Experiments across LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, and LLaDA-1.5 show consistent gains over existing guidance methods with lower inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can recognize events in images and parse sentences, but it remains unclear when they bind visual Agent-Patient structure to linguistic semantic roles across languages whose role cues depend on morphology, word order or construction. We introduce ROLECUE, a controlled diagnostic that pairs 192 validated two-person action images with German, Turkish, Japanese, English, Korean and Bangla sentences in canonical and patient-first orders. The evaluation separates image-only role recognition, text-only role parsing, direct image-sentence matching, response-compliance behavior and an external modular composition of the model's own component predictions. Across eight recent open-weight VLMs, ROLECUE reveals a structured spectrum: some models fail visual or linguistic component tests, some largely solve the diagnostic, some collapse to constant semantic assent and several show component-joint gaps in which reliable image-only and text-only role predictions do not survive direct joint inference. The largest non-degenerate gaps reach 44.9 percentage points, with final bootstrap intervals confirming that the effect is not a point-estimate artifact. These results reveal multilingual component-joint performance gaps and acceptance biases hidden by aggregate VLM benchmarks and show why component diagnostics are necessary before interpreting joint multimodal errors.
bullets: Evaluates Agent–Patient role binding using 192 two-person action images and sentences in six languages.
Separates visual role recognition, text parsing, image–sentence matching, response compliance, and modular composition.
Across eight open-weight VLMs, identifies visual, linguistic, joint-inference, and constant-assent failure patterns.
Finds non-degenerate component–joint gaps as large as 44.9 percentage points, with bootstrap intervals supporting their robustness.
Shows that aggregate benchmarks can hide multilingual role-binding failures and motivates component-level diagnostics.

papers.abstract: SLAM failures remain difficult to avoid in autonomous robotic systems, and undetected failures can propagate to unsafe planning, control, and mission-level decisions. Existing monitoring strategies often depend on prior maps, estimator-internal variables, or redundant sensing, which limits their applicability to deployed and resource-constrained robots. This paper presents a scene-geometry consistency monitor for detecting geometry-manifested SLAM failures using only the geometric output of the SLAM backend. The targeted failures include cumulative drift-induced failures, abrupt misregistration failures, and backend map corruption when they become observable as inconsistency in reconstructed scene geometry. The proposed method represents revisited local regions with recursive latent voxel geometry and evaluates each current observation against a trusted continuation explanation and a weak non-propagated reference explanation. The resulting voxel-wise evidence contrasts are aggregated into a fixed-boundary monitoring signal for online failure declaration and downstream safety response. Experiments on self-collected sequences, GEODE benchmark sequences, multiple robotic platforms, and different SLAM backends show that the monitor responds to failures when they are manifested in backend scene geometry. It achieves 4/4 valid post-onset declarations with no pre-onset alarms on four self-collected sequences, detects geometry-manifested failures in all five corrupted GEODE runs while remaining alarm-free in five geometrically consistent runs, adds only 0.1--0.2\% absolute CPU load, and supports a closed-loop UAV detect--isolate--recover workflow.
bullets: Targets cumulative drift, abrupt misregistration, and backend map corruption that become geometrically observable.
Uses recursive latent voxel representations of revisited regions and contrasts trusted continuation evidence with a weak non-propagated reference.
Aggregates voxel-level evidence into a fixed-boundary online signal for failure declaration and safety response.

Reported experiments achieved 4/4 post-onset declarations without pre-onset alarms on self-collected sequences and detected all five corrupted GEODE runs while staying alarm-free on five consistent runs.
Adds only 0.1–0.2% absolute CPU load and supports a closed-loop UAV detect–isolate–recover workflow.

papers.abstract: Recent large human reconstruction models create remarkable animatable 3D avatars from a single image, but their appearance remains entangled with the illumination and cannot be relighted. In contrast, existing 3D relightable-avatar reconstruction methods typically require person-specific optimization. We present ZARA, a zero-shot feed-forward framework that reconstructs an animatable 3D Gaussian avatar together with its intrinsic attributes from a single image. ZARA couples a pretrained large-scale human reconstruction model with a Material Transformer to inherit geometry priors while learning material-aware Gaussian representations. To preserve localized details, we introduce Gaussian-aligned material feature fusion strategy, which injects multi-scale material features onto individual Gaussians and combines them with geometry tokens. As most human-avatar datasets lack ground-truth material maps, we use pseudo-material labels as conditioning inputs and supervision targets during training. We further introduce MatFace regularization to preserve facial structure and color in albedo prediction under unreliable facial pseudo-material supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ZARA reconstructs animatable and relightable humans within tens of seconds without person-specific optimization or post-processing, outperforming existing baselines in both relighting quality and materials generalization ability. As the ability of recovering the physically-based-rendering attributes of the human, ZARA also enables direct material editing of the avatar's appearance.
bullets: Addresses appearance–illumination entanglement in single-image human reconstruction and avoids person-specific optimization.
Combines a pretrained human reconstruction model with a Material Transformer to predict material-aware Gaussian representations.
Uses Gaussian-aligned multi-scale material feature fusion to preserve localized details and combine material information with geometry.
Trains with pseudo-material labels and introduces MatFace regularization to improve facial albedo structure and color.
Experiments show reconstruction in tens of seconds, improved relighting and material generalization over baselines, and support for direct material editing.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of ZARA and its core network components. Given a single image, the pretrained geometry branch reconstructs canonical Gaussian geometry, while the material branch encodes material maps and predicts per-Gaussian intrinsic attributes. The Gaussian decoding branches predict geometry, pose-dependent geometry offsets, and materials. The material encoder receives the prepared material priors and extracts features that are fused into global material tokens and per-Gaussian material features. The resulting canonical avatar is animated by the target motion and rendered under novel illumination.

papers.abstract: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. The query norm controls the sharpness of the attention distribution, while the key norm determines how strongly a token attracts different queries. These norms therefore carry token-specific information about attention selectivity and token importance. By normalizing both, QK-Norm suppresses this information. This raises a natural question: can we control query-key representations without discarding their sensitivity to magnitude? To address this question, we propose QK-MAP, a Magnitude-Aware Projection for constructing queries and keys. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.
bullets: QK-Norm stabilizes attention by normalizing query and key norms, but removes information about attention sharpness and token importance.
QK-MAP encodes input magnitude as bounded, multi-frequency phase patterns instead of relying on vector-length growth.
Its fixed-norm representations preserve sensitivity to magnitude while reducing periodic ambiguity through multiple learnable frequencies.
Across 190M–7B parameter models, QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than Standard attention and QK-Norm.
Analyses report greater input-scale sensitivity, less attention to the first token, and stronger contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests.

papers.abstract: Cinematic composition questions depend on in-frame geometry that vision-language models (VLMs) use inconsistently. External perception tools can expose this geometry, but naive prompt injection can overwrite useful visual predictions. On ShotBench composition, pre-question geometry reduces Qwen2.5-VL-7B from 49.5% to 46.3%; corrupted measurements lower it to 33.6%. CompositionEvidence derives nine reproducible features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts and supplies their shared 24-dimensional representation through two interfaces. A training-free channel appends gated neutral evidence after the question, reaching 56.2% (+6.7, exact McNemar p=0.0018) and 48.4% under corrupted evidence. A minimal-training channel maps the same representation to four soft tokens with a 7.37M-parameter projector while leaving the VLM frozen; it reaches 61.0% (+11.5). Across nine VLMs, including five commercial models queried through official provider APIs, zero-shot accuracy ranges from 43.8% to 63.0%, and the text channel changes it by +6.7 to -6.9 points; the highest baseline is among the regressions. The effect of explicit geometry depends on measurement reliability and on how the receiving model integrates it.
bullets: Composition questions rely on in-frame geometry that VLMs use inconsistently, while naive geometry prompting can hurt performance.
It derives nine features from frozen detection, depth, and line experts into a shared 24-dimensional representation.
A training-free gated text interface reaches 56.2% accuracy and remains more robust to corrupted evidence than pre-question prompting.
A minimally trained four-token projector reaches 61.0% while keeping the VLM frozen.
Across nine VLMs, geometry changes performance from −6.9 to +6.7 points, showing that reliability and model integration are critical.

papers.abstract: Weight tying reduces the parameter cost of language models, but the usual tied output head is limited to a single softmax. We introduce onóna, a two-table parameterization that increases output expressiveness while preserving input-output weight sharing. The Transformer takes the average of two embedding tables as input, and the output head combines the softmax distributions defined by those same tables. A gate conditioned only on the current input token determines the mixture weight. Its values can be precomputed for inference, and the Transformer body remains unchanged. We evaluate onóna across Dense, Gated DeltaNet hybrid, mixture-of-experts, and Attention Residual architectures at 142M, 330M, and 1B scales. Under matched token budgets, onóna lowers final validation loss and external perplexity in 11 of 12 comparisons and raises the average accuracy over eight downstream tasks in 10 of 12. The one exception on loss is the 1B MoE model. The cost is one extra embedding table and one extra vocabulary projection.
bullets: Addresses the limited expressiveness of a single softmax output head under standard weight tying.
Averages two embedding tables for Transformer inputs and mixes their corresponding output distributions.
Uses a gate based only on the current input token; gate values can be precomputed, leaving the Transformer body unchanged.
Across 12 matched-budget comparisons, it improves validation loss and external perplexity in 11, and downstream accuracy in 10.
Adds one embedding table and one vocabulary projection; the 1B mixture-of-experts model is the sole loss exception.

papers.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) trains agents to adapt to novel tasks from test-time experience, but requires diverse training environments and reward functions. While environments are becoming cheaper to generate, it remains difficult to anticipate every objective an agent may be asked to pursue at test time. Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) learn policies from reward-free data and support zero-shot RL (ZSRL): adaptation to new objectives at test time using a large reward-labeled dataset. Recent work has shown that BFM task inference can instead be performed online without prior task-specific data. We note that this capability positions BFMs and meta-RL as alternative approaches for online adaptation to new reward functions in a fixed environment. We then ask whether we can extend BFMs to compete with meta-RL more broadly, including in novel environments, and identify four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and learning from mixed reward supervision. We study each individually, then propose MetaBFM, a hybrid method that addresses all four. During training, it combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning; at test time, it can interpolate between exploration, exploitation, and ZSRL-style reward inference. We demonstrate that MetaBFM can recover the in-distribution performance of supervised meta-RL while generalizing to reward functions outside the training set. Our work suggests that BFMs and meta-RL are complementary research directions whose combined strengths allow adaptive agents to learn more diverse behaviors from a fixed set of supervised objectives.
bullets: Meta-RL typically needs diverse training environments and reward functions, while BFMs enable zero-shot adaptation from reward-free data.
The work identifies four challenges: environment identification, online data collection, test-time exploration, and mixed reward supervision.
MetaBFM combines supervised reward-following with unsupervised learning during training.
At test time, it balances exploration, exploitation, and zero-shot reward inference.
It matches supervised meta-RL performance in-distribution while generalizing to reward functions absent from training.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) inherit strong textual reasoning capabilities from their language backbones and text pretraining, but often fail to apply the same level of competency to visual inputs. We show that this degradation cannot be attributed to only perception failures, by evaluating models on semantically-equivalent text and rendered-text image inputs: models can accurately read text in the images and recover near-text performance when provided their own transcriptions, but just cannot reason well on the images directly. We characterize this discrepancy as a modality reasoning-access gap, where models fail to route perceived visual content into existing reasoning machinery accessible with text. To bridge this, we propose TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning), which first mines synthetic modality counterfactuals where a model succeeds on a text problem but fails when provided the corresponding rendered image, and post-trains the model on the image input via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. Importantly, although trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, TIGER results in model performance improvements across diverse real-world visual benchmarks including geometric diagrams (MathVerse), multi-disciplinary sciences (EMMA, MMMU), complex charts (ChartQAPro), and embodied spatial reasoning (RoboSpatial-Home). TIGER also complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods, yielding further performance gains. Analysis involving reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching provide support indicating that TIGER helps to align visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/minhngh/Tiger.
bullets: Identifies a modality reasoning-access gap: models can read rendered text in images but struggle to reason over the images directly.
Mines synthetic cases where a model succeeds on text but fails on the equivalent rendered image.
Post-trains on these image inputs using GRPO, with SFT and DPO variants also explored.
Training only on synthetic rendered-text images improves performance across diagrams, science, charts, and embodied spatial reasoning benchmarks.
Activation analyses suggest TIGER aligns visual-to-reasoning pathways with text-reasoning states and complements existing visual RLVR methods.

papers.abstract: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.
bullets: Addresses stale memories and brittle 3D representations when small objects move between household surfaces.
Introduces Hypothesis Scene Graphs, preserving visual evidence for surface objects while keeping persistent furniture topology stable.
Uses scale-aware retrieval, exploration for new surface observations, and verification to confirm or invalidate hypotheses.
Introduces FAROS-Bench for multi-scale search and mid-episode object relocation with memory invalidation.
Performs competitively on GOAT-Bench and substantially outperforms prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

papers.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) estimates the expected return of a target policy from previously collected data without additional environment interaction. While OPE methods for flat Markovian policies are well studied, little work has addressed evaluating hierarchical policies in which a high-level policy selects temporally extended options that generate primitive actions until a termination condition is met. The primary existing approach applies per-decision importance sampling at the option level, but requires option-annotated trajectories and exhibits variance that still grows with the horizon. For non-hierarchical policies, fitted Q-evaluation (FQE) typically achieves lower error than importance sampling by leveraging the classic Bellman equation for policy evaluation; however, a naive extension of FQE to hierarchical policies results in a biased policy value estimate. In this paper, we introduce Intra-Option Fitted Q-Evaluation (IO-FQE), which estimates a value function in the augmented state-option space; this approach enables OPE of hierarchical policies even when we lack annotations of what option was run in the data. We develop two continuous-action instantiations of IO-FQE and show on long-horizon hierarchical continuous control tasks (AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation) that IO-FQE eliminates the bias incurred by a naive application of FQE to hierarchical policies and substantially lowers mean squared-error compared to option-level importance sampling.
bullets: Addresses off-policy evaluation for hierarchical policies composed of temporally extended options.
Avoids requiring annotations identifying which option generated each action in the logged data.
Introduces an intra-option fitted Q-evaluation method based on value estimation over state-option pairs.
Develops two continuous-action variants and evaluates them on AntMaze navigation and OGBench Puzzle manipulation.
Eliminates the bias of naive FQE and achieves substantially lower mean squared error than option-level importance sampling in the reported tasks.

papers.abstract: Latent-action world models learn actions from video without labels, and recent methods aim to share these actions across bodies. Transfer between 2D characters with different body structures remains underexplored. In this paper, we study whether an action learned from one character can make a character with a different body perform the same action. A cat, a blob and a human can all jump, but each moves its body in its own way. The usual transfer gain mixes body motion with screen movement and can assign a perfect score to a model that ignores its action. To address this, we introduce a transfer score that compares the correct action with wrong ones from the same source. We test five training objectives on a new synthetic benchmark of 2D cartoon characters with six body plans, the standard Sprites benchmark, and 431 selected animal and human animations from DeformingThings4D. With a fixed camera, a baseline that only copies the source's screen movement scores 0.71, as high as most learned models. In contrast, with a camera that follows the body, the best model reaches only 0.46 for an unseen animal family and 0.20 for humans. With this camera, a linear probe identifies the action class of unseen animal families with 66% to 86% balanced accuracy (chance 17%). The learned actions therefore retain information about which action is performed, but the correct action closes only part of the prediction error gap for a new character.
bullets: Cross-body-plan transfer is studied for 2D characters such as cats, blobs, and humans performing shared actions.
The paper introduces a transfer score that contrasts the correct source action with incorrect actions from the same source to avoid rewarding screen-motion copying.
Five training objectives are evaluated on a new six-body-plan cartoon benchmark, Sprites, and selected DeformingThings4D animations.
With a fixed camera, screen-motion copying reaches 0.71, revealing that standard transfer gains can be misleading.
Body-following-camera results are lower: the best model scores 0.46 on an unseen animal family and 0.20 on humans, while action classes remain linearly decodable at 66–86% balanced accuracy.

papers.title: Action Transfer Across Character Body Plans in Latent-Action World Models: An Empirical Study of Animated Characters
papers.tldr: The study shows that latent actions retain transferable action information across differently shaped animated characters, but current models achieve only partial zero-shot action transfer when screen-motion shortcuts are removed.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have established themselves as the preeminent paradigm for high-fidelity generative modeling across various modalities, yet their practical deployment is hindered by the severe computational overhead of iterative sampling. While recent feature-caching methods mitigate this latency through feature reuse or forecasting based on integer-order operators, they remain limited in adapting to the non-stationary and highly curved dynamics of DiT latent trajectories. In this work, we reveal that DiT feature evolution exhibits anomalous diffusion characteristics and a certain degree of spatiotemporal heterogeneity, rendering static, integer-order forecasting operators inadequate and prone to error accumulation. To address this, we propose Fractional Anomalous Dynamics Extrapolation (FADE), a unified framework for training-free diffusion transformers acceleration. FADE models DiT feature evolution via anomalous diffusion and employs a Mittag--Leffler fractional operator to better adapt to high-curvature and non-linear latent trajectories of DiTs. Leveraging the empirical observation that these complex dynamics maintain cross-sample stability, we further construct a Look-Up Table with multiple dimensions through offline profiling. This enables negligible LUT-retrieval overhead, spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval during online inference. Extensive evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities demonstrate that FADE achieves state-of-the-art acceleration, preserving exceptional generation fidelity under aggressive skip intervals with negligible latency overhead. Our project page is available at https://youngkinlon.github.io/fade-project-page/.
bullets: DiT sampling is computationally expensive, and existing integer-order feature forecasting struggles with non-stationary, highly curved latent trajectories.
FADE models feature evolution as anomalous diffusion using a Mittag–Leffler fractional operator.
An offline-profiled multidimensional lookup table enables spatiotemporally adaptive parameter retrieval with negligible online overhead.
Evaluations across diverse architectures and modalities report state-of-the-art acceleration and strong fidelity under aggressive skip intervals.
Scope: the method is training-free and relies on cross-sample stability of complex DiT dynamics.

papers.abstract: 1-bit key-value (KV) cache compression can combine quantizer calibration with selective high-precision storage to reduce reconstruction error. We propose Calibration and Fisher-guided Anchors for KV cache compression (CALFA-KV). Offline, we jointly fit a key center, radial normalization parameters, and K/V vector codebooks to match the frozen model's projected attention output. We also estimate channel-wise Fisher-type sensitivities from squared gradients of a reference next-token cross-entropy loss. Online, we use these sensitivities to weight the squared reconstruction errors of each KV state. Here, a KV state is one token's key-value pair within one layer and KV head. We retain the highest-scoring states at high precision under a per-layer, per-KV-head budget. Under exact restoration, we bound the excess risk of score-based anchor selection relative to the optimum at the same anchor budget, where risk is the conditional mean square of the first-order loss change. With a budget of 56 additional FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, CALFA-KV (d8b8) outperforms all evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines on the mean score across seven benchmarks for each of the three models. At the same anchor budget, CALFA-KV (d8b10) uses a nominal index rate of 1.25 bits per channel and narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90--2.01 points on the same metric.
bullets: Offline, it fits key normalization and K/V codebooks to preserve the frozen model’s projected attention output.
It estimates channel sensitivity from squared gradients of a reference next-token loss, then scores KV states by sensitivity-weighted reconstruction error.
Online, it stores the highest-scoring token key-value states at FP16 under per-layer, per-KV-head budgets.
With 56 extra FP16 anchors per layer and KV head, d8b8 outperforms evaluated nominal 1-bit baselines across seven benchmarks and three models.
The d8b10 variant narrows the gap to BF16 to 0.90–2.01 points at a nominal 1.25 bits per channel; the theory bounds selection risk under exact restoration.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. CALFA-KV for 1-bit KV cache compression. (a) Offline joint calibration proposes updates with fixed codeword assignments and tests them using deployment-precision replay after re-encoding. Channel sensitivities are estimated separately from reference-loss gradients. (b) During inference, sensitivityweighted reconstruction errors rank historical KV states for FP16 retention, with up to N anchors per layer and KV head. Attention combines decoded history, restored anchors, and unquantized recent and live K/V. The nominal 1-bit rate refers to codeword indices.

Fig. 2. Layerwise errors relative to a BF16 reference on Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 with a fixed, jointly calibrated d8b8 quantizer. Relative MSE is the sum of squared differences divided by the reference signal energy. No anchors uses zero additional anchors; Random, Unweighted error, and Fisher-guided (ours) each use a budget of 56 additional K/V pairs per layer and KV head. papers.abstract: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.
bullets: Builds an object-centric task graph from instructions and a skill library, then uses execution records to identify capability gaps.
Improves task organization, hand-offs, recovery routes, and repeatedly failing perception, motion, manipulation, or verification skills.
Adopts revisions only after full-task evaluation and paired comparisons, enabling validated local changes to accumulate.
On ten RoboDojo development tasks, average success increased from 30.0% to 86.2%; across eight real-world tasks, it succeeded in 62 of 80 real-robot trials.
Scope: the coding agent operates during development, while deployment uses the retained skills without runtime agent calls.

papers.abstract: We present a hypernetwork that generates the parameters of an implicit neural representation (INR) for a given signal in a single forward pass, without test-time optimization. Existing hypernetworks for this problem either ignore the chain-rule structure of the test-time optimization that produces an INR or, when they preserve it, instantiate the structure with MLPs whose parameter count grows quartically in target-network width. Our central contribution is to show that this parameter-count cost is structural to the MLP instantiation, not to the optimization-oriented principle of preserving chain-rule structure, and to resolve it by replacing the MLP body with attention. The resulting hypernetwork combines three design choices: an output-neuron-centric tokenization that aligns the token axis with each layer's output-neuron axis; an information-flow consistency rule that fixes the role of every cross-attention module from the representation its output should occupy; and a token-space iterative rollout that realizes the five quantities one optimization step on the target INR computes as five cross-attention modules with parameter count independent of target-network width. Across five 2D and 3D INR generation benchmarks, our method outperforms the state-of-the-art single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines; scales to target-network widths at which the MLP-based optimization-oriented paradigm exhausts GPU memory; and produces the highest result on NeRF generation without ground-truth INR weights supervision.
bullets: Existing optimization-oriented hypernetworks preserve test-time optimization structure but can require parameter counts that grow quartically with target-network width.
The method replaces the costly MLP body with attention while retaining the chain-rule structure of an optimization step.
It uses output-neuron-centric tokenization, information-flow-consistent cross-attention, and token-space iterative rollout.
Across five 2D and 3D INR benchmarks, it outperforms reported single-pass and optimization-oriented baselines.
It scales to target widths that exhaust GPU memory for MLP-based approaches and achieves the highest reported NeRF-generation result without ground-truth INR-weight supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One iterative module of the proposed hypernetwork HΩ, illustrated for a three-layer MLP target INR (L = 3); the construction extends to arbitrary L. At iteration t, the forward chain (left, modules ϕi) produces the pseudo-activation tokens τ t i from the parameter tokens ω(t) i , seeded by τ t 0 from zζ through the Cross-Attention (CA) block. The backward block (right) realizes one chain-rule step at each layer: ψτ i and ψω i produce the local Jacobian tokens Jτ ,t i−1 and Jω,t i , which ψδ i−1 and ψ∇ i contract with δti to produce the propagated loss-signal δti−1 and the parameter-gradient tokens ∇ωiL; the backward recursion is seeded by δtL, formed from τ t L and zζ via the concat-plus-CA module. papers.abstract: Predicting where multiple agents will move next is fundamental to autonomous driving, robotics, and any system that must share space with people safely. Modern stochastic predictors read off inter-agent interactions once from the observed past and keep that view fixed throughout the generative rollout, so the reciprocal geometric constraints that emerge as the joint future sharpens are not re-examined. We address this gap with SRA (Spatial Reasoning Adapter), a modular graph denoiser that is integrated into existing diffusion and flow-matching predictors without redesigning their generative cores. At every reverse step, SRA reads the host's current future estimate, builds a sparse Euclidean interaction graph on the predicted trajectories, and returns a residual correction to the host's decoding path. Our adapter consists of three core components: a sparse neighborhood retrieved with a learned query-key score and a geometric bias, a future-conditioned relational feature recomputed on the evolving prediction, and uncertainty-weighted message passing where confident agents act as anchors for uncertain ones. We instantiate SRA on three structurally different hosts (LED, MID, and MoFlow) across four multi-agent benchmarks: SDD, NBA, Soccer, and Football. SRA improves ADE for every host on every dataset, with average gains of 5.8% in ADE and 7.0% in FDE. A cumulative ablation shows that the three components act as one mechanism: only together do they improve every host on every sports dataset, indicating that spatial reasoning over the model's own evolving future, weighted by how far that future can be trusted, is broadly useful across denoising architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/Jaewoo97/SRA.
bullets: Targets predictors that do not re-examine reciprocal geometric constraints as predicted futures evolve.
Adds a modular graph denoiser adapter to diffusion and flow-matching models without changing their generative cores.
At each reverse step, it builds a sparse graph from current predicted trajectories and applies uncertainty-weighted residual corrections.
Combines learned geometric neighbor selection, future-conditioned relational features, and confidence-based message passing.
Improves ADE for all tested hosts and datasets, with average gains of 5.8% ADE and 7.0% FDE; the full component combination is needed for consistent sports-dataset gains.

papers.abstract: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.
bullets: Models mission intent with contracts covering coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources.
Couples simulated UAV missions with causal, resource-accounted execution, linking computation choices to time, resources, and usable observations.
Shows that higher perception recall does not necessarily improve mission completion: one configuration completed 1/16 missions versus 14/16 for a lower-recall configuration.
Finds that ignoring execution-induced observation loss can inflate mission success and reverse strategy rankings.
Jetson-profile replays alter local-versus-remote outcomes; selected GPU replays reduce modeled task energy by up to 28% without changing mission success.

papers.abstract: Learned manipulation policies often rely on wrist-mounted cameras for close-range visual feedback that complements external views of the workspace. However, contact-rich manipulation requires establishing and maintaining contacts that can remain hidden even from wrist cameras. Tactile sensors mounted on fingers can reliably and directly measure contact, without needing visual access. In this work, we show that this feedback enables policies to recover the performance advantage of wrist cameras using scene and egocentric vision together with touch. Our approach incorporates two low-cost tactile arrays into a visuotactile ACT policy, without wrist images during training or deployment. We evaluate six real-world task families spanning placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use. On three contact-rich tasks, we independently vary wrist-camera and tactile availability while keeping the demonstrations, policy architecture, and optimization settings fixed. Adding wrist cameras improves success by 18.3-28.3 percentage points over vision without wrist images. Adding tactile sensing instead improves success by 31.7-60.0 percentage points and yields higher observed success than vision-only policies with wrist cameras on all three tasks, with significant advantages on two under Holm-corrected tests. These results support finger-mounted tactile sensing as an effective alternative to wrist cameras in the evaluated contact-rich settings.
bullets: Wrist cameras may still fail to observe contacts hidden by objects or the robot hand.
The method adds two low-cost tactile arrays to a visuotactile ACT policy using scene and egocentric vision, with no wrist images.
Evaluation covers six real-world task families, including placement, insertion, occluded retrieval, and sustained-contact tool use.
On three contact-rich tasks, touch improved success by 31.7–60.0 percentage points over vision without wrist images and exceeded wrist-camera policies in observed success.
The findings are scoped to the evaluated real-world contact-rich settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising, where decisions about which tokens to commit or remask strongly affect output quality. Existing certainty-aware strategies rely on instantaneous confidence or entropy, but these local signals can be misleading on difficult reasoning problems. We formulate DLM test-time scaling as adaptive allocation of both inference compute and decoding strategies. Our two-stage approach uses a fast base sampler to solve easy questions, then applies frequency-aware remasking to the remaining hard questions. This strategy tracks how often each token's prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens, encouraging samples to explore alternative reasoning paths rather than collapse onto the model's preferred trajectory. Experiments with LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct show consistent improvements over a strong adaptive allocation baseline, with absolute accuracy gains of up to 3.73 percentage points (LLaDA) and 7.33 percentage points (Dream) on MATH-500, and absolute coverage gains of up to 11.39 percentage points (LLaDA) and 10.98 percentage points (Dream) on HumanEval. On questions unsolved by the base certainty-aware strategy after 100 samples, frequency-aware remasking recovers solutions for 3.75% to 18.75% of examples.
bullets: Existing confidence- or entropy-based remasking can be unreliable on difficult reasoning tasks.
The method first uses a fast base sampler, then applies frequency-aware remasking to unresolved questions.
It tracks token prediction changes across denoising steps and preferentially commits frequently changing tokens.
