papers.abstract: The task of visual reasoning relative pose identification (VRRPI) has exposed critical weaknesses in the multi-view 3D spatial reasoning capabilities of modern vision-language models (VLMs). We present a systematic analysis of VLMs' behavior in VRRPI, uncovering stable output biases where VLMs disproportionately predict specific motion patterns regardless of visual evidence. To mitigate these inherent biases, we propose self knowledge re-expression with iterative debiasing (SKR-ID), an annotation-free pipeline that adapts VLMs for VRRPI using only randomly extracted unannotated image pairs. SKR-ID transitions VLMs' output mechanism from generic next-token prediction to task-optimized classification heads. The pipeline proceeds in two stages: (1) a cold-start initialization using debiasing object-centric prompts to anchor motion inference in 2D visual evidence; and (2) a recursive logit-ranking mechanism that enforces statistical parity by using the median logit value as a dynamic threshold. Experimental evaluation across frontier VLMs on standard benchmarks demonstrates that SKR-ID significantly mitigates systematic biases. Our method improves open-source VLMs' Macro-F1 scores from 35.0-45.4% to 53.7-58.0%, without using any annotated data. These results show that SKR-ID can effectively improve 3D reasoning performance from a severely collapsed baseline. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/astudentuser/Codes_of_SKR-ID.
bullets: VLMs show stable, evidence-insensitive output biases in multi-view 3D relative-pose reasoning.
SKR-ID adapts VLMs using only randomly selected unannotated image pairs.
It combines object-centric prompts for cold-start visual grounding with recursive median-logit ranking for statistical debiasing.
Across frontier VLMs and standard benchmarks, open-source models’ Macro-F1 improves from 35.0–45.4% to 53.7–58.0%.
The approach targets severely collapsed baselines and does not require annotated data.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning-trained agents for retrieval-augmented generation retrieve content (passages, knowledge-graph fragments, or hyperedges) and supervise training with outcome rewards on the final answer. Across these paradigms the reasoning route through retrieved content never leaves the language model's hidden state, conflating declarative knowledge with the procedural knowledge that recurs across queries of the same logical type; content-only methods consequently plateau as reasoning depth grows. We introduce PatternBloom, an agentic RAG framework that shifts the unit of retrieval from content (what to read) to logic (how to reason). A first RL stage scores the agent's constructed evidence graph by a frozen oracle's information gain through the Information-Density Reward (IDR), a size-normalized mutual-information surrogate. High-reward trajectories are distilled into a Graph Pattern Memory (GPM) of type-abstracted reasoning skeletons, and a second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward (PAR) to couple policy to memory, turning procedural reasoning into a learnable, externalized structural prior. A 7B PatternBloom outperforms $27$ baselines by $+15.0$ Avg-OOD EM, with the gain compounding with reasoning depth precisely because procedural knowledge, once distilled, is reused rather than re-derived at every query. We release our code at https://github.com/EllenYiGe/PatternBloom.
bullets: Content-only retrieval conflates factual knowledge with recurring procedural reasoning, limiting performance on deeper reasoning tasks.
The framework retrieves abstract logic patterns rather than only passages, graph fragments, or hyperedges.
An RL stage builds evidence graphs scored by the Information-Density Reward, then distills high-reward trajectories into a Graph Pattern Memory.
A second RL stage uses the Pattern-Augmented Reward to integrate these procedural patterns into the agent’s policy.
A 7B model outperforms 27 baselines by 15.0 Avg-OOD EM, with gains increasing at greater reasoning depths.

papers.abstract: Local AI promises capable personal assistants that run on users' own devices, keeping data and computation under their control. Open-weight models that fit on local devices can now handle practical tasks such as coding. Yet current inference engines fall short. Popular engines such as vLLM and SGLang target datacenter GPUs with dedicated host memory, while local engines underuse the memory hierarchy of unified-memory devices. We present Hibana, an inference engine for unified-memory devices that co-optimizes model representation, memory management, and decoding strategy. Model surgery, the process of editing a trained model's architecture to suit its hardware, changes how the model computes, shrinking its memory footprint and data movement. Unified-memory management preserves each agent's state across turns, so long-running agents can resume instantly instead of recomputing their state. Adaptive speculation generates several tokens per step. Hibana codesigns these features around the shared memory capacity and limited bandwidth of unified-memory systems-on-chip to support local multi-agent workloads. On a single DGX Spark serving Qwen and Nemotron models of up to 125B parameters, Hibana completes up to 3.4$\times$ more agentic tasks per hour and delivers up to 3.9$\times$ higher decoding throughput than other established frameworks such as vLLM, NVIDIA Flare, llama.cpp, and TensorFold. Code is available at https://github.com/sharar-project/hibana.
bullets: Targets unified-memory systems-on-chip, which existing datacenter and local inference engines do not fully exploit.
Uses model surgery to reduce model memory footprint and data movement.
Preserves agent state across turns, enabling instant resumption without recomputation.
Applies adaptive speculation to generate multiple tokens per decoding step.
On a DGX Spark with models up to 125B parameters, achieves up to 3.4× more agentic tasks per hour and 3.9× higher decoding throughput than established frameworks.

papers.abstract: Existing methods enhancing an LLM's long-context reasoning capability often rely on data synthesis and follow-up LLM post-training. However, the data synthesis strategy and the post-training recipes are empirically driven and computationally intensive. In this work, we propose a new framework, dubbed LongCapHarness, to instead harness the underlying capabilities for long-context reasoning. The harnessing process recursively revises and updates capability primitive implementation, capability state and control logic through recursive self-improvement on the development set. With neither data synthesis nor LLM post-training, LongCapHarness is applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B. LongCapHarness substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis-based baselines on HELMET and RULER benchmarks; its estimated development cost is less than 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong. We hope these results motivate further research into harnessing the latent capabilities of LLMs to solve tasks beyond their explicit training.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost and empirical nature of data synthesis and post-training approaches.
Recursively updates capability primitives, capability state, and control logic through self-improvement on a development set.
Applied to Llama3-8B and transferred to Qwen2.5-3B without additional LLM post-training.
Substantially outperforms recent data-synthesis baselines on HELMET and RULER.
Estimated development cost is under 50% of the estimated training costs of NExtLong and PolicyLong.

papers.abstract: We study decentralised drone formation, without a central planner, under the conditions that make it hard: nobody knows how many drones are alive, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy. In our controller, ant colony optimisation (ACO) allocates drones to picture positions through claims that behave as reinforced, evaporating pheromone and are gossiped between neighbours, so evaporation doubles as failure detection. A particle swarm optimisation (PSO) law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO also tunes the controller offline. We prove that claims of destroyed drones vanish within bounded time, that conflicts between drones that exchange tables are resolved consistently, that survivors cover the picture to within a factor of two, and that drones cannot collide while their safety cells are feasible. On held-out seeds and with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95-99% of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96-100% of runs at normal difficulty, transferred unchanged to eight unseen shapes and to 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21,088 runs. A CBBA-style baseline that shares the evaporating claims but uses argmax without swaps was at least as reliable as ours once tuned with the same budget, and repaired faster, whereas ours generalised better to unseen shapes. The benefit thus comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning, not from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms. A centralised oracle is faster.
bullets: Uses evaporating, neighbour-gossiped pheromone claims for position allocation and silent-failure detection.
Combines PSO-based flight control with a noise-buffered Voronoi filter for collision avoidance; PSO tunes the controller offline.
Proves bounded disappearance of failed claims, consistent conflict resolution after information exchange, near-complete survivor coverage, and collision avoidance when safety cells are feasible.
Forms target pictures in 95–99% of hardest-regime runs and repairs half-swarm losses in 96–100% of normal-difficulty runs; transfers to unseen shapes and 300 drones.
The tuned baseline was at least as reliable and faster to repair, while the proposed method generalised better; a centralised oracle remained faster.

papers.selection_reason: Decentralised drone swarm formation with pheromone-based failure detection and PSO control fits embodied multi-agent coordination, though it is not learning-based.
papers.title: Decentralised Drone Swarm Formation under Silent Failures with ACO Pheromone Claims and PSO Tuning
papers.tldr: A decentralised ACO–PSO controller forms and repairs drone formations under silent failures and unreliable communication, with strong robustness but no clear reliability advantage over a tuned CBBA-style baseline.

papers.abstract: Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) rollouts interleave model reasoning with tool calls in persistent workspaces. Scaling these rollouts incurs substantial memory costs for concurrent environments, while slow tool calls delay entire rollout batches. We present BunshinRL, an agentic RL rollout system that exploits shared environment state and recurring tool calls through three techniques: memory sharing across environments, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution. These techniques build on BunshinFork, a novel live whole-workspace forking mechanism for containers. BunshinFork reconstructs process trees, shares memory copy-on-write, and preserves file, communication, and GUI state, enabling cached-state reuse and rollback after incorrect speculation. We implement BunshinRL and BunshinFork through Linux kernel module and CRIU modifications. BunshinRL reduces peak memory by up to 43%, total memory consumption by up to 51%, and end-to-end rollout latency by 23%.
bullets: Targets memory overhead from concurrent environments and delays from slow tool calls.
Combines shared environment state, tool-prefix caching, and speculative tool execution.
Introduces BunshinFork, which supports live whole-workspace forks with copy-on-write memory, preserved state, and rollback.
Implemented via Linux kernel-module and CRIU modifications.
Reports up to 43% lower peak memory, 51% lower total memory, and 23% lower end-to-end rollout latency.

figures.caption: Figure 4. BunshinFork architecture. A brief freeze captures a consistent workspace state. The live fork path reconstructs isolated clones that share unchanged pages copy-on-write and allocate private pages on writes. Retained snapshot holders support asynchronous serialization, allowing the source to resume without waiting for disk writes.

Figure 3. Illustration of BunshinRL. Right shows two samples in a simplified rollout step; left shows the on-disk and in-memory workspace snapshot stores for tool call prefix. Reasoning steps’ generated tool call signatures are matched with the tool prefix tree. All initial matched tool calls are skipped until the first miss in tool signature (Tool 3 for R1 and Tool 4 for R2), at which point the corresponding snapshots are used to reconstruct the workspaces. As C3 is not cached in memory, Tool 3 is replayed for R2 and its delta write is added to the C0+C1+C2 snapshot. The samples execute actual Tool 3 for R1 and actual Tool 4 for R2, creating new delta CoW pages. After these calls finish, speculation starts from the resulting workspaces: Tool 4 for R1 and Tools 5 and 6 for R2. The Spec Tool Selector selects tool calls that are likely to happen from previous tool call history. When a reasoning step finishes, its output tool signature is compared with the speculative tool signature. For failed speculation, the system rolls back to the workspace snapshot before speculation.

Figure 5. Linux Process Fork vs. BunshinFork Process-Tree Fork. Left: native fork() duplicates one process as a child of the source process. Right: BunshinFork creates a sibling container and reconstructs the whole process tree inside an independent namespace.

papers.abstract: Most robotic handwriting rigidly mounts the pen and reduces writing to trajectory tracking. A freely held pen instead couples grasp stability, tip motion, and contact force. We present Grip, Trace, Write, a force-aware simulation environment and learning framework for high-DoF handwriting. A two-branch actor separates pen retention from arm-wrist writing while preserving their closed-loop coupling. Training learns a grasp controller, initializes writing from inverse-kinematics demonstrations by behavior cloning, and improves writing through reinforcement learning with rewards on ink, force, time, and retention. Across diverse tasks, the policy improves completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency over behavior cloning and inverse kinematics, and generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese content. These results establish force-aware handwriting as a testbed for dexterous tool use.
bullets: Addresses the coupled challenges of grasp stability, pen-tip motion, and contact force in robotic handwriting.
Uses a force-aware simulation environment with separate but closed-loop coupled branches for pen retention and arm-wrist writing.
Combines grasp control, inverse-kinematics demonstrations with behavior cloning, and reinforcement learning guided by ink, force, time, and retention rewards.
Outperforms behavior cloning and inverse kinematics across completion, precision, force regulation, and efficiency metrics.
Generalizes without fine-tuning to unseen English and Chinese writing content; positioned as a testbed for dexterous tool use.

papers.abstract: Model editing provides an efficient way to update factual knowledge in transformer models. Recent approaches reverse edits by modifying, masking, or decomposing model weights, but make recovery dependent on weight-space interventions. We instead show that pre-edit knowledge can be recovered through input-space interventions alone, without modifying the edited model's weights. We introduce Memento, a prompt-space mechanism for auditing residual knowledge that learns a reusable recovery signal to steer an edited model toward its pre-edit response. Memento supports both continuous recovery prefixes and discrete textual prompts for standard text interfaces. Across three LLMs and five editing techniques, Memento recovers 80.07% of held-out edited facts, achieving a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines, suggesting that editing may suppress the facts without fully eliminating their recoverability. We further investigate whether prompt-space recovery extends beyond model editing. On pristine, unedited LLMs, Memento improves average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference. These results demonstrate the potential of prompt-space recovery for auditing residual knowledge in edited models and investigating the gap between factual knowledge and its accessibility during inference. We will release our source code.
bullets: Model-editing audits typically rely on modifying or analyzing model weights; this work uses input-space interventions instead.
Memento learns reusable recovery signals that steer edited models toward their pre-edit responses, via continuous prefixes or discrete prompts.
Across three LLMs and five editing methods, it recovered 80.07% of held-out edited facts, with a 9.58% relative improvement over baselines.
On unedited models, Memento improved average factual recall by 53.9% relative to standard inference.
The findings suggest editing can suppress factual accessibility without fully removing the underlying knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of MEMENTO’s continuous prompt-space recovery. A trainable prefix Π is prepended to factual prompts and optimized across training facts to recover the original object o from an edited model fθ′ , whose parameters remain frozen. The objective combines supervised recovery (Lrec), preference optimization (Lpref ), fluency preservation (Lflu), and distillation from the pre-edit model (Ldist). Gradients update only Π; the pre-edit model supplies distillation targets during training and is not needed at inference. Without the prefix, the edited LLM answers the edited object (o∗ = midfielder); with it, the LLM produces the original object (o = quarterback).

papers.abstract: Video diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos, but attention over long spatiotemporal sequences makes inference computationally expensive. Sparse attention reduces this cost by computing only a subset of query-key interactions exactly, and recent training-free methods further approximate the remaining interactions. These methods, however, degrade quickly at high sparsity, which limits the achievable speedup. We present ESTRA (Extreme Sparsity Through Refined Attention), a training-free acceleration method that preserves generation quality even at extreme sparsity. ESTRA concentrates exact attention computation on a small set of important key-value tokens and approximates the remaining contributions with cluster representatives. To identify these tokens efficiently, it groups similar queries and uses their representatives to score individual keys. A variance-based correction further refines the attention weights of the cluster representatives, improving the accuracy of the approximation. Experiments on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B show that ESTRA establishes a new quality-efficiency frontier for training-free sparse attention, achieving $3.26\times$ and $4.71\times$ end-to-end speedups at 5% attention density while surpassing Sol-Attn and SVG-EAR in fidelity to dense generation and on most VBench dimensions. Even at 1% density, ESTRA remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5%, while reaching up to $5.39\times$ speedup.
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of attention over long spatiotemporal video sequences.
Selects a small set of important key-value tokens using clustered query representatives.
Approximates remaining attention with cluster representatives and applies variance-based weight correction.
At 5% attention density, achieves 3.26× and 4.71× end-to-end speedups on Wan2.1-14B and HunyuanVideo-13B.
At 1% density, remains more faithful to dense generation than Sol-Attn at 12.5% density, with up to 5.39× speedup.

papers.abstract: Visual data are often expressed through multiple complementary modalities (e.g., images and segmentation masks), each capturing different aspects of the same underlying structure. Most existing multimodal methods adopt a top-down paradigm, learning a shared latent variable through joint training from scratch, which limits scalability. We propose Split and Bridge (SnB), a bottom-up framework for multimodal generation that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time. Rather than learning a unified latent space, SnB generates coherent multimodal samples by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point and then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. This design enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models without joint training, making it scalable and easily adaptable. Across standard benchmarks (PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ) and more complex settings (PIE-Bench++, ROCO), SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence. We show that SnB naturally extends to downstream zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Our results demonstrate that bottom-up generation provides a practical framework that complements existing top-down multimodal approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB
bullets: Addresses the scalability limits of jointly trained shared-latent multimodal models.
Shares a diffusion trajectory until a split point, then uses a bridge module to guide modality-specific generation.
Supports plug-and-play reuse of pretrained unimodal diffusion models.
Achieves a strong balance of sample quality and cross-modal coherence across several benchmarks and complex settings.
Extends naturally to zero-shot co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling.

This flexibility applies SnB in various tasks, like interleaved co-generation (top left pair) and multimodal generation (top right pair). papers.abstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. By predicting policy outcomes under updated estimates of current conditions, world models could enable teams to re-evaluate existing policies without physically executing each candidate, provided predicted performance changes reflect those realized on deployed systems. We identify research priorities for model-based policy re-evaluation, validation of predicted against realized performance, and incorporating shared information into world models to support coordinated team adaptation.
bullets: Environmental, hardware, or team changes can reorder the Pareto set, making previously dominated or new policies viable.
Selecting among existing Pareto-optimal policies may address objective shifts but not changing deployment conditions.
World models could predict policy outcomes under updated conditions, reducing the need to physically test every candidate.
Safe adoption requires validating predicted performance against outcomes on deployed systems.
Shared information should be incorporated to support coordinated adaptation across robot teams.

figures.caption: Figure 1: This is a proposed pipeline for maintaining a shared, current representation of the world using world models after deployment. Distributed agents collect local observations, model predictions are tracked against realized performance, and if the context is out of distribution, the model can be updated. The model is used to evaluate policies when objectives change, or possibly even learn new policies with the updated world models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes using world models for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation in remote robot teams, directly addressing world models for robotics.
papers.title: Multi-Objective Adaptation After Deployment: A Position on World Models for Remote Robot Teams
papers.tldr: World models could help remote robot teams safely reassess and adapt policies after deployment as conditions and objectives change.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding efficiency depends on the number of consecutively accepted draft tokens, yet token-level training objectives do not directly optimize this quantity. We introduce D-REAL (Drafter Reinforcement of Expected Acceptance Length), a post-training method that directly optimizes expected acceptance length for a fixed decoding context. D-REAL weights position-wise draft-target distributional overlap by prefix survival probabilities along a draft-sampled prefix, faithfully capturing the sequential dependence of verification on earlier proposals. By accounting for the parameter dependence of the proposal distribution, we derive an unbiased gradient estimator for this single-round objective under stochastic verification. We evaluate D-REAL on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B as the target model across ten benchmarks. Starting from baselines whose mean acceptance length has plateaued, one epoch of D-REAL post-training consistently improves the benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens across both architectures under greedy (T = 0.0) and stochastic (T = 1.0) sampling, translating into up to a 9.4% end-to-end serving throughput improvement.
bullets: Targets the sequential objective that determines how many draft tokens are accepted, rather than optimizing tokens independently.
Weights position-wise draft–target overlap by prefix survival probabilities to account for earlier proposal acceptance.
Derives an unbiased gradient estimator that includes the proposal distribution’s parameter dependence under stochastic verification.
Evaluated on DSpark and DFlash2 with Qwen3-8B across ten benchmarks and under greedy and stochastic sampling.
Improves benchmark-averaged mean acceptance length by up to 0.23 tokens and end-to-end throughput by up to 9.4%.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of draft-training objectives. Unlike (a) standard token-level losses and (b) D-PACE, which weight token likelihoods along fixed offline reference prefixes, (c) D-REAL directly optimizes expected acceptance length along online draft-sampled trajectories by combining exact local distributional overlap (left inset) with differentiable prefix survival factors (right inset) via stop-gradient proposal denominators.

Figure 2. Per-task cumulative acceptance rate Pr(N ≥ t) across speculative positions t ∈ {1, . . . , 7} for DFlash2 under (a) greedy (T = 0.0) and (b) stochastic (T = 1.0) decoding. Across both regimes and all ten benchmarks, D-REAL consistently slows down prefix survival decay compared to the baseline, yielding compounding gains with draft depth. Y-axis ranges vary by workload and are shared across temperatures; shading highlights the gap, and labels report the position-7 gain in percentage points.

Table 2. End-to-end serving performance of DFlash2 and DSpark on GSM8K in SGLang, measured on an 8-GPU Hopper node (concurrency = 32). D-REAL translates higher acceptance lengths into substantial throughput gains and latency reductions without modifying the inference architecture.

Table 4. Macro-averaged cumulative acceptance rate Pr(N ≥ t) (%) across speculative positions t ∈ {1, . . . , 7} for DFlash2 over all ten benchmarks (τ ≈ 1 + ∑7 t=1 Pr(N ≥ t), where the small systematic positive bias stems from early-EOS block truncation causing position-t rates to be computed conditional on the block reaching t). While D-PACE drops below the baseline at T = 1.0, D-REAL achieves consistent, substantial gains across the entire draft depth.

Table 1. Mean acceptance length (τ ) across ten benchmarks, including one additional verifier-generated token per round. Bold indicates the best results. D-REAL (Ours) consistently outperforms the baseline and D-PACE, particularly under stochastic sampling (T = 1.0).

Table 3. Ablation study on DSpark across representative benchmarks from each domain: GSM8K (Math), MBPP (Code), and C-Eval (Chat). Replacing the static decay with D-REAL’s unbiased dynamic prefix weighting yields consistent gains across all domains and temperatures.

papers.title: D-REAL: Acceptance-Length Optimization with Unbiased Gradients for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: D-REAL directly optimizes speculative decoding’s expected acceptance length with an unbiased gradient estimator, improving acceptance and serving throughput after one post-training epoch.

papers.abstract: In this work, we train agents to act under uncertainty according to specified, belief-dependent rules. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can in theory train agents to follow rules if encoded into well-designed rewards, but in practice, RL fails to perfectly optimize these rewards, leading to ineffective or noncompliant agent behavior. Belief-space planners by construction produce behavior in line with developer specification, but require hand-programming online planners and belief-state estimators, adding significant engineering complexity at scale. We combine the two: we plan offline to generate a dataset of sample trajectories and then distill the plans into a policy that acts on raw observations. We propose two changes to planner distillation that address problems specific to history-based policies: Dual Averaging, a loss that combines per-timestep predictive loss and average loss on task changes, and $ρ$-Optimal Reinforcement, a feedback mechanism that reinforces the policy's own successful rollouts when these are near-optimal. We provide a sufficient condition under which static search problems with noiseless observation models is complete, and show that maximum-likelihood-observation planning implies this condition in static search with continuous beliefs. We create a challenging new domain, Scavenger, where an agent needs to gain information in order to succeed. We evaluate our distilled policy in two versions of Scavenger, one where information is provided visually and one where it is provided as a command in natural language. In either case, the learned policy attains a success rate above 90% in Scavenger, compared with at most 5% for RL. We also find that distilled planners transfer with greater than 60% success to following unseen and intentionally vague commands and greater than 75% success to following floorplans larger than those seen in training.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of making RL agents reliably comply with specified, belief-dependent behavior and the engineering cost of hand-coded belief-space planners.
Distills offline belief-space task-and-motion-planning trajectories into a history-based policy operating on raw observations.
Introduces Dual Averaging for combining timestep and task-change losses, plus ρ-Optimal Reinforcement to reinforce near-optimal successful rollouts.
In the new Scavenger domain, the distilled policy exceeds 90% success in both visual- and language-guided settings, versus at most 5% for RL.
Transfers to unseen vague commands with over 60% success and larger-than-training floorplans with over 75% success.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: An overview of the Scavenger domain. (a) The agent starts in a random room for a procedurally generated floorplan, with a set of visual markers, a geometry visualizing connectivity between rooms, and a visual prior denoting a set of possible locations. (b) The robot must search among possible locations for a hint, either represented visually or as a command in natural language. (c) It succeeds when it approaches the marker hinted at, and then takes a relevant “guess” action when it is sufficiently close to that marker. Guessing before it is certain of the correct marker, or guessing the wrong marker, counts as a failure.

Fig. 4: Results of the generalization study. The policy from our method, trained in Figure 3b, transfers to unseen language commands, to intentionally vague commands, and to problems with vastly more rooms than was seen in training. This shows that our policy learns to comply with physical and epistemic constraints reliably, even in floorplans and given language hints that were unseen in training. Each success rate is calculated based on 50 episodes, and the error bars are binomial standard errors.

Fig. 3: Success rates vs. wall-clock time on Scavenger. The dots on the baseline runs refer to the point in baseline runs where as many simulation timesteps are used for training the policies as our method. In all cases, our method attains at least 18 times the success rate of the baseline RL policies, even while giving the baseline RL policies access to at least 50% more simulator steps for training. Our method attains the highest success rate among the ablations for our feedback mechanism. Note: our method and ablations do not all start at 0 wall-clock time, because there is an initial phase of data generation without policy training for each, longer for the No Feedback ablation since it does not get further policy / planner feedback afterward. The ablations attain much stronger performance than the RL baselines, but start to struggle more with parsing language hints. All methods are run with a single seed.

The robot should be confident that the user has what they need before they leave the house. Left: The robot must first search for the user in the house, who may be in one of three locations. Middle: After finding the user, the robot asks them about what they might need for the day. Right: The robot hears the user is planning to go on a drive to see friends on a rainy day, and then brings them their keys and umbrella.

papers.selection_reason: Distills belief-space task and motion planners into compliant robot policies; relevant to embodied robot learning and navigation.
papers.title: Deploying Physically and Epistemically Compliant Agents by Distilling Belief-Space Task and Motion Planners
papers.tldr: Planner distillation produces agents that follow belief-dependent rules under uncertainty far more reliably than direct reinforcement learning while acting from raw observations.

papers.abstract: Mental simulation, the ability to reason by constructing and updating internal visual states, is central to flexible human cognition, but remains elusive in current multimodal large language models. Latent multimodal reasoning offers a promising route toward this capability by interleaving text with continuous visual latent blocks, allowing models to maintain internal visual workspaces without decoding them into pixels. In this paper, we ask whether these latent visual states actually matter. Through a direct perturbation analysis across representative latent-reasoning MLLMs, we find that they often do not: dropping, replacing, or shuffling generated visual latents has only minor effects on the model's own final-answer probability, while equivalent perturbations to the linguistic reasoning trace are substantially more damaging. We call this failure mode Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): the model appears to perform interleaved visual reasoning, but routes most answer-relevant computation through text. We further diagnose that MSC follows naturally from existing training objectives: visual alignment can make generated latents resemble helper-image embeddings, but it does not require the decoder to rely on them; subsequent text-only supervision further leaves the semantic role of the latent pathway unidentifiable. To address this, we introduce AnchorSim (Anchored Mental Simulation), a contrastive distillation framework that trains models to make their generated visual latents consequential. Across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks, AnchorSim improves performance, while diagnostic re-evaluation shows that visual perturbations now meaningfully affect predictions. Our results expose a fundamental failure mode of latent multimodal reasoning and demonstrate that mental simulation must be anchored to model behavior in order to matter.
bullets: Identifies Mental Simulation Collapse (MSC): perturbing visual latents has little effect, unlike perturbing text reasoning traces.
Attributes MSC to training objectives that align visual latents without requiring downstream reliance on them.
Introduces AnchorSim, a contrastive distillation framework for anchoring generated visual latents to model behavior.
Reports improved performance across multiple visual reasoning benchmarks and stronger sensitivity to visual-latent perturbations.
Shows that effective latent mental simulation requires visual states to be causally relevant to predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AnchorSim. Given an initial image and query, the model produces an interleaved reasoning trajectory consisting of textual thoughts tk and intermediate visual simulations zk. AnchorSim trains the student policy with two complementary signals. First, a visual-blind branch masks the previous generated visual state zk−1 and is stopped from receiving gradients; the student is encouraged to diverge from this blind prediction, preventing “lazy text” reasoning that ignores visual latents. Second, a simulation-anchored teacher, updated as an EMA of the student and conditioned on the ground-truth answer, provides reliable reasoning targets under the full context. The student is optimized to minimize the JSD to the teacher while maximizing the JSD from its visual-blind counterpart, thereby anchoring textual reasoning to the generated visual simulations.

Figure 1: Vision vs. text perturbation impact across four multimodal latent-reasoning models. Each panel reports the mean log-probability (±1 SEM) of the model’s final-answer span. We compare four conditions applied independently to the vision block (blue) and the reasoning text block (purple): Full (unchanged), Drop (removed), Cross (replaced from another sample), and Shuffle (permuted). Step 2 shows them on the vision block; the charts apply them to both blocks in turn. A larger drop from Full indicates that the perturbed block carries more answer-relevant information. In most conditions, perturbing the text block degrades the answer substantially more than perturbing the visual block, indicating that computation is routed primarily through the linguistic stream.

Figure 5: Perturbation analysis. (a) OLS slope S between perturbed and unperturbed answer logprobabilities for Qwen-interleaved and ANCHORSIM, where S ≈ 1 indicates little effect. (b) Closed-loop analysis, where the model regenerates the rest of the trajectory after the perturbation.

Figure 9: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for CoVT-7B on V*Bench. CoVT emits a fixed three-encoder visual-block template per trajectory, so all perturbation conditions are evaluated on the full 100-sample set. Vision-side perturbations leave many samples close to the no-impact diagonal, whereas text-side perturbations move a substantial subset below the diagonal. This shows that the model’s final-answer probability is more sensitive to corrupted reasoning text than to corrupted SAM, depth, and DINO pad hidden states.
Figure 4: Qualitative example on SAT-R. ANCHORSIM-7B achieves better visual–text interleaving and correctly predicts the answer. Blue squares denote visual latent tokens.

Figure 2: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for Mirage-7B. Each panel plots the perturbed final-answer log-probability (y = lpperturbed) against the unperturbed baseline (x = lpfull) for the vision block (blue) and reasoning text block (purple). Points further below the y=x diagonal (dashed) and lower ordinary-least-squares fit slopes (solid lines) indicate a larger performance drop. Across all conditions, the text fit has a lower slope than the vision fit, demonstrating that perturbing the linguistic chain degrades the answer more than perturbing the visual latents.

Figure 15: Qualitative example on CV-Bench-2D. The model must reason about planar spatial relations and object layout. The generated latent states provide compact visual anchors that support relation tracking throughout the reasoning trajectory.

Figure 11: Qualitative example on EMMA. The model solves a diagram-grounded STEM problem by combining textual reasoning with visual grounding. AnchorSim encourages the reasoning chain to revisit visual latents when deriving the final answer, rather than relying only on language priors.

Figure 12: Qualitative example on SAT-R. The task requires mentally simulating a spatial or viewpoint transformation from a real image. The example illustrates how latent visual states can support intermediate spatial reasoning before the model commits to the final answer.

Figure 13: Qualitative example on V*. The question depends on fine-grained visual search over a high-resolution image. AnchorSim helps the model preserve visually relevant details in latent form, allowing the final response to be grounded in localized evidence.

Figure 8: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for SkiLa-7B on the multi-hop subset of BLINK. The layout, axes, and color encoding match Figure 2. Each point compares the perturbed final-answer log-probability against the full-trajectory baseline. Drop and Shuffle are restricted to trajectories with nsketches ≥ 2 (n = 88), while Cross uses all 100 samples. Across conditions, text perturbations produce larger answer log-probability drops than sketch-hidden-state perturbations, indicating that the linguistic reasoning chain carries more answer-relevant computation than the visual sketch states.
Figure 7: Effect of latent size.
Figure 6: Loss ablation.

Figure 16: Qualitative example of multi-hop visual reasoning. The model decomposes the problem into multiple intermediate reasoning steps, each paired with latent visual states. This example illustrates the intended behavior of interleaved visual reasoning: later text should depend on earlier visual simulations rather than bypassing them.

Figure 14: Qualitative example on MMVP. MMVP contains image pairs that expose failures in low-level visual discrimination. This example shows how anchoring the reasoning process to visual latents can help distinguish visually similar alternatives.

Figure 10: Per-sample vision vs. text perturbation impact for Monet-7B on MMVP + V*Bench. Monet emits a single visual latent block per trajectory, so vision-side Shuffle is undefined and omitted. Drop and Cross are evaluated on all 100 samples. Since Monet has no between-block text segments, text-side Drop uses the naive full-text variant. Both vision and text channels carry signal in this single-hop setting, but text perturbations cause larger log-probability drops.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnoses and addresses latent collapse in multimodal LLM reasoning; directly relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Mental Imagery That Matters: Curing Latent Collapse in Multimodal Reasoning
papers.tldr: Latent visual reasoning in multimodal models often does not influence their answers, and AnchorSim trains models to make these internal visual states behaviorally consequential.

papers.abstract: Semantic response caching reuses a cached response for a semantically similar query to improve LLM inference efficiency. However, query similarity alone can lead to unsafe reuse when safety conditions change. Existing approaches improve cache safety through stricter similarity checks, context-aware validation, or response verification, yet they may still miss safety conflicts between the cached response and the new request or introduce unnecessary verification overhead. We argue that safe and efficient semantic caching requires a reuse policy that makes the cached response's safety conditions explicit and uses them to guide the reuse decision with a balance between safety and utility. In this paper, we propose SafeCache, a safety-aware framework that separates candidate retrieval from safety approval and formulates semantic response reuse as a safety-conditioned routing problem. SafeCache matches each cached-response condition against the new request and aggregates the per-condition mismatches into an overall risk score. A separate contradiction guard prevents explicit conflicts from being diluted by strong matches. It further estimates matching uncertainty and calibrates the routing policy under a required unsafe-reuse target and a verifier-call budget to choose among direct reuse, selective verification, or regeneration. Experiments show that SafeCache achieves the better safety-utility trade-off among the evaluated baselines, enabling safer response reuse at comparable cache utility.
bullets: Addresses unsafe cache reuse when a new request’s safety requirements differ from those of a cached response.
Separates semantic candidate retrieval from safety approval rather than relying on query similarity alone.
Aggregates condition mismatches into a risk score and uses a contradiction guard to catch explicit conflicts.
Calibrates routing under an unsafe-reuse target and verifier-call budget to balance safety and cache utility.
Experiments report a better safety–utility trade-off than evaluated baselines at comparable cache utility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SafeCache. From left to right, SafeCache first extracts the reuse requirements of the cached response and the safety facts of the new request. It then matches the two condition sets to compute the condition mismatch and matching uncertainty, while rule- and context-level guards preserve explicit conflicts. Finally, risk calibration produces the routing risk and uncertainty, which are combined with query similarity and the conflict indicator to choose direct reuse, verification, or regeneration. A verified response is reused if accepted and regenerated otherwise.

Figure 2: Necessity of selective verification for SafeCache (α = 0, B = .16). Safety (y-axis, FH↓) and utility (x-axis, VCHR↑) changes when replacing verification in SafeCache (blue) with regeneration (gray) or direct reuse (orange).

papers.selection_reason: Safety-aware semantic response caching for LLM inference; fits efficient AI through latency and compute reduction.
papers.title: Beyond Query Similarity: Safety-Conditioned Cache Routing for LLM Response Reuse
papers.tldr: SafeCache makes LLM response caching safety-aware by routing reuse, verification, or regeneration based on explicit safety-condition matching and calibrated risk.

papers.abstract: World models enable planning through internal simulation, while natural language provides intuitive task specification. Yet, language-conditioned world modeling remains fragmented across domains with disparate action spaces, datasets, and evaluation protocols. We introduce LCWM, a shared task that maps an initial agent-view observation and a language instruction to an action sequence that fulfills the instruction. Its accompanying benchmark, LCWM-Bench, integrates 15 datasets across navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under a shared action interface and evaluation protocol, pairing 142,987 episodes with 428,961 instructions in three styles. We further propose Tiresias, an agent that plans via selective imagination: a language-conditioned diffusion policy generates candidate trajectories, a trajectory ranker shortlists them, and a video-pretrained world model imagines their visual consequences. A visual ranker evaluates these rollouts, complementing trajectory scores to select the final plan. Tiresias achieves competitive planning and imagination performance on LCWM-Bench. Ablations demonstrate the complementary benefits of trajectory ranking and visual verification, while experiments with alternative proposal methods show that the trained rankers remain effective beyond our diffusion policy. Together, LCWM-Bench and Tiresias provide a unified evaluation setting and an effective starting point for studying language-guided planning through world models.
bullets: LCWM-Bench unifies 15 datasets spanning navigation, robotics, 3D gaming, and driving under shared actions and evaluation.
The benchmark contains 142,987 episodes and 428,961 instructions in three language styles.
Tiresias uses a language-conditioned diffusion policy to propose trajectories, then combines trajectory ranking with video-based visual verification.
A video-pretrained world model imagines the visual outcomes of shortlisted plans before final selection.
Ablations support the complementary value of trajectory ranking and visual verification; performance is reported as competitive on LCWM-Bench.

papers.selection_reason: Directly proposes language-conditioned world models with action-conditioned imagination and video-based prediction, fitting interactive and video world model subtopics.
papers.title: Tiresias: Towards Language-Conditioned World Models
papers.tldr: Tiresias enables language-guided planning by ranking imagined action trajectories in a unified cross-domain world-model benchmark.

papers.abstract: LLM agents have made impressive progress in coding and mathematical reasoning, motivating growing interest in learning from long-horizon interaction. Memory supports this process, but plausible lessons can be redundant or reinforce inappropriate actions. Can a memory's source decision provide a practical test for whether to retain it? We localize consequential trajectory steps, extract candidate memories, and replay each source decision with and without its candidate under the same context. This reveals two properties: most candidates barely shift the probed distribution, and both successful and failed source actions can be reinforced or suppressed. These observations motivate Anchor, which tests shift magnitude and source-role alignment before retention. Admitted memories guide later trajectories, enabling experience-driven improvement under a frozen policy. On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, Anchor improves success rate and mean score by up to 19.9% and 17.2%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline for each backbone. With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld cards than unfiltered retention and outperforms all four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.
bullets: Memory candidates often have little effect on action distributions, and successful or failed source actions may both be reinforced or suppressed.
Anchor localizes consequential trajectory steps and replays source decisions with and without each candidate memory.
It retains memories based on both distribution-shift magnitude and alignment with the source action’s role.
On held-out ALFWorld and WebShop tasks, it improves success rate by up to 19.9% and mean score by up to 17.2% versus the strongest backbone-specific baselines.
With Qwen3.5-27B, it retains 41% fewer ALFWorld memory cards and outperforms four WebShop cost-comparison baselines while using fewer tokens.

papers.title: From Reflection to Co-Evolution: Self-Evolving Agents with Locally Verified Memory

papers.abstract: Transparent-interface reconstruction must recover glass surfaces even when most observed color comes from the scene behind them. We present ClearForm, a shared-planar-Gaussian method for jointly reconstructing transparent interfaces and the appearance seen through them. We identify and analyze the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD): when the same transparency-dependent alpha controls both color and geometry, revealing the background can weaken a transparent surface's contribution to geometric reconstruction. We derive its effect on plane-based depth estimation, identify a mechanism that can weaken geometric learning, and quantify the loss of interface support through controlled comparisons. To address this conflict, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. Shared planar Gaussians retain interface contributions in geometry compositing while modeling transmission and sparse reflection in RGB, supported by transparency-aware geometric constraints. To manage the different primitive-visibility requirements of these compositors, we introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by multi-view geometry or RGB reconstruction evidence. On 3D-FRONT-T, ClearForm achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance (CD) and 0.928 F1, compared with 59.18 mm CD for our PGSR reproduction and the reported 34 mm CD and 0.836 F1 for GLINT. On TransLab, it achieves 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR. In matched ablations, dual-opacity compositing reduces CD from 59.25 to 27.09 mm, while DEL improves PSNR by 2.06 dB. Our project page is available at https://hajeongx.github.io/clearform/.
bullets: Identifies the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma, where transparency can reveal backgrounds but weaken geometric learning of glass surfaces.
Uses shared planar Gaussians with dual-opacity compositing: interface support is preserved for geometry, while transmission and sparse reflection are modeled in RGB.
Introduces transparency-aware geometric constraints and Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL) to retain primitives supported by either multi-view geometry or RGB evidence.
Achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance and 0.928 F1 on 3D-FRONT-T, and 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR on TransLab.
Matched ablations show dual-opacity greatly reduces CD, while DEL improves PSNR; the method targets transparent-interface reconstruction with shared planar structure.

Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL) uses visibility in geometric rendering and estimated RGB-loss changes across distinct recently sampled camera views to guide primitive survival.

papers.selection_reason: Joint 3D reconstruction of transparent and opaque scenes using shared-surface Gaussian splatting and dual-opacity compositing.
papers.title: ClearForm: Shared-Surface Gaussian Splatting for Transparent and Opaque Scenes
papers.tldr: ClearForm reconstructs transparent interfaces and the scenes behind them by decoupling geometry-preserving opacity from appearance compositing in Gaussian splatting.

papers.abstract: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.

papers.abstract: Accurate indoor localization on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to the tension between modeling fidelity and computational efficiency. Wi-Fi Channel State Information (CSI) enables low-cost deployment using existing Wi-Fi infrastructure but is heavily distorted by multipath propagation. Transformer-based solutions mitigate these effects but their quadratic complexity limits real-time edge deployment. Ultra-Wideband (UWB) provides geometrically precise ranging yet requires dedicated infrastructure. We present MambaLoc, a cross-modal distillation framework that improves the accuracy-efficiency balance in CSI-based localization. MambaLoc uses a linear-time Selective State Space Model (Mamba) as a lightweight CSI student, guided during training by a UWB-Transformer teacher. A Feature Alignment Module bridges the representational gap between heterogeneous RF modalities, allowing the CSI model to inherit UWB-derived geometric structure without UWB hardware at inference. A probabilistic Gaussian Mixture regression head models multi-modal spatial ambiguity from multipath effects, avoiding the physically implausible averaging of deterministic regression. Evaluations on a real-world dataset show MambaLoc achieves a median localization error of 0.230 m, reducing error by 22.2% over a standalone Mamba baseline, while requiring 65.1% fewer FLOPs and 58% lower inference latency than Transformer-based approaches.
bullets: Targets real-time indoor localization on resource-constrained edge devices using existing Wi-Fi infrastructure.
Uses a linear-time Mamba CSI student trained with a UWB-Transformer teacher, plus feature alignment across RF modalities.
Employs a Gaussian Mixture regression head to represent multi-modal position uncertainty caused by multipath effects.
On a real-world dataset, reaches 0.230 m median error and improves over a standalone Mamba baseline while reducing computation and latency versus Transformer approaches.

papers.abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.
bullets: Targets whole-page generation where every store and item must be catalog-valid, eligible for the request, non-repeated, and correctly nested.
Uses depth-first trie leaf numbering to reduce changing constraints to range lookups over store and item tries.
Validates every generated page independently against the catalog.
A direct GPU trie-walking implementation costs about 5× unconstrained decoding per token; profiling attributes the slowdown mainly to kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization.

A CPU trie-walking implementation overlapping GPU model execution reduces this to about 1.7× unconstrained cost, a 65.9% improvement over the direct GPU version, and also handles item-before-store layouts fastest.

figures.caption: Figure 1. From a ranking pipeline to one decode. (a) The pipeline ranks candidates, then applies the rules. (b) One decode writes the page and checks the same rules at every token.

Figure 2. Where the constraint sits in the page decoder. One decode step. Everything that decides what goes into the mask is the constraint. The trie walk can execute on either side of the boundary between the CPU and the GPU. The three inputs at the bottom carry their sizes in our benchmark and how often each changes. In the full CPU stack (Section 5.5), the constraint box sends a short list of legal tokens, and the GPU applies it to the logits.
Figure 4. One decode step, four ways to build the mask. Schematic, with three groups of two prefix tokens each. Each panel title names the implementation and how it launches (Appendix K).

Figure 3. The structures, on a five-leaf trie. Panel A numbers the leaves depth first, so the leaves under any node form one range, which the node stores as node_lo and node_hi. Panel B shows how we store the trie: per-node arrays hold each node’s leaf range and offsets, and per-edge arrays hold each edge’s token and child node. Node v’s children are edges offsets[v] to offsets[v + 1] - 1, one slice. Panel C runs the legal-child test at the root for a request whose eligible leaves are 1, 2 and 4, on a page that has already used 1 and 2. The test refuses prefix a: the request can reach it, but every eligible leaf under it is already blocked.

Figure 5. The legal set is assembled per request and then narrowed per token. The map cell selects the eligible store set through the map-cell-to-store index. The blocked set then removes what the page has already used. An ahead-of-time compile would need to fix both of these, but only the first one is fixed when the request arrives.

Figure 7. How the request’s filters reach the legal child test. Each filter is a sorted array of leaf ids. For an outer slot the eligible array comes from the map-cell-to-store index and the blocked array from the stores already on the page, each widened to its chain; for an inner slot the eligible array is the chosen store’s menu and the blocked array the items already in its carousel. The test is the one of Figure 3.

Figure 8. Padded or ragged child expansion. Both layouts store the same compressed sparse row arrays; they differ in how a group’s child lists are expanded when its mask is built. (A) Padded gives every row the width of the widest node, a fixed 8,192 slots on the real tries, so the shape is known in advance and the GPU needs no read-back. (B) Ragged lists only the real children, but its length must be read on the CPU before the list can be allocated, which on the GPU is a read-back once per group per step. (C) Each layout suits one placement, which is the interaction of Table 3.

Figure 10. Two things the decoder does not recompute every token. (A) The blocked set changes only when a slot closes, so the memo keeps it per row and adds each new slot, instead of expanding every filled slot to its chain and sorting on every step. (B) Each row keeps its position in the trie, so a step advances one edge; the ablation replays the whole page prefix every step, and its cost grows with page length (Table 16).

Figure 9. Inner subtrie compaction. When a store’s carousel opens, the decoder builds a trie over only that store’s menu and renumbers its leaves from zero, then walks the small trie for the rest of the carousel. Every leaf of the small trie is on the menu, so counting eligible leaves in a node’s range becomes a subtraction instead of two binary searches per child edge. Outer subtrie compaction does the same over the stores of the request’s map cell; it had no significant effect on the GPU, and on the CPU it never ran in the same round as its base, so we cannot separate it from the base. With it, the CPU trie is 16.7 percent faster than the control at light load and 55.1 percent faster when saturated (Table 4).

Figure 11. The full CPU stack: three changes on top of the CPU recipe. Schematic. (A) The overlap walks every group before the first copy, so the walks run under the forward pass and the step no longer waits for them. (B) The tensor trie re-walks the current identifier’s few prefix tokens from the trie root on every query; the page prefix is incremental in both, so this is not the ablation of Figure 10(B). The numpy trie runs the same steps from a cached state, slicing the child edges instead of expanding them, as numpy calls at about 1 microsecond each instead of about 10 by our estimate of dispatch overhead, and returns a short list of allowed ids instead of a vocabulary wide mask. Filled boxes mark the steps that differ. (C) The batched write sends every group’s rows in one pinned copy and a fixed set of kernels per step. None changes which tokens are allowed; together they take the CPU recipe’s 20.1 percent at light load to 65.9 percent (Tables 4, 9 and 17).

Figure 6. Where the three axes act on a decode step. Placement and layout change how the child list is read. Launch structure changes how many times the mask work is handed to the GPU. Each acts on one or both of the two stages that run once per group (the brackets mark which), which is why none of them changes the arithmetic.

papers.title: LEGIT: Live Eligibility Gating over Identifier Tries for Constrained Decoding of Heterogeneous Pages

papers.abstract: Domain adaptive point cloud completion (DA PCC) aims to bridge the geometric discrepancy between labeled source domains and unlabeled target domains for accurate 3D shape completion. Existing methods based on CNNs, Transformers, and Mamba-like sequence models still face challenges from limited receptive fields, high computational complexity, insufficient geometric bias, and serialization sensitivity. Recently, Receptance Weighted Key Value (RWKV) provides a linear-complexity alternative for long-range sequence modeling. However, adapting RWKV to DA PCC remains challenging due to the lack of explicit geometric priors, the mismatch between recurrent modeling and coarse-to-fine generation, and unstable target-domain adaptation. To address these challenges, we propose DAPointRWKV, a novel RWKV-based framework for DA PCC. DAPointRWKV consists of three components: Geometry-Aware RWKV (GA-RWKV) Backbone, RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder (RWKV-PD), and Dual Structural Regularization (DSR). Specifically, GA-RWKV introduces geometry-aware recurrent representation learning, RWKV-PD bridges RWKV token representations with coarse-to-fine reconstruction through local token-guided refinement, and DSR stabilizes target-domain transfer through visible-structure anchoring and complete-shape hypothesis stabilization. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that DAPointRWKV consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
bullets: Targets the geometric gap between labeled source and unlabeled target domains in 3D shape completion.
Introduces a Geometry-Aware RWKV backbone for recurrent geometric representation learning.
Uses an RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder to support coarse-to-fine reconstruction with local token-guided refinement.
Applies Dual Structural Regularization to anchor visible structures and stabilize complete-shape hypotheses during target adaptation.
Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing methods.

(b) The RWKV-Oriented Progressive Decoder is proposed to convert RWKV features into progressively refined point sets through coarse-to-fine reconstruction with local token-guided refinement. (c) Dual Structural Regularization is presented to regularize target-domain completion by enforcing observation anchoring and hypothesis stabilization.

papers.abstract: Recommender systems are transitioning from static retrieval engines into interactive assistants grounded in physical environments. However, current studies largely neglect the combined complexities of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction. To bridge this gap, we introduce SituRecBench, an interactive benchmark for evaluating frontier vision-language models (VLMs) as situated recommendation assistants within high-fidelity 3D environments. We reformulate recommendation as a situated assistance process in which an assistant interacts with a user while sharing the user's egocentric view. Our benchmark simulates real-world shopping environments (e.g., supermarkets and home furnishings stores), requiring assistants to elicit preferences, ground recommendations in the environment, and guide the user to relevant locations through dialogue. The benchmark evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness through a unified interactive protocol. Extensive experiments reveal persistent challenges in spatial grounding and preference elicitation, highlighting limitations in their ability to integrate global contextual information with local observations. SituRecBench provides a rigorous foundation for advancing the development of situated assistants in the real world.
bullets: Targets the combined challenges of spatial navigation, visual grounding, and multi-turn social interaction.
Uses high-fidelity 3D shopping environments, including supermarkets and home-furnishing stores.
Assistants must elicit preferences, recommend visible or nearby items, and guide users through dialogue.
Evaluates dialogue quality, recommendation utility, and navigation effectiveness with one interactive protocol.
Experiments expose persistent weaknesses in spatial grounding and integrating global context with local observations.

papers.abstract: Pose awareness characterizes the extent to which a learned feature space aligns with the underlying object-pose manifold, such that observations with similar poses exhibit greater feature similarity than those with increasingly different poses. While such structure is desirable for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks, visual foundation models pre-trained on individual 2D images typically lack explicit 3D or pose supervision. This raises a fundamental question: Do 2D visual foundation models exhibit pose awareness after large-scale pretraining? To answer this question, we introduce PoseBench, a systematic benchmark to probe pose awareness in pretrained visual features. Our evaluation follows a progressive design: held-out rendered views probe intrinsic pose-aware structure under controlled conditions, while real-image queries evaluate how robustly this structure remains accessible under real-world variations. We further introduce pose-graph-based refinement as a complementary probe of compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold. Across 31 publicly available checkpoints from 10 pretraining families, PoseBench reveals that pose awareness is an implicit but non-uniform property of 2D visual foundation models, and consistent gains from pose-graph refinement suggest that feature spaces retain structure compatible with the underlying pose manifold. PoseBench therefore provides a systematic basis for understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D vision tasks.
bullets: Benchmarks pose awareness through progressively harder probes, from controlled rendered views to real-image queries.
Introduces pose-graph refinement to test compatibility between feature neighborhoods and the underlying pose manifold.
Evaluates 31 publicly available checkpoints spanning 10 pretraining families.
Finds pose awareness is present but varies across models, while refinement consistently reveals additional pose-compatible structure.
Supports understanding and selecting pretrained features for pose-sensitive 3D tasks.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) show strong visual perception capabilities, but existing evaluations largely focus on single-view or multi-view settings with shared camera parameters, leaving the challenge of multi-agent collaborative scenarios underexplored. In such settings, multiple agents observe a shared environment from independent viewpoints, and reliable decisions require reasoning across these independent observations of the same environment. To study this problem, we introduce MaRiO, a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent collaborative reasoning, and evaluate 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs on it. Our analysis reveals three key findings: (1) tasks governed by static perception are generally easier than tasks that require transformational event sequences; (2) most models struggle to resolve cross-agent correspondences, with errors increasing with scene complexity; and (3) models show limited ability to leverage geometric cues present in the scene. As an initial step toward addressing these challenges, we explore geometry-guided synthetic view augmentation that generates intermediate transition frames between agent observations, providing auxiliary spatial context that improves performance in certain categories. Overall, our results highlight that multi-agent collaborative reasoning remains an open challenge and an important direction for multimodal embodied systems. The code is available on the project page: https://omarftt.github.io/MaRiO-page/.
bullets: Introduces MaRiO, a benchmark for multi-agent collaborative reasoning in shared environments.
Evaluates 23 state-of-the-art MLLMs across tasks involving independent agent observations.
Static-perception tasks are easier than tasks requiring reasoning over transformational event sequences.
Models struggle more as scene complexity increases and make limited use of geometric cues.
Geometry-guided synthetic intermediate views improve performance in certain categories, but the problem remains open.

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies based on diffusion and flow matching can model complex, multimodal behaviors, but remain susceptible to covariate shift during closed-loop execution. Existing approaches mitigate such failures through additional demonstrations, policy fine-tuning, or test-time guidance, but often require human intervention, engineered rewards, or other task-specific signals. We introduce GUARD, an anomaly-informed Q-steering framework that leverages the policy's training distribution to construct a dense, failure-anticipatory steering signal. GUARD pairs sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores learned from policy training data and propagates both through a learned Q-function. Its gradients then steer the denoising process toward actions that improve task return while preventing trajectories from entering poorly supported regions, without directly modifying the pretrained policy. Across four Adroit dexterous manipulation tasks, GUARD achieves average success rates of $96.0\%$ and $80.0\%$ under nominal and perturbed dynamics, outperforming the strongest baseline by $21.0$ and $20.0$ percentage points while maintaining the lowest anomaly score. GUARD further demonstrates direct sim-to-real transfer on in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation tasks, achieving $40$ and $25$ percentage-point gains in success rate. These results demonstrate that anomaly signals can serve not only for failure monitoring but also to complement sparse task rewards as effective supervision for robust policy steering.
bullets: Addresses covariate-shift failures in diffusion and flow-matching policies without extra demonstrations, fine-tuning, human intervention, or engineered task-specific signals.
Combines sparse task rewards with dense anomaly scores derived from the policy’s training distribution.
Propagates both signals through a learned Q-function and uses its gradients to guide the denoising process without modifying the pretrained policy.
Across four Adroit tasks, achieves 96.0% nominal and 80.0% perturbed-dynamics success, with the lowest anomaly score and gains over the strongest baseline.
Transfers directly to real in-hand screwdriver rotation and reorientation, improving success rates by 40 and 25 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Feature caching accelerates Diffusion Transformers by reusing intermediate computations across denoising timesteps, yet existing methods share a fundamental blind spot: they treat the standard reference denoising trajectory as the optimisation target, approximating its per-step states and thus inheriting its output as an implicit quality ceiling. We argue that this target is arbitrary -- what truly matters is the ideal result, not the intermediate path taken to reach it. We propose IdealCache, a training-free framework that abandons step-wise imitation of the reference trajectory. Instead, it anchors caching on a per-input ensemble of ideal trajectories constructed from candidate target results, aggregates their geometry into a single graph, and discovers optimal non-uniform schedules via a constrained shortest path on this graph. By decoupling from the reference process, IdealCache breaks the performance bottleneck of trajectory-approximation; our schedules can attain near-lossless fidelity in generation and even surpass on task-specific metrics (e.g., maintaining higher semantic consistency in image editing). Without retraining, IdealCache achieves 6.35x speedup on Qwen-Image, 5.84x on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32x on HunyuanVideo, with competitive or superior quality across tasks.
bullets: Existing cache schedulers optimize approximation of the reference denoising trajectory, imposing an implicit quality ceiling.
IdealCache constructs per-input ensembles of ideal trajectories from candidate target results and aggregates their geometry into a graph.
A constrained shortest-path search identifies input-specific, non-uniform caching schedules.
The training-free method reports speedups of 6.35× on Qwen-Image, 5.84× on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 4.32× on HunyuanVideo.
It maintains competitive or superior generation quality, including higher semantic consistency for image editing.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based generative modeling has emerged as a general computational framework for simulating high-dimensional, structured data across various domains. Understanding its generative mechanisms is paramount for advancing model training and inference in a principled way. Here, we demonstrate that deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal geometric structure invariant to data modalities and diffusion model implementations. This structure can be largely explained by an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.
bullets: Motivates understanding the mechanisms underlying diffusion-based generative modeling.
Analyzes deterministic sampling trajectories across data modalities and diffusion implementations.
Identifies a universal geometric structure shared across these trajectories.
Explains much of the structure using an exactly solvable model based on the optimal linear denoiser.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Deterministic sampling trajectories share a universal structure across data modalities and diffusion model implementations. (a) Intermediate states along sampling trajectories, from random noise (left) to generated data (right). (b) Each trajectory projected onto its three leading principal components, with all starting points aligned (black point). (c) The trajectories aligned through an orthogonal transformation. Each axis in (b) and (c) is scaled independently to make the small deviation from a straight line visible.
