The bottom row shows the distributions of the shape deviation, measured by the root-mean-square error (RMSE), between two independently initialized real trajectories and between a real trajectory and the Gaussian counterpart of another such trajectory. The table reports the deviation of each reference from the real trajectory before and after the transformation, normalized by the Gaussian chord deviation before the transformation. The Gaussian chord is the straight line from the initial noise to the endpoint of the Gaussian flow, the Brownian bridge is pinned to the same two endpoints, and the isotropic Gaussian flow replaces Σ with the scaled identity (trΣ/d) Id (see the Supplementary material for implementation details).

papers.selection_reason: Universal geometric structure in deterministic diffusion sampling; transferable to video diffusion and generative modeling.
papers.title: On the universal structure in deterministic generative diffusion
papers.tldr: Deterministic diffusion sampling trajectories exhibit a modality- and implementation-invariant geometric structure that can be explained by an exactly solvable optimal-linear-denoiser model.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.
bullets: Addresses streaming video queries whose evidence may occur before, during, or after the current scene.
Stores observed moments as timestamp-indexed structured captions for fine-grained, queryable temporal evidence.
Selects a query-specific strategy: retrieve past evidence, read present context, or defer answering for future observations.
Experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show improved question answering through temporal evidence preservation and strategy selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of TimeTraveler. Incoming video frames are encoded into structured captions and stored in a timestamp-indexed Time Dictionary. Given a query, a Temporal Strategy Planner acquires evidence following temporal intent: past queries retrieve relevant captions through similaritybased lookback, current queries access local captions, and future queries continue observation until evidence appears. Then, the retrieved evidence is used to produce the final answer.

Figure 1: Conceptual comparison between prior memory-based SVU and TimeTraveler. Prior methods preserve streaming history as agentic memory [19], pruned tokens [22], or KV-memory recall [24], but rely on a single evidence-access path and do not ensure that retained evidence remains query-recoverable. In contrast, TimeTraveler plans whether each query should be grounded in the past, current scene, or future, and accesses a structured Time Dictionary accordingly.

The retrieved Time Dictionary caption preserves fine-grained details such as on-screen text (“FRONT RAISE”), spatial layout, and highlighted muscle groups, which are essential for answering correctly.

papers.selection_reason: Streaming video QA with temporal strategy planning and timestamp-indexed evidence; directly targets video-language temporal understanding.
papers.title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.tldr: TimeTraveler improves streaming video QA by planning whether to recall the past, inspect the present, or wait for the future using a timestamped Time Dictionary.

papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can surface passages that support a claim, contradict it, or fail to address it, yet existing calibrated grounding methods are typically one-sided and model only supporting evidence. We introduce Conformal Evidence Sets (CES), a two-sided framework that returns separate support and refutation sets with finite-sample inclusion coverage of at least $1-α$ on each side under exchangeability; a Bonferroni union yields joint coverage of at least $1-2α$. On labeled candidate pools from the contrastive VitaminC benchmark, CES closely tracks nominal coverage across $α\!\in\!\{0.05,0.10,0.15,0.20,0.30\}$, with maximum deviations of $3.0$ percentage points for support and $5.4$ for refutation, and reaches essentially the same empirical coverage--size frontier as a test-tuned fixed-threshold heuristic without any test exposure. Stress tests mark the boundary of that guarantee: under FEVER distribution shift both sides under-cover, by up to $12.7$ percentage points, and support-side group-stratified recalibration substantially reduces the support gap. Scorer swaps, hard-negative retrieval, cross-dataset transfer, and a live end-to-end pilot expose a clear separation: when exchangeability holds and relevant evidence is retrieved, evidence inclusion remains calibrated even with an imperfect scorer, whereas the support/refute verdict tracks scorer quality directly. Calibrated evidence coverage and reliable verdicts are therefore distinct properties and should be reported separately.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of one-sided grounding methods that model only supporting evidence.
Returns separate support and refutation sets with at least 1−α finite-sample inclusion coverage per side; joint coverage is at least 1−2α via Bonferroni.
On VitaminC, empirical coverage closely follows nominal levels, with maximum deviations of 3.0 percentage points for support and 5.4 for refutation.
Under FEVER distribution shift, both sides under-cover by up to 12.7 percentage points; group-stratified support recalibration reduces the gap.
Evidence inclusion can remain calibrated despite imperfect scoring, while support/refute verdict quality depends directly on scorer quality.

papers.selection_reason: Conformal two-sided evidence sets for RAG; calibrated retrieval grounding for LLM external memory.
papers.title: Two-Sided Conformal Evidence Sets for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.tldr: Conformal Evidence Sets provide separately calibrated support and refutation evidence for RAG, with guarantees under exchangeability but degraded coverage under distribution shift.

papers.abstract: Reproducibility is important for LoRA-adapted language models used in repeated evaluation, auditing, and decision-making. However, Split-K kernels used to introduce parallelism in low-rank LoRA multiplications can have the unintended consequence of numerical nondeterminism when partial results are combined using floating-point atomic additions. We investigate this non-determinism in vLLM across GSM8K mathematical reasoning, MBPP code generation, and Jev-style structured toxicity decisions on Civil Comments and introduce a deterministic Triton Split-K implementation. Under identical-input replay, Atomic Split-K=8 produces different FP32 shrink outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while our Deterministic Split-K=8 shows no observed variation. Repeated atomic inference changes generated outputs in 17.30% of GSM8K and 14.96% of MBPP comparisons, sometimes altering task correctness. Structured-decision probabilities vary in 81.47% of atomic comparisons, with decision flips. Controlled tracing demonstrates how shrink-output differences propagate into the KV cache and how accumulated cache differences can change token decisions and final answers. Our deterministic Triton Split-K=8 implementation preserves parallelism, achieving 16.8-21.1% latency-based speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02-2.62% additional latency relative to Atomic Split-K=8.
bullets: Floating-point atomic additions in vLLM’s Split-K LoRA kernels cause nondeterministic outputs under identical-input replay.
Nondeterminism propagates through the KV cache, changing generated answers, task correctness, and structured toxicity decisions.
Atomic Split-K=8 varied FP32 outputs in 97.61% of comparisons, while deterministic Split-K=8 showed no observed variation.
The deterministic implementation achieved a 16.8–21.1% speedup over unsplit reduction with only 1.02–2.62% higher latency than Atomic Split-K=8.
Evaluation covered GSM8K, MBPP, and Civil Comments-based structured toxicity decisions.

papers.title: Reproducible LoRA Inference Through Deterministic Split-K Reduction
papers.tldr: A deterministic Triton Split-K implementation removes LoRA inference variability while retaining most of Split-K’s latency benefit.

papers.abstract: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.
bullets: Derives information-theoretic and Boolean-circuit lower bounds for latent state-transition operations and their CMOS dynamic energy.
Finds that DreamerV3-style RSSM rollouts are memory-bandwidth bound, while GPU energy is reported as far above the CMOS energy floor.
Thermal simulations show sustained planning can overheat a millimeter-scale silicon tile, even with ideal copper heat spreading.
Proposes WMPA with near-memory computation, entropy-aware precision, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads.
A 40× lower-power design target is simulated to keep the tile near ambient temperature, suggesting feasibility for thermally constrained robots.

Fig. 3. Measured sustained GPU energy per planning call (mean of 10 trials, with standard deviation) against the 12nm CMOS dynamic switching floor. The gap is 5.91 × 1010 at H = 20, the headline configuration of Section III-D, and rises to 6.08×1010 at shorter horizons because of a fixed per-call overhead.

papers.selection_reason: Hardware-algorithm co-design for action-conditioned world model planning in robotics, directly fitting interactive world models.
papers.title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
papers.tldr: WMPA is a hardware–algorithm co-design that targets the severe energy, bandwidth, and thermal costs of embedded world-model planning in robots.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) in medical retrieval-augmented generation must be able to say when a retrieved report contradicts the X-ray, so understanding whether they can detect such conflicts is important for safe deployment. The sycophancy mask hypothesis holds that these models internally detect conflicts but refuse to report them, concealing a detected contradiction. We introduce a three-part diagnostic that separates concealment from uncertainty: representation probing, activation steering, and two-way forced choice. Across four instruction-tuned VLMs on chest X-rays, we confirm behavioral suppression of contradiction and find that a linear probe separates matched from mismatched inputs, beyond what a simple CLIP model achieves. Steering the learned conflict direction never elicits contradiction, and forcing a binary choice does not recover one; instead, cross-modal attention to the image drops on mismatched pairs. We conclude that these models fail to contradict because the mismatch registers as hedged, gated uncertainty rather than concealed knowledge, calling for re-grounding and uncertainty surfacing. Code is available at https://github.com/mohamed-eldagla/Uncertainty-Not-Concealment/.
bullets: The study examines whether VLMs can detect when retrieved reports conflict with chest X-rays.
A three-part diagnostic combines representation probing, activation steering, and forced-choice testing.
Across four instruction-tuned VLMs, probes distinguish matched from mismatched inputs, but steering and forced choice do not elicit contradiction.
Mismatched pairs reduce cross-modal attention to the image, supporting an uncertainty-based explanation of sycophancy.
The findings motivate re-grounding and explicit uncertainty surfacing for safer deployment.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The diagnostic framework. A single observation (internal signal present, behavioral CONTRADICTS absent) is ambiguous between concealment (H1) and uncertainty (H2). Three tests (steering, forced choice, and cross-modal attention) disambiguate them; in every case the observation matches H2.
Figure 2: Activation steering (InternVL2-8B): robust CONTRADICTS stays at 0% at every α; SUPPORTS falls from 89.8% to 83.1% while INCONCLUSIVE rises from 8.5% to 16.9%; INVALID remains 0–3.4%.
Table 2: CLS probe AUC for C0 vs C2+C3 (mean ± std over 5 folds); C4 excluded.
Table 1: Behavioral verdicts (%) by condition, robust first-verdict parsing with multi-label outputs labeled INVALID. CONTRADICTS is 0% everywhere.

papers.selection_reason: Mechanistic study of sycophancy and uncertainty in medical VLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM behavior.
papers.title: Uncertainty, Not Concealment: A Mechanistic Reappraisal of Sycophancy in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Vision-language models appear to avoid contradicting conflicting medical reports because mismatches trigger gated uncertainty, not concealed knowledge.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for resource management across the Cloud-Edge continuum. However, embedding LLMs directly inside latency-sensitive control loops places inference latency, execution jitter, and hallucination risks on the critical path. This study argues for a different use of LLMs: a continually instruction-tuned intent compiler that runs once per management intent or declared context change, above a fast, deterministic tactical controller that handles all low-latency runtime actions. We formulate intent compilation as a continual instruction tuning problem, because management intents arrive sequentially and accumulate while infrastructure and workload contexts drift. Unlike recent LLM-based management frameworks, our design scores the model's outputs by execution, so that catastrophic forgetting can be measured in the executed objective of the underlying controller. On a continuum simulator with a 2B backbone and parameter-efficient adapters, preliminary results show that naive sequential tuning forgets earlier intents in the executed objective, that replay of stored examples nearly prevents this forgetting, and that the tuned compact compiler performs on par with simpler translators while being more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/lilanpei/continuum-intent-compiler.
bullets: LLMs are kept out of critical control loops to avoid inference latency, jitter, and hallucination risks.
The LLM runs once per intent or context change, translating intent into actions for a fast tactical controller.
Sequential tuning is evaluated through the controller’s executed objective, exposing catastrophic forgetting of earlier intents.
Replay of stored examples nearly prevents forgetting in preliminary continuum-simulator experiments.
The compact compiler matches simpler translators and is more robust than a grammar parser to rephrased intents.

Top: the outer loop, in which the compiler, tuned offline on the update batch, turns an intent and its context into (?̂?, ?̂? ) and the validation gate admits them to the tactical controller or rejects them. Bottom: the inner loop, in which the tactical controller acts at every epoch on the continuum simulator. Measured outcomes return only to the offline adapter update. Dashed arrows depict exchanges that happen only during offline label search.

Table 3: The tuned compiler against the translation baselines on the Stream I test set. Each entry is the mean gap (4) over the test intents (lower is better).

papers.selection_reason: Continual instruction tuning with replay to prevent catastrophic forgetting; directly relevant to continual/online learning.
papers.title: Continual Instruction Tuning for LLM-based Management of Continuum Resources
papers.tldr: A continually instruction-tuned LLM can compile management intents for Cloud–Edge resources while a deterministic controller handles latency-sensitive execution, with replay reducing forgetting and improving robustness to rephrased intents.

papers.abstract: While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have improved automated radiology report generation, they remain prone to hallucinations, necessitating clinically meaningful risk-control methods. Conformal prediction (CP) provides statistical guarantees, yet existing CP approaches rely on uncalibrated automated extractors and fail to account for the clinical relevance of errors. We introduce clinical admissibility criteria (CLARITY), a framework for evaluating radiology reports that explicitly distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor deviations. To eliminate reliance on automatic judges, we collected radiologist annotations of MLLM-generated reports using CLARITY. By benchmarking CP strategies and automatic evaluation metrics against these expert annotations, we demonstrate that commonly used admissibility proxies systematically fail to detect clinically relevant errors. Our findings reveal that automated admissibility judgments are largely decoupled from true clinical admissibility.
bullets: MLLM-generated radiology reports can hallucinate, creating a need for clinically meaningful risk control.
The framework distinguishes clinically consequential errors from minor report deviations.
Radiologists annotated generated reports using the CLARITY criteria, avoiding reliance on automated judges.
Benchmarking shows common CP strategies and automatic metrics fail to reliably identify clinically relevant errors.
Automated admissibility judgments are largely disconnected from true clinical admissibility.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Qualitative comparison of admissibility assessments. Reference-based automatic assessment maps a candidate and reference report to clinical labels and then compares those labels. This procedure can penalize a correct finding that was omitted from the reference and treats discrepancies equally without accounting for their clinical consequence. CLARITY instead uses image-grounded radiologist judgments of both relevance and accuracy. The labels and arrows, rather than color alone, distinguish the assessment pathways.

Figure 2: Comparison of CheXbert and CLARITY. Distribution of CheXbert positive-label F1 scores for 970 generated reports from 97 studies, grouped by radiologist-assessed CLARITY admissibility. Points show individual reports.

Table 1: Association of automatic metrics with CLARITY. Spearman correlations are computed after study-level averaging; 95% confidence intervals use 2,000 study-cluster bootstrap samples and two-sided P values use Holm correction across 14 metric variants. RadCliQ scores are sign-inverted so higher values consistently indicate better reports. The sample-size column gives studies/reports after metric-specific exclusion of undefined values.

Table 2: Empirical coverage and prediction-set size for conformal miscoverage α = 0.30. The fixed disjoint CheXbert-to-CLARITY evaluation uses the primary F1 threshold of 0.4 and reports one run.

papers.selection_reason: Evaluates conformal prediction for MLLM radiology report generation; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reliability.
papers.title: A Clinical Evaluation of Conformal Prediction for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
papers.tldr: CLARITY uses radiologist annotations to evaluate conformal prediction for chest radiograph report generation and shows that automated admissibility proxies often miss clinically consequential errors.

papers.abstract: A robot that keeps learning after deployment is corrected by several people in turn, and one of them may later ask to be removed. We show that whether the robot can forget that person depends on how people correct it. The goal of removal is the robot that would exist if the person had never been there, which we compute exactly in two simulated tasks with scripted users. When users correct the robot by taking over control, an ordered log of training updates is enough: retraining on the remaining sessions in their original order gives a robot as close to the goal as training noise allows. Deleting the person's data and retraining in one pass does not, even when the other users' corrections do not depend on the removed person, because it loses the order of training. When users only nudge the robot's action, the other users' corrections carry the removed person's influence, and no method we tested recovers the goal robot. Continuing to train without the person removes most of their habits, but not what their data in the training buffer keep alive. The log can identify one clearly harmful user, but not rank users by influence better than counting their corrections.
bullets: The target is the robot that would have resulted had the removed user never provided corrections.
For takeover-style corrections, replaying the remaining sessions in their original order nearly recovers this target; one-pass retraining after deletion does not.
For action-nudge corrections, other users’ updates can preserve the removed user’s influence, and tested removal methods fail to recover the target.
Continued training without the user removes many habits but cannot erase influence retained in the training buffer.
The correction log can identify a clearly harmful user, but does not rank user influence better than simply counting corrections.

papers.selection_reason: Online robot policy learning and forgetting user corrections; directly relevant to robot learning and continual/online learning.
papers.title: Who Taught the Robot That? Removing One User's Corrections from a Robot Policy That Learns Online
papers.tldr: Removing one person’s influence from an online-learning robot depends strongly on how corrections are provided and how training history is retained.

papers.abstract: Deepfake videos generated by advanced generative models pose serious threats to digital security, misinformation control, and media forensics. Although numerous detection methods have been proposed, their reported performances are often based on heterogeneous preprocessing pipelines, inconsistent data splits, and model-specific training protocols, hindering fair architectural comparison. This work presents a controlled and reproducible comparative study of convolutional neural networks (ResNet-18 and EfficientNet-B0) and a transformer-based architecture (ViT-B/16) within a unified, face-centric deepfake detection framework. All models are trained using identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization settings, and data splits on Celeb-DF v2 and FaceForensics++, and results are validated across three independent random seeds with bootstrapped confidence intervals. Experimental results show that while CNN-based models perform competitively at the frame level, their performance degrades after video-level aggregation. In contrast, ViT-B/16 demonstrates more stable video-level performance, achieving 92.8\% [95\% CI: 91.7--94.0] video-level accuracy and an AUC of 0.950 [95\% CI: 0.934--0.964] on Celeb-DF v2 (3-seed bootstrapped). Cross-dataset evaluation across the same three random seeds reveals a large, asymmetric generalization gap (AUC 0.79 FF++$\rightarrow$Celeb-DF vs. 0.64 Celeb-DF$\rightarrow$FF++), indicating that in-domain video-level stability does not transfer to unseen manipulation domains. These findings indicate that global self-attention improves robustness and video-level stability for deepfake detection within a given data domain, while highlighting the need for further work on cross-domain generalization.
bullets: CNNs perform competitively at the frame level but degrade after video-level aggregation.
ViT-B/16 achieves 92.8% video-level accuracy and 0.950 AUC on Celeb-DF v2, with bootstrapped confidence intervals across three seeds.
The study uses a unified face-centric pipeline with identical preprocessing, augmentation, optimization, splits, and evaluation across ResNet-18, EfficientNet-B0, and ViT-B/16.
Cross-dataset performance shows an asymmetric generalization gap: AUC 0.79 from FaceForensics++ to Celeb-DF versus 0.64 in the reverse direction.
Results support improved in-domain stability from global self-attention, while emphasizing limited cross-domain robustness.

papers.selection_reason: Video-level deepfake detection and temporal aggregation analysis fit video understanding and temporal video representation.
papers.title: Beyond Frame-Level Accuracy: Analyzing Video-Level Stability in Transformer-Based Deepfake Forensics
papers.tldr: A controlled comparison finds that ViT-B/16 provides more stable video-level deepfake detection than CNNs in-domain, but this stability transfers poorly across unseen manipulation domains.

papers.abstract: Computer vision (CV) for policing has centred on recognising objects such as seized weapons, while body-worn video (BWV) is still reviewed by people, with existing AI tools using only its audio. Multimodal video AI could make BWV review faster and cheaper. At the object level, we present the KnifeHunter dataset, developed with UK law enforcement, with over 25,000 images of 543 knife classes and a protocol reflecting investigative conditions, and KHNet, a retrieval architecture fusing local and global features, which with about 125,000 distractor images attains 85.7% and 63.4% mean Average Precision (mAP) on the medium and hard protocols. At the event level, we present an evaluation protocol for video understanding pipelines, which describe a video as events and a transcript, that scores transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation and unsupported events. Whether each event is supported by the recording is labelled by a judge validated against blinded human labels. We apply it to complete pipelines, three 2026 omni-modal models and our hybrid NarrativeBridge-PAL-GPT-5 pipeline, on UKBWV-27, a pilot stress-test set of 27 publicly released UK BWV recordings (118 minutes). On this set the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures, yet it leaves 13.6% of predicted events unsupported and misattributes 27.7% of utterances, and every pipeline degrades on recordings from edited releases, long recordings and noisy audio. We propose readiness levels separating assistive tasks from those requiring verification of every output.
bullets: Introduces KnifeHunter, a law-enforcement-developed dataset with over 25,000 images across 543 knife classes and investigative evaluation protocols.
Presents KHNet, which fuses local and global visual features for knife retrieval, achieving 85.7% mAP on the medium protocol and 63.4% on the hard protocol.
Proposes an event-level evaluation framework covering transcription, speaker attribution, event detection, temporal localisation, and evidential support.
On 27 UK body-worn-video recordings, the hybrid pipeline leads on five of six measures but produces 13.6% unsupported events and misattributes 27.7% of utterances.
Performance declines for edited releases, long recordings, and noisy audio; the paper recommends readiness levels distinguishing assistive uses from outputs requiring verification.

papers.selection_reason: Multimodal video understanding pipelines for event detection, temporal localization, and transcription fit video understanding.
papers.title: From Weapons to Events: Evaluating Evidential Support in Multimodal AI for Policing
papers.tldr: The paper evaluates multimodal AI for policing at both knife-image retrieval and body-worn-video event understanding, finding promising performance but substantial unsupported events and attribution errors that require human verification.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D reconstruction turns an uncalibrated monocular stream into a dense point cloud in a single inference pass, orders of magnitude faster than classical structure-from-motion (e.g., COLMAP), and reliable on the weakly textured, repetitive surfaces where keypoint matching fails outright. However, raw point clouds lack the object identity, physical properties, and watertight volume required for robot learning. This gap widens under robot-native capture. A camera mounted on a robot constrained to a few degrees of freedom sees each object only partially, and the repetitive, weakly textured structure of an office makes distinct workstations nearly indistinguishable, leaving redundant and partial observations that downstream reconstruction cannot resolve. Existing image-to-3D generation methods struggle with these conditions, hallucinating geometry under incomplete views and confusing repeated instances. We present OfficeTwin, a robot-native framework that converts these incomplete observations into simulation-ready digital twins. OfficeTwin first imposes metric and structural constraints, then exploits the office's structural redundancy by registering repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame, where complementary observations recover geometry occluded in any single view without hallucination. On a real office scan, OfficeTwin recovers every cubicle as an individually watertight, metric solid, outperforming feed-forward reconstruction and generative baselines that fail to produce simulation-ready assets.
bullets: Addresses incomplete, weakly textured, and redundant office observations from cameras with limited robot motion.
Imposes metric and structural constraints before reconstruction.
Registers repeated cubicles into a shared canonical frame to recover occluded geometry without hallucination.
Produces individually watertight, simulation-ready cubicle models on a real office scan.
Outperforms feed-forward and generative reconstruction baselines that fail to create simulation-ready assets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the OfficeTwin pipeline, converting RGB frames of a redundant office into a watertight, metrically scaled Manhattan digital twin in five phases: (1) VLM-based metric scaling; (2) gravity-aligned structural parsing and cubicle identification; (3) wall-bounded 3D SAM3 instance growth; (4) canonical cross-instance registration for occlusion completion; and (5) consensus denoising and Manhattan solid fitting.

Figure 5: Ablation of key designs: failure (left, red) vs full pipeline (right, green). P2: raw C-shaped cut leaks 3D growth, inflating cubicles (5.80×4.90m vs 1.81×2.42m). P4: vanilla ICP is distracted by cabinet planes (spread 0.137m vs 0.044m on pose faces). P5: alpha-shapes leave open edges (66 vs 0). Removing any step breaks the twin.

Figure 3: Single-cubicle reconstruction from a partial view (top) and a redundant multi-cubicle frame (bottom). Left to right: feed-forward reconstruction with Poisson surfacing (purple; ceiling removed), single-image generative reconstruction (blue), and OfficeTwin (green). Red boxes mark the SAM3D failures analysed in Sec. 4.2

Figure 2: Full-scene reconstruction (ceiling removed). From left: TSDF fusion yields an inseparable hole-riddled mesh and structureless Poisson surface; Pi-Long/VGGT-Long yields a scale-ambiguous cloud; OfficeTwin recovers 23 individual, watertight metric solids instead of one fused mass.

Figure 4: Phase 2 topology extraction. (a) Gravity-aligned cloud (ceiling removed). (b) Near-vertical points (wall candidates). (c) Manhattan plane fitting extracts wall skeletons. (d) Walls classified as partitions (orange) or back walls (blue). (e) Cutting desk planes with walls isolates 23 trajectory-independent cubicles (green regions, red centers).

Table 2: Redundancy consistency evaluation. Repeated cubicles act as mutual references: cross-instance corroboration lifts surface coverage from 21.0% to 68.6%, yielding 23/23 watertight instances without ground-truth meshes.

papers.selection_reason: Robot-native 3D reconstruction of redundant scenes is relevant to embodied perception and 3D scene understanding for robot learning.
papers.title: OfficeTwin: Realizing 3D Reconstruction of Redundant Scenes through Partial Viewpoint Perception
papers.tldr: OfficeTwin turns partial, repetitive robot-captured office views into watertight, metric 3D digital twins by aligning repeated cubicles and combining their complementary observations.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents accumulate sessions of up to millions of tokens, far more key-value (KV) cache than one GPU holds, so serving systems keep a small budget of tokens and evict the rest. Eviction methods differ in which tokens they keep but share one goal: that the tokens a later step needs are still cached. We show this is not enough. In 100K-token coding sessions on Qwen3-8B with a 2,048-token budget, a planner-guided policy that keeps over 99% of the needed tokens resident still fails late steps increasingly often: its accuracy falls from 93% to 64% as the gap between a definition and its use grows from 2K to 90K tokens, at residency 0.996. The needed tokens are resident but unretrievable: what grows is their rotary-position distance to the query. We present PACE (Planner-Aware Context Engine), a KV-cache engine that couples plan-aware retention, in which the agent's planner tells the cache which context future steps will read, with bounded positions, which renumber kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below 8K at any session length. In a pre-registered evaluation on fresh tasks, PACE passes 97% of hidden unit tests at 100K tokens, against 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV under the same budget, and needs both components: either alone reaches 63% (the combination beats each, p < 10^-4). The result holds with length: in 1M- and 2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with definitions written 0.9M and 1.8M tokens before use, PACE passes 99% and 100% of checks and recalls every session fact, while bounded positions without foresight falls from 33% to 13%; PACE holds under 0.7 GB of KV state where the full cache would need 147-295 GB. Renumbering is exact, costs no measurable perplexity, and adds 9% wall time. On Mistral-7B, whose coding ability caps it at 40% even with nothing evicted, PACE stays at that ceiling while retention alone falls below it.
bullets: Long sessions can exceed one GPU’s KV-cache capacity, requiring aggressive token eviction.
Even when over 99% of later-needed tokens remain cached, accuracy drops as their rotary-position distance from the query grows.
PACE uses the agent’s plan to retain future-relevant context and bounds rotary distances by renumbering retained tokens.
On 100K-token Qwen3-8B coding tasks with a 2,048-token budget, PACE passes 97% of hidden-unit tests versus 42% for H2O and 3% for SnapKV.
The method scales to 1M–2M-token sessions on one 24 GB GPU, with 9% added wall time and no measurable perplexity cost.

figures.caption: Figure 2: PACE inside the engine’s KV-cache manager. The planner’s dependency graph becomes a per-span foresight bonus that decides which tokens stay; bounded positions renumber the kept tokens so their rotary distance to the query stays below L; persistent sessions carry the cache across steps; evicted context is tiered and restored when the plan needs it.

Figure 1: Keeping the right tokens is not enough. 100K-token coding sessions, Qwen3-8B, KV budget 2,048 tokens. papers.selection_reason: KV-cache engine for long-horizon LLM agents directly targets cache memory efficiency, token retention, and long-context processing.
papers.title: PACE: Keeping the Right Tokens in the KV Cache Is Not Enough for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
papers.tldr: PACE shows that retaining the right KV-cache tokens is insufficient for long-horizon agents unless their positional distance remains retrievable, and combines plan-aware retention with position renumbering to preserve long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Geometric foundation models estimate dense geometry and camera parameters from monocular images, but reliable SLAM also requires consistent scale and accurate data association across successive reconstructions. We present DASH-SLAM, a monocular SLAM system that integrates metric depth predictions from pretrained Depth Anything 3 into a shared-keyframe pose graph without task-specific fine-tuning. DASH-SLAM derives scale corrections from depth ratios at shared anchor images and accumulates them across reconstructions, with a damping factor controlling their influence. These corrections rescale odometry translations, loop constraints, and map geometry. Experiments on TUM, Replica, and 7-Scenes show that DASH-SLAM outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We evaluate performance using both rigid and similarity alignment to distinguish metric-scale fidelity from accuracy up to scale. We further evaluate DASH-SLAM on four challenging sequences in perceptually-degraded environments from the Unified Autonomy Stack field dataset, covering tunnels, fog, and a frozen lake. On these sequences, DASH-SLAM outperforms the foundation-model SLAM state-of-the-art and maintains tracking where classical SLAM methods fail.
bullets: Addresses inconsistent scale and data association across monocular reconstructions.
Uses metric depth from pretrained Depth Anything 3 without task-specific fine-tuning.
Estimates scale corrections from depth ratios at shared anchor images and accumulates them with damping.
Rescales odometry translations, loop constraints, and map geometry.
Outperforms state-of-the-art methods on standard benchmarks and challenging tunnel, fog, and frozen-lake sequences, maintaining tracking where classical SLAM fails.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. DASH-SLAM overview. The front end selects keyframes from the incoming image stream, and the inference stage constructs submaps using Depth Anything 3. The back end propagates metric scale across consecutive submaps through their shared anchor frames. The loop-closure thread detects revisited places and passes loop constraints to the back end, which optimises the global pose graph.
Fig. 3. Ground truth and estimated UAS trajectories after Sim(3) and SE(3) alignment. Crosses mark the last ORB-SLAM3 poses before tracking failures.

papers.tldr: DASH-SLAM enables calibration-free metric monocular SLAM by propagating depth-derived scale corrections across shared-keyframe pose graphs.

papers.abstract: Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.
bullets: Compares truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across four long-context benchmarks.
Evaluates evidence recall, token retention, and downstream reader accuracy using the same selected contexts.
Reports strong but task-specific recall: BM25 reaches 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong, while dense retrieval reaches 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval.
At 32K tokens, BM25 obtains 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval obtains 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy.
Finds that evidence-recall rankings do not consistently predict downstream answer accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Directly evaluates context selection under token budgets, fitting token pruning/eviction and long-context efficiency for language models.
papers.title: CoRA-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation by Context Selectors Under Token Budgets

papers.abstract: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.
bullets: Addresses the lack of affordable, flexible, and accessible platforms for agricultural robotics research and education.
Combines four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation.
Uses an end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify framework spanning perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous verification.
Demonstrated lane following, row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop task verification under varied lighting and soil conditions.
Its proof-of-concept scope and reconfigurable architecture support component testing, rapid prototyping, experimentation, and hands-on training.

papers.abstract: A phone screen can be wrong in ways that need no reference: a label that runs off the screen, letters that touch, a line that breaks one character before its end, one button with sharp corners among round ones. We ask whether a model can box every such fault on a screenshot, given no target design and no reference image. Such a critic could serve as a cheap first pass over generated pages before a designer reviews them, but only if it stays silent on clean pages. ScreenProof poses this target-free critique over three families of faults: general faults, local style faults (one element breaks the style its page sets) and text layout faults (letter spacing, line height, line breaks). A data engine makes each fault in page code and records the changed element's box, and hard negatives change every sibling alike. No frontier judge is reliable: frontier models flag 18-62% of clean real screenshots and 18-82% of clean generated pages, find 47-72% of text layout faults, and rarely find a foreign icon (5-19%). Our small critic ProofJudge (Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA), trained on code-made pages with one to four faults each and keeping a finding only when it is confident, reaches F1 0.48, the highest of all judges (Gemini 4 Argon 0.37; open models at most 0.15; 0.46 even without the confidence cut), and is the only fault-finding judge within 15% false alarms on clean pages (2% real, 9% generated), the property such a first pass needs, at about a hundredth of Argon's cost. It finds the most general faults (59%) but fewer local style faults than Argon (25% against 41%) and fewer text layout faults than the API judges (43%; Gemini 4 Argon 47%). Against a named brand the task is harder still: models know a design language about as well as its public documentation states it.
bullets: Targets three fault families: general UI errors, local style inconsistencies, and text-layout problems.
Generates faults directly in page code, records the altered element’s box, and uses hard negatives where all siblings change consistently.
ProofJudge, a Qwen3.5-9B model with LoRA, reaches F1 0.48 and limits false alarms to 2% on real clean pages and 9% on generated ones.
It detects general faults best (59%), but is weaker on local style faults (25%) and text-layout faults (43%).
Named-brand critique remains difficult; models largely know a design language only as well as its public documentation describes it.

papers.abstract: We present Jais 3, a fleet of six open, Arabic-centric agentic language models ranging from 0.9B to 375B parameters. Jais 3 is built to complete tasks for Arabic speakers, not only to answer questions in plain text: it is trained to plan multi-step tasks, call tools and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, operate a terminal, search the web, and read, edit, and produce PDF, spreadsheet, and presentation files, while communicating with the user in Arabic. Instead of pretraining from scratch, we adapt each model of the fully open K2 Horizon fleet to Arabic through continual pretraining, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), final token preference optimization (FTPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We combine natural Arabic text with translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic, and replay the base model's own training data to keep its reasoning, agentic, and English abilities. Jais 3 covers Modern Standard Arabic and the major regional dialects, follows instructions with Arabic-specific constraints, and inherits the 512K-token context window of K2 Horizon (all models except the 0.9B). To our knowledge, its 375B model is the largest open Arabic-centric language model to date. For evaluation, we revisit how Arabic models are assessed, moving to fully generative evaluation on audited Arabic benchmarks. Across model sizes, Jais 3 matches or outperforms open-weight models of comparable size on Arabic and agentic benchmarks, with particularly strong agentic capabilities and Arabic instruction following, and far fewer hallucinations. We release the weights and the checkpoints from every training stage of all six models, together with samples of the training data, the data recipes and training configurations, the training logs, the audited benchmarks, and the evaluation code.

bullets: Covers models from 0.9B to 375B parameters, including what the authors describe as the largest open Arabic-centric model to date.

Adapts the open K2 Horizon models to Arabic through continual pretraining, SFT, FTPO, and RLVR, using natural, translated, transliterated, and synthetic Arabic data.
Supports Modern Standard Arabic and major regional dialects while retaining reasoning, agentic, and English abilities; most models have a 512K-token context window.
On audited generative Arabic and agentic benchmarks, it matches or outperforms comparable open-weight models, with strong agentic and instruction-following performance and fewer hallucinations.

papers.abstract: Modern Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference is constrained by GPU memory. This constraint is mitigated by expert offloading, which stores part of the model's weight in host memory and executes on demand. Though MoE architecture has computation sparsity, more GPUs are needed for serving increasingly larger frontier models. However, existing expert offloading systems overlook this need and fail to scale performance with additional GPUs. We present AdaOffload, a general and efficient multi-GPU hybrid expert execution framework that effectively handles heterogeneous hardware and workloads. We co-design GPU-CPU parallelism and GPU-CPU co-execution for decode and prefill with online workload observation that adapts to different hardware, workload, and batch size heterogeneity. We evaluated AdaOffload on five different platforms with varying GPU capability (L4, Pro6000, B200), number of GPUs, CPU capability, and NUMA topology on three different frontier open-weight models (284B to 753B). AdaOffload achieves $1.9\times$ to $15.5\times$ throughput speedups across different models over state-of-the-art systems.
bullets: Targets GPU-memory limits and poor scalability of existing expert-offloading systems as models and GPU counts grow.
Uses a multi-GPU hybrid execution framework that adapts online to hardware, workload, and batch-size heterogeneity.
Co-designs GPU–CPU parallelism and co-execution for both decode and prefill phases.
Evaluated across five hardware platforms and three frontier open-weight models ranging from 284B to 753B parameters.
Reports 1.9×–15.5× throughput speedups over state-of-the-art systems across evaluated settings.

papers.abstract: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs.
bullets: Addresses noisy foundation-model masks and identity–geometry coupling in object-aware 3DGS.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.
bullets: Addresses the limits of one-model-per-prompt routing and fixed ensembles for heterogeneous requests.

papers.abstract: External state should become more valuable as a reader becomes more capable, yet long-context evaluations measure memory utility at a single model scale. This paper formulates scale complementarity: the absolute gain from external state increases when reader capacity and a compact state budget are jointly scaled. ASCENT realizes this principle with a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and a bounded query-conditioned readout; every language model remains frozen. Under log loss, the value of a nested refinement equals its target-relevant conditional information; a full factorial makes the reader-by-state interaction identifiable. Official 16K BABILong experiments show Qwen2.5 accuracy gains of 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters, with both adjacent directional contrasts significant after family-wise correction. At 7B, Foundation accuracy rises to 33.25% while four-slot ASCENT answers every question, which caps the gain at 66.75 points; the 3B-to-7B accuracy increment is -15.88 points [-20.55, -11.20]. The accuracy-side claim is therefore established from 0.5B to 3B; the 7B conclusion rests on the non-saturated negative-log-likelihood factorial. A three-model by three-state factorial yields co-scaled negative log-likelihood gains of 0.388, 2.099, and 7.406 nats at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B; all interaction and gain contrasts retain positive simultaneous lower bounds. Five public 7B-8B readers obtain 66.75-85.63 point gains, and ASCENT exceeds task-trained retrieval checkpoints at the two larger shared scales. Controls, baselines, systems accounting, matched-hardware reproduction, and a cross-architecture sensitivity analysis accompany the experiments. The results establish scale-complementary external state under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.
bullets: Addresses the lack of scale-sensitive measurements of external-memory utility in long-context models.
Uses a target-blind causal writer, nested typed state, and bounded query-conditioned readout while keeping readers frozen.
Formalizes scale complementarity through conditional information and factorial reader-by-state interaction analysis.
On 16K BABILong, Qwen2.5 accuracy gains were 10.50, 78.88, and 82.63 percentage points at 0.5B, 1.5B, and 3B parameters.
Results support the claim from 0.5B–3B on accuracy and across 1.5B–7B on negative log likelihood, under the evaluated benchmarks, metrics, and state schema.

papers.abstract: Long-term conversational question answering can require several separated dialogue turns that support an answer only together. We introduce EviCover, a retrieval approach designed to retain this complementary evidence. It converts questions into observable evidence requirements, checks requirement coverage using retrieved source identifiers, and selects turns jointly. We track annotated support sets - the benchmark-labeled dialogue turns associated with each question - through retrieval, reranking, and final answer-generation context. We evaluate the baseline memory pipeline on generated, human-verified LoCoMo conversations and human-written REALTALK conversations, and examine EviCover on REALTALK's 108 multi-hop questions. Compared with the hybrid lexical/dense baseline, support-turn recall among 60 candidate turns rises from 0.526 to 0.575, and recall in the final ten-turn context rises from 0.349 to 0.379. The evidence funnel identifies separate discovery and selection failures, while paired answer evaluation shows that greater evidence recall does not yet establish a correctness gain. This analysis locates where complementary evidence is lost and distinguishes evidence retrieval from its use in answer generation.
bullets: Long-term conversational questions may require multiple separated dialogue turns jointly.
EviCover converts questions into evidence requirements, checks source coverage, and jointly selects turns.
Tracking annotated support sets reveals distinct evidence losses during retrieval, reranking, and context construction.
On REALTALK’s multi-hop questions, support-turn recall improves from 0.526 to 0.575 among candidates and from 0.349 to 0.379 in the final context.
Paired evaluation finds that better evidence recall alone does not establish more correct answers.

papers.abstract: Existing LLM post-training quantization techniques determine precision before inference begins, yet the precision a model requires varies dynamically across prompts, layers, and inference phases. We present AutoEMatic, a full-stack co-design that adapts the precision of weights, activations, and the KV cache at runtime. A lightweight policy selects each layer's precision at every prefill and decode step from two runtime signals: the entropy of the next-token distribution and the magnitude of each layer's update to its hidden states. This runtime adaptation is made practical by AutoFP, a multi-scale floating-point format that derives 2-, 4-, and 6-bit precisions from a single NVFP4 base format. We realize AutoEMatic on two targets: GPU kernels that execute AutoFP on NVFP4 Tensor Cores, and an accelerator whose vector MAC datapath executes all AutoFP formats natively. Across reasoning and agentic benchmarks, AutoEMatic improves accuracy by up to 21.7% over NVFP4 and matches group-scaled FP6 accuracy on most benchmarks, using 4.9 bits per weight versus 4.5 for NVFP4. On GB300 GPUs, AutoEMatic retains approximately 90-98% of NVFP4 decode throughput across the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, the AutoEMatic accelerator reduces latency by 1.6-2.3x and energy by 7-23% compared to an accelerator with NVFP4-only datapath at iso-accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of fixed-precision post-training quantization, whose optimal precision varies by prompt, layer, and inference phase.
Uses next-token entropy and per-layer hidden-state update magnitude to select weight, activation, and KV-cache precision at each prefill and decode step.
Introduces AutoFP, a multi-scale floating-point format supporting 2-, 4-, and 6-bit precision from a shared NVFP4 base format.
Improves accuracy by up to 21.7% over NVFP4 and matches group-scaled FP6 accuracy on most evaluated benchmarks, at 4.9 bits per weight.
Maintains roughly 90–98% of NVFP4 decode throughput on GB300 GPUs; a dedicated accelerator achieves 1.6–2.3× lower latency and 7–23% lower energy at iso-accuracy.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have continuous deficiency in spatial reasoning tasks that require \emph{mental spatial transformation}, such as reasoning under hypothetical changes in viewpoint or position, known as perspective-taking tasks. Existing approaches either scale linguistic reasoning or augment VLMs with static geometric representations, but neither directly enables active transformation of the represented scene. World models offer this capability, yet existing systems typically communicate through synthesized RGB images, introducing a latent-to-pixel-to-latent bottleneck. We introduce \emph{WorldMind}, a framework for test-time scaling of spatial reasoning through latent world simulation. Given a query and observation, the VLM selects useful spatial transformations, while a world model executes them and exposes aligned intermediate latent features directly to the VLM. The resulting latent evidence is incorporated into subsequent reasoning steps, enabling iterative spatial simulation without repeatedly decoding imagined states into pixels. To optimize this interaction, WorldMind further employs process-verifiable reinforcement learning that rewards reasoning progress only when the associated action and latent transition are valid. WorldMind thus scales spatial reasoning by allocating additional inference-time computation to active world simulation rather than generating more language or pixels. Across VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny, WorldMind achieves an average improvement of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation.
bullets: Targets VLM deficiencies in mental spatial transformations, including hypothetical viewpoint and position changes.
The VLM selects useful transformations, while a world model executes them and returns aligned latent features directly for iterative reasoning.
Uses process-verifiable reinforcement learning to reward only valid actions and latent transitions that make reasoning progress.
Achieves average gains of 16.0% over the base VLM and 8.3% over the strongest RGB-based world simulation across three benchmarks.
Scope: focused on visual spatial reasoning and perspective-taking tasks evaluated on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench, and MindCube-Tiny.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of WorldMind design. To ensure proper latent world simulation, WorldMind first trains an adapter that selects latent features from the world model and aligns them with a frozen VLM. Then, it fine-tunes the VLM in two stages: (1) supervised fine-tuning with simulated reasoning trajectories; and (2) process-verifiable reinforcement learning, which further optimizes action selection and reasoning using intermediate and final rewards.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.
bullets: Addresses embodiment, viewpoint, action-space, and temporal differences between human demonstrations and robots.
Learns self-supervised temporal representations with cycle consistency to discover cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation.

papers.abstract: We extract visibly pushdown grammars (VPGs) from neural language models in a fully black-box setting. Our work builds on the VPL* framework, which learns VPGs from recurrent networks by exploiting access to the target's internal state. First, we replace the white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees. The resulting algorithm applies unchanged to transformer language models and, more generally, to any acceptor exposing only binary decisions. Second, we further observe that the original framework only ever queries the target on well-formed sequences that can be accepted by the most permissive VPG (called BParse) with the target's ranked alphabet. That is, VPL* is blind to the target's behavior outside BParse. Thus, we propose to sample trees directly instead of sequences and call the target with all the resulting sequences in order to provide an error estimate of how far the target deviates from being a VPG. Last but not least, we develop a learner that captures a tree automaton describing discovered behaviors of the target outside BParse, which results in a larger learnable space. We evaluate the approach on several cases, including transformers trained with Dyck grammars and synthetic targets designed to be outside BParse.
bullets: Replaces VPL*’s white-box equivalence oracle with PAC sampling over trees, enabling use with transformers and binary-decision acceptors.
Samples trees directly to estimate how much a target deviates from being a visibly pushdown language (VPL) acceptor.
Learns a tree automaton for target behaviors outside BParse, expanding the space of learnable behaviors.
Evaluates the approach on Dyck-trained transformers and synthetic targets outside BParse.

papers.abstract: Clinical trial screening requires assessing large numbers of patient-trial pairs to prioritize candidates for detailed eligibility review, often under restrictions on sharing patient records. We introduce TrialJev, an open-weight eligibility scorer that uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models and a pointer head to score natural-language answer options in a single forward pass, without autoregressive decoding. Trained on TREC Clinical Trials 2021 and evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen TREC 2022 synthetic patients, TrialJev achieves 80.97% (Qwen3.5-27B) and 81.84% (Qwen3.8-27B) accuracy, compared with 79.87% and 79.93% for LLMs fine-tuned on the same data to generate verdicts. In matched batch-1 measurements, verdict generation takes 2.45-2.70 times as long as the one-pass inference of TrialJev at 9B-27B. Under a common development-fitted decision correction, the two 27B TrialJev models reach 80.99% and 81.88% accuracy, compared with 81.28% for the proprietary hosted Jev API; paired confidence intervals include zero. TrialJev runs locally on a single GPU, requiring approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B, without transmitting patient text to an external model API. An A/B-logit ablation shows that avoiding decoding, rather than the pointer head alone, accounts for the measured efficiency advantage. TrialJev is intended for first-pass prioritization of candidate trials, complementing rather than replacing explanatory models and clinical review. Evaluation is limited to synthetic patients and implementation-specific timing, and clinical use has not been validated. Adapters, pointer heads, and model cards are released on Hugging Face.
bullets: Uses LoRA-adapted Qwen models with a pointer head to score answer options in one forward pass without autoregressive decoding.
Evaluated on 6,975 eligible-or-excluded pairs from 50 unseen synthetic patients in TREC Clinical Trials 2022.
Achieves 80.97%–81.84% accuracy, comparable to or above same-data fine-tuned verdict-generating LLMs and statistically compatible with a hosted Jev API after correction.
Runs locally on a single GPU, taking approximately 178 ms per pair at 27B and avoiding transmission of patient text to external APIs.
Designed for first-pass prioritization, not explanatory assessment or replacement of clinical review; clinical use remains unvalidated.

papers.title: TrialJev: Open-Weight Single Pass Eligibility Scoring for Patient Trial Screening

papers.abstract: The development of deep learning-based medical AI depends on high-quality annotated data. Yet, dataset creation remains constrained by the need for expert radiologist annotations, limiting curated datasets to relatively small cohorts. To overcome this limitation, recent efforts increasingly aggregate disparate public datasets into large-scale dataset collections. However, combining datasets at scale often obscures data provenance, introducing substantial risks of reuse propagation, unintended leakage, bias amplification and distorted data distributions. In this work, we study these problems on a massive collection of 565k 3D radiological images across 1034 public datasets and provide practical resources to address them. Firstly, we formalize dataset collections as a distinct paradigm in medical image analysis and characterize their structural challenges, including reuse propagation, duplication, and provenance fragmentation. Secondly, we perform a large-scale empirical study of duplication on this collection and demonstrate extensive exact and near-duplicate reuse across public datasets via perceptual hashing and manual tracing, identifying a lower bound of 118k duplicate pairs. We make the perceptual hashes publicly accessible for comparison through our website, providing researchers with a standardized reference for identifying potential overlaps and shared provenance. Thirdly, since hashing alone cannot detect all duplicates, we introduce MAP (Metadata for Aggregation and Provenance), a lightweight, portable metadata profile for documenting provenance, known overlaps, and deduplication decisions in dataset collections. Our contributions help dataset collections shift from coarse aggregations to reliable and provenance-aware data scaling mechanisms in medical image analysis. A web tool supporting our work is available at https://mic-dct.dkfz.de/.
bullets: Analyzes 565k 3D radiological images from 1,034 public datasets.
Identifies challenges including reuse propagation, duplication, provenance fragmentation, leakage, bias amplification, and distorted distributions.
Finds at least 118k duplicate pairs through perceptual hashing and manual tracing.
Publishes perceptual hashes and a web tool to help researchers identify overlaps and shared provenance.
Introduces MAP, a portable metadata profile for recording provenance, overlaps, and deduplication decisions.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Cross-dataset overlap network revealed by exact and near-duplicate 3D medical images. Node size indicates the number of images in a dataset, edge size indicates the number of duplicate links associated with a dataset, and shaded regions denote connected components in the overlap graph. The largest component contains 107 datasets, including widely reused datasets and collections such as AMOS, KiTS, and AbdomenAtlas, illustrating that public dataset collections are not independent flat unions but part of a densely connected reuse ecosystem. Because perceptual hashing detects visual identity rather than causal lineage, edges should be interpreted as evidence of image-level overlap rather than complete provenance relationships.

papers.abstract: A language model that never had to forget would keep every document it has read and every turn it has spoken, and answer from any of it. This paper shows that two stock models can do that on unmodified weights by manipulating their geometry. Rotary attention turns each pair of key dimensions, a plane, at its own rate. The slow planes turn once in thousands of tokens and carry the address a query matches when it reads a far key; the fast planes turn once in a few tokens, and the order of the tokens inside a span is already written into its keys and values by the time the span leaves the near window. At distance the position blurs, and what attention reads is a bag rather than a sequence. A far span is read by its words: under competition it is read only if it is visible at the query of the question's own handle word, and a read through a description rather than a word fails at distance in every model measured, a 70B included. These facts allow a trick. What sits in the far part of attention does not have to be the history as it was; it can be installed ahead of the prediction. The design keeps a near window of 8K tokens at their true positions and changes what lies beyond it with the prompt: every far key and value goes to the host exact, a word index finds the units the request's rare words name, a far window of slots inside the trained range holds them while the request is encoded, and a rare word the model generates fetches its units mid-generation with one exact re-encode. Implemented in llama.cpp on Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, the design reads planted single needles at 99 to 100 of 100 and three-key discrimination at 88 to 100 of 100 from 32K to one million tokens, scores 70.8 on RULER against 69.9 for dense attention on Llama-3.1-8B at 128K and 67.8 against 75.5 on Mistral-7B at 32K, and at 128K prefills at 1.85 times and decodes at 1.65 to 1.68 times stock speed.
bullets: Rotary attention preserves address-like information in slow dimensions but loses order for distant spans, making far-context retrieval largely word-based.
The method keeps the nearest 8K tokens at true positions and remaps distant keys and values into trained-range slots selected using rare query words.
During generation, rare generated words can trigger an exact re-encoding to retrieve additional relevant units.
On Mistral-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, it retrieved planted needles with 99–100/100 accuracy and achieved 88–100/100 on three-key discrimination from 32K to 1M tokens.
At 128K, it reported 1.85× faster prefilling and 1.65–1.68× faster decoding than stock speed, with task scores varying by model and benchmark.

papers.selection_reason: Modifies attention geometry (rotary attention) to enable stock models to handle unbounded context (up to 1M tokens) with improved speed, contributing to efficient attention mechanisms.
papers.title: Retrofitting Unbounded Context onto Stock Language Models
papers.tldr: A prompt-driven KV-cache remapping strategy gives unmodified language models practical million-token context by preserving an 8K near window and selectively staging relevant far-away text.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid state estimation and language-grounded motion understanding from robot recordings ties training coverage to the robot's motion repertoire. Human motion datasets offer broader coverage, yet transferring this knowledge requires overcoming differences in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances. To enable this transfer, we propose a unified inertial encoder whose shared inertial interface uses kinematic IMU synthesis to represent human and humanoid motion at corresponding body sites. Within this common input space, joint training on human and kinematically retargeted humanoid motion combines velocity estimation and motion--text alignment with continuous-time encoding and sensor and motion randomization. The resulting model transfers zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation, real-robot training trajectories, or fine-tuning, achieving the lowest velocity error among evaluated methods across five datasets, including 0.099m/s on real G1. Its motion-description retrieval also extends to retargeted G1 motion categories observed only in human training, demonstrating how human motion knowledge can support the generalization of humanoid inertial odometry and language-grounded motion understanding.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between human datasets and humanoid robots in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances.
Uses kinematic IMU synthesis to create a shared inertial representation at corresponding body sites.
Jointly trains velocity estimation and motion–text alignment with continuous-time encoding and sensor/motion randomization.
Transfers to a physical Unitree G1 without simulation, real-robot trajectories, or fine-tuning.
Achieves the lowest velocity error among evaluated methods across five datasets, including 0.099 m/s on real G1, and retrieves motion categories seen only in human training.
