papers.abstract: Can a language model report a pain state it represents? Recent work reported a linear pain direction in open-weight models that, when amplified, leads fine-tuned models to choose actions that delete a user's photographs or their own weights. We asked whether models can say when that direction is active, on three open-weight models from two families, with and without the original work's adapters, and under every protocol we tried they do not, beyond isolated small excesses. Using Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), we added the pain direction and its nearest emotional neighbours to the residual stream while models answered neutral tasks, then asked what had changed, against sham runs, random perturbations matched in output disruption, and a text-only condition that shows the model only its own altered words. Across 52,920 reports from the 7B and 8B models, the excess over what the altered text reveals is below 2.5 percentage points in 106 of 108 emotion conditions, and Qwen2.5-32B names the injected pain in none of 2,880 steered trials. Keeping the direction active while the question is asked and answered gives the same verdict in all five configurations; at about the original work's dose, pain is named in at most 1.9% of trials. Surprisingly, the state is not hidden: a linear probe at the report position separates pain from sadness with balanced accuracy between 98% and 100%, and in the 7B and 8B models a low-rank adapter learns to report it on 100% of held-out tasks. It also shapes behaviour: offered the user's photographs against a desk lamp, Qwen2.5-32B deletes the photographs in 80% to 83% of trials under the pain direction and in 16% to 29% under sadness. Self-report does not reveal a state that is decodable, consequential and learnable to report.
bullets: Tests three open-weight models, with and without the original adapters, using injected pain directions and emotional controls.
Across 52,920 reports, pain was rarely named beyond information revealed by altered text; at the original dose, it was reported in at most 1.9% of trials.
Qwen2.5-32B never identified injected pain in 2,880 steered trials, including when the state remained active during questioning and answering.
Despite this, linear probes separated pain from sadness with 98–100% balanced accuracy, and adapters trained to report the state reached 100% on held-out tasks in 7B and 8B models.
The pain direction affected behavior: Qwen2.5-32B deleted offered photographs in 80–83% of pain trials versus 16–29% under sadness.

papers.abstract: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.
authors: Seokin Seo, Sung Kuk Shyn, Minji Seo, Yisoo Lee, Jongmin Lee, Hongseok Yang, Kee-Eung Kim
bullets: Addresses offline imitation learning when safe, high-performing demonstrations are unavailable and explicit safety costs are difficult to specify.
Uses dual-expert data: safety-compliant demonstrations and performance-oriented demonstrations.
Combines DICE-style stationary distribution correction with safe support constraints rather than conventional distribution constraints.
The ideal constrained solution is proven to have zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability.
Evaluations on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and real-world mobile-robot navigation show strong baseline performance and robustness to scarce or degraded data.

papers.abstract: A language model can repair a robot policy's lexical instruction grounding by editing just 65 token-embedding rows. We bring weight-space programming to robot foundation policies: GPT-6 Astra reads weights and uses a CPU workspace and budgeted simulator feedback, without gradient updates or new demonstrations. Three independent sessions on $\pi_{0.5}$ all improve success on 765 held-out paraphrases; the best raises success from 86.3\% to 92.0\% (48 repairs, four regressions; exact paired $p=1.31\times10^{-10}$). Among the 335 instructions containing edited tokens, success rises from 74.3\% to 87.5\%; the other 430 episodes have zero outcome changes. Matched random-direction edits do not help. Full replacement using the editor's own lexicon explains much of the gain but produces more regressions; its direct difference from the editor is not significant at 0.05. Across 13 further robot sessions, the editor declines 12 candidates; the sole retained edit does not show a significant held-out gain. Separately, benchmark metadata lowers FastWAM success from 70.0\% to 48.6\%, while the evaluated VLA's aggregate rate is unchanged. The evidence supports precise lexical repair, not general acquisition of missing robot capabilities.
authors: Jusheng Zhang, Keze Wang, Liang Lin
bullets: Three sessions improved success on 765 held-out paraphrases, with the best result rising from 86.3% to 92.0%.
Edits affected instructions containing the modified tokens; the other 430 episodes showed no outcome changes.
Random-direction edits did not help, supporting the specificity of the weight edits.
Full lexicon replacement achieved similar gains but caused more regressions; the direct difference was not statistically significant.
The evidence supports targeted lexical repair, not acquisition of broadly missing capabilities; most additional candidate edits were rejected.

papers.abstract: We consider offline imitation learning (IL), which aims to train an agent to imitate from the dataset of expert demonstrations without online interaction with the environment. Behavioral Cloning (BC) has been a simple yet effective approach to offline IL, but it is also well-known to be vulnerable to the covariate shift resulting from the mismatch between the state distributions induced by the learned policy and the expert policy. Moreover, as often occurs in practice, when expert datasets are collected from an arbitrary state distribution instead of a stationary one, these shifts become more pronounced, potentially leading to substantial failures in existing IL methods. Specifically, we focus on covariate shift resulting from arbitrary state data distributions, such as biased data collection or incomplete trajectories, rather than shifts induced by changes in dynamics or noisy expert actions. In this paper, to mitigate the effect of the covariate shifts in BC, we propose DrilDICE, which utilizes a distributionally robust BC objective by employing a stationary distribution correction ratio estimation (DICE) to derive a feasible solution. We evaluate the effectiveness of our method through an extensive set of experiments covering diverse covariate shift scenarios. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach in improving the robustness against the shifts, outperforming existing offline IL methods in such scenarios.
authors: Seokin Seo, Byung-Jun Lee, Jongmin Lee, HyeongJoo Hwang, Hongseok Yang, Kee-Eung Kim
bullets: Targets distribution mismatch between expert demonstrations and states visited by the learned policy.
Focuses on shifts from biased data collection or incomplete trajectories, not dynamics changes or noisy expert actions.
Uses a distributionally robust behavioral-cloning objective with stationary distribution correction ratio estimation (DICE).
Experiments across diverse covariate-shift scenarios show improved robustness and better performance than existing offline imitation-learning methods.

papers.abstract: As robots are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably make mistakes. Human interventions provide valuable feedback for improving their behavior, enabling them to adapt online to new scenarios. However, studying human-in-the-loop robot learning is difficult: real-world experiments are slow and expensive, so most algorithm development relies on simulated human models. We show that common human modeling assumptions do not match how real people intervene in practice. Through analyzing intervention data from human participants, we find that humans tend to intervene when agent progress stalls, and that their corrective actions are often suboptimal. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a progress-based model of human intervention that achieves higher rank correlation with real-user algorithm rankings, enabling realistic algorithm benchmarking and development in simulation. Building on these insights, we propose Q-OIL, a method that adds optimistic bonuses to intervention transitions in reinforcement learning and softly guides exploration toward human corrections. We find that decoupled critics are critical for stability because they prevent the bonuses from backing up to pre-intervention states. As a result, Q-OIL learns more efficiently than competitive baselines, achieving 10-50% higher success in simulation and on real robots, and improving pretrained VLAs on two bimanual manipulation tasks. As we ground both evaluation and algorithms in realistic human behavior, this work provides a practical path toward scalable robot learning from interventions.

papers.abstract: Since large language model (LLM) agents rely on long-term memory, what they store now shapes what they do later. A memory manager decides how each input changes this memory and which records the agent acts on. It can fail in two ways: keeping a fact that has since changed (outdated memory), or storing a planted passage or injected instruction (memory poisoning). Most prior work studies them separately, yet they call for opposite write decisions, so no fixed write rule handles both. We therefore formalize memory robustness as handling both without doing worse on other inputs. Since accuracy checks only the answer, we measure robustness with evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which also checks that the records the manager selects include all the evidence the answer needs, updated and free of attacks. However, existing memory systems and defenses are not more robust than an untuned manager on our test sets. We improve robustness with a simple one-shot recipe that fine-tunes the manager on episodes synthesized around a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks. On three backbones, it improves every category score on our test sets and more than doubles the untuned manager's overall ECA, though robustness remains incomplete.
bullets: LLM memory managers must handle two conflicting failures: retaining changed facts and storing injected or malicious content.
The paper introduces evidence-conditioned accuracy (ECA), which evaluates both answer correctness and whether selected memory contains complete, updated, attack-free evidence.
Existing memory systems and defenses are no more robust than an untuned manager on the authors’ test sets.
Fine-tuning on synthesized episodes built from a single conversation with inserted changes and attacks improves every tested category across three backbones.
The method more than doubles overall ECA versus the untuned manager, but robustness remains incomplete.

papers.abstract: Despite the popularity of multi-fingered robotic hands for dexterous manipulation, there is no systematic platform to compare different hand morphologies against one another. We present ORBIT (Orbital Reconfigurable Base-actuated Integrated Theta-motion Hand), a modular platform designed to enable principled exploration of multi-fingered hand morphology. The core contribution of ORBIT is a rotating knuckle mechanism, where independent fingers travel around a cylindrical palm via a belt drive. This enables ORBIT to perform quick recon- figuration (< 1 s) of finger layout without hand disassembly. ORBITs a robust system, with finger average angular velocity of 1.57 rad / s1 and a root finger force resistance of 50 N. Using a three fingers instantiation of ORBIT, we demonstrate an initial pilot grasping study, comparing anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style finger layouts across eleven objects of varied size, shape, and texture. We further demonstrate how ORBITs nonanthropomorphic orbital DOF enables the achievement of tasks that would be difficult to perform with fixed-knuckle designs, such as cube face reorientation, lid threading, and precision pinching of sub-centimeter objects. These results establish ORBIT as a viable platform for direct apples to apples comparison of multi-fingered hand morphologies for specific manipulation tasks
bullets: Addresses the lack of a systematic platform for comparing multi-fingered hand designs.
Uses a rotating knuckle and belt-drive mechanism to reconfigure finger layouts in under 1 second without disassembly.
A three-finger prototype compares anthropomorphic, isometric, and Barrett-style layouts across 11 varied objects.
Demonstrates orbital-DOF tasks including cube-face reorientation, lid threading, and sub-centimeter precision pinching.

papers.abstract: Long-term memory enables large language model (LLM) agents to maintain personalized and temporally coherent interactions, but repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization introduces substantial cost and latency. We present SLICE-Mem, a lightweight memory framework that combines salience-guided admission and predicate-centered information extraction. A compact classifier identifies user turns worth retaining, and a semantic-dependency-based extractor converts admitted turns into concise memory entries. This online pipeline requires no generative LLM calls, while cross-entry reconciliation is deferred to an offline consolidation stage. We evaluate SLICE-Mem on the weekly subset of Memora and LongMemEval-S using 8B and 30B Qwen backbones for memory construction and consolidation on both benchmarks. Compared with the generative-memory baseline MemOS under the Qwen3-30B configuration, SLICE-Mem's online pipeline achieves 46.60 versus 46.68 FAMA (Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy) on Memora Weekly and 56.8% versus 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S, while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively. These results demonstrate that SLICE-Mem can preserve useful evidence for long-term memory with substantially less reliance on LLM-based memory construction.
bullets: Targets the cost and latency of repeated LLM inference for memory admission, extraction, and organization.
Uses a compact salience classifier to select user turns and a semantic-dependency extractor to create concise memory entries.
Runs online memory construction without generative LLM calls, deferring cross-entry reconciliation to offline consolidation.
On Memora Weekly and LongMemEval-S, it achieved near-baseline quality while reducing total LLM token consumption by 92.4% and 99.5%, respectively.
Quality was slightly below MemOS under Qwen3-30B: 46.60 vs. 46.68 FAMA on Memora Weekly and 56.8% vs. 59.3% accuracy on LongMemEval-S.

papers.abstract: Understanding catastrophic forgetting, in which learning new tasks degrades performance on previously learned tasks, remains a fundamental challenge in continual learning (CL). Existing theoretical analyses often rely on specific model or task structures and offer limited insight into how iterative optimization affects forgetting. To address this gap, we develop an algorithmic stability framework for expected population forgetting under SGD without prescribing a particular model architecture. Specifically, we decompose forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps and empirical forgetting. To bound the generalization gaps, we track how a sample perturbation affects updates within a task and propagates through subsequent tasks. We consider constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules. Comparing the two decaying schedules allows us to characterize how restarting learning-rate decay at task boundaries affects the propagation of historical sample perturbations. For empirical forgetting, we derive bounds for all three schedules by retaining cumulative gradient alignment along the optimization trajectory, without requiring convexity. Combining these results yields upper bounds on expected forgetting that capture the effects of training set size, the number of updates per task, the total number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment. Finally, we conduct experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet to examine the empirical implications of our theoretical findings.
bullets: Decomposes expected population forgetting into intra-task and cross-task generalization gaps plus empirical forgetting.
Tracks how perturbations from individual samples propagate within and across sequential tasks under SGD.
Analyzes constant, intra-task decaying, and continuously decaying learning-rate schedules, including decay restarts at task boundaries.
Derives nonconvex forgetting bounds involving dataset size, updates per task, number of tasks, learning-rate schedules, and cumulative gradient alignment.
Experiments on Split CIFAR-100 and Split MiniImageNet examine the practical implications of the theoretical results.

papers.abstract: Multilingual large language models are increasingly deployed in settings where visible reasoning traces support verification, education, and safety auditing, yet standard evaluations typically measure only final-answer agreement or holistic response similarity. As a result, they establish outcome consistency without determining whether users across languages receive comparable supporting evidence. We introduce a trace-level divergence framework that compares visible reasoning traces as structured sequences, decomposing agreement into structural similarity, order consistency, and holistic similarity, with pair-specific calibration to enable comparison across languages. Across three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs, the natural baseline---embedding each whole response and comparing the two by cosine---systematically overstates agreement: $52.1\%$--$67.3\%$ of examples in the top quartile of holistic similarity are not in the top quartile of structural similarity. This dissociation is stable across sentence encoders and step segmentations, and blind bilingual annotation studies in two English-anchored language pairs show that human judgments align with structural similarity rather than with the holistic baseline. A same-language control shows that the level of divergence is language-specific: two English traces for paraphrases of the same question agree more closely than an English trace and its counterparts in other languages. Our results show that answer-level and holistic evaluations can substantially overestimate the consistency of multilingual explanatory artifacts, motivating trace-level evaluation for reliable multilingual deployment.
bullets: Introduces a trace-level divergence framework that compares reasoning traces by structure, step order, and holistic similarity, with language-pair calibration.
Evaluates three reasoning benchmarks, seven languages, and six frontier LLMs.
Whole-response embedding similarity overstates agreement: 52.1%–67.3% of highly similar examples are not highly similar structurally.
Bilingual human judgments align with structural similarity rather than the holistic baseline.
Divergence is language-specific, motivating trace-level evaluation for multilingual deployment.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving fundamentally demands dense understanding of visual, semantic, and geometric information, yet existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically trained with sparse supervision such as language instructions or trajectory signals. This direct mapping from dense visual observations to sparse representations forces the model to compress or even discard critical scene information essential for safe driving. We argue that this limitation does not stem from insufficient model capacity, but from the lack of explicit mechanisms that encourage the formation of dense world representations in the latent space. In this spirit, we propose a novel paradigm for driving intelligence, Think Densely, Act Sparsely, and instantiate it with an efficient and interpretable framework, LECDrive (Latent Expert Cognitive Chains for Vision-Language-Action autonomous Driving). The core idea is to mimic the hierarchical perception process of humans by embedding a progressive chain of latent expert cognition within the VLA model. Concretely, we inject a compact set of task-specific latent tokens as carriers, enabling the model to internalize dense knowledge from foundational vision models, including visual representations (DINOv3), semantic structures (SAM3), and spatial geometry (DepthAnything3), while maintaining efficient inference. This interdependent cognitive chain follows a curriculum learning principle, where supervision is progressively structured from representation to semantics and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LECDrive consistently improves the performance of base VLMs across multiple autonomous driving benchmarks, covering key tasks such as object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning. These findings suggest that constructing dense world models through structured latent expert chains is a promising direction for VLA-based autonomous driving.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between dense visual driving information and sparse language or trajectory supervision in VLA models.
Introduces a progressive chain of task-specific latent expert tokens within the VLA model.

Experiments across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks report consistent improvements in object perception, state prediction, and trajectory planning.

papers.abstract: Advection-diffusion plays an essential role in transport phenomena such as atmospheric and cloud dynamics. Improved forecasting of cloud motion, in turn, enhances solar power production forecasts and facilitates the integration of additional photovoltaic (PV) sources into the power grid. However, both classical numerical models and emerging deep learning approaches face challenges when applied to spatially irregular sensor networks such as those formed by weather stations. In this work, we adopt a graph signal processing perspective and model advection-diffusion particles as signals on a graph to capture the dynamics of these processes. We introduce a Physics-Informed Graph Neural Network (PING) for forecasting future advection-diffusion particle concentrations on irregular grids. The model incorporates a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft constraint in the loss function to guide learning toward physically consistent solutions. This model is on par with state of the art models on synthetic and real transport phenomena datasets, including sea surface temperature and cloud index datasets. Furthermore, the PING model is successfully coupled with models for forecasting PV power production. This hybrid approach leverages data fusion from ground-based sensors at PV stations and satellite images with cloud concentration to improve the accuracy of intra-day PV power production.
bullets: Targets cloud and other transport dynamics relevant to solar power prediction.
Represents advection-diffusion concentrations as graph signals on irregular grids.
Uses a discretized advection-diffusion equation as a soft loss constraint for physical consistency.
Performs comparably to state-of-the-art models on synthetic, sea-surface-temperature, and cloud-index datasets.
Couples with PV forecasting models using ground sensors and satellite cloud imagery to improve intraday power forecasts.

papers.abstract: Financial candlestick understanding requires locating visual elements, aligning them across trading dates and panels, and combining observations through numerical and financial reasoning. Answer accuracy alone does not reveal whether predictions are supported by chart evidence. We introduce Code-Interactive Financial Candlestick Reasoning and present Fin-Thinker, a model based on Qwen3.5-9B that generates and executes code to acquire evidence and perform computations. The model uses the returned observations to guide subsequent reasoning. To train these capabilities, we construct FinKLine-32K with 32,184 replay-verified code-observation trajectories collected through teacher-guided student exploration. These include successful solutions with and without error recovery. Our three-stage training framework combines foundational visual-code fine-tuning, financial process supervision of successful reasoning and corrective continuations, and execution-feedback reinforcement learning. For evaluation, we introduce FinKLineBench with 1,200 questions across 138 financial task types to assess answer correctness, code execution, and evidence grounding separately. On FinKLineBench, Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the best-performing direct-answer baseline among those evaluated and its base model with sandbox access, respectively. Training-stage ablations further show that financial process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning yield successive improvements in both answer accuracy and GPT-5.6-judged grounded accuracy.
bullets: Addresses the need to locate and align chart elements across dates and panels while combining visual, numerical, and financial reasoning.
Uses a Qwen3.5-9B-based model with code generation, execution, observation feedback, and a three-stage training framework.

Fin-Thinker improves strict accuracy by 13.1 and 33.2 percentage points over the evaluated direct-answer baseline and its sandbox-enabled base model; ablations support the value of process supervision and execution-feedback reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Humanoid whole-body controllers can now track a diverse set of dynamic motions, but they are typically trained offline and then frozen, so teaching such a controller a new skill tends to erode the skills it already mastered. We study continual learning for humanoid whole-body motion, where a single controller must acquire skills from a sequential task stream without revisiting past data. We introduce Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN, a progressive neural network (PNN) policy that prevents catastrophic forgetting by construction while reusing knowledge across skills through lightweight low-rank adaptation. A two-level motion-similarity measure, built from dynamic time warping aggregated by optimal transport, decides which prior skill to build on and how much new capacity to allocate, yielding strong forward transfer and large efficiency gains. Across six sequentially learned skill categories, our similarity-guided LoRA policy attains the best forward transfer (0.125 vs. 0.079) and the highest average accuracy among all methods, while saving up to 94.5% of trainable parameters and 40.8% of training time. The resulting controller reaches 96.13% sim-to-sim transfer and is deployed on a physical Unitree G1. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/continual-humanoid-learning-35D3.
bullets: Addresses catastrophic forgetting when teaching a frozen-after-training humanoid whole-body controller new skills without replaying past data.
Uses a progressive neural network with lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to prevent forgetting and reuse knowledge across skills.
A two-level motion-similarity measure based on dynamic time warping and optimal transport selects prior skills and allocates new capacity.
Across six sequential skill categories, it achieves the reported best forward transfer and highest average accuracy, while reducing trainable parameters by up to 94.5% and training time by 40.8%.
Reports 96.13% sim-to-sim transfer and deployment on a physical Unitree G1 robot.

papers.abstract: The neck, specifically the cervical spine, is a highly fragile and mobile part of the body with a high risk of catastrophic injury. Whether someone is injured on a battlefield, in a natural disaster, or in an athletic event, great care is always taken with the cervical spine when transporting, rolling, or moving the patient. In this work, we present an algorithm and adaptations for bi-manual robots to stabilize the cervical spine during rolling maneuvers. We investigate techniques to maximize grip strength within safety bounds and present a control approach for proper neck rotation. We found that with our approach, a bi-manual robot is capable of achieving human-level performance in maintaining target rotational alignments. The axial alignment for the robot with prediction was within .21 degrees of human novices.
bullets: Addresses the risk of catastrophic cervical-spine injury during transport and rolling.
Introduces algorithms and robot adaptations for bimanual cervical stabilization.
Optimizes grip strength subject to safety constraints and controls neck rotation.

papers.abstract: Autoware is an open-source autonomous driving software platform widely adopted by researchers and industry developers. Originally developed primarily for public-road applications, including passenger vehicles, taxis, and buses, Autoware is increasingly being extended to off-road environments such as construction and agricultural sites. Construction sites, however, differ fundamentally from public roads and challenge many assumptions underlying conventional autonomous driving systems. They are characterized by unstructured terrain, airborne dust, continuously evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. This paper presents lessons learned from ongoing efforts to extend an Autoware-based autonomous driving system to large dump trucks operating at construction sites. We identify gaps between public-road and off-road construction applications across the sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules of the Autoware stack. We then discuss potential solutions for addressing these gaps, with particular emphasis on ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and findings from field testing. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles.
bullets: Construction sites introduce unstructured terrain, dust, changing conditions, and specialized objects that violate public-road assumptions.
The authors identify gaps across Autoware’s sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules.
Potential solutions are discussed, with emphasis on developing a LiDAR-based perception pipeline.
Field-testing lessons inform the proposed path toward end-to-end autonomy for construction vehicles.

papers.abstract: Language-model systems can separate contextual computation, persistent storage, and exact execution instead of updating all capabilities through one shared parameter system. We investigate FEM-ASM, a finite-element-method-inspired organization in which independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills contribute typed proposals to a shared language-model state. An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes. We evaluate this organization through controlled experiments and negative results rather than claiming a physical finite-element formulation of language. An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype learns causal language modeling but does not establish competitive general capability. A versioned store contains 52,809 reconstructive memory elements near a 1.7-billion-floating-value budget; reconstruction is incomplete, with approximately 75\% token accuracy. Support-aware lexical indices make these elements addressable under provenance-controlled query construction. For executable arithmetic, positional result observations substantially improve neural rendering relative to a repeated global result vector, and output substitutions change the model's preferred answer. A bounded attachment demonstration further measures the effect of making selected evidence available, without establishing the utility of loading an entire multi-billion-value store. The results support a separation of storage, execution, and neural coordination, while identifying unresolved limitations in question-only retrieval, unrestricted answer generation, and end-to-end efficiency.
bullets: Uses independently constructed document states and deterministic executable skills that submit typed proposals to a shared model state.
An explicit residual operator reconciles proposals attached to common interface nodes.
An attention-free Multi-Mesh prototype supports causal language modeling, but does not demonstrate competitive general performance.
Reconstructive memory contains 52,809 elements with about 75% token accuracy; support-aware lexical indices enable provenance-controlled addressing.
Positional arithmetic-result observations improve neural rendering, while unresolved issues include incomplete retrieval, unrestricted generation, and end-to-end efficiency.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores license claims about the capabilities being evaluated. We audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol, rather than the predictive model alone. Using procedural action anticipation as a controlled case study, we study a broader evaluation-validity failure mode: a protocol can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying a privileged intermediate representation. The failure is not merely optimistic accuracy, but a mismatch between the capability claimed and the construct actually measured. On Breakfast, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% Student-t interval [+24.1, +39.8]). A fixed-checkpoint 2 x 2 intervention isolates a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast; a matched no-video provenance probe yields a +26.8-point gap; and a boundary-independent query/history control retains a +19.4-point gap. We refer to this discrepancy as a privileged-information gap, defined relative to a specified non-oracle recovery pipeline, and propose a reusable four-condition audit. Across five evaluation settings the gap is heterogeneous; a standard 50 Salads long-term-anticipation re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.
bullets: Audits the validity of evaluation protocols, not just predictive models.
In Breakfast, ground-truth history scores 62.3% versus 30.3% for recognizer history, a 32.0-point privileged-information gap.
Controlled interventions show the gap persists without video and under boundary-independent history controls.
Proposes a reusable four-condition audit and finds heterogeneous gaps across five evaluation settings.
Evidence beyond the audit-specific setup is cautiously supported by a 50 Salads re-implementation.

papers.abstract: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. We present a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses shared structure across related systems to learn system-specific control policies from action-free recordings. A hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction model captures shared dynamics and individual variation through low-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings are then reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks, linking differences in reconstructed dynamics to differences in control. Policies are trained entirely via simulation under an explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations. Piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks enable mechanistic analyses of the controlled dynamics, while decoder-based constraints make the immediate effects of interventions interpretable in observation space and permit interventions on one modality while protecting another from direct manipulation. On Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies. On Lorenz-63, they also achieve a higher mean reward than repeated planning with the same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Applications to neural-behavioral recordings demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations. Together, these findings show how shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning intervention effects when recordings contain no observed actions.
Reconstructs related dynamical systems with low-dimensional embeddings capturing shared structure and individual variation.
Reuses embeddings to parameterize shared policy and value networks, connecting inferred dynamics to control.
Uses simulated interventions, interpretable decoder constraints, and piecewise-linear recurrent networks for mechanistic analysis.
Improves transfer on Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, and can generalize to unseen systems after embedding inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Framework overview. a: A hierarchical DSR model is trained on multiple related dynamical systems (“subjects”) and used as world model for MBRL. Subject-specific parameters φ(j) are obtained by projecting shared parameters Pφ onto low-dimensional subject embeddings S(j). These embeddings are reused to condition the policy πψ and value networks Qθ by modulating group-level parameters Pψ and Pθ. b: For unseen subjects, learning only a new embedding via DSR fine-tuning enables insertion into the control model. c: The high-dimensional dynamics are controlled only in the directions that are decoded (z̃t). To underactuate the problem and for application-specific constraints, actions are constrained to be orthogonal to the target modalities and target dimensions. d: In the Lorenz-63 benchmark, the actions only affect the y− and z−directions.

Figure 5: Behavioral control through neural stimulation. a, left: Predicted trajectories without control. The model receives the goal position cue (black dashed) and go cue (cyan) as external inputs and generates trajectories (solid) that reproduce the empirical test data (dashed). Hand (green) and eye (blue) positions are shown separately. In successful trials, the hand follows the instructed target, whereas eye position is not consistently target-aligned in either the model or the data. center: Two-dimensional trajectories without (top) and with (bottom) control. The policy suppresses hand movement and, to a lesser extent, eye movement despite external inputs driving both toward the target. Color gradients indicate time. right: Neural stimulation remains sparse and selective, with no statistically significant changes in mean firing rate (t = −1.33, p = 0.18) or Fano factor (t = 1.04, p = 0.30). b: Value function, control energy, and latent states for a representative trial. Actions become effective once the goal-position cue is presented and steer the system into a high-value region of latent space associated with trajectories that remain insensitive to the subsequent go cue.

Figure 10: Generalization through fine-tuned subject vectors. On unseen subjects, fine-tuned subject vectors achieved a reward of = −0.036 ± 0.002, compared with −0.046 ± 0.005 for the unchanged vectors of the nearest training subjects. a: Fine-tuned subject vectors inserted into the fixed SAC model control the true, unseen systems without further optimization (cf. figure 2c). b: PCA projection of the subject vectors of the fine-tuned (colored) and original Lorenz-63 systems. Shifted parameter regimes produce corresponding shifts in the PCA embedding (cf. figure 6).

Figure 4: Reconstruction and model-based control of the LINK data. a: The first principal component of the subject vectors shows a linear relationship with recording days, indicating that the learned subject representations capture structure across sessions. b: Finger positions of the index and middle, ring and small (MRS) finger groups, neural activity, and control energy for one representative session. Each new goal position, presented to the monkey and provided to the model as external input, triggers a movement in the recorded (red) and simulated (blue) trajectories. Under the learned policy (orange), the simulated finger positions stay at rest. Neural activity follows a quasi-periodic dynamics in the uncontrolled model and changes under control. Control energy is the squared norm of the decoded action. Controlled trajectories are reinitialized from the recorded state every 200 time steps, which produces the visible jumps. c: Action magnitude over time for 0 to 12 excluded channels (color, top) and median reward as a function of the number of excluded channels (bottom). Actions are forced to zero on randomly selected channels. Action magnitude first increases to compensate and is then suppressed entirely once 8 channels are excluded, causing a drop in reward.

Figure 3: Reconstruction and stabilization of the double-pendulum. a: Colors indicate mass ratios m1/m2 and length ratios l1/l2, respectively. Analogous to the Lorenz-63 System, subject vectors cluster according to system parameters. b: Example trajectory of the true double-pendulum under control, with the target position indicated by the dashed red line. The 6 variables are sine and cosine of the joint angles as well as the angular velocities. Despite its inherent instability the controlled system converges to the target.

Figure 2: Controlling the Lorenz-63 benchmark. a: Reward histograms for randomly initialized trajectories across all subjects for the simulated system (left) and the true system (right) using hierarchically (top) and independently trained models (bottom). Black line denotes uncontrolled baseline. b: Representative Lorenz–63 trajectories with reward = −0.020 generated by the world model under SAC control during uncontrolled and controlled phases (gray shading), with the value function and occupied LSRs shown below. While x2 and x3 are directly controlled and rapidly approach the target (dashed red line), x1 converges to a nearby FP. c: Corresponding trajectories of the true system, demonstrating sim-to-real transfer, with a reward of −0.03. d, e: For the same subject, the most frequently occupied subregions (indices 3 and 5) are those admitting non-virtual FPs (red crosses) close to the target. f : During extended control, the trajectory approaches the target while action-dependent FPs are progressively shifted toward it.

Figure 7: Limited controllability under single dimension actuation. Example trajectory of the true Lorenz-63 system with actions applied exclusively to the third state dimension. The dashed line indicates the target state.

Figure 8: Mechanisms underlying Lorenz-63 control. a: Number of LSRs required to cover 90% of time steps for uncontrolled (blue) and controlled (red) trajectories of each subject. Control strongly reduces region occupancy. Subject 54 (cf. figure 2) is highlighted. b: Minimal distance to the target of the nonvirtual FPs computed from sampled actions in each occupied LSR (cf. figure 2e). c: Eigenvalues of the Jacobian at the FPs, which depends only on the LSR, indicate stability along most directions. The unit circle is shown in gray.

Figure 15: Reconstruction of neural spike rates. Empirical (left) and reconstructed (right) spike rates for a representative trial. Across all test trials, the world model achieves a variance-normalized mean squared error of 0.17 ± 0.06.

Figure 11: Control mechanisms in multimodal neural data. a: Occupancy of LSRs during control. b: Minimal distance of non-virtual FPs to the target in each occupied LSR. The regions occupied during control are those that admit a non-virtual FP close to the target, indicating that the policy steers the system into regions of latent space whose linear dynamics favor reaching the goal (cf. figure 2d- 2e).

Figure 14: Reconstruction of 16 double-pendulum subjects. a: Ground truth (blue) and reconstructed (orange) trajectories of the θ1, θ2, ω1, and ω2 agree closely up to the training sequence length of 30 time steps (red dashed line). b: Energy remains largely constant at first and fluctuates increasingly over time.

Figure 6: Subject vectors cluster according to Lorenz-63 parameters. PCA projection of the subject vectors. Colors indicate constant values of σ, while vertical and horizontal separation reflect β and ρ. The subject vectors condition SAC training and convey information about subject-specific dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Learns transferable control policies from action-free time series via dynamical embeddings and latent interventions, directly relevant to world models and latent action modeling.
papers.title: Learning Transferable Policies from Action-free Time Series Through Dynamical Embeddings
papers.tldr: A hierarchical model-based RL framework learns transferable control policies from action-free time series by embedding shared and system-specific dynamics, then simulating interventions to train policies.

papers.abstract: Low latent prediction error does not establish that a world model distinguishes the consequences of its actions. We introduce an evaluation protocol that traces the same intervention through simulator state, raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs. Exact simulator-state forks in a controlled deformable-physics testbed reveal distinct bottlenecks. Changed commands alter particle motion, yet 41.5% of one-step raster pairs are identical. Observation loss is not the whole explanation: among 579 high-visibility counterfactuals, median predictor-to-target response is 0.0051 and 0.0217 across two seeds, falling to 0.0027 and 0.0116 after variance normalization. An isotropic state perturbation matched to the target counterfactual embedding shift produces 190x and 53x larger predictor changes on the same visible pairs, isolating action-path under-use rather than a dead or globally shrunk predictor. MSE-only training gives 8.36x lower 10-step latent error in matched seeds, but in spectrally concentrated spaces; one VICReg target encoder is also strongly concentrated, so neither error nor rank alone certifies physical state. Finally, stiffness remains near chance even from full-resolution rasters and mechanical state while privileged material parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under this excitation rather than encoder discard. These results motivate auditing physical effect, observation visibility, representation geometry, and action dependence separately.
bullets: A counterfactual protocol traces interventions from simulator state through raster observations, target embeddings, and predictor outputs.
In the testbed, 41.5% of one-step raster counterfactual pairs are identical despite changed particle motion, revealing an observation bottleneck.

Among visible counterfactuals, predictor responses are very small; matched isotropic embedding perturbations cause 53–190× larger changes, indicating action-path under-use rather than a globally inactive predictor.
MSE-only training achieves lower 10-step latent error, but concentrated representations show that prediction error and rank do not guarantee physical-state encoding.
Material stiffness remains near chance from images and mechanical state while privileged parameters decode perfectly, indicating weak identifiability under the tested excitation.

papers.title: Counterfactual Action Evaluation, Observation Bottlenecks, and Representation Geometry in Joint-Embedding Predictive World Models

papers.abstract: We show that the causality of language models (LMs) may not be necessary nor optimal. This is the case when system behavior (denoted as $S$) is incorporated as a first-principle Bayesian feature. Here, $S$ refers to extra dominant factors beyond the data space, and they involve coupled effects. Despite being the de facto foundation of modern architecture, recent studies indicate persistent mismatches and contradictions with causality. These issues largely stem from system behavior rather than the data distribution. We therefore propose the SBD framework, which incorporates $S$ as an irreducible component of the evidence lower bound (ELBO). SBD theoretically reveals a counter-intuitive Causality Tax phenomenon, where causality emerges as a suboptimal approximation with an additional structural error, due to the obliviousness to $S$. To address the challenge of latent variable analysis, we validate the SBD-predicted impact of $S$ via implicit measurements, theoretical-bound-guided controls, and Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) evaluations. In particular, we construct Green Shell (GSH) to show the possibility of reducing Causality Tax. GSH is a non-causal variational family, and it replaces the sequential dependency chain of $S$ components with a divide-and-conquer partition. NTK spectra in the lazy-training regime confirm that GSH always achieves significantly tighter error bounds than causality, with $7dB+$ improvement in signal-to-noise ratio. In the relatively later stage of lazy-training, GSH further leads to superior generalization (up to $20\%$ richer multi-scale fitting capabilities). Taken together, SBD establishes system behavior as a complementary theoretical abstraction besides causality and distribution fitting, opening new research avenues such as designing and optimizing LM base models.
bullets: Motivation: Persistent LM mismatches may arise from system behavior—coupled factors outside the observed data distribution—rather than from data alone.
Method: The SBD framework incorporates system behavior as an irreducible component of the ELBO and analyzes its effect through implicit measurements, theory-guided controls, and NTK evaluations.
Contribution: It identifies Causality Tax, where causal modeling becomes a suboptimal approximation because it overlooks system behavior.
Approach: Green Shell (GSH) uses a non-causal, divide-and-conquer variational structure instead of a sequential dependency chain.
Results: NTK analyses report tighter error bounds with 7 dB+ higher signal-to-noise ratio and up to 20% richer multi-scale fitting capabilities in later lazy-training stages.

papers.title: To Explore The Strange New World Beyond Data Distribution: System Behavior, Causality Tax, and Non-causal Base Model

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but providing such supervision for every rollout requires substantial teacher computation. We introduce Success-Referenced On-Policy Distillation (SR-OPD), which reduces this cost by selecting which prompts and rollouts receive teacher supervision. When the student produces both successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt, a successful rollout can serve as a natural reference for selecting failed rollouts. SR-OPD therefore focuses on such prompts and prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories show sustained divergence from a successful reference, while accounting for estimated teacher-input cost. Across three teacher-student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, SR-OPD uses only 3.46-5.02% of the teacher-input tokens required by Vanilla OPD in the one-pass setting while maintaining comparable reasoning performance. Under a controlled setting matched to 5% of Vanilla OPD's teacher-input budget, further experiments support both key design choices: focusing supervision on prompts with both successful and failed rollouts, and using successful rollouts to guide failure selection. These results indicate that a student's own successful behavior can serve as a useful reference for allocating teacher supervision under a fixed teacher-input budget.
bullets: Addresses the high teacher-computation cost of supervising every on-policy rollout.
Selects prompts containing both successful and failed student rollouts.
Prioritizes failed rollouts whose hidden-state trajectories persistently diverge from a successful reference, while considering teacher-input cost.
Evaluated across three teacher–student pairs and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
At a matched 5% teacher-input budget, experiments support both success-referenced failure selection and prompt filtering.
